Headline: Blood tests find high level of cancer-causing forever chemical in residents near factory
Body: This video can not be played Thornton-Cleveleys resident Sam Hammond was shocked by the level of chemicals in her son's blood Blood tests have found "really high levels" of a cancer-causing forever chemical in dozens of people living near a major chemical factory in the UK. The residents, from Thornton-Cleveleys, Lancashire, have been told they could be at elevated risk of serious health conditions from the substance, known as PFOA. The village has been under investigation for years by the Environment Agency over contamination of soils and locally grown food from the substance, which is a type of forever chemical - so-called because they do not easily break down. That investigation said high levels likely came from the nearby AGC Chemicals factory, which used it in their manufacturing processes until 2012. Sam Hammond and her husband, both from the village, have been told they were at increased risk of health impacts from PFOA. However, she told the BBC was more shocked by her son's result. "When we opened the results...it was like, my God, that is ridiculously off the scale. "I feel guilty because I've introduced [my children] to that way of life. I know it isn't my fault, but the guilt is horrific. Knowing that I've offloaded what levels I probably had over the years into those children when I breastfed them - that's heartbreaking," she said. Forever chemicals are a group of substances, also known as PFAS, that are resistant to water and oil and are in thousands of everyday products, such as clothing and cookwear. But because they do not break down easily they have raised health concerns. PFOA has been banned in the UK since 2020 because it was classed by the World Health Organization (WHO) as a Group 1 carcinogen, which means there is clear scientific evidence it can increase the risk of cancer. The Environment Agency and Wyre Council have been testing the area close to the AGC Chemicals factory since 2024 to determine if it has been contaminated. They found PFOA at elevated levels in the soil, eggs and locally grown vegetables. Two allotment sites have now been closed and are due to be classified as contaminated land, while residents within 1km of the factory have been advised to peel any fruit or vegetables grown in their gardens. Those investigations concluded the PFOA was likely to have come from the factory having been carried in the air. Residents previously asked the council to test their blood for the chemical. But according to the UK Health Security Agency, PFAS monitoring is not currently recommended because "tests are unlikely to provide clear information for individuals". Instead independent tests were offered by Manchester Metropolitan University, paid for by investigative journalists Watershed and Law for Change - which funds cases covering environmental issues. Forty-nine residents volunteered, and they were told their blood test readings on Wednesday. Andrew Molloy found out he was in the highest-risk category. "I was half expecting it to be just normal," he said. "Because the investigation here has all been focused on - you're only really being at risk if you eat fruit and veg from the garden or grow your own eggs - which I don't." Andrew's home was built on land that used to be part of the factory. He underwent the tests because he was worried about persistent health problems in his family. "One of the first things I'm going to do is take [the results] to my GP and at least get it on my record. They seem to refuse to do anything related to this, but now I have hard information and data," he said. Mario Panteli, who was visibly shaken by his results, which were among the highest, said it was "quite emotional, a shock". He added: "I bought a property, assuming that this is our forever home. I'm going to have to stop my children from going in the garden, front and back. I feel constricted, like I'm in a cage now." Dr David Megson, who carried out the testing at Manchester Metropolitan University, said the results made him feel sick. "To me, it shows something seriously wrong has happened to that community in that area, that the levels were far higher than anything we would have ever expected to see in the general population." Andrew Molloy expected his results would be normal The UK does not have any recommendations about acceptable PFAS levels in people, although the US and Germany do. Of the 49 residents tested, 70% had readings that could leave them at increased risk of adverse health effects, according to these countries' guidelines. Possible effects include a higher risk of reduced thyroid function, kidney cancer, testicular cancer, elevated cholesterol, pre-eclampsia and ulcerative colitis. Having elevated forever chemicals in their blood is not a guarantee residents will develop these conditions, but US and German authorities have suggested anyone with elevated levels should be offered further health screening. More than 100 residents, including those who had their blood tested, are now considering taking a group legal action against AGC Chemicals to claim damages for the contamination Sarah Moore, partner at law firm Leigh Day - which is representing some residents - said compensation could be sought for financial losses on residents' homes and the impact it has had on their use and enjoyment of the land. She said damages could also be sought "in relation to the health risks, which we now consider to be a significant issue as a result of the testing we've been doing locally". The case would be "groundbreaking in the UK," she added and would be the first time a community has brought a legal claim over contamination from forever chemicals in the country. Overseas, one of the biggest legal cases over PFOA contamination was in West Virginia, in the US, which was depicted in the 2019 film Dark Waters. In that case, DuPont and Chemours Co settled more than 3,500 PFOA lawsuits for a total of $671m (£526m). Both companies have always denied any wrongdoing. Panorama: The Truth About Forever Chemicals Reporter Catrin Nye reveals how PFAS can affect health and contaminate the environment, and she asks if the UK government is doing enough to keep us safe. The factory in Thornton-Cleveleys first started operating in the 1950s, when ICI manufactured coating for non-stick frying pans using PFOA. AGC Chemicals took over the factory in 1999 and continued using PFOA until 2012, when it switched to a replacement chemical called EEA-NH4, which was also found in the blood of 10 residents tested. A spokesperson for AGC Chemicals said the site manufactured chemicals long before the company was established. "Since the wider multi-agency investigation is still ongoing and no formal determination of land contamination has been made, we cannot speculate on future outcomes or next steps," they said. Earlier this month, AGC Chemicals said the factory would close later this year after deciding there was no "viable solution to keep the site operating in the context of a volatile and competitive market". Have you been affected by the issues raised in this story? Share your experience. UK launches plan to tackle 'forever chemicals' amid growing concerns Tests on carcinogen found in gardens and allotments Egg warning over carcinogenic chemical near plant Dr Steve Hajioff, a specialist in public health, who was not involved in the Thornton-Cleveleys blood testing, said PFOA levels could have been even higher in the past, given the factory stopped using the substance in 2012 and it does break down over time. He said the levels measured in Thornton-Cleveleys are associated with elevated risks of serious health condition, but added: "If you increase the risk of something really rare, like kidney cancer or testicular cancer, by 30%, then the chances of an individual getting affected are still pretty low." Moore said she was representing residents in the community who were pregnant and worried about their children, as well as those who have families who were refusing to visit their homes over concerns about the risks. "What we're looking at in Thornton-Cleveleys at the moment might be seen as something of an outlier. My worry is that it's the tip of the iceberg, it's just the beginning," she added. The researchers said further blood testing should be done in the wider community to understand the scale of the issue. A previous report into PFAS in Jersey recommended that residents with elevated levels should be offered treatment, including cholesterol-lowering medications and blood letting - a treatment where blood is gradually withdrawn from a vein, allowing the body to naturally replenish it. Wyre Borough Council, which is overseeing the investigation into the site, said: "We recognise that PFAS is an emerging area of scientific research and will continue to press for updated advice and guidance from expert health agencies on behalf of our communities as further evidence becomes available." Headline: Waste sector crisis could see rubbish piling up on streets, experts warn
Body: The large landfill site at Mount Vernon, Glasgow, has just a few weeks of 'void' space left Scotland's waste sector is on the verge of a crisis which could see rubbish piling up on the streets, experts have warned. They say the combination of significantly reduced landfill space and a breakdown of Glasgow's main incinerator have created a "perfect storm" which could see waste left uncollected. Industry representatives are due to meet ministers to discuss their concerns but say there's no obvious short-term solution to avoid the crisis. The Scottish government said was working with stakeholders to maintain resilience and  identify contingency arrangements should they be required. Landfill capacity in Scotland has been shrinking as operators wind down their operations ahead of a forthcoming ban on sending black bag waste to landfill sites. That had been due to come into effect at the start of this year, but was delayed until January 2028after a Disclosure investigationreported that 100 lorry loads of waste would have to be sent to England by road each day. David Balmer says rubbish will soon have nowhere to go and be left on Scotland's streets Last year there were 10 sites which took in most of Scotland's residual waste – the material left over after recyclable and compostable materials have been separated out. However, that has now been reduced to just three, one of which is in administration. The problems have been exacerbated by the breakdown of Glasgow's main incinerator at Polmadie, which has been out of action since April. Welding cracks were identified during routine inspections and the facility is not expected to resume operations until next March. Much of the city's household waste is currently being diverted to a large landfill site at Mount Vernon - but its operator, Patersons, says it only has a few months of space available for burying the rubbish. The amount of rubbish being processed there has increased from about 2,000 tonnes to 5,000 tonnes a week. An application to extend the site has been refused on appeal by the Scottish government. The operator estimates that it will be full by the end of the year. The ban on sending black bag waste to landfill was designed to encourage more recycling, with the residual waste being sent instead to incinerators where it is burned to create electricity. The proposals sparked a rapid rise in plans to build waste to energy facilities, which led in 2022 to a ban on new applications This was introduced because of concerns that Scotland would end up with more incinerators than needed to deal with the available waste, particularly if recycling rates increased. But the amount of household waste being recycled has barely changed in a decade. A fresh report published last month by Zero Waste Scotland concluded that most incinerators are operating well below their maximum capacity, which suggests the capacity gap might have been miscalculated. Several more sites are under construction, including the South Clyde Energy Centre at North Cardonald, but are not expected to be ready quickly enough to address the current issues. Several sites in the north of England, some of which are understood to have received waste from Scotland, have been shut down by the Environment Agency following investigations into suspected illegal waste activity. Landfill manager David Balmer, who works with Mount Vernon's operator Patersons, said it was possible that Scotland would quickly run out of landfill space. He said the Polmadie breakdown had created a perfect storm. "Could you see waste on the street? Absolutely," he said. Balmer said councils and waste management contractors were under an obligation to collect the rubbish. "But if they can't process it further down the line, what's the easier solution? "The easier solution is to leave in the streets at the moment, pending a solution. The problem is we can't see a solution." Waste consultant Alasdair Meldrum, of Albion Environmental, says he has not seen such a looming crisis in almost 40 years of working in the industry. He says there are already commercial operators who are struggling to find outlets to send their waste, with some being sent hundreds of miles to locations in England. Meldrum added: "There's no easy solution. There are a number of landfill sites that could develop more void space but you can't do the engineering work in the winter. "There's no real short-term solution. We've got ourselves into a real problem." Experts say 80% of the waste in black bags could be recycled One possible solution is for householders to reduce the amount of black bag waste they generate by sending more for recycling. However, rates of recycling have barely changed in Scotland over the last decade. Zero Waste Scotland has estimated that more than half of domestic residual waste could be recycled. One of the biggest elements is food waste which, if collected separately, could be processed through anaerobic digestion. However, environmental group Friends of the Earth Scotland believes its policy which is to blame rather than the actions of individual households. Kim Pratt, circular economy campaigner, says there has been far too much focus on incineration and not enough on reducing how much waste is in the system. She added: "That makes all these problems much easier to solve. It reduces the expense for households, it makes it easier to meet the landfill ban and it reduces the need for incineration." The Grrec energy-from-waste incinerator in Glasgow has been out of action since April Glasgow City Council said general waste was being disposed of at a range of alternative sites, including other energy from waste facilities. A spokesman added: "We are satisfied there is sufficient capacity in the overall system to ensure general waste is disposed of appropriately while the Grrec is offline for repair. "Residents should continue to use their household bins as normal. Recycling services are unaffected by the current issues." The council and Viridor, which operates the incinerator, say they are working to bring the facility at Polmadie back on line once repair work is complete. The Scottish government's climate action secretary Gillian Martin insists that shifting to an economy where materials are kept in use for as long as possible, rather than being routinely disposed of, is essential. She acknowledged a need for "sufficient strategic landfill capacity" to be available during the transition process while some materials cannot yet be recycled or reused. She added: "We've been working closely with stakeholders to monitor capacity, maintain resilience and identify appropriate contingency arrangements should they be required." Headline: Seahorse habitats 'healing' thanks to eco-moorings
Body: The research was carried out by Kira Dunn of Southampton University Scars caused to rare seahorse habitats by boat anchors off the Dorset coast are starting to heal, thanks to the installation of new moorings. In 2021, Studland Bay Marine Partnership began installing the first of dozens of eco-moorings in a bid to reverse damage to delicate seagrass meadows. A new scientific study has now provided the first evidence that eco-moorings can help restore seagrass, with some scars shrinking by more than 90% over four years. David Brown, chair of the partnership steering group, called the results "incredibly exciting", adding: "The impact has been beyond our expectations." Seagrass habitats store carbon, support biodiversity and help protect coastlines from erosion, but are declining globally due to pollution, development, disturbance andclimate change. The research, conducted by Kira Dunn as part of her MSc in Marine Biology with Oceanography at the University of Southampton, analysed monitoring data collected since the first eco-moorings were installed. Studland Bay is home to protected spiny seahorses Using sonar surveys, historical satellite imagery and five years of monitoring data, the study tracked recovery across 39 damaged areas of seabed. In the area where 10 trial eco-moorings were installed in 2021, the size of bare patches in the seagrass decreased by an average of 93.6% between 2021 and 2025, shrinking by around 57 sq m each year. In a second study area, where traditional chain moorings remained until 2023, the scars reduced by 65.4%, around 15.9 sq m a year. Studland Bay has been a designated a Marine Conservation Zone since 2019 and is home to one of the UK's largest seagrass meadows, supporting species such as the protected spiny seahorse and short-snouted seahorse. The bay also became a voluntary no-anchor zone in 2021. Dunn, who graduated this year, said the research project had been "rewarding and positive". She said: "It's incredibly encouraging to see how quickly this important habitat can regenerate when given the opportunity." Traditional boat anchors cause damage to delicate seagrass Dr Ken Collins, of the University of Southampton, who supervised the study, said: "Studland Bay is becoming a powerful example of how practical conservation measures can reverse habitat damage and deliver measurable environmental improvements." Brown, who is also lead ecologist for the National Trust, said: "These results are incredibly exciting, and a huge encouragement to all the organisations and individuals who have given so much time and support to the partnership. "The impact has been beyond our expectations, and thanks to robust monitoring and research, we have the science to prove how the eco-moorings benefit seagrass and all the species that rely on it." Studland Bay Marine Partnership is made up of conservation charities, boating organisations, academics, statutory bodies, community groups and businesses, with the aim of restoring Studland's seagrass. Partners include Dorset Wildlife Trust, Natural England, the National Trust, the Seahorse Trust and the University of Southampton. Headline: ‘It’s hard to sell a house when it’s covered in baboon faeces’: Cape Town divided over plan to remove its monkeys
Body: Two troops of chacma baboons are breaking into homes and shops but animal rights activists insist coexistence is the answer Cape Town’s city council has said it will “imminently” round up two baboon troops coming intorepeated conflict with residents. The animals will be sterilised and permanently moved to a newly constructed sanctuary. The plan has been fiercely criticised by animal rights activists, who say the monkeys should remain roaming freely, and that less destructive options have not been properly considered. Cape Town’s baboon problem has been brewing since the 2000s, after the city stopped culling troops in the late 1990s after pressure from the public. But in the past two years it has reached boiling point. A2025 censusfound that the population had grown by a third since 2000, from 360 baboons to 493, now living in 12 managed troops. As a result of the population boom, troops of chacma baboons on the city’s peninsula regularly rip off roof sheeting, sneak into unlocked cars and raid food pantries. Some monkeys are now staying up late into the night to break into homes in Simon’s Town and nab snacks from convenience stores. Residents can no longer barbecue or host garden parties for fear of the marauding baboons. “It’s depreciated property values because it’s hard to sell a house when it’s covered in baboon faeces and paw prints, and you know they’re coming every day,” said Justin O’Riain, a behavioural ecologist at the University of Cape Town who has long studied the local baboons. Cape Town’s geography is partially to blame. Much of the problem is confined to the Cape Peninsula, a narrow sliver of land stretching from the city centre to Cape Point. Here, baboons are boxed in between the steep, protected area of Table Mountain national park and the sprawling urban development that stretches to the Atlantic Ocean. “The underlying issue is that baboons will seek low-lying land. That is their natural drive – it’s better access to water and more productive vegetation,” said Joselyn Mormile, who leads the Cape Baboon Partnership (CBP), a nonprofit organisation that works with the city and local conservation authorities to manage the baboons. “But throughout the peninsula, we’ve developed most of those places. It’s a constant battle between the two.” Initially, the CBP’s2025 management planproposed to move four troops to a sanctuary. That was revised, Mormile said, to give two other troops living in the northern section of the peninsula “the benefit of the doubt to see if they can adjust in that remaining space … We believe that they could settle quite nicely.” The baboons have proved an especially divisive – and expensive – issue. Cape Town’s baboon management programme costs about 20m rand for 18 months (£920,000), with full-time rangers watching over most of the troops to try to head off any trouble. In addition to moving the Waterfall and Seaforth troops to a sanctuary, a baboon-proof northern boundary fence will be erected between urban areas and nearby mountains. Animal rights activists, who have been staging peaceful protests for months, andsome scientistssay the city should build a fence to exclude the Waterfall and Seaforth troops rather than remove the animals from their environment. However, O’Riain said it was likely that the baboons would simply move along to the next area of low-lying land where the fence ends, as there was not enough food for the baboons behind the proposed southern fenced area. Opponents argue that removing the other baboons will cause long-term psychological distress and social disruption, and that the baboons play an important ecological role by dispersing plant seeds. Chacma baboons are not considered endangered. And the welfare of the animals is already in question: baboons are being poisoned, hit by cars, chased by dogs and shot. “No one should ever shoot a baboon, but if people feel the authorities are not doing anything, they will take action – and that action is never nice,” O’Riain said. “Just a few days ago, a baboon was shot straight through the chest. “How many more millions of rand are we going to throw into these troops only to end up in exactly the same place in another 10 years’ time?” he said. “Which is shocking baboon welfare, shocking baboon health, and a very poor quality of life for the people who are living in these areas.” Find moreage of extinction coverage here, and follow the biodiversity reportersRebecca Ratcliffe,Phoebe WestonandPatrick Greenfieldin the Guardian app for more nature coverage.

Headline: How climate change is reshaping Britain's trees
Body: Stephanie James says growers are having to adapt as hotter, drier summers become more common One of the UK's biggest tree nurseries says it is already changing the species it grows as hotter, drier summers reshape conditions for growers. Frank P Matthews, based in Tenbury Wells, Worcestershire, produces more than a million trees every year, supplying garden centres across the country. After what it describes as a challenging growing season, the family-run business has introduced new drought-tolerant species, reduced water use and adapted the way it irrigates its trees. Managing director Stephanie James said growers had little choice but to adapt to a changing climate. "We've phased out some species that aren't doing so well and introduced others that thrive in hotter conditions," she said. Rainwater collected in lagoons helps the nursery keep its trees watered during dry spells Among the varieties now being grown are cercis, lagerstroemia and koelreuteria, which are better suited to warmer weather. The nursery captures rainwater and stores it in large lagoons, providing a vital supply during dry spells. "We wouldn't be able to grow trees like this if we didn't have them," James said. The business has also begun using a compost additive that reduces water consumption by about 30%. "It means the water doesn't run through the pots quickly. It spreads horizontally and takes its time," she said. Container-grown trees are watered using drip irrigation systems that deliver small amounts of water regularly to keep compost moist while minimising waste. About 2,000 tree species are grown at the site near Tenbury Wells Elsewhere on the site, bare-root trees are grown in fields and irrigated using water extracted under licence from a nearby river. When water levels fall below a certain point, irrigation stops and the nursery relies on the resilience of the trees themselves. As well as adapting to changing conditions, the nursery says diversity will be increasingly important as the UK's treescape evolves. "If you look around the country, a lot of the ash are dying," James said. "We need to keep replanting new and diverse species. "The key to mitigating climate change from a tree point of view is planting a wide range." The nursery, which grows around 2,000 different species, is encouraging people to plant trees as part of National Tree Week in November. Despite this summer's dry conditions, James said autumn remains the best time to plant because roots have time to establish before the following growing season. Her advice for gardeners is simple: use plenty of bark mulch. "Mulching is very key to reducing water loss and helping to protect that root system," she said. Headline: What are my children exposed to? Why I want testing for cancer-causing chemicals
Body: This video can not be played Michael Phillips played at Llwyneinion lagoon as a child and wants people like him to be tested When she moved to the countryside two years ago, Natalie Dugdale thought it would be the perfect spot to raise her family. Close to a lagoon in north Wales, she thought she could walk her baby, toddler and dogs on public footpaths. But when she watchedMichael Sheen's BBC documentaryrevealing the lagoon's history as a dumping ground of cancer-causing chemicals known as PCBs, Natalie was shocked. Now she is part of a group of people who are worried they may have been poisoned by years of exposure to toxic waste, and are campaigning for voluntary blood testing across Wales. But Wales' public health body has said it does not recommend blood testing for PCBs, saying it would cause more concern. Michael Sheen followed up campaigner Douglas Gowan's concerns about dumping carcinogenic waste Public Health Wales (PHW) said the tests did not provide "a reliable means of assessing an individual's exposure to contamination or the potential health impact". Members of a newly formed campaign group for those living alongside some of the sites concerned have told BBC Wales they had been left "frightened and upset" and said testing would help provide "peace of mind". Natalie could not believe her local lake in Llwyneinion, just outside Wrexham, had actually once been a dumping ground for potentially dangerous chemicals and wants to see blood testing introduced. "I was really upset because having young children, what are they being exposed to?," said Natalie, 33. Natalie Dugdale is calling for public health bodies to test people that are worried they may have been poisoned by years of exposure to toxic waste Llwyneinion lagoon was recently branded "a shame on Britain", following the documentary into historical dumping of PCBs by US chemical giant Monsanto, which had factories in Wrexham and Newport. Nel Byers, who walks around the area with her three-month-old daughter Wren, said that blood testing was needed "for people's own peace of mind" as well as showing "on a national scale" whether these communities had heightened results. "I had no idea about all of this until the doc came out," said the 33-year-old from Trevor. Nel Byers, her fiance Otis Proctor and their three-month-old daughter Wren live near the former Monsanto works in Wrexham and want to know how they may have been affected by toxic chemicals in the ground "But it was very scary because there are areas where my children play on that have been dumping grounds - and we had no idea." Sheen's Buried programme teamfound elevated levels in soil samples taken in an area open to the public beyond the fenced-off lagoon, as well as at 13 other suspected dumpsites for the firm's toxic waste across the country. "We need to be proactive now and voicing our concerns for future generations," added Nel. "If they get the blood testing done they might actually start doing something about it." Llwyneinion lagoon is one of the most notorious dumpsites of the toxic chemicals Their call comes afterprivately funded testing found high levels of other so-called forever chemicalsin dozens of people living near a chemical factory in Lancashire. Michael Phillips played at Llwyneinion lagoon as a child and, decades later, developed a rare cancer in his shoulder. The 63-year-old said many of his friends had died because of similarly rare cancers, which he now suspects were linked, although no proven link has been established. "I would say every person that played in the pool that was close to me, apart from one friend who had an operation to get rid of it, is dead," said Michael.  "It's got to stop." Michael was also found to have "very high" levels of PCBs in his blood - after private testing commissioned for the documentary. The banned chemicals were once widely used and revered for being non-flammable and hard to break down - but are seen today as the first "forever chemicals" which are building up in the environment, threatening wildlife and human health. Michael, Nel and Natalie have both now joined a newly formed campaign group - made up of hundreds of residents living alongside the former Monsanto works in the villages of Cefn Mawr, Acrefair and Trevor in north-east Wales. Buried with Michael Sheen What is the truth lying beneath our feet? Michael Sheen uncovers claims of conspiracy, complicity and denial over alleged toxic 'forever chemical' contamination in south Wales. One of their calls - alongside a national soil testing programme - is for voluntary blood testing, led by PHW. One of the group's founders pointed to the fact the documentary had to rely on a large-scale study from the US to assess and compare PCB levels in the local residents it had tested. "There's a huge potential here for Wales... to really lead the way and show the rest of the UK how to handle this risk," said community councillor Katie Witherden. "It would give people answers about what they have or haven't been exposed to - and I think all of us deserve the right to have the choice to know that." There are 12 locations in Wales that were sites of concern for Douglas Gowan PHWissued a statement,externalin response to calls from residents and politicians - including the Welsh Affairs Select Committee of MPs - saying a programme of blood testing was "not recommended". It argued that testing would "not tell us how or where people may have been exposed" as there were many potential PCB sources in the wider environment - including food, and materials in homes and buildings. There was no treatment for higher levels of the chemicals so there was a risk too of "causing worry among people who are found to have PCBs in their blood", it added. Natalie said she found the response "disappointing", adding: "I think a lot of people are already frightened and it's more frightening not knowing." Katie agreed that "people are already worried" and said: "We know they can't treat PCBs and that's not what we're asking for." Her husband Steve Witherden is the Labour MP for Montgomeryshire and Glyndŵr, and described PHW's response as "chilling". Councillor Katie Witherden and her husband Steve, the Labour MP for Montgomeryshire and Glyndŵr, are campaigning for public testing for those who could be affected by PCBs "My hope is that they revise their position," he said. "There's a real strength of feeling from people who've lived near to these sites or worked in them, a real clamouring." Dr Dave Megson, of Manchester Metropolitan University, who was also involved in the Buried documentary testing, argued the US and other countries in Europe were well ahead of the UK in advancing the use of blood testing for alleged chemical contamination. While it could not prove that cancers and other health impacts were caused by PCBs, he argued: "There's so much information that we can pull out if you use those non-standard tests and do some advanced science." PHW acknowledged the health authority's refusal to back calls for blood testing was "a difficult message". "We appreciate that the communities are worried and that is understandable, but the testing isn't necessarily going to give any good answers," said Prof Sarah Jones, consultant in environmental public health at PHW. "Generally when we do any sort of testing we want to be able to put things right for people and that's what we can't do here." This video can not be played Sheen told MPs that Wales' first minister had initially declined his request for a meeting over toxic pollution claims She argued there were too many "unknowns" about the impacts of concentrations of PCBs on the body and no treatment for those found to have elevated levels in their blood. "All we could do is give [people] a number that we can't really interpret and then we can't make right." She felt this could "create even more worry and that is a health harm in itself". "There is nothing that blood testing can do that would magically take those worries away - it would only potentially magnify them," Jones said. Asked whether the cost of implementing a blood testing regime was also a factor, she said: "No... this is not about money." Rather than blood testing, Jones argued public authorities should focus on taking "whatever steps need to be taken to make these [suspected dumpsites] as safe as possible". Dr Will Mackintosh, from the Royal College of GPs Cymru, said it may be that "additional support" would be required for GPs in future, in communities where concerns had been raised about alleged contamination. "It's clearly something which obviously large numbers of people are concerned about, and general practice has a role in responding to that as best as we can," he said. The Welsh government said "addressing the issue of contaminated land is a key priority for this government". "We will develop a Wales-wide strategy to progressively restore post-industrial land so that communities are no longer exposed to potential risks," it said. "This will include strengthening the 'polluter pays principle' while we continue to press for environmental justice by raising the importance of seeking UK government funding direct with the UK Treasury." Monsanto does not exist any more and Eastman Chemical Company, responsible for the firm's legacy production in the UK, has not responded to BBC Wales' requests for comment. Headline: Thousands without water and roads closed after burst pipe
Body: Areas of Crawley are flooded and about 9,000 homes have water supply issues Thousands of homes in parts of West Sussex have water supply issues and a number of roads have flooded after what police are describing as a "significant" leak. Roads around the Southgate Roundabout in Crawley have been closed on Sunday morning due to the burst water pipe, Sussex Police said. Southern Water said around 9,000 customers were impacted and it was setting up bottled water stations. A company spokesperson said: "Our teams are on site and working as quickly and safely as possible to repair the burst and restore supplies." The company said customers were experiencing a loss of water supply or low pressure in the following areas - Woolborough Road, Holmcroft, Southgate, Tilgate and Furnace Green. It reported at 12:00 BST that supplies had returned to some homes. The Southern Water spokesperson added: "Restoring water to customers as quickly as possible remains our highest priority." John Boulton, who is 82, and his partner are without water. He said: "It's pretty disgusting, really - we pay so much for the water supply." Boulton said he had just paid £22 for bottled water in a shop. The water main burst in the early hours of Sunday morning causing extensive flooding Southgate Avenue, Crawley Avenue and part of the A23 are currently closed, according to Southern Water. Sussex Police has asked that people avoid the area while emergency services manage the situation safely. The County Mall shopping centre in the town has been temporarily closed due to the water outages. Southern Water said its teams were working to make the repairs as quickly as possible Martin Lawrence was making deliveries in the area at 05:00 BST. He toldBBC Radio Sussex: "I came across this massive flood going across the road. "There was a large amount of water going from one side of the roundabout to the other and going into an underpass. "I've never seen so much water in my life." Resident Ryan Beck said: "We have no water pressure in the upstairs of our house. "And all the underpasses are flooded." Southern Water says when supplies return, water may be discoloured or have bubbles in it. The company says this is normal and discolouration usually clears once the network settles. If the water is cloudy and white, customers are urged to leave it in a glass for a few minutes to see if it clears, as it could be trapped air. If the water if brown or black, people are told to run their tap for a few minutes and it should clear, and to try again after 20 minutes if it does not work the first time. Southern Water says it is fine to use supplies as normal once it runs clear. The company said a chlorine smell or taste was also "perfectly normal" and came from small amounts that remained in supplies. Customers are also being urged to run their taps for a short amount of time to help bring through water, as there could be air locks in pipes. Headline: Bumblebee project seeking to help rare species
Body: The project will focus on Cornwall, Kent and the North Pennines A project is under way to try and help one of the UK's "most threatened" species of bumblebee. The Bumblebee Conservation Trust is leading a £907,000 three-year scheme alongside the University of Cambridge to recover the Moss carder species. It said the initiative would focus on landscapes across Cornwall's coastal grasslands, dunes and heathland as well as grazing marshes and sea walls in Kent and the upland fringe landscape of the North Pennines. During the project, the trust said it would work with landowners to trial "small-scale habitat interventions" to identify those which work well while gaining a better understanding of the species' behaviour and needs. More news stories for Cornwall Listen to the latest news for Cornwall Moss carder bumblebees are largely found in small, fragmented populations, according to the trust. It said it was distinctive with a velvety covering of ginger-yellow hairs across its body and no black hairs. The trust said habitat loss and fragmentation were likely to have a bigger impact on the Moss carder than many other species as it typically foraged closer to its nest than most other bumblebees. Amy Plowman, head of conservation and science at the trust, said: "This is a hugely exciting and ambitious three-year project that gives us a real opportunity to turn the tide for one of the UK's rarest bumblebees." Moss carder bumblebees are largely found in small, fragmented populations Funding worth more than £530,000 has been provided to the project by Natural England's Species Recovery Programme. Tylan Berry, Natural England's species and nature recovery networks senior officer, said the Species Recovery Programme was helping "take practical action to halt species decline and support nature recovery across England". Berry said the Moss carder was "one of England's most threatened pollinators". "Projects like this demonstrate how targeted investment can support practical conservation action on the ground," he added. Follow BBC Cornwall onX,external,Facebook,externalandInstagram,external. Headline: Trump meets US-backed Venezuelan president for first time since Maduro seized
Body: Delcy Rodríguez was pictured alongside the US president on the sidelines of the summit in New York US President Donald Trump has held talks with Venezuela's interim President Delcy Rodríguez at the UN General Assembly, their first face-to-face meeting since the White House backed her to take over the South American country's government. Rodríguez succeeded Nicolás Maduro shortly after US forces conducted a raid on the Venezuelan capital Caracas and seized him. The pair met a few kilometres from the New York jail where Maduro is awaiting trial for drug trafficking and other charges. Rodríguez said they discussed "advancing a cooperation agenda in strategic areas such as energy, mining, and security". US Secretary of State Marco Rubio and White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles also attended the meeting. Rodríguez's government has signed an agreementallowing the US to control more than 65 billion barrels of its oil-  more than a fifth of the country's reserves. It grants a US-led company 100-year concessions over 17 oilfields in Venezuela. Trump previously called it "the biggest oil deal in world history". During his address to the UN on Monday, Trump said the US and Venezuela control "more than 60%" of the world's oil, adding: "To the victor belong the spoils." Rodríguez is due to address the UN on Wednesday. She previously served as vice-president to Maduro and was sanctioned by the US in 2018, but the measureswere lifted in April this year. She was sworn in as interim president by Venezuela's National Assembly days after the US raid with the White House's blessing. Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado hasrepeatedly been barred from re-entering the country. Former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro to face trial next June

Headline: 'I have never felt heat like that' - a survivor on watching 33 cellmates die in Nigeria
Body: Usman Muhammad survived but 33 others died in the cell and four others died later in hospital Usman Muhammad pauses by the entrance to a tiny Nigerian prison cell and leans his forehead against the wall unable to speak. The day before he had been trapped inside the stifling room, measuring roughly 6m  (19.7ft) by 3m (9.8ft), with more than 50 other prisoners. Thirty-three of his cellmates died in the cramped conditions in the prison in Minna, the capital of Nigeria's Niger state - and four died later in hospital. The mass deaths caused an outcry and sparked protests, including attacks on public buildings, as relatives and locals demanded answers. Federal officials had initially blamed the deaths on a diphtheria outbreak but exactly what happened is now the subject of an investigation. "I have never felt heat like that in my life. When we touched each other's bodies, it felt like fire burning," Muhammad tells the BBC once he is able to gather his thoughts. When he was locked inside, there was standing room only amid humidity levels of more than 90%, which in some circumstances can be dangerous to human health as it prevents the natural cooling mechanism of sweat drying on the skin. The temperature outside was above 25C and the only ventilation came from a small, high-up window. "One of us fainted and we started knocking at the [cell] door. When [a guard] came we asked him for water. He looked at the guy that fainted and closed the door.  That's how they started dying one after the other," Muhammad says. Like the others who had been detained, the young man, in his 20s, is an artisanal miner, eking out a living searching for precious metals at mine sites. The federal government has tried to crack down on this alleged illegal activity as it says it costs the country revenue, damages the environment and can be linked to wider criminal activity. Officers from the Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps (NSCDC) had arrested a large group of miners near Minna last Tuesday and Wednesday. The prisoners were held at its detention centre in the city, but the NSCDC has not shared either the names or the number of those it was holding. This video can not be played The BBC's Madina Maishanu shows the conditions inside the cell where so many died As the hours inside the cell wore on, the heat and dehydration became unbearable and Muhammad says some of the detainees began drinking their own urine and collecting sweat from their bodies to try to stay alive. He describes seeing people in distress and struggling to breathe. "People were calling for help, some were already very weak." But no-one came to help, he and others allege. "While in the cell, we were shouting and telling them that people were dying," another survivor Adamu Isah told the Reuters news agency. "We tried to break down the door when they refused to open it… At one point, a security officer came to the door. "We were shouting and telling him that people were dying, but he said it wasn't his problem if people died." Finally, on Thursday, the cell door was opened and the guards saw the dead bodies. The NSCDC has not directly responded to the accusations of neglect and maltreatment but has said that 24 of its personnel are now in custody in connection with the deaths, including its suspended Niger state commandant Suberu Aniviye. "The people who were killed are not flies. How can this go unlooked? We will get to the bottom of this," Niger state Governor Umaru Bago told the BBC. The only air coming into the cell was from a small window high up on the wall As the organisation involved is a federal body rather than a force under his jurisdiction, such as the police, the governor is unable to exert direct influence but he welcomes the investigation that has been ordered by the government in capital, Abuja. A 10-member committee has now been set-up to determine exactly what happened. It has two weeks to establish the causes of the deaths and identify who was responsible and can recommend legal action against anyone found culpable. No officer, regardless of rank, would be protected and any attempt to obstruct the investigation would be taken seriously, Interior Minister Olubunmi Tunji-Ojo said. As he leaves the cell after talking to the BBC, Muhammad says he hopes that by speaking out he can help find justice and bring some closure to this traumatic event. Headline: Hundreds of wildflowers to be planted at meadow
Body: Friends of the Lake District wants to plant 1,500 wildflower plants at land at Mazonwath A project to preserve vulnerable vegetation and wildlife will see hundreds of wildflower plants introduced to an upland hay meadow. Friends of the Lake District (Fold) wants to plant 1,500 wildflowers on land at Mazonwath, in Little Asby, Cumbria, to help reintroduce many native species lost through some farming practices. A spokesperson for the environmental charity said plant roots were good for moisture retention and soil health, with their texture playing a part in slowing the flow of overland water. They added: "Conservation work like this is really important to help our insects and birds have a home into the future." Fold is calling for volunteers to help join the planting efforts on 13 October and more information on how to join is available on the charity's website. The charity will be planting great burnet, bird's foot trefoil, black knapweed, cranesbills, oxeye daisy and vetches. The organisation is working with Cumbria Wildlife Trust as part of the Cumbria Seed Bank Project, which aims to reverse the decline of grassland habitats in the county. Volunteers are needed for a planting event at Mazonwath next month The two-year project in partnership with Kew Millennium Seed Bank, aims to collect, store and sow seed from rare and declining grassland species that are found in Cumbria. A Fold spokesperson said: "The aim is not only to introduce harder-to-establish plants that are missing from grasslands, but to also use this project to inform future work to safeguard vulnerable populations of plant species in Cumbria, so that these wildflower species are not lost forever." Headline: Elephants use medicinal plants to treat themselves, researchers find
Body: Accounts from local experts revealed that wild elephants used more than 35 plants, many of which have known medicinal uses African elephants use dozens of different medicinal plants to treat themselves and their families when they are sick. This is the conclusion of a study which interviewed people who live and work alongside the elephants in the Mount Elgon region of Kenya. These particular animals have long intrigued scientists with their extraordinary behaviour - they are known as salt-mining elephants, because they go into caves  and scrape the rock with their tusks to extract minerals for their diet. This newly published research suggests that the same elephants use several different plant species in the forest for medicinal purposes. Camera traps set up by the Mount Elgon Foundation captured the elephants 'mining' for salt in caves, to supplement their diet One of the lead researchers, Dr Elodie Freymann from Brown University in the US, said the study raised the question of whether destruction of forest habitat deprives animals - and humans - of the medicines they need to thrive. "This shows just how entangled our medicines are with the non-human world," Dr Freymann told BBC News. The researchers say the forests are 'natural pharmacies' for the elephants The scientists collaborated with the conservation charity theMount Elgon Foundation,external. They interviewed local people, including wildlife scouts and community elders. Accounts described elephants selecting particular plants when they seemed unwell, and mothers reportedly giving medicinal plant material to their calves. From this, the researchers concluded that the elephants use 35 different plant species, and that 25 of those are known locally to have medicinal uses. Wild chimpanzees filmed using forest 'first aid' Wounded orangutan seen using plant as medicine The study,published in the journal Scientific Reports,external, did not name the interviewees - keeping participants anonymous so they felt free to share their stories. Their accounts reveal some intriguing details. In one testimony, a wildlife scout described seeing elephants using a plant known as Angurweet "as medicine to give to babies". Angurweet is used as a remedy for ailments including stomach ache. The scout, who  described elephant mothers mixing it in their mouths - "removing the leaves and chewing it until smooth, along with the roots of some other trees". He also recounted  that he had seen mothers mix this plant material with their own milk. "They give it to the babies, who chew on it themselves and spit out the solids". Professor Michael Huffman, a primatologist based in Japan, currently at Nagasaki University, said this particular account was "tantalising", but more evidence would be needed to prove that elephants provided bespoke medical treatment for their calves. The scientists have already embarked on gathering that evidence - giving the local wildlife experts they worked with cameras to record the behaviour they witness. They are also analysing plants that the elephants use - looking for new medicines that the elephants themselves may have discovered. Another lead reearcher on the project, Dr Fabien Schultz from the Bernhard Nocht Institute for Tropical Medicine in Hamburg, told BBC News: "Local knowledge has given us a map". "We [now] want to follow the elephants and investigate whether they select particular plants in particular health contexts, and whether those plants have relevant biological activity." The study identified 35 different plant species that the animals use Many animals treat themselves with plants and other natural remedies. The earliest scientific accounts of elephants practicing "self-medication" date back to the early third century. Roman author Claudius Aelian in his text De Natura Animalium (On the Nature of Animals) described an elephant that, after being wounded by spears and arrows, consumed flowers and oil from an olive tree. The elephant made a full recovery. Centuries later, these scientists are delving into what we can learn from wildlife about the properties of plants in the forest habitats they evolved in. "There are medicine-producing organisms on this planet that have this incredible capability," Dr Freymann told BBC News." Medicine factories that exist all around us." Researchers worked with local experts to identify plants the elephants use Prof Huffman, who was not involved in this study, added: "We now know that mosquitoes and drosophila (flies) self-medicate, bees self-medicate, as do many other species all the way up the evolutionary ladder to the great apes of Africa and Asia. "WIth each new species studied, we have gained a greater understanding of our medicinal past." For Dr Freymann, the findings also contain a lesson for our future. "So many of the medicines we buy in a pharmacy were derived from compounds from trees, algae, from fungi, from coral reefs. "It's a win-win for us to protect these forests and keep those natural pharmacies around... long enough that we can discover new natural products that could save us down the line."

Headline: Eating garden weeds to survive in Russian-occupied city cut off from food and water
Body: Oleshky has been under Russian occupation since 2022 and its people are now trapped "Two more civilians died last night," says Halia, before her phone connection cuts off. She is trapped in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky, which she says is "constantly shelled" and cut off from food and water. Three days later she tells me the two who were killed were a husband and wife. She knew them well. They were bringing home a bag of food from the closest neighbouring town of Radensk, 23km (14 miles) away, but were unable to get home before a curfew imposed by Russian occupation authorities. They were then killed by a drone. Four separate sources have confirmed the deaths of two civilians carrying food on 20 September. Halia does not want to share their names for fear she might be identified. Her name has been changed to protect her safety. Hers is just one of the many harrowing accounts the BBC has heard from residents in the front-line city in southern Kherson in recent days. Occupied by Russia since 2022, Oleshky is trapped between the Dnipro River, which separates it from Ukrainian positions, and Russian forces. It is also one of the cities where thousands of people lost their homes afterthe collapse of Nova KhakovkaDam in 2023, flooding buildings up to their rooftops. Ukraine and Nato accused Russia of blowing up the dam, while Russia blamed Ukraine. Oleshky was home to 24,000 people before Russia's full-scale invasion. Now the Ukrainian government estimates that some 6,000 people remain in the city and its surrounding areas, including 200 children. Residents say children remaining in wider Oleshky are suffering from malnutrition, a lack of medical services, and are "degrading" without access to education. Many have also told the BBC independently there is only one hospital partially operational, opening a few days a week to perform critical amputations. Ukraine has attempted to deliver supplies to the area but has not had success in recent months. To stay or risk the 'Road of Death' - Ukrainian civilians trapped in frontline city Earlier this week the Kremlin acknowledged that Oleshky faced "a critical situation" and "problems with supplies of food and medicine", but added that "Russia's military was working to resolve them" and blamed Kyiv. The local population is living under a "full blockade" by Russian forces, according to Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha. Speaking at the UN General Assembly in New York on Tuesday, Sybiha called on the international community to pressure Russia into allowing humanitarian aid into the city. Oleshky was flooded after the collapse of the Nova Kakhovka Dam in June 2023. Inside Oleshky, Halia faces a daily struggle to survive. "There is no food here in the city," she says, adding that the last food delivery was back in May. "I eat once a day, a dinner only," she says. "I make some plain bread, sometimes I can have it with a tomato, or with some honey, and a tea. That's it." Many residents have turned to cooking garden weeds as they have run out of the vegetables they managed to grow over the summer, she explains. Oleshky has been without gas or electricity since 2023, so residents have had to find other solutions Which weeds are safe to eat and how to boil them has become a topic of discussion on local Telegram messaging chats, along with calls between residents to sell, swap or share pieces of food. No shops are open any more in Oleshky, with residents unable to source either clothes or hygiene products. The city has had no electricity, gas or water since the Kakhovka dam was attacked three years ago. While some residents have risked travelling on foot along mined roads out of the city in search of supplies, it is now deemed too much of a danger. These residents were able to get out of Oleshky in spring this year Warning: Distressing and graphic descriptions of dead bodies below. Working out how many people have been killed in Oleshky is difficult. The UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine has recorded reports this year ofat least 29 civilians killed and 54 injured in Oleshky and Hola Prystan,external- about 24km to the east. Local volunteers estimate that number could be significantly higher. Ksenia Arkhipova has been counting the dead since she managed to escape Oleshky in summer 2022 - a few months after it was taken by the Russian army. She is a volunteer who is involved in attempts to deliver food and medicine and facilitating evacuations to Oleshky. Locals trust her with their sensitive personal information. "I've been putting together a spreadsheet of all those who died as soon as I find out about it, with their names and dates of birth – I've got around 1,200 people now," she says. "Sometimes I don't have time to update it, as the list grows one or two people longer every day: someone was killed by a drone, someone else stepped on the landmine." While the BBC cannot independently verify these figures, one local resident has given her personal account of losing her loved ones. Both her parents were killed in Oleshky this summer, said Tetiana - also not her real name. She confirmed their identities to the BBC with their dates of birth and photos, but asked not to have them published for her own safety. "They were shot inside their home. Russian soldiers came there and wanted to take it," she said. Largest attack on Moscow sees Ukraine fire hundreds of drones, mayor says A four-minute warning isn't enough: Russia's new relentless missile tactics exhaust Kyiv residents Russia hits Ukrainian train shortly after Boris Johnson and top European officials leave station Burying the bodies of people killed in Oleshky has been restricted by Russian occupation authorities, residents say. This has made counting the dead even harder. They "do not allow us to bury the dead if they were killed by a drone, stepped on a landmine or were killed in any other way", said Tetiana. Russia's occupation authorities demand those deaths are confirmed by post mortem examination carried out by a Russian doctor, the BBC has been told. That is not possible in Oleshky. Only those who die of natural causes could be buried, she added, and as a result, "some bodies have been on the streets since December". Bodies are "either getting piled" up in the local hospital morgue, "where there's been no power since winter", says volunteer Ksenia Arkhipova, or "stray dogs eat them". That detail has been verified by the BBC based on numerous pictures obtained from residents. They are all too graphic to publish. "This is a tool of psychological pressure," says Ester Vrataryova, the co-founder of charity Humanity, which helps people in Oleshky and the wider Russian-occupied territories of Ukraine. "If you try to bury a dead body, you'll become the next one," she says. This video can not be played Watch: Ukraine's race to counter a new type of Russian drone

Headline: Africa's richest man helps fund $660m fuel pipeline between Ethiopia and Djibouti
Body: Aliko Dangote made his fortune from cement in Nigeria Nigerian billionaire Aliko Dangote has announced that he is helping to fund a new $660m (£500m) fuel pipeline between Ethiopia and Djibouti The project will include a 120km- (75 mile-) pipeline connecting Djibouti's Damerjog port to a distribution facility in Dewele, Ethiopia, as well as storage capacity of about 400 million litres. It is expected to begin operations within 18 months. Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed said the pipeline, which would be a joint venture between Dangote and Ethiopia, is expected to reduce the time needed to transport fuel from Djibouti's port to the Ethiopian capital, Addis Ababa, from five days to one. The first phase will transport key petroleum products, including jet fuel, diesel and petrol. Speaking at the ground-breaking ceremony, Dangote, Africa's richest man, said the project would strengthen Ethiopia's energy security and make its fuel supply chain more resilient. Landlocked Ethiopia relies heavily on Djibouti's port for imports, including petroleum products. The new infrastructure is expected to reduce pressure on existing transport systems supporting industries, including transport, aviation, agriculture and construction. Djibouti is also expected to benefit from increased port activity, job creation and higher government revenues. The project is part of Dangote's wider expansion of infrastructure and manufacturing businesses across Africa. Dangote Cement has production capacity of about 55 million tonnes a year, while his oil refinery in Nigeria currently has capacity to process 700,000 barrels of crude a day and is seeking to double that to 1.4 million barrels a day. The refinery recently listed 4.1 billion ordinary shares on the Nigerian stock exchange, aiming to raise about $1.63bn (£1.2bn). In Kenya, the company is due to break ground next week on a proposed 700,000-barrel-a-day crude oil refinery in Lamu. Headline: Why families are being urged to look closer on autumn walks
Body: James Benwell says searching for fungi can turn an ordinary family walk into an outdoor adventure From fairytale toadstools to fungi that look like birds' nests, experts say some of Britain's most unusual mushrooms are beginning to emerge as autumn arrives. Hidden in parks, woodlands and nature reserves, species ranging from the bright-red fly agaric to the rare red cage fungus can be found by anyone willing to slow down and take a closer look. For James Benwell, of the Birmingham and Black Country Wildlife Trust, searching for fungi has become a way to explore the outdoors with his young son. He said mushroom spotting can transform an ordinary walk into an adventure, revealing colourful and unusual species that many people pass by without noticing. Across the West Midlands, fungi enthusiasts have recorded everything from tiny bird's nest fungi in Birmingham city centre, to fly agaric mushrooms growing beneath woodland birch trees and a rare red cage fungus discovered in Cannon Hill Park. Many species can go unnoticed among fallen leaves, rotting wood and the bases of trees, but Benwell said taking the time to look more closely opens up a hidden world. "Every walk becomes interesting and exciting if you're exploring and if you're looking for new things," he said. Magpie inkcap mushrooms get their name from their black-and-white appearance, Benwell said With more than 15,000 species of fungi found in the UK, experts are encouraging people to photograph and record what they find, rather than pick them. Interest in fungi has grown in recent years, according to Lucas Large, chairman of the West Midlands Fungus Group, who said the organisation regularly attracted newcomers to its activities and fungi forays. Benwell added one of the attractions was the variety of shapes, colours and forms that can be discovered throughout autumn. "Sometimes you've just got to look through the leaf litter a bit, and you'd be amazed at the colours and different shapes and sizes of mushrooms you can find when you do look," he said. The fly agaric's distinctive red cap and white spots have made it one of the world's most recognisable mushrooms Among the most recognisable species is thefly agaric,,externalthe striking red mushroom covered in white spots that has become closely associated with folklore and popular culture. Benwell described it as "the mushroom of fairy tales". "It's in Alice in Wonderland, it's in Super Mario Brothers... It's everywhere as part of fairy tales and folklore," he said. "But there are still adults who've never seen it." The bright-red cage fungus attracts flies with its distinctive smell Other species offer equally unusual sights. Bird's nest fungi resemble miniature nests complete with tiny eggs, while the rare red cage fungus forms a vivid crimson lattice structure. The latter was spotted in Birmingham's Cannon Hill Park last year, in what Benwell said was only the second recorded sighting of the species in Birmingham and the Black Country. "UK-wide, you're only talking hundreds of records ever. It's not a common species at all," he said. Large said the red cage fungus also had another notable characteristic. "It smells horrible," he said, explaining the fungus attracts flies which help spread its spores. After more than a decade studying fungi, Large said the rarest species he had seen in the region was the coral tooth fungus. "It formed this enormous kind of white, coraloid fruiting body," he said. Bird's nest fungi get their name from their resemblance to tiny nests filled with eggs While the colourful displays may encourage people to learn more about fungi, experts are warning against assuming wild mushrooms are safe to eat. Several species found in the UK can cause severe illness or death if consumed, including the death cap mushroom, whichthe Woodland Trust says is responsible for most fungus-related fatalities.,external Large said there was no foolproof shortcut to determining whether a mushroom was poisonous. "The only way to do it is to know which one it is, or be sort of certain that you've got a particular species," he said. Benwell agreed and said people without specialist knowledge should avoid picking wild mushrooms. "There are mushrooms that will harm you, that will make you sick or even kill you in this country," he said. "The best place to get your mushrooms if you want to eat them is the supermarket." Lucas Large describes the coral tooth fungus as one of the rarest species he has seen in the region Instead, people are encouraged to enjoy fungi where they are found, whether in Birmingham city parks, the woodlands of Cannock Chase, Sutton Park or the Wyre Forest. When searching with his son, the pair follow a simple rule. "No licking, no picking, no kicking." For Benwell, that approach allows families to enjoy the excitement of discovery while ensuring the region's remarkable fungi can be appreciated by everyone who passes by. Headline: Flood-hit farmer welcomes prevention projects
Body: James Winslade said the floodwater was on his land for three months in 2014 and ruined the soil A farmer who saw his land devastated by flooding has welcomed the allocation of funding towards flood prevention measures. Somerset Council has allocated a government grant of £50m on flood prevention work, including dredging, improvements to pumping stations and flood warning systems. James Winslade, a farmer near Burrowbridge in Somerset who saw "every bit"of the family's 900 acres underwater in 2014, hopes the money can help prevent future disasters. "It's brilliant to have that money. Dredging and permanent pumps mean we can get water moving a lot quicker," said Winslade, adding he was keen for work to be completed. "The trouble is, the money hasn't been spent. Now we're catching up from lack of investment," Winslade added. "I'd like to actually see work being done on the ground." Winslade, whose family has farmed on the Somerset Levels for three generations, was among people who had to evacuate during the floods which made international headlines. 'AI helped diagnose my daughter's rare condition' 'I thought it was perimenopause but it was incurable cancer' Henry superfan, 8, shows off vacuum collection In June, the Department for Environment, Food, and Rural Affairs announced that Somerset Council would be allocated £50m for flood resilience. Since then, the council has developed a flood resilience programme consisting of 15 projects the money will be spent on. The first allocation will be about £650,000 for communities, emergency response, and to fund gully maintenance ahead of the coming winter. One of the community projects is My Community, a Somerset Council programme supplying residents with home maintenance and installation of flood-resilient washing machines, toilets and showers. Federica Smith-Roberts, Somerset Council's lead member for communities, climate change and environment, said an advisory board with people from key agencies and the community has been working on a draft programme "with the aim of moving at pace to deliver some key measures as soon as possible". "The My Community programme will be a crucial part of this," she said. Bryony Sadler said she is not entirely happy with all of the projects Somerset Levels resident and flooding campaigner Bryony Sadler said: "Some of the projects that are being used I'm not in favour of. "No matter how good your drainage system is, unless it's unblocked, that water is still going to be here and it's going to affect us and then we can't go to the shop and the railway is flooded." Some of the funding will go towards improving pumping stations Some of the funds will go to help the Internal Drainage Boards carry out additional dredging and desilting work. And about £3m will help the Environment Agency (EA) improve existing pumping stations across Somerset. "With winter fast approaching, we're pleased Somerset Council has confirmed that flood resilience funding will reach communities before challenging weather sets in, and we'll continue working closely with the council and partners on the programme," an EA spokesperson said. Headline: US states declare emergency as powerful storm brings flooding and power cuts
Body: This video can not be played Watch: Huge waves pummel northeast US as storm barrels through Tens of millions of people across the north-eastern US have found themselves in the path of a powerful weekend storm bringing coastal flooding, power cuts, travel chaos and cancelled stadium events. The so-called nor'easter brought "dangerous coastal flooding and beach conditions, strong winds and heavy rainfall" to areas including New York City and Boston on Saturday, the US National Weather Service (NWS) said. States of emergency have been declared in New York and New Jersey, both of which faced a coastal deluge in some areas. Rain and strong winds were forecast from Virginia to Maine. In Brooklyn, New York City, a man was killed by a falling tree. This video can not be played BBC Weather presenter Helen Willetts look at the impacts of the powerful Nor'easter The nor'easter has caused widespread power cuts. More than 160,000 households, nearly all in the north-eastern US, have lost electricity, according to tracker PowerOutage. More than 2,400 flights were delayed and another 1,199 grounded on Saturday, according to FlightAware. A full moon was projected to worsen coastal flooding. Streets and homes were inundated with floodwater in the coastal New Jersey communities of Surf City and Manasquan on Saturday. Surf City, New Jersey, was among coastal communities flooded NWS said in its alert: "Prepare immediately for significant inundation in low-lying areas near the shore, including roads underwater and impacts to homes and businesses." In New York, officials are warning of wind gusts of up to 55mph (86km/h) throughout the weekend, leading to downed trees and power lines. "Don't travel if you don't have to," NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani told residents in a video message. "Do not drive or walk through floodwater." In the Boston area, the Red Sox moved the last game in their series against the Chicago Cubs to Sunday afternoon in Florida. Residents on kayaks in a Beach Haven West, New Jersey, neighbourhood A professional football match between Red Bull New York and St Louis City SC was also cancelled. The Global Citizen Festival concert in New York City's Central Park, which was to be headlined by Lauryn Hill, Wyclef Jean and John Legend, will not go ahead. Ed Sheeran's Boston concert was also among events called off due to the weather. Sheeran's concert at the Gillette Stadium in the Boston area was cancelled for safety reasons, the venue said.
