Headline: Europe's car makers are in crisis. Will the threat of war rescue them?
Body: Europe's car makers are in crisis. Will the threat of war rescue them? It's green, bulging and intimidating. Ford's latest vehicle looks like a pick-up truck that has been through an Incredible Hulk transformation. Based on its popular Ranger series, this beefy number parked outside the front door of Ford's Dagenham plant can carry a load of two tonnes, tow up to four tonnes and is also shouldering the hopes of the 2,000-strong workforce that still makes engines here. Inside the factory, the three-litre diesel engines that will power this camo-painted beast drift down a production line that has seen output cut from 90,000 engines a year to about half that over the last decade. Ford is hoping that a pivot towards military vehicles can help fill the void created by what the company's UK boss calls the most challenging environment since the invention of the motor car. Once mighty, the European car industry is starting to look puny and is hoping surging defence budgets as Europe re-arms can help it flex its industrial muscles once more. Ford is part of a bid for the British Army's Light Mobility Vehicle (LMV) programme Ford is part of a joint venture with defence specialists General Dynamics and Ricardo bidding for a Ministry of Defence (MoD) contract to supply 9,000 vehicles over the next five to seven years to replace the Army's ageing Land Rover-based fleet. Lisa Brankin, chair of Ford UK, says it is a chance to showcase their abilities to respond quickly to defence needs: "As a manufacturer you look at every opportunity that comes at you and this is a great opportunity that we would love to take advantage of." This is not the first time Ford has busied itself with defence work. Ahead of World War Two, Ford's factory in Dagenham, east London, was the largest car plant in Europe. When war broke out, civilian car assembly stopped completely, and the factory was converted entirely to military production. Between 1939 and 1945, the Dagenham plant built 360,000 vehicles for the Allied war effort. Ford workers in Manchester manufactured 34,000 Rolls-Royce-designed Merlin engines, which powered Spitfires and Hurricane fighter planes. Eighty years later, the UK and European car industries are hoping that the engines of war can help defend against what one supplier told the BBC was a "terminal decline". As Europe feels compelled to commit hundreds of billions to ramp up defence spending in the face of the menace from Russia and US reluctance to be Europe's protector, car makers that are under commercial attack from Chinese rivals have taken notice. So can the rearmament of Europe save an auto industry and a supply chain facing crisis? Ford is far from the only car company that sees defence as a growth industry - and one that can utilise the growing overcapacity at car plants across Europe. French car maker Renault has signed a strategic agreement with defence giant Thales to produce military drones - targeting an output of up to 1,000 units per month. The French military and Directorate General for Armament want to tap into Renault's mass-production capabilities to bypass traditional, slower defence supply chains. Meanwhile, Volkswagen has agreed to sell an under-used factory in Osnabruck, western Germany, which will become a military manufacturing hub in a joint venture with an Israeli-based defence investor. Jaguar Land Rover (JLR), which makes the Land Rover, is also bidding for the same contract as Ford - as the Army retires its existing Land Rover-based fleet by 2030. JLR has also established a new dedicated business unit to support its global military ambitions. It makes sense for under-utilised auto manufacturing capacity to switch to defence, says Mike Hawes of the Society for Motor Manufacturers and Traders (SMMT) trade association. The UK car industry and its suppliers are heavily reliant on a few big manufacturers – Nissan in Sunderland, Toyota in Derbyshire, BMW in Oxfordshire and the biggest of them all by value of output, JLR at multiple sites in the Midlands and Merseyside. And Hawes says the supply chain is very vulnerable. "UK automotive output has been in decline over the last eight or nine years," he says. "We're probably half of what we were 10 years ago. Now, that's obviously going to hit the supply chain because they're not making the same number of parts. So they've got capacity. They may be quite dependent on one particular manufacturer as well." So they will welcome "the opportunity to broaden their customer base and potentially move into defence", he says. Just two weeks ago, JLR announced it was cutting 4,000 jobs from its 30,000-strong UK workforce in order to reduce costs to stay competitive with international – particularly Chinese – rivals. Dave Roberts of the firm Evtec, which supplies cooling systems components to JLR, is worried about the implications of this. "JLR is the critical mass in the UK automotive manufacturing space," he says. "It is the glue that holds the whole of the sector together. Because remember, when you're making volumes for JLR, they're significantly higher than any other car maker in the UK. "If they suffer, the ripples run deeper through the supply chain." Earlier this week, major JLR suppliers urged the government to help automotive manufacturers move into aerospace and defence, warning that large-scale car production in the UK faces long-term decline.  Executives have warned of a "visible crack" in the UK automotive supply chain In an open letter to the prime minister, chancellor and West Midlands Mayor Richard Parker, industry leaders argued Britain's automotive supply chain was "not in decline" but "in the wrong market". The letter was signed by executives representing businesses with more than 8,600 direct employees, alongside the Confederation of British Metalforming, which represents about 75,000 workers. Signatories to the letter said the redundancies were "the first visible crack" in a UK automotive supply chain supporting about 183,000 manufacturing jobs. Across Europe, the industry is facing what Sigrid de Vries, director general of the ACEA auto industry manufacturers' association called "a perfect storm". Car makers are spending billions to shift to electric vehicles and insist that government sales targets for EVs are outpacing consumer demand. And the EVs people are buying are increasingly from the biggest new threat to the industry – China. In the early 2000s, Western firms saw China as a land of opportunity. The country's rapidly growing middle class had plenty of money and a seemingly insatiable appetite for cars, including the most profitable upmarket models. It was a lucrative business – the Chinese market once accounted for half of Volkswagen's profits. However, it didn't last. China wanted a home-grown car industry and lavish state funding was ploughed into making the country a leader in high-tech businesses, including electric cars. Today, the Chinese market is overloaded with brands, both foreign and domestic, and is characterised by cut-throat competition. Chinese car makers have focused their attention on foreign markets, and have used the transition to electric vehicles as a pathway to gaining market share. The likes of BYD, Chery and Geely are moving aggressively into Europe. For European brands, all of this could not have happened at a worse time. The loss of the steady stream of profits from China, and the emergence of Chinese rivals on their home turf, has come after they invested heavily in producing electric vehicles (EVs). But EV sales have not increased as quickly as expected. Executives admit they have struggled to match the low production costs and development speed of the Chinese insurgents. The result is that European manufacturers are now rushing to cut costs, while wondering what to do with expensive factories capable of producing millions more cars than they are able to sell. Volkswagen has already announced plans to cut 100,000 jobs over the next few years. Whereas once closing plants in Germany would have been unthinkable, the company has now shuttered one in Dresden and may shut down four more. That includes a site in Zwickau, where VW spent over €1bn (£857m) converting production lines to build electric vehicles - a process that was completed just four years ago. Industry estimates indicate that western European car plants have roughly 2.5 million vehicles worth of annual spare capacity. Little wonder that car makers are jealously eyeing soaring defence budgets across Europe. Sigrid de Vries says car makers are well placed to help Europe rearm. "Many of the capabilities that defence needs are needed for and also delivered by the automotive sector," she says. "So automotive manufacturers and suppliers possess industrial assets, they possess manufacturing expertise, logistics capabilities, also advanced technologies. They have vast and also very integrated supply chains that may be relevant for Europe's broader defence preparedness objective." But it is not that simple – security protocols, political and economic rivalries within Europe plus the fact that unless you're actually at war, the volumes will not replace the mass consumer market, all of which present challenges, she says. "These are two very different worlds," she says. Governments want to invest in their defence capabilities and that is why it's now, more than ever, interesting for manufacturers and suppliers to see what's possible, but it will not be enough to address the underutilisation of manufacturing capacity we currently see."  If defence can't plug the yawning gaps in UK and European car manufacturing production – is it time for the henhouse to rent a room to the fox? In other words, let Chinese companies move into European production facilities? To offset the immense fixed costs of running idle assembly lines, legacy European and UK automakers are opening their doors to Chinese rivals. Stellantis – owners of the Vauxhall, Fiat, Peugeot and Citroen marques – has taken a 20% stake in Chinese EV maker Leapmotor and production of the Chinese brand started in Poland two years ago. (Leapmotor then moved production to Spain after Poland voted to impose steep tariffs on Chinese EVs while Spain abstained – an example of how trade politics can get complicated.) Nissan and Chery International UK have signed a non-binding Memorandum of Understanding for the study of contract manufacturing for Nissan to manufacture Chery vehicles at its Sunderland plant. VW CEO Oliver Blume said in April of this year that Volkswagen was considering sharing spare European factory capacity with Chinese joint-venture partners. In one sense it could be a win-win. European factories would have extra work while Chinese manufacturers could avoid high tariffs when selling into the US and the EU by making and exporting the cars in and from those markets. But building cars in Europe does not automatically mean creating or saving European supply chains. Some plants may only perform final assembly while many of the components – especially batteries – may continue to come from China. Cultural treasures are being destroyed worldwide - so why is no-one being punished? War may be coming. Are we psychologically ready? Why a fresh wave of North Korean soldiers may fight in Russia's war in Ukraine Car making is still seen as central to countries' sovereign manufacturing capability – in the old days the mantra was: "What's good for General Motors is good for America." You could say the same for Volkswagen, Mercedes and BMW for Germany and JLR for the UK. Car plants are often the major employer in their area and support local supply chains, so job losses can hit particularly hard. That's why countries go to great lengths to protect and preserve them. Australia is a case in point. When its final locally made car left the production line in 2017, it didn't just lose a car industry, it lost an engineering mindset and key skills, says Dave Roberts of Evtec. "Over the next decade... ripple effects crept into all manufacturing," he says. "So they lost infrastructure capability. They lost advanced manufacturing capability. "They're vulnerable. They're not resilient in those sectors anymore." Ford UK's Lisa Brankin acknowledges 9,000 engines over five to seven years is a far cry from the 90,000 per year the plant used to produce – but she insists every little helps. "It is a drop in the ocean but every single opportunity is worth having, isn't it?" A spokesperson for the Ministry of Defence says it wants UK industry to play a "central role" in delivering thousands of modern light mobility vehicles. The spokesperson adds: "We are backing British businesses and supporting our defence industrial base with 85% of our defence spending currently staying in the UK, driving reindustrialisation and making defence an engine for growth." It's understandable why a declining European car industry wants to gatecrash the spending splurge in the defence sector. But even if they can, right now it is hard to see how they'll ever be able to wield the muscle that they once did. It has been replaced by a line chart showing EU defence spending, both actual and projected, from 2018 to 2029. Headline: Scientists discover why Kent meningitis outbreak was so severe
Body: Scientists say they have discovered why the bacteria responsible for the UK's worst outbreak of meningitis B in Kent earlier this year proved so dangerous. More than 20 young people, mostly students, were infected inthe March outbreak, linked to a Canterbury nightclub. All needed hospital treatment, while nine ended up in intensive care and two died. Experts at the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) and the University of Oxford,who have looked at the DNA of the bacterium,external, say it picked up some genetic material from other bugs found naturally in the throats of some people. This exchange created a new strain or variant that then spread between clubbers and caused severe illness. Experts stress the meningitis vaccine currently being offered to more than a million young people starting university protects against it. Young people can book to get their Men B vaccine at high street pharmacies across England. There are walk-inappointments too,external. Two doses offer the best protection. First doses are available until 31 December 2026, with second doses available until 31 March 2027. Dr Charlene Rodrigues, consultant in Pathogen Genomics at UKHSA, said: "This investigation shows just how quickly and dramatically these bacteria can change. "The fact this outbreak variant was able to spread to so many young people was due to the social environment, a place where lots of close social mixing takes place." Speaking exclusively to the BBC, she said bacteria are known to undergo changes like this, known as horizontal gene transfer. Such changes can make infections more severe, and may mean they get past the immune system because people haven't encountered them before. These events, while rare and unpredictable, could happen again, so experts "should not take their eye off the ball", she added. Scientists say speed and severity ofthe Kent outbreak was very unusual. It was described as "unprecedented" and "explosive" at the time, with so many infections happening in one place and over a very short period. Two people died - a 21-year-old University of Kent student and Juliette Kenny, a sixth-form pupil at Queen Elizabeth's Grammar School in Faversham. The outbreak is thought to have started in a nightclub called Club Chemistry in the city centre, which was popular with university students. It's likely one person brought the infection in with them, and then it spread that evening. Meningitis is passed through close contact - including kissing and sharing drinks or vapes. Dr Rodrigues suspects the very same genetic changes that made the strain so dangerous may also explain why the outbreak was short-lived and did not continue to spread. People were generally too sick to be silent carriers who can pass it on unknowingly to others. Prof Robert Heyderman, an expert in infectious diseases at University College London, said the outbreak strain could have been carried by healthy people for some time before the conditions were right for the outbreak to occur. Following the Kent outbreak, a one-off menB vaccination programme was launched to protect young people heading to university this autumn. Advisers are asking the government to consider introducing MenB jabs routinely for secondary school-aged people at around the age of 15 to better protect them against a disease that can be deadly. Anyone concerned about symptoms of meningitis or sepsis, which can include fever, headache, stiff neck, sensitivity to light, a rash that does not fade under pressure, difficulty breathing and muscle pain should seek medical help immediately. Headline: Brazil's Lula bans online gambling ahead of presidential election
Body: Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva announcing new economic measures in São Paulo Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva has announced a ban on online gambling, just days before an election in which he is seeking a fourth term as the country's leader. The left-wing leader, who is running against the son of the incarcerated former Brazilian President Jair Bolsonaro, signed a provisional order on Friday that "prohibits all sports betting and online casinos". The online gambling industry in Brazil was legalised in 2018 and has since been blamed for widespread household income losses due to addiction. Flávio Bolsonaro accused his rival of playing politics, while Brazilian football teams said the ban could lose them income due to betting firms pulling their sponsorships. Lula described the industry as a "cancer" in his announcement, adding that "either we remove the tumour, or it kills us". The move comes just over a week before the first round of Brazil's presidential election. Recent polls have the 80-year-old leader almost neck-and-neck with the younger Bolsonaro. Lula also separately signed a bill to establish criminal offences related to fixed-odds betting – the most common type of online sports betting. Punters and bookies will have until 5 October to withdraw any existing funds from online betting accounts, while new deposits have been barred. The new measures must receive congressional approval within 120 days to remain in force. Lula acknowledged online betting was allowed under the former President Michel Temer's administration but said that it had grown "without regulation under Bolsonaro's management". He said in a statement on X that there were "no restrictions" particularly for preventing children and teenagers from accessing online betting. "We won't allow betting companies to profit at the expense of Brazilian families' income and lives," the president added. Lula described how he had heard from families who had sold everything in their houses because of their gambling addictions. Earlier this week at the UN General Assembly, Lula accused the industry of "transforming addiction into profit". But Flávio Bolsonaro called the gambling crackdown "populist, hypocritical and politically motivated" during a campaign rally in Rio de Janeiro on Friday, according to Reuters. Grêmio, one of the so-called "big twelve" Brazilian football teams, noted ahead of Lula's announcement that sports betting firms had become "one of the main sources of revenue for sports" since they were made legal. It said a change in the law "will not only be an open door for illegal betting, but a fatal blow to Brazilian football, leading many clubs to insolvency". The main clubs were paid 1.1bn Brazilian reais ($212m; £160m) by sports betting firms in 2025, while the industry took in 62.5bn reais at the same time, broadcaster Globo reports. Most types of gambling, such as casinos and slot machines, are illegal in Brazil, but ever since online betting was legalised in 2018, it has exploded in popularity. About 59.9% of Brazilian adults support banning internet betting, a survey by Atlas and Bloomberg published this week has found. The Brazilian Institute for Responsible Gaming (IBJR), a trade body representing around 75% of the domestic betting sector, said a total ban on fixed-odds betting jeopardised the industry as a whole – and potentially 58-73bn real in revenue. "The ban also doesn't eliminate existing demand," it said in a statement, adding that anyone turning to illicit betting would no longer have "access to protection mechanisms provided in the regulated environment". It urged the federal government to strengthen betting regulations rather than outlaw online and fixed-odds betting entirely. Headline: Spain battles climate change on several fronts
Body: Farmer Juan Ángel Izquierdo says it is hard not to worry about wildfires In a small green meadow in the Gredos mountains, west of Madrid, a couple of dozen cows belonging to Juan Ángel Izquierdo and his family are grazing. The only noise is the gentle clang of the bells around the animals' necks. This would be an idyllic scene were it not for the blackened pine and oak trees all around, the legacy of a devastating recent wildfire. "It was immense, I've never seen anything like it," says Izquierdo, whose family have been farming here for 200 years. The fire, in late July, merged with two others, burning a total of around 80,000 hectares (200,000 acres), making it the biggest blaze Spain has ever registered. It consumed more than two-thirds of Izquierdo's land and killed 12 of his 85 cows. Another eight animals had to be put down because of their injuries. All the hay he had gathered to feed his cows in the winter was also burned. "For us farmers, the summers are becoming more and more worrying, because they are getting hotter," he says. "It rains less, the wet season ends earlier and the autumn starts much later." For farmers, such conditions are synonymous with fires. "If you don't think about the wildfires too much, you feel okay," Izquierdo says. "But when a fire starts in a nearby village you start wondering – 'and what if we're next?'." Wildfires are one of several symptoms of climate change which in recent years have had a substantial impact on Spain's economy, as well as contributing to shocking human tragedies. World Weather Attribution, an international research organisation, found that the extreme conditions that drove record-breaking fires in Spain and Portugal in 2025 were40 times more likely,externalto happen due to the warming climate. "The ultimate reason for the greater frequency and intensity of these kinds of fires has to be attributed to the increase in greenhouse gases caused mainly by the generalised use of fossil fuels," said Ernesto Rodríguez Camino, president of the Spanish Meteorology Association. The Socialist Prime Minister, Pedro Sánchez, has described the fires in dramatic terms, placing Spain in the front line of an environmental crisis. "The climate emergency kills," he said in July, during a visit to the southern province of Almería where a wildfire claimed 15 lives.  Research found that extreme heat and resulting fires in Spain were now 40 times more likely This year, around 300,000 hectares of land have been burned in Spain, according to the European Forest Fire Information System (EFFIS), approximately half the total affected in the entire European Union. In the last 40 years, damage caused by Spanish fires each year has exceeded 200,000 hectares on eight occasions – three of those since 2022. 'This landscape is completely charred': Inside the village at epicentre of Spain's wildfires 'It's a hell of a situation': Spain grapples with devastating wildfires Farming insurance association Agroseguro estimated that 16,000 hectares of crops had been destroyed by mid-August this year, a major blow for Spain's agri-food industry, which contributes 9% of the country's GDP. The local authorities in Castilla y León, the region most heavily affected by this year's massive fire near Madrid, are offering compensation – between €5,500 ($6,300; £4,700) and €25,000 ($29,000; £21,000) to each farmer – depending on the damage suffered. But Izquierdo estimates that this will cover less than half of his losses. For decades, Spain's warm climate has been a boon for one of its other biggest industries - tourism. Sun-drenched resorts along the Mediterranean coast, and in the Balearic and Canary Islands, have driven the country's growth as a tourist hub. This year, close to 100 million foreigners are expected to come to Spain, making it the second most-visited country in the world, just behind France. Yet there are signs that the heat is becoming too much for some travellers. A study by researchers at Madrid's Rey Juan Carlos University found that it can as adeterrent to potential visitors.,external "When there is a heatwave, the number of overnight stays drops in the destinations that we've studied, and there is also a drop in arrivals from some of Spain's biggest markets," says María Dolores Sánchez, an economist who co-authored the report. "Tourism represents 13% of Spain's GDP, so this could have repercussions in the medium term when it comes to Spain's competitivity." The city of Toledo, near Madrid, saw temperatures soar above 40C on numerous days this summer The medieval city of Toledo is on the plains of Castilla-La Mancha, far from Spain's coastline, but its rich history and winding streets have made it a popular destination for those seeking an alternative to the country's beaches and bars. However, this summer tested their tolerance of heat, with the country registering a record-breaking 61 days of heatwaves that continued into early September. Toledo repeatedly saw temperatures in excess of 40C. "It's quite difficult to do the tours in the summer," says guide Diego Esteban, of the company Visit Toledo. "We need to adapt, whether it is those of us who work in the tourism industry or the locals." When leading tours in the summer months, Esteban makes sure that there are frequent stops, drinking water is provided and that the itineraries include plenty of shade. However, he would like to see more shade and drinking fountains available. He says the heat has started to change the timing of the tourist season, bringing many more visitors during the cooler months of spring and autumn. Warmer summers have also encouraged the so-called "coolcation" trend, whereby Spanish travellers seek out cooler areas to spend their holidays, typically in the north of the country. Another consequence of Spain's warming climate has been drought. In 2024, after three years of minimal rainfall, the north-eastern region of Catalonia temporarily introduced stringent restrictions on water use, including a 25% reduction for industry and an 80% reduction for crop farming. Heavy rainfall since then has lifted the restrictions, but the drought had a major impact on the local economy. The most dramatic and tragic natural phenomenon Spain has seen in recent years were flash floods that killed 237 people in the east of the country in October 2024, centred on the Valencia region. Spanish meteorological research group Climatoc-Lab described it as "a manifestation of how global warming alters the hydrological cycle". The Valencia Chamber of Commerce estimated that the floods caused €4.5bn in direct damage. Thousands of businesses were affected, some literally washed away by the floodwater, while others were able to resume operations after a lengthy recovery. "It was a disaster, both in terms of the lives lost and the impact on businesses, on workers, employers and ordinary people," says Laura Llácer Álvarez, manager of the Fepeval federation of industrial parks in the Valencia region. Spain's geographical position, along with its climate and topography, make it unusually vulnerable as global temperatures increase. Germanwatch, an independent environmental organisation, ranked Spain the world's 20th most affected country in its climate risk index for 2024, just behind Nigeria and Mali. Yet there are those who see an upside for the economy. "Climate change affects how we produce, how we invest and how we consume," says Julián Cubero, head of economics of climate change at economic think tank BBVA Research. He points to how heat can act as a drag on economic activity. "We all work worse when it's hot," he says. However, he adds, a greener economy can create new jobs with greater productivity. "The key is to realise that if we don't act, growth will slow down, and if it's handled right it can become an opportunity," he says. Would you buy branded clothing from your favourite tech firm? Headline: As Merz scrambles for support, Germany's identity crisis is laid bare
Body: Friedrich Merz has led Germany since 2025 A set of bumper local elections has thrown Germany, and its government, off balance. Chancellor Friedrich Merz may now be a man on borrowed time. His coalition government is in crisis. But this breakdown of business as usual in Germany has been brewing for years. It's a nation wrestling with new, uncomfortable and unresolved realities. Think of certain stereotypes about Germany, and think again. A country dominated by boring, consensus-driven politics? Not any more. A confident, powerhouse economy at the cutting edge of car-making? Yesterday's story. A nation that can be used as a byword for impressive efficiency? The trains don't even run on time. Many Germans I've spoken to feel their nation has drifted away from the things that once anchored their identity. And the question of what next is, as yet, unanswered. That uncertainty is currently embodied by a beleaguered chancellor weakened by bruising regional election results. The far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) party has made strong gains in recent local elections In the last fortnight, Friedrich Merz's party was beaten to first place in Berlin, pummelled in the polls in Saxony-Anhalt and pushed out of parliament altogether in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania. A lifeline for Merz is that no-one, within his own centre-right CDU party, is yet willing to challenge the chancellor openly despite persistent rumours of a Kanzlertausch (chancellor swap). But he is on thin ice, with record low approval ratings among voters who often describe him as arrogant and out of touch. It is a problem that in government circles is sometimes more politely referred to as a "communication" issue. Those who back the Chancellor say it is time to double down on much-needed reforms, alongside its centre-left SPD coalition partner, and find a better way of talking to people. Swapping chancellors is not the answer as anyone would face the "same challenges", argues Jürgen Hardt, foreign policy spokesperson in parliament for Merz's CDU and its sister party, the CSU. Hardt pointed out that the CDU/CSU fared far better in other regional elections earlier this year, when we spoke minutes after Merz addressed party lawmakers at a closed-door meeting in the Bundestag. "I think Friedrich Merz knows about his deficits," says Hardt. "He will work on him and we will work on us as (a) party. And hopefully we will convince the people in the next months that we are on the right way." Merz came to power in 2025, promising to get tough on immigration and boost Germany's ailing economy. He appeared to offer a dynamism that might act as an antidote to the former dull, unhappy drumbeat of centre-left leader Olaf Scholz's bickering three-way coalition. Olaf Scholz and his three-way coalition struggled in power, and he was ousted in 2025 And Merz's allies would claim he has had some success. This week, leading economic institutes raised the country's growth forecasts for 2026 and 2027 above 1% while illegal entries into Germany – and Europe – are down year on year. But that will not eliminate public anxieties, on either issue. Households and businesses continue to endure high energy costs while fears persist that China is cannibalising German industry, including its iconic car sector. It is a brutal reversal of Germany's old recipe for success: cheap Russian gas that powered a booming export-driven economy. And when it comes to immigration, the focus is now less on new arrivals and more on concerns about public safety, welfare costs and integration. While there are local exceptions, voters appear to be losing faith in Germany's two principal governing parties (CDU and SPD). Enter the rising force in German politics, Alternative für Deutschland (AfD): a party that alarms security officials with its Russia-friendly stance and contains regional branches that are classed as right-wing extremist by domestic intelligence. Smears and misrepresentations, argues the AfD, as it claimed its third victory ever in a state election last Sunday in the north-eastern state of Mecklenburg-West Pomerania. Its co-leader, Alice Weidel, told me this week that Friedrich Merz's days were numbered. The AfD are a divisive force, with their recent local election wins sparking protests The AfD has survived numerous scandals in recent years to now top the polls nationwide, at around 28%. It carries the swagger of a party making the political weather. It has capitalised on a nostalgia for the past alongside an anxiety in the present as it consolidates its strongholds in the former communist east. An AfD placard I saw in Berlin read "Berlin braucht Ordnung" (Berlin needs order). It is the as yet untested promise that this party can bring back a lost sense of stability. But in Germany's capital it was in fact Die Linke (the Left) that topped the polls last Sunday in a further blow to the country's traditional "big tent" parties. The victory has put fresh scrutiny on Die Linke, as it faces allegations of antisemitism. The party leadership has insisted it is committed to protecting Jewish life. This round of regional elections has encapsulated the country's fault lines: the eroding support for Germany's political centre, and a polarising debate on the AfD. Rarely in post-war Germany has a set of local polls generated so much upheaval at home and interest abroad.

Headline: Who are the Houthis and what do they want?
Body: The Houthis captured key coastal areas in their recent rapid advance Yemen's civil war has flared up in recent weeks as the Iran-backed Houthi movement, which controls much of the country's north-west, seized large strategically important stretches of the Red Sea coast in a rapid offensive. The territory includes the port of Mokha, which overlooks the Bab al-Mandab Strait, a chokepoint for global shipping. Oil prices have risen on fears of further disruption to the global economy, following six months of war between the US, Israel and Iran. Hundreds of people have reportedly been killed on both sides during the Houthis' advance, which came after the collapse of a four-year informal ceasefire. The UN says more than 120,000 people have been displaced by the escalation. Neighbouring Saudi Arabia, which opposes the Houthis and backs Yemen's internationally-recognised government, has launched air strikes, while the Houthis have fired drones and missiles at south-western Saudi Arabia. The group has also targeted commercial vessels linked to Saudi Arabia in the Red Sea. How escalating Saudi oil crisis could drive up prices everywhere The Houthis are an armed political and religious group from northern Yemen which champions the country's Shia Muslim minority, the Zaidis. They declare themselves to be part of the Iranian-led "axis of resistance" against Israel, the US and the wider West - along with armed groups such as Hamas and Lebanon's Hezbollah movement. Formally known as the Ansar Allah (Partisans of God), the group emerged in the 1990s and takes its name from the movement's late founder, Hussein al-Houthi. His brother, Abdul Malik al-Houthi, has been its de facto leader since 2004. In the early 2000s, the Houthis rebelled against Yemen's long-time authoritarian president Ali Abdullah Saleh. They wanted greater autonomy for the group's homeland in the north of Yemen. The group seized the capital Sanaa after the 2011 Arab Spring, when a popular uprising forced Saleh to hand power to his deputy. The Houthis have continued to grow in strength, with troop numbers estimated to have risen to 350,000 last year, and now control between one-quarter and one-third of Yemen's territory, but 70-80% of its population - about 30 million people. The group wants an end to a Saudi blockade, control of the whole of Yemen and access to Yemen's oil and gas revenues. The Houthis have controlled northern Yemen since 2014 Neighbouring Saudi Arabia feared the Houthis would take over Yemen and make it a satellite of its regional rival, Iran. In 2015 Saudi Arabia formed a coalition of Arab countries that intervened on behalf of Yemen's internationally-recognised government. But years of air strikes and ground fighting were unable to dislodge the Houthis from most of the territory they seized, and also triggered one of the world's worst humanitarian crises. A temporary ceasefire was brokered in 2022. Soon after the start of the Gaza war in October 2023, the Houthis began firing drones and missiles towards Israel and at merchant vessels in the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden, saying they were acting in support of the Palestinians. Western countries deployed warships and the US, UK and Israel carried out air strikes. An Israeli strike killed senior Houthi figures including the prime minister of its self-declared government. In 2025 the US and the Houthis agreed to stop targeting each other. However the Houthis resumed missile attacks on Israel after the US and Israel attacked Iran in February 2026, having paused them after the October 2025 ceasefire in Gaza. The informal ceasefire between the Houthis and the Saudis began to unravel in July. The Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea. They said they were retaliating for what the Houthis say is a years-long Saudi blockade, and for an air strike on Sanaa airport. This was followed by a rapid Houthi advance in September that captured as much as 130km (81 miles) of the country's Red Sea coastline as well as the island of Perim. The move gave the Houthis significant control of the strategic Bab al-Mandab Strait, but they have insisted that they pose no threat to international shipping, except for Saudi-linked vessels. The Houthis' actions have caused renewed concern about disruption of world oil supplies. Bab al-Mandab has become an increasingly important route for oil exports from Saudi Arabia since shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, on the other side of the Arabian Peninsula, was curtailed due to the US and Israel's war with Iran. The situation has also been exacerbated by Houthi attacks on Saudi oil installations, as well as an attack on the East-West Pipeline blamed on Iran-backed Iraqi militias, and the escalation threatens to again draw in Western powers. Media reports said both the Yemeni government and Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman had urged President Trump to strike the Houthis following the offensive. Trump did not do so, saying the Houthis had agreed not to hit US targets. The UK meanwhile agreed to a Saudi request todeploy a military aircraft to help refuel Saudi Arabian fighter jetsfor "purely defensive missions". Lightning Houthi advance in Yemen may bring dangerous new dimension to Iran war Saudi Arabia and Western powers say Iran smuggled weapons - including drones, and cruise and ballistic missiles - to the Houthis during Yemen's civil war in violation of a UN arms embargo. A panel of UN experts concluded in 2024 that the Houthis had been transformed into a powerful military organisation due to the transfer of materiel, assistance and training from Iran's Revolutionary Guards, Lebanon's Hezbollah movement and Iraqi specialists. And a report in May 2026 by Conflict Armament Research (CAR) - after the start of the Iran war - found that whereas in the past Tehran shipped finished weapons to the Houthis, it was now increasingly sending parts which its proxies were able to assemble and was also sharing increasingly advanced missile technologies. Iran has denied supplying weapons to the Houthis and says it only supports them politically. Headline: What is kratom, the 'gas station heroin' alarming officials in the US?
Body: Jeffrey Deaver, a 58-year-old retired timber cutter in the state of Washington, has taken kratom for four years to help with severe chronic hip and knee pain. He discovered the herbal product when he couldn't find relief from doctors and while waiting for surgeries. Scared at first, he "started small", but then took more until his pain went away. "It was like a miracle," Deaver said. "I could sleep. I could function. "I just don't know what I'd do without it." Kratom - a herb with opioid-like effects - has grown in popularity in the US over the last decade, and is typically purchased over the counter and consumed in pill or liquid form. This week, investigators found packaged kratom in the possession of two deceased University of Mississippi students. Although their deaths were not attributed to kratom, officials are now issuing warnings about its consumption. For years, anti-kratom advocates have pushed for bans, and in some countries, like the UK, it's illegal. But Kratom is not regulated by the US Food and Drug Administration and is legal in some states, including Mississippi. Here's what we know about it: Kratom is a tree that is native to Southeast Asia in countries like Thailand, Malaysia and Indonesia. It's been used for centuries for its stimulant properties, grounded and consumed similar to tea. As its popularity spread around the globe, it entered the US market as a supplement around 2016. "That's really where the problems began," said Dr Shane Speights, dean of the New York Institute of Technology College of Osteopathic Medicine at Arkansas State University. In the US kratom is mostly sold in highly concentrated forms either via pill, powder or liquid, Speights said. It's also widely available - found everywhere from convenience stores and petrol stations to vape shops. Also, because of the supplement classification, kratom products are not federally regulated. "There's no way to know exactly what you're getting," Speight said. "You could go and create something in your basement, market it as a supplement, and nobody's really going to check and see what's in it." Kratom is often marketed as a safe, natural herbal supplement that helps with pain management, anxiety and depression. In lower doses, its stimulant properties create a "caffeine-kind of buzz", Speights explained. Because of its opioid-like effects, it has also been used with the goal of curbing addictions to actual opioids like fentanyl. Those properties stem from the way the plant's compounds - like 7-Hydroxymitragynine - activate various hormones, including dopamine. "It's almost like taking a narcotic," Speights said. "At higher doses, it can create more euphoria and give you more of a general high." Hallucinations are possible, too. The higher doses also pose greater risk for adverse side effects. That includes central nervous system (CNS) depression - which is "where the deaths come in," Speights said. CNS can result in cardiovascular collapse and loss of breathing. Withdrawal symptoms and addiction are also risks, said Jana Wu, director of clinical integration at the addiction treatment centre Mountainside. "It affects marriages, relationships," she said. "I've seen people lose jobs, spend thousands of dollars a month on it." Because it's easy to develop a high tolerance to the herb, users may need to take an increasing amount to achieve the same effect over time. "I've worked with people that were taking like up to 20 pills a day," Wu said. Experts told the BBC that the biggest dangers come from the fact that kratom is not federally regulated. "Is there a safe dose?" Speights said. "My answer is going to be no because -  I'm going to go back to this - we don't know what's in it." Kratom is banned in 11 states: Alabama, Arkansas, Connecticut, Indiana, Kansas, Louisiana, Massachusetts, North Dakota, Tennessee, Vermont and Wisconsin. Massachusetts was the last state to make it illegal, issuing a temporary emergency order in August. Ten years earlier, the US Drug Enforcement Agency (DEA) had moved to classify kratom as a Schedule 1, the most dangerous level for drugs, calling it "an imminent hazard to public safety". But the effort failed a few months later, after the justice department said it received "numerous comments from members of the public challenging" the attempt. That leaves states to take action, like Arizona, which recently sued a company  selling kratom beverage products. Groups opposed to kratom want states to do more, saying "gas-station drugs are poisoning our communities". Pro-kratom groups like the American Kratom Association are pushing for bans  against synthetics "posing as natural kratom". Internationally, kratom is banned in the UK. In Europe, the laws vary by country. In Malaysia, where the kratom tree is native, consumption and sale are banned under the Poisons Act of 1952.

Headline: Farmers' fury as race for £233m funding compared to 'scramble for Oasis tickets'
Body: Many farmers rely on government payments to manage their land in more environmentally-friendly ways Thousands of farmers missed out on vital government funding after online applications for a £233m green scheme for the whole of England closed down in under six hours. Farming and environmental groups condemned the race to secure the sustainable farming incentive (SFI) funding, with some comparing it to a "frantic" online scramble to secure Glastonbury or Oasis gig tickets. The post-Brexit scheme, which replaced EU subsidies with payments for farmers to look after nature and provide "public goods", opened at 10:00 BST on Tuesday but had run out of budget by 15:48 BST. The government said farmers had responded "in force" to the scheme and there would be further funding opportunities for 2027. The SFI scheme had been shut without warning last year so demand from farmers was expected to be high The National Farmers' Union (NFU) is calling for the government to explain why the scheme opened and closed so quickly, with so many farmers left out of pocket. It said it wanted "clarity and urgency" from the government and added that it had made "repeated warnings of a lack of sufficient budget". NFU vice-president Robyn Munt said: "The rapid uptake of the scheme comes as no surprise. Its closure in less than six hours shows the scale of demand there is from farmers to deliver for the environment and to invest in farm resilience. "The current cashflow pressures facing farmers and growers only exacerbates that demand as they look for certainty and clarity for the year ahead." Vicki Hird, agriculture lead at the Wildlife Trusts said "the scramble for green farming schemes was worse than the dash for Oasis tickets". She added: "The budget has been inadequate for far too long and the Treasury must recognise this and allocate far greater funds to ensure climate resilience in farming in the next budget." The SFI scheme is vital for many farmers who have turned large swathes of their land over to nature-friendly schemes, such as planting hedges, creating wildflower margins and protecting the soil. Whenthe scheme was suddenly closedwithout notice last year, there were concerns that some farmers might turn their backs on environmental work if they could not access the payments and demand for Tuesday's scheme was expected to be high. The Nature Friendly Farming Network (NFFN), which helps farmers to manage land in environmentally-friendly ways, criticised the "frantic scramble" and said farmers had "faced a desperate race against time" to secure their funding agreements. Cambridgeshire arable farmer Martin Lines, who leads the NFFN, said: "This entire SFI system, with windows opening and closing within a few hours, isn't fit for purpose. "We need to find a better way based on continuous, whole-farm agreements, not doors that slam shut on day one because the money has already gone." He pointed out that after years of extreme weather, many farmers were relying on the funding to help adapt their farms to climate change and become more resilient. The Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) said it would provide further information on future opportunities for funding applications in 2027 "soon". A Defra spokesperson said: "This year we ensured small farms and those new to SFI were prioritised - with an exclusive first window in the summer. "In anticipation of high demand in the second window, ministers decided to allocate an additional £20m to the fund, on top the £50m announced by the prime minister in August, so that we could fund as many agreements as possible." Farming Minister Stephen Morgan added that the SFI had been designed to be simpler to apply for and that farmers had "responded in force". "This is a scheme that works for farmers, backs food production, and delivers practical, sustainable land management, supporting the aims of our farming roadmap, our long-term plan for English farming," he said. Headline: Trump's Board of Peace unveils $2.45bn Gaza recovery plan
Body: Reconstruction has yet to begin in Gaza almost a year after a ceasefire came into force US President Donald Trump's Board of Peace has announced a $2.45bn (£1.85bn) Gaza recovery plan at a meeting on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly. The funding will be spread across 66 programmes over six months, and directed at housing, diesel generation and waste removal, among other needs. But the board admitted substantial donations were still needed, with $18bn pledged but only $280m handed over so far. It estimates full recovery and reconstruction will require about $71bn over the next decade. The board also did not set out a date for the start of reconstruction in Gaza, where Trump's plan to end the war has largely stalled almost a year after Israel and Hamas agreed a ceasefire. The disarmament of Hamas has been a key sticking point. The Palestinian group has agreed to give up its weapons in exchange for a phased Israeli troop withdrawal from the 60% of Gaza currently occupied. But Israel has insisted that it must fully disarm before any pullout. Violence has also continued in Gaza amid the deadlock, with near-daily Israeli strikes, and living conditions for the 2.1 million people living there remain dire. Jared Kushner, a Gaza Executive Board member and Trump's son-in-law, conceded that the Gaza Recovery Programme faced "different delays on different things, for whatever reason". "The goal of today was really just to show you that we're really fully committed to doing it," he told the meeting of board members and stakeholders. He was joined in New York by US envoy Steve Witkoff, who said that "real progress" had been made over the past year. "All of the hostages are home. There is a ceasefire, imperfect as it may be, but it still exists. Humanitarian efforts have achieved historic results, with billions of dollars donated and pledged to meet urgent needs and support the long work of recovery," Witkoff added. In addition to fundraising, the plan faces significant challenges including how to ensure security for those operating in Gaza, overhaul internal governance and find consensus between Israeli and Palestinian officials. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio told a separate news conference on Wednesday that "a number of countries have stepped forward and pledged financial assistance" and the board was "looking for more that will participate in that". Michael Eisenberg, an Israeli-American Board of Peace member, told the BBC's Newshour programme what the next steps were likely to be. "Because it's a war zone, you need to remove unexploded ordnance. And then there are still hundreds of kilometres of tunnels underneath Gaza which need to be destroyed as well. "Once that's all done, Gazans can get to rebuilding again: whether it's housing, or better sanitation, or other things," Eisenberg said. Jared Kushner (R) conceded that the plan faced "different delays on different things" In August, the Board of Peace's high representative for Gaza, Nickolay Mladenov,criticised Israel's continuing air strikes on Gaza, as well as the actions of Hamas. Mladenov warned that a collapse of last October's ceasefire would be "a point of no return" for the region. At least 1,408 Palestinians, including more than 300 children, have been killed in Israeli attacks in Gaza since the ceasefire began, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN. The Israeli military says five of its soldiers have been killed in combat since the ceasefire and one contractor was killed in an "operational accident". Reconstruction has also yet to begin in Gaza, where an estimated 80% of all structures have been destroyed or damaged during the war, leaving more than 60 million tonnes of rubble piled up. More than 1.9 million people - about 90% of the territory's population - have been displaced, many of them multiple times, and 1.2 million of them are currently living in tents or makeshift shelters, with limited access to clean water and sanitation services, according to the UN. The Board of Peace was created as part of Donald Trump's 20-point Gaza peace plan, which he unveiled alongside Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in September last year. Hamas agreed to return all 48 remaining hostages being held in Gaza in exchange for Palestinian prisoners in Israeli jails and Gaza detainees, and to the idea of handing over the governance of Gaza to Palestinian technocrats. In July, Hamas said it had accepted a disarmament plan for Gaza which would see it lay down its arms, provided Israel ends "all forms of aggression" and withdraws its forces from Gaza. But that was later rejected by Netanyahu, who said the military would stay in Gaza until Hamas was "genuinely" disarmed. The Board of Peace was originally thought to be an international organisation intended to bring peace to Gaza, but later expanded to include conflicts worldwide. The war was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, in which about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage. Israel responded by launching a military campaign in Gaza, during which more than 73,920 people have been killed, according to the territory's health ministry. Headline: From Nagaland to a path to the Oscars: Indian film brings a rarely seen world to global cinema
Body: This video can not be played Watch: Indian film brings a rarely seen world to global cinema There is something pleasingly improbable about Angh. The film comes from Nagaland, a mountainous state of fewer than two million people on India's northeastern frontier, and is in Konyak, a tribal language unfamiliar to most Indians, never mind audiences abroad. It was director Theja Rio's first feature and most of its cast faced a camera for the first time. And yet, at the Toronto International Film Festival this month, this quiet film won the Platform Prize, a major juried award. The award is intended to recognise films with a particularly distinctive directorial voice. The jury praised Rio's "refreshing perspective" and the film's portrait of a world rarely encountered on the international screen. The win also gives Angh an unusual route towards the 2027 Academy Awards. Under new rules, winners of designated prizes at six international festivals can qualify for consideration in the International Feature Film category without relying solely on their country's official submission. This does not make Angh an Oscar nominee. But it does place a Konyak-language film from one of India's smallest states inside a global conversation from which such stories have been almost entirely absent. Rio still sounds slightly startled by it. When we speak in Delhi, roughly 72 hours after the win, he has barely had a moment to breathe - Toronto, flights, interviews, more interviews. "There were a lot of good films in the competition", he says, including films by far more seasoned directors. His producers were confident. "They thought we were going to win. I wasn't." He is also less solemn than Angh might suggest. Before cinema, he wanted to be a rapper - "a kid from Compton instead of a kid from Nagaland", as he puts it. His tastes still range happily from Black Thought, the lead rapper of American hip-hop group The Roots, to his favourite filmmaker, the Iranian director Abbas Kiarostami. But for his first feature, he turned close to home. Set in the early 1960s, Angh follows Anghba, the ageing hereditary chief of a Konyak village, and his young son, as the world around them changes. The Konyaks are one of Nagaland's 17 major tribes, concentrated in the eastern district of Mon, where such chiefs are known as Anghs. Even today, some older men bear facial tattoos associated with the Konyaks' historical practice of headhunting. Anghba is the ageing hereditary chief of a Konyak village in Nagaland in the film Anghba and his son are among the last in their region to hold to an ancestral faith as Christianity spreads. Then an American missionary, played by Scottish actor Douglas Henshall, arrives. The father resists but the son is now curious. Rio says the idea for the film came a few years ago, when he was visiting Mon for another project. What struck him was how closely different generations seemed to live alongside one another there. Within a single family, he says, a grandfather might be a former headhunter, his face still tattooed; two generations later, his grandson might play guitar in a rock band. "It feels like you've jumped on a time machine," Rio says. "The past and the present sort of coexist together." The year also matters. Nagaland, which was earlier part of Assam state, formally became an Indian state in December 1963, during a period of profound political and social change. By then, Christianity had been spreading among Naga communities for decades, bringing changes extending beyond religious belief into customs, rituals and everyday life. From right: Theja Rio poses with Nancy Nisa Beso, the film's producer, and actors Anglong Konyak (who plays the village chief, Anghba) and Sobino Rengma (who plays the son, Amao) Dr B Amo Konyak, a scholar of Konyak society, says the changes during this period were almost like a disappearance. Some practices were lost; others "survived in fragments" - in the memories of elders, in family heirlooms. What had once been part of everyday life became heritage. But Dr Konyak says culture did not simply stop. People carried parts of it into new religious and social worlds. Traditions survived, but changed meaning as they changed form. It's this moment of transition that Rio wanted to capture. "The past 50 or 60 years have brought extraordinary churn," he says, widening the distance between generations. In Angh, he explores this through the relationship between the father and son who "intimately love and care about each other very deeply", even as their worlds begin to pull apart. Critic Siddhant Adlakha was struck by the ambiguity the film captures. "Progress and tradition can be nonlinear, even entwined," he says, "rather than strictly opposing forces." Angh traces the relationship between a father and son as they reconcile with larger changes The film is yet to reach a wider audience, but its brief trailer offers a glimpse of how Rio constructed this world. Mist hangs over steep green hills; figures move through forests and village paths; fire and lamplight pick faces out of the darkness. The landscape is beautiful but not merely picturesque - a small world held together by ritual, family and geography, while something larger presses in from beyond its edges. Adlakha singles out the quiet close-ups of Anghlong Konyak, the first-time actor who plays the chief, and the "gentleness" with which Rio captures his "subdued rage". What the camera saw mattered almost as much as where it was looking from. Konyak people have long been viewed from the outside. Dr Konyak points to explorers, colonial officials, missionaries and photographers drawn to tattooed faces, ornaments, weapons and headhunting, while the lives behind them often receded from view. The forest plays a central part in the storytelling of the film Rio was conscious of inheriting that history. "There have been several films and documentaries made about Nagaland," he says, "but these sort of films tend to follow the gaze of the explorer rather than the subject." With Angh, he wanted to reverse that gaze, asking viewers to "step inside the shoes of these characters". The change is subtle but consequential. The Konyaks are no longer an exotic remnant of the past, but people living through what Dr Konyak describes as "love, grief, conflict, faith, uncertainty and generational change". Konyak advisers worked on dialogue, costume and production design, and much of the cast was drawn from first-time Konyak performers. The forest, too, belongs to the people moving through it. Adlakha says Rio treats it "not just as a setting, but as a home with a history", much as an urban filmmaker might treat Mumbai or New York. Rio and cinematographer Adam Pietkiewicz shot Angh on 16mm film, drawing on photographs and footage of missionaries and Naga communities from the 1950s and 60s. They wanted to recreate the grain, texture and atmosphere of those archival images, while shifting the point of view from outsider to subject. It was an evocative choice - and a logistical headache. Unlike digital footage, the exposed film could not simply be reviewed on set. Every four or five days, the cans had to be sent to Mumbai for processing, while the crew carried on shooting without knowing exactly what they had captured. The film also stars Sottish actor Douglas Henshall, who plays a Christian missionary There were more prosaic problems too. During a night shoot with Henshall, an old Second World War Jeep was supposed to be driven into frame. It behaved perfectly through rehearsals. But when the cameras began rolling, the engine refused to start. After repeated attempts, the crew managed to capture just one take of the Jeep entering the frame. "It was a very difficult night," Rio says. Angh may be Rio's first feature, but its journey places it within a widening map of Indian cinema, especially in the northeast. Adlakha points to filmmakers such as Assam's Rima Das and Meghalaya's Dominic Sangma whose work, he says, reveals "how complex and multifaceted the idea of Indian cinema happens to be". Rio thinks Nagaland still remains at the edge of that scene. Its film industry is, as he puts it, "at a very nascent stage", with little of the reach enjoyed by India's established filmmaking centres. But he hopes some of the attention around Angh travels back with it. There are, he says, "so many talented filmmakers with so many beautiful stories that are yet to be told". For now, though, Rio is looking forward to something more ordinary - getting back to Nagaland. "I want to play football with my friends."

Headline: Track UK's latest migration numbers - net migration, visas, asylum and small boats
Body: Track UK's latest migration numbers - net migration, visas, asylum and small boats UK net migration has dropped to the lowest level, outside of the Covid pandemic, since 2012. How does that sit alongside other key migration measures, including asylum applications, small boat arrivals and visas granted? Scroll down to find out more about the latest key figures, and get answers to key questions on a range of topics. Between 1 January and 23 September 2026, a total of 18,565 people crossed the English Channel by small boat from France. This was down by 42% on the same period the previous year. These crossings have become the most common way for people to be detected entering the UK illegally since 2020. Nearly all those who arrive by small boat claim asylum. Under international law, this means they are allowed to stay in the country while their asylum application is considered. Small boat arrivals made up 40% of asylum applications between July 2025 to June 2026. Boats that arrived in the UK from 24 September 2025 to 23 September 2026 carried an average of 67 people. This has more than doubled since 2021. Experts sayovercrowding in boats makes crossings riskier. At least 84 people died while attempting to cross the Channel in 2024, according to the United Nations (UN). When looking at the scale of small boats crossings, the number of these arrivals is about 5% of the size of total immigration into the UK from January 2025 to December 2025. The government has pledged to“smash the gangs”behind these crossings in order to reduce the numbers. People from Eritrea accounted for 18% of all arrivals from July 2025 to June 2026. In the latest figures covering January 2025 to December 2025, at least 2,335 people who arrived by small boat were found to be potential victims of human trafficking or other forms of modern slavery, according to the Home Office. Another 4,712 people were detected entering the UK without permission via other methods including hiding in vehicles, travelling on ferries or through airports from July 2025 to June 2026. This was down by 17% on the same period the previous year. There are also individuals who arrive legally, for example via a work or study visa, and then overstay their limit. The total number of people who live in the UK illegally after arriving legally is not known. An asylum seeker is someone who wants to be in the UK because they say they cannot live safely in their own country due to persecution or violence. The government must house an asylum seeker if they cannot financially support themselves while their claim is being considered. There were 89,089 people in asylum accommodation as of June 2026. About 18% of those people, 16,021, were in hotels. These are used when there is not enough shared housing available, such as houses of multiple occupation (HMOs) orformer military sites. The governmenthas pledged to stop the use of hotelsby 2029. More people are in hotels across the south of England than elsewhere in the UK, while HMOs are more common in the north of England and Scotland. A modern browser with JavaScript and a stable internet connection is required to view this interactive Type in a postcode or the name of a local council below to see how many asylum seekers are housed in the area A total of 85,891 people applied for asylum in the UK from July 2025 to June 2026. This was down by 21% on the same period in the previous year. Most people who arrive in the UK by small boat claim asylum, but they were only 40% of all asylum seekers from July 2025 to June 2026. The rest include people who arrived by other illegal means or who came to the UK legally and applied for asylum while holding, or just after holding, a valid visa. It can take years for the government to decide whether someone should be granted asylum. In June 2026, 40,168 people - across 32,401 asylum applications - were waiting for an initial decision. The number of people awaiting an initial decision was down by 56% on the previous year. As of June 2026, a further 90,341 refused asylum applications were part of a second backlog, waiting the outcome of an appeal in the courts. This was up by 51% on the previous year. Together, these initial decision and appeal cases form the government’s total asylum applications backlog,which it has pledged to clear. Refugee status was granted in about 38% of asylum decisions made by the Home Office from July 2025 to June 2026. About 39% of asylum appeal cases concluded between January 2026 to December 2026 resulted in a previous refusal decision being overturned. The government requires people who are in the UK, but no longer have permission to live or work in the country, to leave. This is called a return and can happen voluntarily or involuntarily. People can lose the right to be in the UK for different reasons, such as a visa expiring, an asylum claim being refused, or by receiving a criminal conviction that results in deportation. There were 40,605 returns from July 2025 to June 2026. This was up by 8% on the same period the previous year. That number of returns is equivalent to about 6% of total emigration from the UK from January 2025 to December 2025. Of all returns from July 2025 to June 2026: 5,962 had been convicted of a criminal offence12,568 had lodged an asylum claim at some point3,310 had arrived in the UK by small boat People from India made up 27% of all returns from July 2025 to June 2026. The UK istrialing a scheme with Franceto return people who arrived in the country on a small boat. For every person the UK sends back to France, the UK will accept an equal number of asylum seekers. This is called the "one in, one out" deal. As of 30 June 2026, 1,087 people have been returned through this arrangement. Returns can happen in different ways. "Enforced returns", which includes deportations, means the government arranges transport to return people to a different country. In some cases, people are escorted by officers. All other returns are "voluntary". This means a person has agreed to leave and may receive government help with travel and other costs to help facilitate the return. Some people classed as leaving the country voluntarily do so completely independently and withoutany government knowledge or involvement. Independent returns made up 34% of the total from July 2025 to June 2026. Most people who come to the UK do so legally, after being granted a visa before they travel. A visa gives someone permission to enter or stay in the UK for a specific purpose, such as work, study or joining family members. There were 727,487 people who came to the UK via visas from July 2025 to June 2026, not including visitors or people transiting through the UK. This was down by 15% on the same period the previous year. That does not mean all those people travelled to the UK, only that they were approved to do so. The most common type of visa people came to the UK on was study, which made up 53% of all visa entries from July 2025 to June 2026. People from China were the most common group to come to the UK on study visas, making up 23% of the total. Together, people from China and India accounted for nearly half of all study visas. This has been the case for many years. The EU and UK monitor the number of people crossing borders in the Mediterranean and English Channel by sea without permission. There were 139,288 sea arrivals to the UK, Greece, Italy, Spain and Cyprus from August 2025 to July 2026. Crossings to the UK accounted for about 22% of the combined total. Sea arrivals into mainland Europe peaked in 2015, when the UN saidmore than a million peoplecrossed the Mediterranean. The top three countries with the most people claiming asylum from April 2025 to March 2026 were Spain with 133,795, Italy with 124,740 and France with 111,320. The UK ranked at number five for asylum claims over the same period when compared with 26 other European countries with populations over one million. When adjusted for population size, the UK ranks at number 10 for asylum applications per 100,000 people. Net migration measures the overall change in a country’s population due to migration over a given period. It is everyone coming into the country (immigration) minus everyone who leaves (emigration). The latest available data to compare the UK with other European nations is January 2024 to December 2024. At that point, the countries with the biggest increase in their population were Spain with 626,000, Germany with 494,000 and the UK with 331,000, after taking into account the people who left the country, and those who arrived. When adjusting for population size, the UK was in position 11 for increase in population due to migration, alongside 13 other European countries with comparable data per 100,000 residents. Is the government meeting its pledges on illegal immigration and asylum? Why do Channel migrants want to come to the UK? Find out more about people crossing the Channel in small boats Produced by: Rob England, Libby Rogers, Jess Carr, Aidan McNamee, John Walton, Becky Dale, Allison Shultes, Chris Kay, Steven Connor and Scott Jarvis. Graphics by: Jez Frazer, Zoe Bartholomew and Joy Roxas Figures from government and other official sources can be revised between publications. This page shows data as presented in the latest available release. Immigration, emigration and net migration *The net migration figure for the UK will not exactly equal immigration minus emigration because the Office for National Statistics (ONS) publishes it as a rounded number. Immigration and emigration estimates,externalfrom the ONS are updated twice a year. Net migration figures use the internationally recognised definition of a long-term migrant: "A person who moves to a country other than that of their usual residence for at least a year." Visas for legal migration The total number of visa entries only includes visas that have been granted. It does not include visitor visas or transit visas, where the UK is not the final destination. Visa figures record when permission was granted, not when or whether someone arrived in the UK. If a person was granted more than one visa within the year shown, each visa is counted separately. Work visas refer to new individuals granted permission, or extensions of existing permission. This includes categories such as seasonal work, health and care, domestic worker and youth mobility visas. Study visas include all individuals sponsored by approved UK education providers, as well as those on short-term study visas. Family visas allow someone to come to or remain in the UK to live with close family members already here. This includes joining a spouse, partner, child or parent, or coming to care for a relative. The "Other" category includes visas outside work, study and family routes. This covers humanitarian schemes such as the Ukraine Sponsorship Scheme and the British National (Overseas) route. It also includes family permits for people from European Union or European Economic Area countries. Asylum applications and accommodation Home Office figures for asylum seekers in hotels are published under the category "contingency accommodation - hotel". The number of people in all other forms of accommodation includes non-hotel contingency accommodation, as well as initial, dispersal and "other" accommodation. To show how evenly accommodation is distributed, a scale compares each local authority's share of people in that type of accommodation with the UK-wide average for areas using the same accommodation type: Less than half – more than 50% below the average share Lower than – between 25% and 50% below the average share About the same as – within 25% of the average share Higher than – between 25% and 100% above the average share More than double – more than 100% above the average share Backlog figures for people waiting for an initial asylum decision include both main applicants and dependants. Open appeals against refused asylum applications refer to individuals. Figures on appeals are published every three months by the Ministry of Justice, at a different time from other government asylum statistics. It also includes a small number of appeals against revocation of protection. Small boat crossings and other irregular arrivals Small boat crossing figures and the average number of people per boat are takenfrom the Home Office daily data,external. Entering the UK without permissionis an offence under immigration law,external, but asylum seekers are generally not prosecuted if they claim asylum on arrival. In some cases, people have been prosecuted alongside other offences, such as people smuggling or re-entering after deportation. The International Organization for Migration (IOM)collects figures on people who have died,externalor gone missing while crossing from mainland Europe to the UK. These reports are based on information from French and UK officials (such as police or coastguard) and media sources. The IOM considers them an undercount because there are no official statistics. The figures may include people who died in the Channel itself, as well as those who died while travelling to a crossing point. Data on modern slavery includes final decisions only. Modern slavery covers human trafficking, slavery, servitude and forced labour. Figures for other entries without permission combine all recorded irregular arrivals that were not by small boat. This includes inadequately documented air arrivals, recorded detections at UK ports, and other recorded detections within the UK. Returns and deportations People who are denied entry at the border and then leave the UK are not included in the returns figures on this page. Returns involving the government are grouped into three categories. Enforced returns (which include deportations) are cases where the Home Office requires someone to leave and arranges their removal, usually because they have no legal right to remain or following a criminal conviction. Assisted voluntary returns are when someone agrees to leave the UK and receives government support, such as help with travel documents, flights or reintegration assistance. Controlled voluntary returns are when someone leaves the UK voluntarily without being forcibly removed, but their departure is formally recorded by the Home Office. Independent returns are referred to by the government as "other verified returns," and refer to individuals who have left the UK without People returned after a criminal conviction include non-British citizens convicted in the UK of any criminal offence, or convicted abroad of a serious criminal offence. UK migration compared with other countries Sea arrival figures are taken from the UNHCR European sea arrivals dashboard and combined with UK Home Office small boat data. Asylum application, immigration and emigration figures for European countries are the latest available data from Eurostat for: Austria, Belgium, Denmark, Finland, France, Germany, Greece, Ireland, Italy, Netherlands, Portugal, Spain, Sweden, Czechia, Estonia, Hungary, Latvia, Lithuania, Poland, Slovakia, Slovenia, Bulgaria, Romania, Norway, Switzerland and Croatia. UK population figures are from ONS, National Records of Scotland and the Northern Ireland Statistics and Research Agency 2024 mid-year estimates. European population figures are from Eurostat as of 1 January 2024. To ensure comparability with the UK, European countries with populations under one million are excluded from per-capita comparisons of net migration and asylum applications. For net migration comparisons, only countries that include asylum seekers or refugees in their immigration figures are included. These are: Austria, Belgium, Estonia, France, Germany, Greece, Ireland, Italy, Netherlands, Norway, Slovenia, Spain and Switzerland. Portugal was also excluded as it did not have net migration data available for 2024, it will be re-included in future updates. What do you want BBC Verify to investigate?
