Headline: We ship our gym equipment all over the world
Body: Greg Bradley's company has secured contracts with high profile customers all over the world When Greg Bradley started the his gym equipment company 14 years ago, someone told him he would never sell outside the island of Ireland. "I remember thinking, 'I'm going to prove you wrong'," he said. "Thankfully, we have been able to do that." BLK BOX is based in Newtownabbey - but it has secured contracts with high-profile customers all over the world, from sports teams like Manchester United to chains like PureGym. Bradley is just one of many success stories, with official figures showing economic activity in Northern Ireland in the second quarter of this year grew faster than the UK and Republic of Ireland. BLK BOX works internationally across the EU and markets like the US, Sri Lanka, Maldives, India, Australia and has grown its workforce to 180 staff. Bradley said Covid had made people realise the importance of their health and "a lot of young people are into going to the gym". "We have won high profile contracts and expanding internationally across France, Spain, Germany and other countries," he told BBC News NI. He added thatthe Windsor Frameworkhad also been advantageous compared to  English competitors. "We've been able to win a contract with a large French gym chain, Stade Français rugby team, so it's actually worked out good for us and we are really doubling down on that. "There's still a bit of an education process with it, not everyone knows that we can ship frictionlessly across Europe, they are a bit scared of tariffs but once you explain it, everyone is really interested." Northern Ireland's economic output rose by 2.3% in the year to June Figures from the Northern Ireland Statistics and Research Agency (NISRA),externalshow Northern Ireland's economic output, which is broadly equivalent to UK GDP, rose by 1% in the second quarter to June and by 2.3% over the year. UK GDP increased by 0.4% over the second quarter and by 1.2% over the year. Ireland's GDP increased by 10.2% over the second quarter, but its Modified Domestic Demand (MDD), which removes the distorting effects of globalisation, experienced a decline of 0.8% over the quarter. The growth in Northern Ireland was driven by an increase in the production sector, which includes manufacturing. Output in the services sector, which is the largest part of the Northern Ireland economy, also increased in the last 12 months. Daniel Duckett said rising petrol prices in particular will affect the cost of goods While these figures suggest the Northern Ireland economy ended the first half of this year in a position of strength, there are real concerns that rising energy and food costs could put businesses under significant pressure in the months ahead. Pastry chef Daniel Duckett closed his east Belfast patisserie in the last year, but has now re-opened in partnership with Knott's bakery chain in Forestside shopping centre. Duckett said that Knott's has the buying power for ingredients so "they can control costs a little bit better than we would have been able to". "They have been able to absorb a lot more of the costs that we would have been paying before," he added. Duckett said rising petrol prices in particular would affect the cost of goods. He added: "We have to think, how much do we deliver to the shops? Because that will also affect our petrol prices that fill up vans that travel across Northern Ireland." He said weather and global warming also affected many products the business brings in, such as tropical fruits, vanilla, cocoa, sugar cane. "Those are things that are definitely affected bystorms and El Niño. I would try to brace myself for that as well." Duckett added: "For the second half of the year we will have to be vigilant about where those products that have to travel far come from, as petrol prices will have to factor in to that." Headline: Children as young as 13 are getting ketamine bladder damage
Body: Children as young as 13 are getting ketamine bladder damage, doctors running a dedicated NHS clinic for it have told the BBC in an exclusive interview. Medics at Alder Hey Hospital in Liverpool say some patients - they have had over 100 referrals since opening last May - describe "peeing a jellyfish", which is some of the bladder's protective lining being shed. Prolonged damage can lead to incontinence or uncontrolled peeing, and even kidney failure. Many children at the clinic had been taking ketamine for a year or more, meaning some may have started when they were 12 or younger. Some with emotional trauma say the ketamine, sold for pocket money prices, helps "shush" or quieten their brain. Ketamine's most common form is white or pale-brown grainy powder that is often inhaled (snorted) or sometimes injected by users. It can be a liquid or a crystal form too. The drug is a general anaesthetic so it reduces or blunts sensations in the body. Users say it can make them feel dream-like and detached, chilled and relaxed. But it can also cause extreme harm. Prof Rachel Isba who runs the clinic told the BBC some of the children she has seen had started wetting the bed or having to go to the toilet more often and in a hurry. "Sometimes they don't always make it. They might have accidents...and a lot of them report pain in their bladder. "They describe this feeling of weeing over broken glass. It's very painful." She says, unfortunately, some of them will use the ketamine to treat the pain. "Ketamine is a very good pain reliever. It's an anaesthetic, and so they get into a vicious cycle or 'K loop', which makes their bladder worse," says Isba. She says ketamine is very cheap, "pocket-money level". "And you only need a small amount to feel an effect." She says some children find it hard to quit if their mates are still doing it. "There's use going on at school. That's really difficult. And, unfortunately for many of these children they are not able to attend education for various reasons." Some had pre-existing conditions like ADHD, while others had been in and out of the care system. Ketamine abuse in children and young people is on the rise in the UK. TheAlder Hey doctors,externalsaw one young patient in 2023, nine in 2024, and then "a rapid escalation" in 2025, which led them to open the bespoke clinic in May. They get about one referral every week from GPs or emergency departments in Cheshire, Merseyside and other nearby regions. Of the first 60 they saw, 43 were girls. Despite its name, "ketamine bladder" can affect the entire urinary tract, including the kidneys and ureters. Symptoms include an urgent and frequent need to urinate. This can be very painful and the pee can be blood-stained. Although stopping using ketamine can help, sometimes the damage can be so serious that the bladder needs surgical repair or even removal. Some users experience abdominal pain and spasms, or "K cramps" too. There are reports that heavy users are getting liver damage, but it is difficult to separate harms from other things people may also be taking, including other street drugs and alcohol. Isba says cannabis and alcohol are still more popular, but ketamine is "probably up into third place". Children at the clinic often say they have also tried other drugs, drank alcohol, and vaped. About three out of every 10 people who frequently use ketamine get bladder issues, says theBritish Association of Urological Surgeons,external. Sometimes it is reversible, if the drug use stops. Given the risks, there have been calls to reclassify it as a Class A drug - like cocaine and heroin - but the Advisory Council on the Misuse of Drugs has recommended to government that ketamine should remain a Class B controlled substance, like amphetamines and cannabis. Isba says children are disadvantaged when it comes to accessing services. "There are definitely some children out there who are under the age of 16 who if they were 18 would be offered an inpatient detox stay. But because we don't have those facilities in the UK, they are not able to access that and that feels unfair. Particularly for the ones who are ready to stop." Headline: Could an iced coffee freeze you out of the job market?
Body: This video can not be played Watch: Is it OK to take an iced coffee to a job interview? Would you bring an iced coffee to a job interview? The question on the internet's lips this week started life, as many do, in a TikTok video. "Don't waltz into your interview all casual with an iced coffee, it just looks like you didn't have time to finish your coffee beforehand," said US recruiter Caitlin Wehniainen. It's what her Gen Z job candidates are doing, she said, warning it makes it look like the interview is "just a stop on your list of errands for the day". The post has started what Wehniainen calls the Great Iced Coffee Debate of 2026. Some believe turning up with an iced matcha latte in hand is a cardinal sin. They say it's unprofessional, too informal, and a distraction. Others feel this is an overreaction - distracting from how difficult it is to secure a job - or even just get an interview in the first place. In a subsequent LinkedIn post, Wehniainen says she "was never saying that bringing coffee makes someone a bad candidate. "My point was simply about avoiding distractions." Can an iced latte actually hurt your chances of getting a job? What in the World Hanad, 28, works for an energy supplier in London. He likes iced coffee but wouldn't bring one to an interview. "A job interview is all about first impressions," he says. "Anything can deter the employer from employing you. "Iced coffee is something a lot of teens drink… it would look immature and too informal." Hanad says he wouldn't take an iced coffee to an interview He would never bring along an energy drink for the same reasons. But he says water or a hot coffee would be okay. His colleague Tsvetina, 24, thinks a potential employee shouldn't be judged by what they bring to the interview, nor their dress code. "I think we should be moving away from these traditional corporate stigmas. What matters is what the person is actually communicating during the interview." Aisha, 28, says she would take along an iced coffee. "I think it shows that I have come early enough to get iced coffee." She wouldn't bring a fizzy drink, however. In general, she thinks a lot of employers like to see personality in a candidate. "It makes you stand out from other people who are coming [applying] for the job." Katy feels there is a sexist element to the controversy around Wehniainen's post Katy, 25, a personal assistant in events, says she personally wouldn't turn up to a job interview with an iced coffee. But she sees the controversy around Wehniainen's post as "a bit sexist, because it's usually girls who drink iced coffee". "If it was a hot coffee, which is more masculine, there wouldn't be a discourse about that." Young people trying to land their first job are facing multiple challenges. The number of graduate vacancies in the UKhas almost halved in the past year, as employers cut entry-level roles in favour of AI and battle rising costs. Around one in eight people aged 16-24 are not in education, employment or training - so called Neets. Young workers in the US are alsostruggling with a tight jobs market,externalas hiring slows. Lucy Cooper is the founder of Spark, a design and branding recruitment company in London. She says her industry - marketing - is really tough right now, and she doesn't know of any Gen Z candidates who would risk turning up to an interview with an iced coffee. You could "seem too relaxed and a little bit flippant, like you're not taking it seriously enough, or you are interviewing the employer rather than the other way round". "I think people at junior level are very conscious about not doing anything that could jeopardise their chances," she says. She adds that it would be fine to accept a coffee offered by the employer, however, or drink one on a video interview. Dan Craddock, director at Hays, says employers shouldn't rely on "snap judgements". "It's important not to read too much into a single item a candidate brings to an interview. "Whether that's an iced coffee, a bottle of water or a notebook, employers are ultimately assessing the skills, experience and behaviours that will make someone successful in the role." Chris Mason, co-founder of Intelligent People - a specialist recruitment agency for the tech industry, says focusing on ice coffees alone "does seem to be an overreaction on the US recruiter's part". He advises candidates to "try to do everything possible to project the right image and attitude". He warns bringing snacks or specialist drinks may undermine the impression candidates will want to give - that they're "serious and focused on the interview". He says the main issue they see with some younger candidates is a lack of preparation, not being punctual, and not researching the role, organisation or interviewer. Headline: US strikes on Ecuadorian fishing boats raise humanitarian concerns but Trump admin not wavering
Body: Attorney says fishers ‘losing their livelihoods’, but Marco Rubio maintains US still willing to ‘blow up ships if need be’ While the US secretary of state,Marco Rubio, was being decorated in Quito by Ecuador’s president for “helping to promote peace in the region”, 10 Ecuadorian fishers whose boat had been blown up by US forces were adrift in the eastern Pacific. On 8 September, a day before Rubio arrived, a US patrol vessel intercepted the fishing boat Don Rufo in international waters nearEcuador. “The gringos were all armed as if they were going to war,” said the boat’s captain, Mero Calderón, 50. “I tried to show them our catch to prove that we were there working, but they wouldn’t listen,” he added. “They brought two huge bombs aboard, took us to their ship, handcuffed and blindfolded us, and blew our boat to pieces,” said Calderón, who along with five other fishers, was handed over to local authorities. But another 10 crew members were fishing farther out to sea in a smaller boat that was not equipped to make it back to shore. The Ecuadorian navy only rescued them on 10 September, when Rubio was already in Peru preparing to return to the US. US Southern Commandpostedan edited 14-second video of the operation and said “intelligence confirmed” that the vessel was being used by a gang as a “floating refuelling station” for speedboats allegedly carrying drugs – which the fishers deny. It was one of eight operations involving Ecuadorian boats in just more than two weeks – the lateston 16 September– to follow the same pattern. Unlike the nearly 70 US airstrikes in the Pacific and Caribbean that have killed 234 people since last year, crews were removed before the vessels were sunk. Also, rather than unilateral US attacks, the new wave of operations has the open support of Ecuador’s far-right president, Daniel Noboa, who is calling them “joint operations”. Donald Trumphas compared the drug trafficking operations to the campaign against the Islamic state. “Like ISIS, they should be killed, exiled or detained as enemy combatants without the possibility of release, which is what we’re doing,” Trump said on Tuesday. Some analysts see the shift as an indication that the US’s military strategy against drug trafficking in Latin America has entered a new phase. “Noboa has offered Ecuador as a ‘laboratory’ for the implementation of this new phase,” said Will Freeman, a fellow for Latin America studies at the Council on Foreign Relations. Although Ecuador does not produce cocaine like neighbouring Colombia and Peru, over the past decade it has become a major trafficking hub because of its access to the Pacific, including the area where the attacks on boats have been taking place. Noboa has responded with acontroversial “iron-fist”approach to the gangs, issuing repeated states of emergency and expanding the role of the armed forces. This crackdown however has done little to reduce violence, and instead has erodedhuman rights. The most notable example of human rights abuse came last year in the case of the “Guayaquil Four”, the forced disappearance of four Afro-Ecuadorian boys between the age of 11 and 15. All four boys were found dead, there bodies charred and dismembered. Despite pushback from voters, Noboa signed an agreement with the White House authorisingjoint operationsand granting US military personnel involved in counter-narcotics operations immunity from criminal prosecution. The operations have also extended to land, with US troopstaking part in raidslast Thursday. “Noboa is interested in the optics of a very lethal crackdown and in making Ecuador a place where the Trump administration can refine those methods and show them off,” said Freeman, who has also reported on the boat attacks in Ecuador forthe New Yorkermagazine. Trump has pressured Latin American presidents to join an anti-drug cartel coalition he created calledShield of the Americas. With Peru and Colombia recently joining, the group now includes all but the few countries still governed by the left, such as Mexico and Brazil – where a far-right senator is aserious contenderin October’s election. So far, the coalition’s primary goal appears to have been increasing joint operations against alleged drug traffickers. Adam Isacson, director for defence oversight at the Washington Office on Latin America, expects joint operations to expand across the region. Isacson stressed that though more people are being turned over to local authorities instead of killed, the US is “still doing the bad old stuff”. On 19 September, four peoplewere killedin the Caribbean. As with the other airstrikes, the US has not disclosed their identities or any of the alleged evidence linking them to criminal activity. During his trip to Ecuador, Rubio said the decision on what approach to take was “a strike-by-strike or operation-by-operation determination” that depended on the threat and location of the boat, but that the USwould “stillblow up ships if need be”. Human rights organisations have described the airstrikes asextrajudicial killings,and a special rapporteur for the UN human rights council has concluded that there are “reasonable grounds to believe” that they constitute “crimes against humanity”. Despite Trump’s claims,available datashow they have hadno impacton the volume of cocaine entering the country. Journalists and human rights groups have managed toidentify some of the victims, who in many cases were innocent or, when suspected of involvement in criminal activity, poor people at the bottom of trafficking networks. In Ecuador, the local NGO Permanent Committee for the Defence of Human Rights estimates that more than 220 fishershave been subjected to“violent boardings, arbitrary detentions, enforced disappearances, torture and the destruction of vessels” in this year’s US operations. None of the fishers remains in custody and, while some are still facing prosecution, many have already been acquitted forlack of evidence. “Fishers are losing their livelihoods when the US destroys the boats. Besides, if the US says the vessels were being used to refuel drug boats, why destroy the evidence?” said the committee’s lawyer, Fernando Bastías. A US Southern Command spokesperson said it conducts operations “in compliance with US and international law” and that leaving boats “intact could permit their reuse by criminal networks”. Although the US and Ecuador have celebrated the recent operations on social media, three cases from earlier this yearremain unclaimed. The first was on 20 January, when the fishing vesselFiorella disappearedwith eight crew members on board; days earlier, some of them had told relatives they were being monitored by drones and by a vessel on which they said they had seen a US flag. Human rights organisations and journalists identifiedtwo more caseswith similar patterns in late March, although the fishers survived. The Washington Postreportedthat the three cases were part of a covert CIA programme, and the agency declined to comment. A US Southern Command spokesperson said it had no knowledge of, nor were its forces “involved in the incidents described in reports involving the Fiorella”. Both the husband and brother of María Mero, 43, were aboard the Fiorella: Gabriel Aladino Mero Delgado, 44, and Jefferson Ariel Mero Cueva, 25. “Where did they take them? Do they have them in the US, in a prison somewhere? We don’t want any trouble; we just want them to send them back to us,” she told the Guardian. The families say they have spent months trying to get answers from the Ecuadorian government, so far without success. “They were fishers, not criminals. Let the great president come here to my house and see whether I have luxuries, anything that would show I’m a drug trafficker. No, because all of us here are poor, and we just want our loved ones back,” added Mero.

Headline: Bangkok roads submerged as flood disaster declared
Body: This video can not be played Disaster declared as heavy rain sparks Bangkok flooding A flood emergency disaster has been declared across Bangkok after more than 300mm (12in) of rain fell since Thursday, leavingroads in the Thai capital submerged. On Sunday, Bangkok's Metropolitan Authority said the rains have subsided, but canal water levels remain high. The city's governor has warned that the flooding is not yet over. People have been urged to stay at home and those living close to the city's network of canals have been advised to move their belongings to upper floors. Thunderstorms are common in Thailand at this time of year but extreme weather in recent days has inundated Bangkok's drainage system, causing traffic chaos on roads that are already famously congested. Canals across the Thai capital have burst their banks, leaving roads under water Somkid Pheuk-ngam, a 67-year-old who lives near a canal just north of central Bangkok, told the AFP news agency: "The water keeps coming in. It's hard to go out now. It's like at my waist level now. "I cannot go anywhere. I have been closing my shop for two days now." She said water levels in the city appeared to be worse than in 2011, when Bangkok was impacted by nationwide flooding. Hundreds were killed across Thailand then in an extreme weather event that lasted for three months. So far, no casualties have been reported in Bangkok from this latest flooding. The Thai Meteorological Service has forecast more heavy rain through the week, though the area of low pressure causing the downpours of recent days is expected to move towards central Thailand. All 50 of Bangkok's districts were declared emergency zones. On Saturday, Chadchart Sittipunt, the city's governor, said the east of the city had been hardest hit, AFP reported. He continued: "The rain keeps falling and we are doing our best. We are trying to pump the water out, but the water in canals are full... The risk areas are those who live near canals. Every canal is now filled." Disaster declared as heavy rains spark Bangkok flooding Teen rocker Nene Royal becomes first Thai to win America's Got Talent

Headline: Butterfly populations 'could crash' due to weather
Body: The Gatekeeper species was the most-spotted butterfly across the counties Butterfly and day-flying moth numbers recorded across Devon and Cornwall this summer have been "very good" - but experts fear prolonged hot and dry weather could lead to a decline. Nearly 5,000 people took part in the Butterfly Conservation's 2026 big butterfly count in Devon, recording 77,151 insects during the three-week count. It said nearly 3,000 people took part in Cornwall, spotting 47,712. Professor Richard Fox, head of science at the conservation, said adult butterflies loved hot weather, but warned they could be on course "for a population crash". "The extreme droughts in 1976 and 1995 had severe impacts on butterfly populations, with some species never fully recovering," he said. One of the standout species was the Painted Lady More news stories for Devon Listen to the latest news for Devon The charity said strong butterfly numbers were "likely" down to favourable conditions for caterpillars in spring, followed by the hot, sunny weather enjoyed by adult butterflies during the summer months. However, it said previousdrought conditions across much of the UKmay have caused food plants used by caterpillars to wither before they had finished feeding. The charity said it feared the full impact may not become clear until next year. Fox said many species were already under pressure, with 80% of the UK's butterfly populations having declined since the 1970s. "So many are already struggling for survival without these extreme weather pressures," Fox said. He added: "With increasingly hot, dry summers and droughts predicted to become more and more frequent due to climate breakdown, degraded habitats and already depleted butterfly populations, some species may be pushed further and faster towards extinction, which is a very sombre thought. "They are, quite simply, less resilient to these events, which means we could be looking at very difficult years ahead." The charity has urged people to help wildlife recover by planting more trees and shrubs, installing water butts to store rainwater and leaving areas of grass uncut. The gatekeeper was the most commonly spotted butterfly in Devon and Cornwall. The meadow brown took the second spot in Devon, followed by the red admiral. In Cornwall, the red admiral took second spot, followed by the painted lady. Butterfly Conservation said the painted lady was one of the standout species with 6,955 recorded in Devon and 6,033 in Cornwall. The migratory butterfly enjoyed a strong year nationally. Painted ladies undertake one of the world's most remarkable insect migrations, travelling from Africa to the UK over several generations, crossing the Sahara Desert and Mediterranean Sea. Headline: Iran must stop arming Houthis in Yemen, G7 says ahead of UN General Assembly
Body: This video can not be played Watch: Why is the Bab al-Mandab Strait so important? Iran must "end its arming of and support" for the Houthis in Yemen, the foreign ministers of G7 nations have said in a joint statement. The G7 also condemned "in the strongest terms" Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, adding that the recent escalation in fighting against Saudi-backed pro-government forces in Yemen represented a threat to regional and global energy security. Thousands of refugees have fled Yemen in recent days after the Iran-backed group seized territory along the country's Red Sea coastline, including near the Bab al-Mandab Strait, the gateway to a key global shipping route. Iran has previously denied supplying weapons to the Houthis and says it only supports them politically. Yemenis flee across Red Sea as Houthis and Saudi-backed forces escalate war Houthis say they targeted Saudi capital with ballistic missiles The G7 statement comes ahead of the annual UN General Assembly in New York, where Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian is due to speak. "We call on the Houthis to immediately cease all military actions, all threats and attacks against civilian shipping, and to return to the political process in good faith," said the foreign ministers of the UK, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan and the United States. It went on: "Their reprehensible actions constitute a dangerous pattern of escalation that risks further exacerbating the conflict, undermining international trade and creating global economic instability." "Looking forward, we will continue to support the legitimate Government of Yemen and reaffirm our strong commitment to the unity, sovereignty, independence, and territorial integrity of Yemen," the ministers said. Their statement was issued following a meeting on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly. This video can not be played Watch: Video shows strike on a market in Yemen, but it's not clear where the projectile originated from. Meanwhile, the Houthis accused Saudi Arabia of targeting civilians in Yemen in its air strikes across the group's territory. Houth-run Saba news agency reported that a pre-dawn strike on a house in the Red Sea port city of Mokha on Tuesday killed six people, including two children and a woman. Saba also said that nine detainees were killed in an attack on a prison in al-Hazm, in Jawf province, on Monday night. The Houthis' health ministry said two members of one family were killed in a strike on Jawf province on Monday, and that one person was killed in Taiz. The Saudi-led coalition backing Yemen's government has not yet commented. Meanwhile, government-run media reported that civilians were injured in a Houthi missile attack on a market in the Mudaribah wa al-Ara district of Lahj province, about 20km (12 miles) east of Houthi-controlled territory. Verified CCTV footage showed a munition hitting an area crowded with people and vehicles, causing a large explosion. People flee as the air is filled with dust and smoke. There was no immediate comment from the Houthis. The UN estimates that in all,more than 120,000 Yemenis have been displacedby the sudden surge in fighting along Yemen's Red Sea coast. Earlier this month, the Houthis, who had already seized most of the populated parts of Yemen, took control of Bab al-Mandab, a narrow, maritime chokepoint where the southern Red Sea flows into the Gulf of Aden and the wider Indian Ocean. This video can not be played Watch: Inside a camp for Yemeni refugees in Djibouti Saudi Arabia has retaliated with hundreds of air strikes in the region. The Houthis have also launched hundreds of drones and missiles at cities and infrastructure in south-western Saudi Arabia, including the capital city, Riyadh. Prime Minister Andy Burnham has saidthe UK will provide"defensive air-to-air refuelling" support for Saudi Arabia, involving a single British aircraft, a Voyager, based out of RAF Akrotiri in Cyprus. Burnham said the announcement followed a request from Saudi Arabia for "military support", which he agreed to on the advice of Defence Secretary Wes Streeting and Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband. A diplomatic source told AFP that France has pledged support as well, and says is ready to work on "securing" Saudi energy infrastructure via a "strictly defensive approach". Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman has also requested military support from President Donald Trump, US media reported. Trump has wavered for weeks over whether to act on a Saudi request for help in fighting the Houthis, the New York Times reported on Monday. The US president had earlier told Fox News that he was in "deciding mode" as he considered options for the next steps in the war against Iran. On Sunday, US embassies across the Middle East issued new security alerts as fighting between the Houthis and the Saudi-backed coalition in Yemen intensified. The Houthis declare themselves to be part ofthe Iranian-led "axis of resistance"against Israel, the US and the wider West - along with armed group such as Hamas and Lebanon's Hezbollah movement. Although Iran has denied arming the Houthis in violation of a UN embargo, the UK and other Western powers have said their naval forces have repeatedly intercepted Iranian weapons shipments bound for Yemen during the civil war. A panel of UN experts also concluded in 2024 that the Houthis had been transformed into a powerful military organisation due to the transfer of materiel, assistance and training from Iran's Revolutionary Guards, Hezbollah and Iraqi specialists. Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that began in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the government from the capital, Sanaa. The conflict escalated in 2015, after the Saudi-led coalition of Arab states intervened in an attempt to restore the government's rule. A four-year-old informal ceasefire began to unravel in July, when the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea. The Houthis said they were retaliating for a Saudi blockade of ports and airports in their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom. Since taking control of Bab al-Mandab, they have said they pose no threat to international shipping but reiterated that they would continue to target vessels from Saudi Arabia.

Headline: Ten climbers missing after avalanche hits Himalayan base camp
Body: The avalanche struck Himlung Himal, a mountain popular with overseas climbers At least 10 Nepalese climbers who were preparing to lead an expedition in the Himalayas are missing after an avalanche hit a base camp on Sunday morning. The climb's organisers said the local guides were at a staging point close to the Himlung Himal peak in Manang district when the avalanche struck. Forecasts showed there was heavy snowfall around the 7,126m (23,380ft) peak in recent days, which lies on Nepal's border with Tibet. Poor weather has hampered rescue efforts, with helicopters and rescue teams unable to reach the site. Bibhuti Chand Thakur, of Himalaya Holidays Trekking, told news agency AFP: "Eight members of our expedition team and two more from another company have been reported missing." The Nepali team had been sent ahead of foreign climbers to prepare the camp, manage the route and fix ropes on the mountain. Nepal's mountain districts have seen persistent rain and snow in recent days, creating treacherous conditions for the country's economically important climbing tourism industry. Climbers were forced to leave Mount Manaslu, the eighth highest peak in the world, earlier this week due to the rising threat of avalanches. The latest death of Nepali climbers comes less than two months aftersix lost their lives on Broad Peak in Pakistan, including renowned British-Nepali mountaineer Nirmal Purja. Extreme weather further south in the neighbouring Indian region of Uttar Pradesh has killed more than 50 people, officials there said. It comes as efforts to recover bodies continues on the Nepal-Tibet border, where more than 6,000 people are still missing after a massive flood and landslide in August. More than 1,400 people are confirmed to have died after a glacial collapse in the Himalayas sent vast quantities of water and debris careering down the Trishuli River valley, sweeping away settlements. Headline: The treasured 'eternal snow' on this tropical island is about to disappear forever
Body: Only small patches of snow remain on Papua's Sudirman Range The mountains of Papua are not far from the equator, but they've been topped with "eternal snow" for centuries. The peaks in this Indonesian region on the world's second-largest island, just north of Australia, have offered scientists countless insights into the Earth's climate history. They're also the epicentre of the spiritual universe for many Papuans - a Mecca or a Vatican, as one activist puts it. But now, nearly all the snow is gone. A century ago, the 300km (190-mile) stretch of the Sudirman Range had snow and permanent ice on all four of its major peaks. But now there are only small areas around Puncak Jaya, also known as Carstensz Pyramid, with any snow at all. These are expected to entirely disappear in a year or two. Glacier cover around the peak has shrunk from nearly 1,900 hectares (4,700 acres) in the 19th Century to about 16 hectares (40 acres) today. Almost entire glaciers have vanished within a human lifetime. "There is a profound unfairness in this," says Marie Šabacká, a Czech glacier ecologist who travelled to Puncak Jaya last March in a bid to be among the last scientists to study Papua's "eternal snow". She says the tropical glaciers in Papua are unique because they are separated from other glacier systems by thousands of kilometres. Papua is home to the "last remaining tropical ice" between the Andes and Himalayas. Ice cores taken from the slopes of Puncak Jaya preserve a record of climate history. Scientists can use them to obtain information about atmospheric conditions in the region and understand changes in the planet's warmest ocean waters that surround the island - the tropical Pacific and Western Pacific Warm pool. But this archive is disappearing before scientists have had time to fully study it. The snow cover has reduced dramatically since this photo, taken in 1936 The retreat of Papua's glaciers is driven by the same forces affecting ice around the world, Šabacká notes, a warming atmosphere caused by human activity, including the burning of fossil fuels like coal, oil and gas. As temperatures rise, the freezing point moves higher up mountains, so more precipitation falls as rain instead of snow, even in places that once saw regular snowfall. El Niño events can accelerate this process, while local factors such as cloud cover, snowfall and mountain topography influence its pace. The mountains in Papua are just 450km (280 miles) south of the equator, where "permanent ice can survive only at very high altitudes and within a narrow range of climatic conditions", Šabacká says. A small increase in temperature, a higher freezing point or shift from snowfall to rainfall can determine whether a glacier survives at all, she adds. The glaciers' retreat is evidence the Earth has been warming over a long period - and their disappearance "removes both a biological habitat and part of a culturally significant landscape". Šabacká, seen taking samples from Puncak Jaya, says Papua's vanishing glaciers are unique as they are so far from other glacier systems At least five groups of Indigenous people have had strong spiritual ties to Puncak Jaya for generations. The Moni people refer to it as Mbainggela, and believe their ancestors watch over the mountain. To the Amungme people, the range is known as Nemangkawi, or the "White Arrow". "Parents and grandparents prayed their children would have hearts like the White Arrow, never straying from the proper path," says Elfrida Natkime, a young Amungme woman. "It symbolises honesty, purity and moral integrity." According to traditional Amungme beliefs, Nemangkawi symbolises how people should live. Amungme environmental activist Adolfina Kum stresses how important the peak is to her people - and how traditions and cultural foundations risk being shattered as the ice melts. "How would Muslims feel if Mecca were destroyed? How would Catholics feel if Rome or the Vatican were destroyed?" she asks. "For the Amungme people, that is what it feels like when Nemangkawi is destroyed." The mountain holds immense spiritual significance for Indigenous people like Justinus, a man from the Moni tribe For many Indigenous Papuans, the disappearance of the glacier is not an isolated event. The discovery of vast copper and gold deposits transformed the region during the 20th Century, and the development of extractive industrial projects have reshaped parts of the landscape. Entire mountain faces have been excavated and roads, industrial infrastructure and settlements have transformed surrounding valleys. Papuans say the development has brought jobs, roads, education and economic opportunities, but also environmental degradation and decades of social conflict. Some have lost access to their ancestral lands as mining expanded. The BBC has approached Freeport, which operates Papua's Grasberg mine, one of the world's largest gold and copper operations, for comment. "Every time I see the mountains, I feel amazed, but I also feel sadness," says Elfrida Natkime. "Since the company came, I have seen the exploitation. But the development has also provided a livelihood for many people." This 3D rendition by Klaus Thymann's Project Pressure shows ice coverage at the date of capture in 2025 As local communities watch their sacred landscapes change, scientists and explorers are racing to document what is left. Using drones and three-dimensional mapping techniques, Danish researcher Klaus Thymann and his team have created a detailed model of what remains. From the early 2000s to 2025, the glaciated area has receded by 95%, he says. "There's almost no ice left. Those are the facts." Thymann says glaciers are "incredibly powerful" as indicators of climate change. "When people hear that something described as 'eternal' is disappearing, it triggers a reaction," he explains. Adolfina Kum believes communities "lose an important source of strength" when sacred mountains, forests or ancestral places are disturbed. "I often describe it as pulling out the roots of a tree. Once the roots are removed, the tree loses its foundation." What is El Niño and why could it mean record temperatures? Headline: Pomp over progress in Xi’s US summit with Trump is a win for China
Body: While US president hailed visit as ‘great’, almost nothing of substance was achieved on resolving thorny issues Key takeaways from the Trump-Xi summit in Washington If the Beijing meeting between Donald Trump and Xi Jinping in May was the “stalemate summit”, the second round of talks between the presidents of the US and China this week seemed to give up entirely on the idea of breakthroughs. Instead, it was described as a celebration of “diplotainment” rather than diplomacy, where pomp prevailed over progress and where one of the main outcomes was the news that two giant pandas would soon be sent from China to Atlanta zoo. Trump rolled out the red carpet for Xi’s arrival on Wednesday and broke with decades of precedent to meet the Chinese leader at Joint Base Andrews. Thus began a three-day state visit that involved a tour of Trump’s new helipad and the Marine One helicopter, and a 90-minute meeting that Trump described as “great” and that revealed, according to Trump, that Xi “has great interest in granite”. “The biggest takeaway is that Trump has been displaying anextraordinary degree of deferenceto Xi Jinping,” said Julian Gewirtz, who served as a senior China official in the Biden administration. But what of actual substance? Expectations going into the summit were low. But the outcomes somehow still fell short. One of the biggest issues in the US-China relationship is trade. Last year, as Trump unveiled successive rounds of tariffs on Chinese goods, the White HouseaccusedChina of unfair practices that it said contributed to the loss of 3.7m US jobs and inflated the trade deficit. The tariffs were supposed to suppress the volume of Chinese imports to the US and put pressure on China. To some degree, they worked. The US trade deficit withChinain 2025 fell to $200bn, down from nearly $300bn in 2024. But experts have noted that some of this shortfall is made up for by Chinese goods being shipped to the US via third countries, a trend underlined by the fact that China’s trade surplus surpassed a record $1tn last year. With the US and China accounting for 43% of global GDP, their trade war has far-reaching implications for the world economy. So it was a relief not just to Beijing and to US consumers when the two countries agreed a temporary trucein Busanlast year. That truce is due to expire in November. China, where the economy is heavily reliant on exports, was reported to be pushing for the truce to be extended until the end of Trump’s term, in January 2029. On Thursday, it was revealed that Xi’s first state visit to the US in more than a decade had resulted in a mere two-month extension. That reflects “the lack of preparation for this summit beyond the pomp and circumstance”, said Neil Thomas, a senior fellow at the Asia Society. William Yang, a senior analyst at the International Crisis Group, said: “This summit largely achieved symbolism and ritualism over substance. That is very clear.” The short extension “reflects the level of fundamental differences that still exist between the two countries over a variety of issues”. China’s most powerful response to Trump’s tariffs was the decision to block the export of rare earths, critical minerals vital to US manufacturing and military supply chains. That seemed to skewer Trump’s leverage over China. Gewirtz said: “Beijing’s retaliation … seems to have had a profound effect on [Trump] and his administration’s willingness to take risks vis-a-vis China.” Apart from the trade war agreement, the summit failed to achieve any meaningful progress on thorny issues in the US-China relationship such as artificial intelligence, Taiwan, the wars in Iran and Ukraine, and human rights. On Taiwan, which Beijing considers to be the most important issue in the relationship, Xi put pressure on Trump to weaken the US’s support for the self-governing island that China claims as its own. According to the Chinese readout of the Xi-Trump meeting, Xi told Trump he hoped “the US side will adhere to the correct position of opposing Taiwan independence”. For the US to state that it “opposes” Taiwanese independence would be a rhetorical shift from the current position of “does not support” such a claim, and would be a move welcomed by Beijing. Trump has not yet commented on whether he agreed to such a statement. But it does seem he is no closer to approving a $14bn arms sale package for Taiwan, a sale that Beijing would like to see disappear completely. On Thursday, US Senate Democrats lambasted Trump for opting for “pageantry over purpose” and for failing to deliver agreements on “the economic and security issues that will shape America’s future”. Trump ignored recent warnings about the dangers posed by AI, writing on social media on Thursday: “I want ​to leave it exactly where it is,” adding: “That is China’s position also.” For China, the lack of big news from the visit is a win in itself. “The summit went excellently from the Chinese perspective,” Thomas said. Xi “got a huge amount of respect from the American president, the full state visit treatment [and] really great images beaming back to China of the Chinese and the American presidents interacting as peers on the global stage, without having to make any meaningful concessions or compromises.”

Headline: Scottish drivers hit as diesel passes £2 a litre across the country
Body: Conflict in the Ukraine and the Middle East have driven up prices on forecourts The price of diesel has exceeded £2 a litre at hundreds of Scottish forecourts, according to analysis by BBC Scotland News. Some of the highest prices can be found at garages in Scotland's islands, where fuel is 50p a litre more expensive than that sold at supermarkets in the central belt. Hauliers have described the cost to their businesses as "devastating" and say it now costs £250 a week more to fill up a lorry. Motoring organisation the RAC said it expected the UK average price of diesel to hit a new record high over the weekend. The ongoing conflict in the Middle East and the Russia-Ukraine war has pushed up the cost of crude oil, leading to higher fuel and energy costs. The UK government said it continued to protect British people and business, and  there would not be an increase in fuel duty this year. Dave Neil, who runs a haulage firm in Orkney, said fuel costs were "challenging" Analysis by BBC Scotland News suggests there are at least 226 sites - stretching from the Borders to Shetland - where the price of a litre of diesel is greater than £2. Some of the highest prices are in island and rural areas, including 238.8p and 223p in the Hebrides and 209.0p and 208.9p in the Northern Isles. South Uist-based haulier Norman MacAskill said it cost 32p a litre to fill a lorry's tank when he started in the haulage business 40 years ago, but it was now £2.22. "Anyone who is running a lorry is absolutely devastated when they get their fuel bill at the end of the month. There's no business on earth that can withstand that increase in costs," he said. MacAskill's haulage firm, N D MacAskill & Son, transports livestock around Inverness, Dingwall and Stirling but also further afield. "We do a bit of livestock haulage from the north of Scotland down to the north of England," he said. "It's a devastating cost on a fuel run on that job," he said. MacAskill added: "This has been going on every year for the last 10 years now. The cost of running a haulage business has just gone over the top. "There are dozens of haulage firms that have been established 50-60 years with big numbers of lorries going to the wall. When is this going to stop?" Dave Neil, who runs Sinclair Haulage which serves Sanday, Stronsay and Eday in Orkney, said his business was spending £400 a week more on diesel than it was before the summer. "It's a challenging situation," he said. Neil said he was forced to add an extra fee to his customers' costs. "It's probably the fairest way," he said. "When the fuel price drops we can take that surcharge away." The Road Haulage Association (RHA) said fuel was costing operators roughly £250 a week extra per vehicle. It has called on the UK government to scrap any planned fuel duty rises in January, March and April and to introduce an essential user rebate for coaches, lorries and vans. Managing director Richard Smith said: "It's happening elsewhere. Spain, France and Italy already give commercial vehicle operators a diesel rebate. It's about time we caught up. Crofter Amy Henderson said life was hard enough for people already National Farmers' Union Scotland said rising prices were another unwelcome cost for farmers and crofters. A spokesperson said: "Fuel is a significant input cost for farm businesses and increases feed directly into the cost of producing food. "With many farmers currently working through harvest and other intensive autumn operations, there is no scope to reduce fuel use." Crofter and musician Amy Henderson, from Kiltarlity, added: "It is just deflating. Life is hard enough as it is." She said she was having to make "logistical decisions" around whether to use her car or truck. Henderson added: "I have to take it into consideration when quoting prices for performing." James Dunbar of New Start Highland said rising fuel costs were affecting the families the charity supports Inverness-based charity New Start Highland uses vans to collect and deliver donated items, such as furniture, to people in need. Chief executive James Dunbar said: "Rising fuel prices have a direct impact on us as a charity, as well as the individuals we support. "Transport is core to our operations, from collecting and delivering furniture so those facing crisis and hardship can access essential items, to running our enterprise services like removals and house clearances." He said the charity was in the process of moving to a fully electrified fleet, but he said rising fuel costs directly affected the families it supported. The RAC said the average UK record price of diesel would "almost certainly" be surpassed over the weekend. Head of policy Simon Williams said: "The average UK price of diesel is teetering on the brink of a new all-time high at 198.32p, taking the cost of a 55-litre fill-up for a family car to £109. "The UK now has the most expensive diesel in Europe by 12p a litre - ahead of Finland and the Netherlands." He added: "Petrol is now averaging 173.6p – its highest price in more than four years. Petrol has risen nearly 12p in September and more than 40p since the Iran war began. "Diesel is up 14.5p this month alone and 55p since 28 February." Hauliers have called for an essential user rebate for coaches, lorries and vans The AA said its campaigning had persuaded the UK government to set up pump-price transparency. It said there were nowwebsites and phone apps,externaldrivers could use to check for the latest pump prices and where to find cheaper fuel. The AA said there should be no scrapping of the Treasury's 5p cut in fuel duty, which was first introduced in March 2022. It added that there was a "good argument" for diesel getting further relief. A spokesperson said: "While many big businesses pass the extra cost of diesel onto their customers, often via a sliding scale of fuel surcharges, smaller businesses don't automatically. "These include taxi drivers, craftspeople, domestic repairs, vets, farriers and many who rely on vehicles to look after their customers." The UK government said it had extended the temporaryfuel duty cut,externaluntil 31 December. A spokesperson said: "Since the outset of the war in Iran, this government continues to protect the British people and businesses from this crisis. "This means drivers benefit from the extension of the 5p fuel duty cut, with diesel 11p per litre cheaper until the end of the year than it would have been compared to plans inherited from the previous government." Headline: UK diesel price close to all-time high
Body: Diesel prices in the UK are expected to hit record levels over the weekend as the fallout from the US-Israel war with Iran continues to drive up costs. The average price of a litre of diesel at the pump stands at 198.32p, according to the RAC motoring body. That's close to the all-time high of 199.09p recorded on 25 June 2022, following Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Simon Williams, head of policy at RAC, said the June 2022 high would "almost certainly be surpassed over the weekend as retailers continue to pass on the increases they're seeing when they buy new supply". Over the past seven months, the Iran war has severely disrupted the production and transportation of wholesale oil across the region, causing the price of fuels made from oil to surge. Motor fuel prices fell back when the US and Iran agreed in June to a framework deal to end the fighting, but rose again as tensions resurfaced. Meanwhile, US President Donald Trump has responded to rising diesel prices by mulling a ban on US diesel producers selling overseas, in a move which could push up the UK price even higher. Crude oil is a key ingredient in petrol and diesel, which means that higher wholesale costs make filling up a car more expensive. The price of petrol and diesel is also heavily influenced by demand and refining capacity. Analysts say every $10 (£7.44) per barrel increase in the oil price pushes up pump prices by roughly 7p a litre. Since the war began, the price of a barrel of Brent crude – the global benchmark for wholesale oil prices – has been very volatile. Generally speaking, news of further conflict drives the price up while hopes of an end to the war pushes the price down. Before the conflict, Brent was about $70 a barrel, but the fighting saw it peak at above $120. In early July, after the framework deal was signed, prices fell back to near the $70 a barrel mark. The price climbed back up again after peace talks collapsed and it is now above $100 a barrel. Before the war began, the average price of petrol was 132.83p per litre and diesel was 142.38p. At 198.32p for a litre of diesel, the price is now near a record high. Meanwhile, petrol has hit an average 173.6p a litre, which is the highest in more than four years but lower than its peak of 191.5p during the summer of 2022. Williams said: "Sadly for drivers, there appears to be no end in sight to high prices at the pumps." Because transporting oil is a slow process, price movements in wholesale oil markets take about a fortnight to show at the pump. Fuel retailers have denied accusations of price gouging during the conflict. The official markets regulator said it had "not seen evidence of retailers actively changing their pricing strategies to take advantage of the crisis". Agovernment scheme called Fuel Finder,externallets drivers compare the cost of fuel offered by petrol stations across the UK. In May, the then Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer saida planned 5p increase in fuel duty due in September would be postponeduntil the end of December because of the conflict. RAC has said there is "a very strong case" for leaving fuel duty at its current level, at least until the end of the Parliament. No evidence of widespread fuel price-gouging, watchdog says Drivers can compare fuel prices at different petrol stations - how does it work? The Middle East conflict sent global oil prices soaring as it effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz — one of the world's key water transport routes for oil, liquid natural gas and other essential commodities — limiting global supplies. About 20% of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas normally passes through the waterway. Even if a deal is agreed to reopen the strait, experts warn it will take time before normal levels of shipping through the Strait of Hormuz resume, and the impact of the war will continue to affect the global economy for potentially months to come. While Trump has suggested he might ban US producers from selling diesel overseas, he has not done it yet and views differ on how serious this threat is. If it does happen, many agree it would hurt the countries which heavily depend on US diesel, such as the UK and several European countries. Others note that, while the ban would be likely to reduce US diesel prices in the short-term, it could have unintended effects that could hurt US production – and put pressure on US diesel prices – in the long-term. Why and how is US blockading Iranian ports in Strait of Hormuz? Oil price predicted to remain above $100 for rest of year The UK is heavily reliant on oil and gas imports, with the majority coming from the US and Norway. The price of oil on the global market determines how much the UK pays for it. Although the UK does get some oil from the North Sea, most of that is exported for refining elsewhere. Headline: Venezuela's interim president promises election after Maduro ousted
Body: Venezuela's interim president, Delcy Rodríguez, has announced that elections will be held as part of a transition to "full democracy", but did not specify a date. Rodríguez was sworn in just days after her predecessor in office, Nicolás Maduro, was seized by US forces and taken to New York to face drug-trafficking charges. She has enjoyed the backing of the Trump administration despite her previously close ties to Maduro. The opposition in Venezuela has slammed her for not setting even a tentative date for elections. Critics of her government have long denounced the 2024 election, after which Maduro was declared president and she vice-president, as fraudulent and say theyhave vote tallies to back up their claim. Speaking at the UN General Assembly on Tuesday, Rodríguez insisted that "there will be elections in Venezuela" and that the Venezuelan people would determine "the right moment" when to hold them. The interim president, who was a close ally of Maduro and served as his vice-president until his ouster by the US, did not mention the jailed former leader once. Less than nine months after the US raid on the Venezuelan capital, Caracas, in which the presidential couple was seized and about 100 people killed, she instead thanked US President Donald Trump "for his willingness to take the path of diplomatic relations and cooperation". She also said that her government and the Trump administration were "working seriously to resolve existing differences through dialogue", adding that the two nations were paving "the way for energy relations, the promotion of security, the common fight against transnational crime and economic cooperation for the benefit of both peoples and our continent". Unlike Rodríguez, President Trump did make ample references to Maduro during his speech to the assembly, calling him an "outlaw dictator, a real criminal". Trump also celebrated the signing of what he said was "the largest oil deal in history covering 65bn barrels of oil" which the US has struck with Rodríguez's interim government. "To the victor belong the spoils," he stated, adding that "if necessary, we will use our unmatched military might to secure the vital national interest of the United States". This video can not be played Watch: Why is the US-Venezuela oil deal so controversial? While he did not mention elections in his speech at the UN, Trump told the LA Times earlier this month that he did not think Venezuela was ready yet. The two leaders also briefly met Tuesday on the sidelines. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who attended the meeting, said that the two presidents had discussed elections. However, he appeared to urge Venezuelan opposition politicians to be patient. Rubio insisted that first, there would have to be a "political transition process" to rebuild the institutions necessary to have free and fair elections. "What we don't want to see (…) would be that someone is elected, and they inherit a complete catastrophe, economic and social," he said. Rubio also pointed to negotiations under way between Venezuela's interim government and some members of the opposition as a sign of progress. Critics of Delcy Rodríguez protested in New York ahead of her speech at the UN Critics of the negotiations have, however, pointed out that Venezuela's most prominent opposition leader, María Corina Machado, is not part of the talks. Machado, who left Venezuela in December to receive the Nobel Peace Prize in Oslo, has not been able to return to the country since. One of her advisers said that she had made three attempts to travel to her home country this week but that all three had been thwarted. Machado remains barred from standing for office - a ban imposed under the Maduro government - and Interior Minister Diosdado Cabello has in the past said that should she return, the authorities would have "a surprise" in store for her. Headline: Four civilians killed in Pakistani strikes in Afghanistan, Taliban says
Body: Flames and smoke rise from an area struck by an air strike in Kandahar on Thursday Afghanistan's Taliban government said a wave of Pakistani air strikes had killed four civilians in the latest escalation between the two sides. The strikes hit provinces including Kandahar, the Taliban's base of power, sources told the BBC. A resident told AFP news agency they heard a jet, followed by a large explosion and then a fire in the city. Pakistan said its forces had struck 10 targets in Afghanistan, without specifying their locations, adding the strikes were "strictly limited to identified military objectives". It's the second wave of Pakistani air strikes on Afghan territory in the past week, and comes after a deadly attack on a police facility in Pakistan on 18 September. In a statement, the Taliban said there would be an "appropriate response" following the attack, while Pakistan said any further "provocative act" would be responded to. Taliban government spokesman Zabihullah Mujahid said the attacks were in Afghanistan's Kandahar, Paktia and Khost provinces. In Paktia, an official said jets had bombed the Afghan Armed Forces' 203 Mansouri Corps, which is controlled by the Taliban, without providing any information on casualties. In Khost, a spokesman said houses were damaged in the strikes, with no casualties reported. Abdullah, a local eyewitness, told Reuters news agency the strikes happened around midnight. "People were shouting, and there was panic all around," he said. "Afterwards, the village elder arrived and called out to the houses, asking if anyone was killed. Thankfully, no one was killed." Another local, Salamat Khan, told Reuters that "there is no military base here, nor are there any military personnel", adding "there are only the homes of ordinary civilians". A Taliban security official inspects the scene of Pakistani air strikes in Khost Zabihullah Mujahid labelled the attack as "reckless, careless, and hostile", and said it "will have adverse consequences for the Pakistani military". Pakistan's Information Minister Attaullah Tarar said the strikes were "deliberate, precise, calibrated, and proportionate, and strictly limited to identified military objectives directly linked to the attempted attacks against Pakistan". The Taliban and Pakistan had enjoyed three months of relative calm, until fighting reignited following anattack on a mosque at a police compoundin north-western Pakistan last week, which killed at least 31 people, according to AFP. A group linked toTehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), which has waged a violent campaign against Pakistan for years, claimed the attack. Islamabad has accused Kabul of harbouring the TTP. Afghanistan's Taliban government denies this, saying militancy is Pakistan's internal problem. Following the attack on the police facility, Pakistan said earlier this week it launched air strikes in the Afghanistan-Pakistan border region, killing 28 militants. Farid Dehqan, a spokesman for the Taliban government in Kunar province, told the BBC that three people were killed and four others were injured in the strike. The UN mission Unama also confirmed that at least three civilians were killed. An attack in Afghanistan's Kunar province has killed at least three civilians, according to the UN Then on Wednesday, Pakistan said it detected drones launched from Afghanistan into its territory and that all of them were "neutralised". Taliban officials denied that their government had launched drones against Pakistan that day. Unama said in July that cross-border armed violence between Taliban government forces and Pakistani security forces killed at least 499 civilians and wounded 1,216 others between October 2025 and June 2026. The worst single incident occurred in March, whenmore than 269 people were killed,externalin a Pakistani air strike on Kabul, which the Afghan Taliban said hit a drug rehabilitation centre. Islamabad denied the charge, saying it "precisely targeted military installations and terrorist support infrastructure". The neighbouring countries had agreed a ceasefire in March, but international mediation has failed to produce a lasting resolution. During a meeting on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly earlier this week, Pakistan's Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar called for "concrete and verifiable" measures to ensure that Afghan territory is not used for "terrorism". Headline: Faisal Islam: The two big decisions the chancellor must make
Body: Chancellor John Healey will give his Budget on 28 October "It is tough," John Healey admitted to me earlier this month when I asked him if there had been too much doom-mongering? "Conflicts, uncertainty, driving up inflation, driving up interest rates. But we've got great strengths. We've got good reasons to be confident about the future of Britain," he insisted. The new scheme to try and help young people get on the property ladder, announced on Saturday, was aimedat boosting confidencein the economy. But the chancellor is now facing two big decisions before his inaugural Budget on 28 October. Firstly, about the longevity of the economic pressures caused by the Iran War, and then about how to sustain a modest but notable uptick in economic spirits, through yet more global turbulence. In his first weeks as chancellor the oil price fell as low as $75 a barrel while the yield - the effective interest rate - on 10-year government bonds was 4.9%. Just over two months later oil has largely traded above $100 and the 10-year yield is at around 5.4%. It is the ultimate double whammy for a chancellor facing his first Budget. Yet there is something unusual about this energy shock. It could quickly reverse, as illustrated earlier in the summer when assumptions about a de-escalation in the US Iran conflict led to sharp falls in energy prices and yields. In New York last week both President Trump and his Iranian counterpart President Pezeshkian suggested November's US midterm elections were connected to when the war might end. The Iranians would wait until after the elections to seek peace because the war's impact on the cost of living - particularly soaring diesel costs - could damage him electorally, the US president told the UN General Assembly. The Iranian president said his nation "didn't want it to get to the midterms". Both sides in this war are feeling the economic squeeze of conflict. The vote on 3 November is six days after the Budget. No-one could rely on there being a settlement by then, but it is plausible. So the Budget tax, spend and borrowing forecasts could be based on a prolonged conflict, which is actually on the cusp of ending, or even already ended. The chancellor has to therefore decide whether to plan for the worst, and make some painful permanent tax and spend decisions, or buy some time. One option is to let borrowing take some of the strain, by tolerating a reduction in the £24bn of headroom - room for manoeuvre against the government's self-imposed borrowing rules - left by his predecessor, Rachel Reeves. This year's headroom will be judged in three years rather than four, so there is some rationale as to why a smaller number over a closer target might be appropriate. And while higher inflation means higher interest costs, it also means higher cash tax receipts, at a time when thresholds continue to be frozen. There is a second consideration. The hopeful optimism "vibes" strategy of the Burnham administration appears to have had some impact. The longest-running UK consumer confidence survey has hit a two-year high. Among younger people it has not been this high since before Brexit. Some data companies call it a "Burnham bounce", although the weather and World Cup were also factors. There is evidence, more mixed, that business optimism has also perked-up in recent months, possibly because of earlier falls in energy prices, though this has been clouded by anticipation of possible tax rises. The Institute of Directors business group said this was despite, rather than because of, the new government. While no-one should get too carried away with these turnarounds, they do stand in contrast to the admitted mistake of the Starmer government in talking up consumer pain two years ago. The question for the chancellor is whether better consumer and business spirits can be reconciled with the need for a "challenging" Budget? Indeed, it's important to determine how much of the summer global bond market shock is solely down to the impact of the Iran war and how much is more structural. Governments are facing new and intense competition in bond markets from the world's biggest AI businesses. In addition, the UK has had recent, prominent political and economic uncertainty. Right now the bond markets are like a pack of wolves stalking red deer, probing for weaknesses. "At times like this you don't want to be at the back of the herd," said one very senior former Treasury adviser. UK and US warned to take action on spiralling debt costs by IMF Unexpected UK borrowing surge adds to pre-Budget pressure on chancellor Government borrowing, bonds and yields explained In response, the Treasury has pointed to the UK having the highest growth and the fastest falling borrowing of the major G7 countries so far this year and our overall energy prices starting to decouple from high and volatile gas prices. However,the IMF chief Kristalina Georgieva this week dismissedthe idea that advanced nations could pause their fiscal homework, while the Gulf situation calmed. "Bring debt levels down, make fiscal consolidation as a priority… it is impossible to stress strongly enough how critical it is to get the courage to take the steps that are necessary," Georgieva told me, acknowledging the UK's "fairly consistent, credible" plans. Then there is the curious conundrum of British productivity. Last year, the government's official forecaster the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR)downgraded the UK's productivitypeformance, leading to a notable hit to the public finances. Now the UK's productivity record has been upgraded materially by the Office for National Statistics, although this is because of fewer hours worked. There could therefore be an argument to reverse some of that downgrade. Separately, the new chair of the OBR Jonathan Haskel is known for his argument that official statistics understate investment in intangibles like software and data. His latest research suggests AI-related investment is already visible in US productivity figures, and he has long been optimistic about tech's impact on the future. While it seems unlikely that such factors will make it into the OBR's calculations next month, there is a real debate here. Officially, however, part of the job at the Budget is to identify cuts to fund the Defence Investment Plan, inherited from Sir Keir. That's before funding the additional move to 3% of GDP and a new social care system. Even a promise of less welfare spending looks like being built on an upfront investment in jobs for young people. One change from last year is that so far, the government has parked the "pitch-rolling" with a silence that would rival the Trappist monks. Instead, policy announcements are strategically timed such as the "Your First Home" scheme just as the Labour party conference got underway. We can expect to hear plenty more as the Budget nears.

Headline: Developing El Niño becomes strongest on record weeks before expected peak
Body: Wildfires fuelled by El Niño are affecting around 12.5 million people across Indonesia, according to the country's health ministry. The developing El Niño climate phenomenon is now the strongest on record, according to scientists monitoring Pacific Ocean temperatures. Daily sea surface temperatures in a key region of the central-eastern Pacific were 3.05C above average on 19 September - exceeding the previous record of 3.02C set during the very strong El Niño of 2015. Some longer-term measures of El Niño have not yet hit record levels but this is likely to change, with the peak not expected until later this year. El Niño can causemajor shiftsin weather patterns around the world, with the Met Office saying many of the expected impacts are already being felt. El Niño set to be 'strongest in living memory', says Met Office What is El Niño and why could it mean record temperatures? El Niño is a naturally-occurring pattern, which happens about every two to seven years and tends to last for around a year. Trade winds that typically blow from east to west across the Pacific Ocean can weaken or even reverse, allowing warm water to spread eastwards. Heat is then released from the ocean into the atmosphere which can boost global temperatures and drive changes in weather patterns around the world. Forecasters track the development of El Niño by watching temperatures in a key region of the Pacific Ocean. When these are consistently 0.5C above normal, an El Niño is declared. There are different ways of measuring the strength of El Niño, however. The records that have now been broken relate to daily measurements of sea surface temperature compared with the long term historical average. This is called the Oceanic Niño Index (ONI). Many scientists - including forecasters in the USA and Australia - also consider an alternative measure known as the Relative Oceanic Niño Index (RONI). This measures how warm the key El Niño region is relative to the rest of the tropical oceans, meaning it takes into account the background warming caused by climate change. By the RONI index the current El Niño is not yet a record-breaker - but it is likely that more announcements will follow in the coming weeks. Professor Adam Scaife, Head of Long Range Prediction at the Met Office, said: "We have been signalling for months that the developing El Niño will be an unprecedented event. "The fact that it has already exceeded previous records – with several weeks to go before it peaks later this year – shows the enormity of this El Niño." Every El Niño is different, therefore impacts on global weather patterns are not guaranteed. And the unprecedented strength of this El Niño does not necessarily mean it will have unprecedented impacts on the weather. Professor Scaife said: "Scientists are still assessing whether the impacts will be in proportion to its magnitude, but we are already seeing expected effects worldwide." El Niño increases the odds of storms and floods in some regions and of drought and wildfires in others. This video can not be played Watch: How does El Niño affect world weather? El Niño years tend to bring below-average monsoon rainfall in India, which is already being reflected in this year's data. Statistics from the India Meteorological Department show that, until 22 September the southwest monsoon had brought 15% less rain than normal. Another typical impact of El Niño is reduced hurricane activity in the Atlantic due to changes in wind patterns high in the atmosphere. So far in 2026 there have been no Atlantic hurricanes, setting a new record forthe latest date without a hurricane formingsince satellite monitoring of storms began. Other possible effects - some of which are already being felt - include the increased risk of floods in coastal parts of Ecuador, Peru and the southern USA, and the enhanced threat of drought and wildfires in Brazil, Australia and Indonesia. These weather impacts can have significant knock on effects for on crop yields, food security and economies around the globe. The UK is thousands of miles from the tropical Pacific and so the effects of El Niño tend to be less clear-cut than in other regions. However, it does bring the increased chance of wet and stormy conditions across north-west Europe during the late autumn and early winter. Aforecast released by the Met Office this autumnstated that there were already "signals for increased rainfall and storminess in autumn here in the UK", especially into November and December. The winter of 2015 and 2016, which coincided with a very strong El Niño, brought a succession of major storms delivering what experts at the time described as the most extreme flooding on record. In addition to storminess, El Niño can also be associated with UK cold spells in the late winter - but the link is not a strong one and the past evidence is mixed. The so-called Big Freeze of winter 2009/2010 was, at the time, the coldest in three decades - and this coincided with an El Niño. However, 2006/2007 was also an El Niño winter and that was unseasonably warm. As this unprecedented El Niño approaches its likely peak towards the end of 2026, scientists will continue to monitor its development - and its impact on weather around the world.
