Headline: How Ceuta, football and Israel are shaping Morocco's election
Body: Moroccan voters will find candidates from 27 parties on the ballot Disillusioned young voters in Morocco were courted with viral football slogans, promises of one million jobs and anti-Israel rallying calls ahead of Wednesday's parliamentary elections. Yet, for many young Moroccans, politics remains deeply disconnected from reality. "I have no hope for this election. I'm ashamed of our political scene. It's a complete circus," Siham Azeroual, 32, an environmental activist who lives in the Atlas region, tells the BBC. The outcome of the vote will decide the make-up of the next government, just weeks after 60,000 people risked their lives to cross from the North African country to the Spanish enclave of Ceuta - a sign of the lack of opportunities many young people feel they have at home. Morocco operates as a constitutional monarchy where political parties compete for 395 seats in the House of Representatives, the legislative chamber. Yet executive power remains closely tied to the crown. King Mohammed VI, the 63-year-old monarch, appoints the prime minister from the political party that comes first in the election, but also presides over the Council of Ministers - the country's most important policy-making body. The current campaign also follows a wave of Gen Z protests that erupted in September 2025 over unemployment, healthcare and living costs. Demonstrators chanted slogans like "freedom, dignity, and social justice" which escalated to "get out Akhannouch", a reference to current Prime Minister Aziz Akhannouch. More than 2,400 people faced prosecution following the unrest. Despite the crackdown, some young activists are choosing to enter the political arena. Some 60,000 people swam from Morocco to the Spanish territory of Ceuta in late July Hamza El Kharroubi, 29, was briefly arrested during the protests. He is now running for parliament with the little-known Environment and Sustainable Development Party, which has a green agenda. "As a young person, I don't have much hope. I joined this party because they wanted more Gen Z faces and they are allowing us to speak freely about our demands," El Kharroubi tells the BBC. He comes from Tetouan, just 34km (21 miles) from Fnideq beach, where the migration wave to Ceuta started in late July. Some 60,000 people crossed, both Moroccans and other nationalities. At least 100 people died in the largest migration surge to the enclave in recent history. "We want justice for the families of those who died crossing to Ceuta. We want compensation for their families," El Kharroubi says. He argues that the crossing was widely linked to economic hardship and unemployment. The International Monetary Fund (IMF) estimates overall unemployment stood at 13% last year, while youth unemployment - between the ages of 15 and 24 - reached 37.3%. El Kharroubi says his goal is not to compete with established heavyweights - but securing a voice in parliament to build toward 2031. "As young people, we have to enter the parliament so by 2031 we have strong young politicians who can compete for a seat in the government." Morocco's FA president Fouzi Lekjaa is beloved by fans for helping put the Atlas Lions on the world football stage Fouzi Lekjaa, head of the Royal Moroccan Football Federation and a senior politician who works in the finance ministry, has emerged as the kingdom's newest political sensation - and a definite heavyweight. Credited with helping the Atlas Lions - as the national men's football team is known - become global contenders, Lekjaa joined the centrist Party of Authenticity and Modernity (Pam) in July. Videos of his campaign rallies have gone viral in the football-mad nation that is jointly hosting the next World Cup along with Spain and Portugal. The clips show crowds chanting "Sir" which means "Go" in Moroccan Arabic - the iconic catchphrase from Morocco's historic 2022 World Cup run, when it became the first Arab and African side to make it to the semi-finals. Lekjaa has promised to make Morocco sixth in the world in education and healthcare, to match the Fifa ranking of the men's football team. Pam is competing against 26 other parties, including Prime Minister Akhannouch's National Rally of Independents (RNI). In its bid for a second term, RNI has renewed a pledge to create one million job opportunities by 2031. Political expert Rachid Aourraz, from the Moroccan Institute for Policy Analysis (MIPA), remains sceptical about this promise. "The slogan 'one million jobs' has become an overused electoral slogan. There is also talk of raising the minimum wage, but what is proposed cannot withstand a structural inability to create stable net jobs," Aourraz tells the BBC. He adds that major parties "do not compete over an alternative model", but rather over how to implement public policies set by a royal vision. Huge pro-Palestinian protests often take place in Rabat Also seeking a political comeback is the Islamist Justice and Development Party (PJD) - using anti-Israeli sentiments to woo voters. Morocco normalised ties with Israel in December 2020 along with several other Arab countries, under the US-brokered Abraham Accords. Led by populist former Prime Minister Abdelilah Benkirane, the PJD is campaigning heavily on  a promise to end diplomatic ties with Israel. He says the normalisation was a "mistake" made by his party which led the government between 2016 and 2021. Bilateral ties were hit during the Gaza war with weekly protests taking place in the capital, Rabat, against the Israeli diplomatic presence. During the conflict the Israeli liaison office was closed and direct flights between the two countries were suspended. Yet despite an outpouring of pro-Palestinian protests, with tens of thousands taking to the streets and setting ablaze the Israeli flag at the height of the war, it was announced earlier this month that Israel and Morocco had agreed to open full embassies in their respective countries. This followed a meeting between their top diplomats and the US ambassador to the United Nations. "We have to speak up," Benkirane told supporters at a campaign rally in Marrakesh. "If we work hard, the king will close the Israeli embassy. The king does not like going against his own people," he added, warning of "the dangers of Israel and Zionism in Morocco". More than half of Morocco's total population of roughly 38.8 million is under the age of 35 - though only 4% of the more than 15.8 million registered voters are aged between 18 and 24. "I am not keeping up much with the campaigns - but I noticed the same faces as usual," says Hiba, a 27-year-old Moroccan living in Canada who preferred not to use her last name. She lives in Montreal which has a large Moroccan diaspora of about 104,000 people, according to the 2016 census. Many of last year's Gen Z protests were more vocal outside the country, where young Moroccans were able to express their anger without fear of repercussions. Hiba, who co-organised several Gen Z protests in Montreal, says she would have considered voting had she been able to find a proxy in Morocco - which is how those in the diaspora can cast their ballot. "Gen Z protests didn't go in vain. We achieved something. At least now we see more debates with young people on state TV," she says. Azeroual, the environmental activist, agrees. But having lived through both the 20 February movement in 2011 that changed the constitution and the recent Gen Z movement, she believes change must come from a multi-faceted approach. "I think young people should focus on the microscale - rather than running for office, helping build communities and connecting with people and then building up to the top," she says. Despite not being fully convinced by any political campaign, she says she will be heading to her local polling station to cast her ballot. Headline: UK warned over ballooning debt costs and slower growth ahead of Budget
Body: The UK has been warned over ballooning debt costs and slower economic growth ahead of Chancellor John Healey's first Budget next month. The UK was among countries facing downgraded growth forecasts in a report by the influential Organisation of Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) on Wednesday. That came as the head of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) told the BBC thatBritain and the US needed toreduce debt due to spiralling borrowing costs. The ongoing conflict in the Middle East and the Russia-Ukraine war has pushed up the cost of crude oil leading to higher fuel and energy costs, which in turn has driven up inflation around the world. The UK economy will grow by slightly less than expected next year, according to the OECD which now expects growth of 1% next year rather than 1.1%. However, it said the UK had proved more resilient than expected this year, upgrading its forecast for growth 0.9% to 1.1%. Meanwhile, IMF head Kristalina Georgievatold the BBC on Tuesdaythat global economic shocks had been "pushing debt levels up like a staircase not to heaven" but that governments had taken "no action to contain that service cost". "[It's] time to take that action," she said, adding that "courage" was needed by politicians to take the necessary steps. Inflation has also pushed up the cost of interest on government debt, which alongside anunexpected surge in government borrowingin August has added to the pressure on Healey. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said on Wednesday that the UK's high level of borrowing had left it "over-exposed" to global shocks. However, he said he stood by his point - made a year ago -  that Britain should be less "in hock" to investors in the bond markets. At the time, the comments spooked investors due to fears he was calling for spending restraints to be eased. Burnham has made easing the cost-of-living for households one of his key aims, while the government is under pressure to spend more on defence. He and Healey face a difficult balancing act, trying to offer more support to households while sticking to Labour's manifesto commitments on tax and the government's self-imposed fiscal rules. The impact of higher fuel prices next year depends on how long supply disruptions last, and stockpiles of oil and supplies from outside the Gulf states have helped cushion the effects on economies so far, the OECD said. Budget airline Ryanair will put up prices next summer as a result of persistently higher oil prices. Chief executive Michael O'Leary said ticket prices will be "materially higher", adding that carriers are in an "almost unprecedented" situation. Ryanair's fuel bill could jump by $1.5bn (£1.1bn) next year to $7.5bn, he said. Risks to the global economy include weaker-than-expected returns on AI investment and climate-change related supply shocks, the OECD said. Next year, global growth is expected to also be 0.1% lower, with countries affected including Australia, Canada, and the Euro-area. Weather-related shocks, including from a strong El Nino, could hit farmers and help push up food prices, it added. In addition, tariffs and export restrictions on trade continue to add to uncertainty, it said. New US tariffs from July as part of the Trump administration's ongoing volatile trade policy have raised its effective tariff rate by 1%. This video can not be played 'Get on top of your debt issues', IMF boss tells governments Chief Secretary to the Treasury Emma Reynolds said: "Despite unprecedented pressures and conflict in both the Middle East and in Europe, the UK economy is showing strong resilience." She added that the government is "already giving families space to breathe" and "starting the big, long-term changes needed to create good jobs and growth in every postcode". However, Conservative shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith said the OECD urges countries to "control spending and improve public sector efficiency". "Instead, this government is trying to find new ways to tax you whilst having to pay interest rates on their borrowing which are the highest in the G7," he said. Ruth Gregory, deputy chief UK economist at Capital Economics, said that the UK had "so far remained resilient to higher energy prices", but most of that reflected businesses having built up stock and households not putting so much disposable income into savings. However, this effect would be temporary, with growth more muted next year. She added that the "drag" on the economy from energy prices would pick up, while as a percentage of the UK's economic output, debt interest payments are forecast to hit levels seen in the mid-1980s.

Headline: Your pictures as equinox marks the start of astronomical autumn
Body: Astronomical autumn has officially started after the equinox took place in the early hours of Wednesday. It happened at 01:06 BST on 23 September, according to Royal Museums Greenwich. It is a precise moment in time when the Sun crosses the celestial equator and neither hemisphere is tilted towards or away from the Sun, meaning day and night are roughly equal in length across the world. While the equinox itself cannot be seen, the day has cultural and spiritual significance for some people. Gatherings took place at sites including Stonehenge and Glastonbury Tor (pictured above), where people came together to mark the occasion and watch the Sun rise. Autumn's arrival is very clearly spelled out in photo taken in Wakefield, West Yorkshire The autumn equinox may mark the start of astronomical autumn, but it does not necessarily mean there will be a sudden change in the weather. The first signs of autumn are already around us with falling leaves and conkers on the ground, and as the Sun gets lower in the sky and the days shorten, temperatures generally fall as we head further into autumn. So far this September, UK mean temperatures have been above average overall, according to the Met Office. BBC Weather Watchers captured some beautiful equinox photos and here are a few favourites of those sent in so far. A spider's web is beautifully crafted in amongst the autumn leaves The sunrise over Malborough in Devon on Wednesday filled the sky with tutti-frutti pink and orange colours Fairytale-style toadstools popping up and changing autumn leaves are some of  beautiful signals that autumn is here. Although the equinox happens at the same moment everywhere, the change in hours of daylight is not the same across the UK. The further north you go, the bigger the difference between the long days of summer and the short days of winter. That means places in northern Scotland are losing daylight more quickly at this time of year than parts of southern England. Leaves are already turning red and oranges setting off the mist still shrouding the fields behind Sunrises like this one in Ventnor on the Isle of Wight, will will get progressively later as autumn continues Around the autumn equinox the changes are particularly noticeable as sunrise gets later and sunset earlier. The word "equinox" comes from Latin and means equal night. At the equinox, the daylight measurement is taken from the point when the centre of the Sun is at the horizon, and is 12 hours sunrise to sunset and 12 hours sunset to sunrise. However, it is the top edge of the Sun which is visible first at sunrise and last at sunset. Because of light refraction - light being bent by the atmosphere - there is still light for a time when the Sun is not directly visible. This adds extra time to daylight hours. In autumn, this means that the time when day and night are actually equal happens after the equinox. This is known as the "equilux", which means equal light. This year, that happens in the UK on Friday 25 or Saturday 26 September, depending on your latitude. Headline: Trump and Xi come face-to-face as US and China battle to win the AI race
Body: This video can not be played A red carpet and military flyover - How Trump welcomed Xi "Whoever wins AI, WINS!" US President Donald Trump has been blunt about his AI ambitions, as well as about who he considers the US's main rival to be: China. His Chinese counterpart, Xi Jinping, has not said anything so forthright - but it seems he holds a similar view. "China very much sees it as a race, they very much think China should be the leading force in AI - they see AI as a power maximiser," says Rebecca Arcesati, from the Mercator Institute for China Studies. You can look beyond the rhetoric for evidence of this: AI has been a cornerstone of China's technological ambitions for more than a decade, whether Xi emphasises it publicly or not. For Trump, beating China to AI supremacy outweighs any risks of the technology to humans - something he hasdescribed as "a hoax". China's foreign ministry warned that "narratives of threat" and confrontation hinder global AI governance, calling for cooperation to ensure it benefits all. It means when the two presidents sit down on Thursday there will be few more important topics than their AI ambitions - and what they say and decide will matter to the whole world. The US and China are locked in a race to develop AI There's no doubt the US and China are global leaders in AI but who is ahead depends on how success is measured. American companies lead on so-called frontier models, with the highest-performing systems on most benchmarks coming from firms such as Anthropic, Google and OpenAI. In February 2025, an AI model by China's DeepSeek "briefly matched the top US model" and as of March 2026, Anthropic's top model led the pack "by just 2.7%",according to researchers at Stanford University,external. Part of the US advantage stems from the vast sums being invested in leading AI companies as the frontier labs burn through mountains of cash to build the infrastructure to train new models. OpenAI boss Sam Altman called for a coordinated slowdown of advanced AI development The stock market is booming and a large part of the US economy's expansion relies on the enormous growth - and projected profitability - of AI companies. So that might partly explainwhy President Trump sees AI as key to US success. Another factor limiting China's ability is the sweeping government restrictions placed on US companies that prevent them from selling advanced microchips to Chinese firms - these are crucial for developing cutting-edge models. Despite the chip restrictions, new AI models are coming out almost monthly in both countries and it's unclear what "winning" the AI race would actually mean, or whether there is a finish line at all. Many companies are racing to develop artificial general intelligence (AGI), a theoretical form of AI capable of learning, reasoning and performing a wide range of tasks at or above the level of humans. The Chinese AI industry has so far focused not on creating frontier models but releasing what is known as open weight models - downloadable and tweakable in a similar way to open source software. This contrasts with the approach taken by many US firms, which largely focus on proprietary models accessed through paid subscriptions or company platforms. Chinese open weight models are being released at a rapid pace, with benchmarks showing the country's top models trailing US rivals by only a few months. Models such as Moonshot AI's Kimi K3 have become popular in China and overseas because they perform close to the frontier models while remaining freely downloadable and adaptable. Beijing's focus is more about deploying the technology across its economy, China analyst Lizzi Lee from the Asia Society Policy Institute said. "AI isn't the moon landing," she said. "The US may lead at the frontier, while China could still gain enormous economic and geopolitical leverage by making capable AI cheap, open and ubiquitous." Yang Zhilin co-founded Moonshot, one of China's most successful AI models, in 2023 AI is also very energy hungry, and China is very well placed there, Rebecca Arcesatitold Tech Lifeon the BBC World Service. "Chinese AI companies are able to access the electricity they need for a much lower cost and that really is an advantage," she said. In robotics - a field of AI that some believe will be world-changing - China has become theworld's biggest manufacturer of robots, with more than two million working in the country's factories, the International Federation of Robotics estimated. The nation is also the world's biggest maker of humanoid robots, accounting for more than nine-tenths of global shipments in the first half of the year, according to independent policy institute Chatham House. Chinese AI developers have showed "remarkable resilience and innovation" in spite of the shortage of advanced American chips, analyst Lian Jye Su from tech research firm Omdia said. But US officials and AI firms have also alleged that Chinese developers closed the gap by using distillation - a technique that enables models to learn from more advanced platforms. China's foreign ministry said in response that AI development was "fuelled" by the country's "vision of extensive consultation and joint contribution for shared benefit". China and the US may be in fierce competition, but their governments' approaches to safety concerns are markedly different. While some in the industry have recently warned that AI could pose an existential risk to humanity, Chinese researchers seem less concerned about that and are more worried about potential misuse of the technology and cyber war. Responding to concerns over AI, Trump has said the US already has sufficient rules in place and that the only guardrails AI needs are a "high IQ" president. "We're leading now over China by a lot, and everyone else, and we're going to keep it that way," Trump said this week, adding that the US was not going to "stifle the growth of something that will be bigger than the industrial revolution". Washington has prioritised innovation and sought to reduce regulation in an effort to "keep American labs ahead", said information security officer Jayant Dave from cybersecurity firm Check Point Software Technologies. China is the world's biggest manufacturer of robots Beijing has taken a different strategy to the US hands-off approach. Xi urged the country's leaders to keep a close eye on AI's risks and ensure the technology was always "under human control". "China has taken a relatively cautious and centrally-coordinated approach," introducing guides on data usage and algorithms before many other countries, helping to address many underlying concerns, Dave said. The use of guidelines, though not legally binding, sets expectations while giving developers room to innovate, said National University of Singapore AI ethics lecturer Jonathan Sim. Despite calls for international cooperation, it remains unclear how the AI superpowers plan to address the technology's potential dangers - if at all. The two countries have previously cooperated on existential threats such as nuclear weapons, but that was based on a shared understanding of the threat, which is not currently the case with AI, Dave said. "Washington worries about capability escaping control. Beijing worries about capability threatening domestic stability," he added. Trump has dismissed proposals for an industry-wide slowdown, arguing that it could allow Chinese developers to close the gap. Ahead of the Trump-Xi summit, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng discussed establishing a notification mechanism for serious AI incidents. While the messaging from Trump on China in recent weeks has been "more antagonistic", the fact that AI is expected to be on the agenda was a "good start", said policy analyst Leia Wang from the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace. What we don't want, she added, was for an "unhealthy version of the race narrative to perpetuate", potentially escalating an already fierce rivalry in AI. Headline: Reports of violence against women in Gaza surge, UN agency finds
Body: There has been a sharp rise in reports of violence against women and girls in the Gaza Strip, including early and forced marriage, according to a series of recent reports from the UN Population Fund (UNFPA). One report, which analyses data collected by 10 organisations, says,externalthe protracted crisis in war-torn Gaza has "created conditions in which women and girls face escalating risks of gender-based violence". It also warns that there has been a "severe escalation" in the number of early and forced marriage incidents in the second quarter of this year. Both are considered types of gender-based violence (GBV) by the UN. Another report presenting testimony from 230 women in crowded displacement camps in Gaza City and Khan Younis,externalmakes for a grim read, describing the violence they have experienced or witnessed. Some readers may find some of the details in this report distressing One displaced woman in a school-turned-shelter in Gaza highlights how rape victims are often married to their rapists to avoid shame and scandal. "When rape cases are discovered in schools, you find weddings and celebrations at the school the next day," she says. Another woman tells how last year, at the time of famine, "a man married off his 14-year-old daughter in exchange for two bags of flour so he and his [other] children could eat". Six women in different displacement camps shared stories of such exchanges - which would have been unthinkable before the conflict between Israel and Hamas began in 2023. Although data collection to establish actual figures remains tricky, in the second quarter of this year, the UNFPA says the number of reported cases of early and forced marriage had increased by 123% on the first quarter. Early or child marriage involved girls aged 12 to 17. "The trends are shocking," says Nestor Owomuhangi, the UNFPA representative to Palestine. He says that the extreme circumstances over the past three years - which have seen tens of thousands of people killed, mass destruction and multiple waves of displacement in Gaza - have broken down social structures, so "everything is eroded... there is no system". While food markets have reopened, many cannot afford the goods on offer, there is still extreme poverty and hunger with reliance on charitable handouts. Nearly all the population of more than two million Gazans have been driven from their homes, leaving most living in squalid tent camps or damaged buildings. Public services have largely collapsed, and Israeli air strikes have continued despite the ceasefire. About 1.2 million Palestinians in Gaza are living in tents or makeshift shelters Prior to the war, girls in Gaza outnumbered and outperformed boys at every level of education above primary school. Now, with prolonged school closures, many children have dropped out of education. For boys there is pressure to find informal work to help support their families, for girls there are heightened issues around safety. Living among strangers, without privacy, in a socially conservative society, there are complaints of heightened sexual harassment and abuse - many families see marrying their daughters as a way to protect them and preserve modesty. The UNFPA report - based on research carried out in late 2025 and early 2026 - reveals how girls orphaned during the war are especially vulnerable. One woman in a Gaza City camp interviewed for the report says she attended the wedding of two girls from her family, aged just 14 and 15. "Their uncles married them off very young. Do you know why? Because their father and mother were martyred, and their uncles wanted to get rid of the responsibility and expenses," the woman said. "By God, they don't understand what marriage or life is." The Women's Affairs Center in Gaza - a Palestinian NGO which works with the UNFPA - and other support groups have documented distressing cases of girls who have been married and suffered abuse, often becoming pregnant. They say that those in their early teens are much more likely to have miscarriages and underweight babies than adult women. "We see adolescent pregnancies going through the roof because of child marriage," says Owomuhangi. "A child who is at an age when the body is not fully developed to sustain another body, who is hungry, in unhygienic circumstances, who doesn't know how to take care of the infant, who doesn't even know how to take care of herself, the consequences of that pregnancy are always really, really bad." The UN and most humanitarian organisations categorise marriages of girls under 18 as early marriage. Even before the war, this was more common among Palestinians in Hamas-run Gaza than it was in the occupied West Bank, but it was declining. The law in Gaza allows exceptions to the minimum marital age of 17 with parental consent and authorisation by a judge. Court officials can approve marriage for those as young as 14 years and seven months old, although a local Sharia expert told us that "legal safeguards" had been removed when Islamic courts - which officiate over family matters for Muslims - were closed for a large part of the war. About 700,000 children missed formal in-person schooling for almost three years The BBC has been speaking to some families in which bereaved relatives were married. Zuhair, who is 25, says his uncles pushed him to marry a 16-year-old girl from his extended family after her father - her sole guardian - was killed in an Israeli air strike. Challenged on why he agreed to go ahead with the plan, he said: "One of the reasons that led me to marry her was that there was no one to take care of her. That's the first point." "If it were not for the war, she would still be a young girl spoiled by her father. She would be going to school," Zuhair adds. "She still has a child's mindset, not a mature mindset. She misses school, her family, friends. She even misses simply sitting at home." A couple says they allowed their 17-year-old son to marry his 16-year-old cousin after their older son and the girl's father were killed. The teenager is now pregnant so will not return to school. "She needs to care for her child," her father-in-law says, "her education would be in vain." Aid agencies say the dangers for women could be greatly eased by improving humanitarian conditions Sexual violence in Gaza remains acutely under-reported in large part due to fear of stigma and retaliation. UN safety audits have shown particular risks to women and girls at night, causing them to avoid camp toilets and bathrooms. The latest analysis report by the UNFPA-led task force stated that incidents of sexual violence, including rape and sexual assault, "have become critical in Gaza". They accounted for 2.7% of total reported incidents of GBV from April to June 2026 - up from 2.1% in the quarter before; this represented a 61% surge in absolute case numbers. This rise is being linked to efforts to raise awareness and provide better ways to make confidential reports. Demographic data indicated that the majority of survivors were women aged 18-59, followed by adolescent girls at 8% and adult men at 5%. Women who are widows or have husbands who are detained or missing are at increased risk of sexual abuse and exploitation. Nearly one in four households is now reportedly headed by a woman - double the proportion before the war. "One widow was looking for a tent, and a [camp] representative told her, "I'll give you a tent, we'll put you in our camp, and you can come stay with me tonight," recalls a woman in Gaza City, interviewed for the UNFPA report. Aid agencies argue that the dangers for women in Gaza could be greatly eased by improving humanitarian conditions. There are calls for Israel to allow higher quality shelters into the territory as well as equipment to upgrade latrines and sanitation as well as lighting. Israel restricts items it classes as having a potential dual use for military purposes. There are ongoing efforts to improve education and healthcare and longer-term plans for campaigns to combat domestic violence and child marriage. While the course of so many lives in Gaza has already been permanently changed, women say they hope for a future in which they at least feel safer. If you have been affected by any of the issues in this story, help and support is available in the UK atBBC Action Line. Headline: Spotlight on new coaches as road to Afcon 2027 begins
Body: Pitso Mosimane (left) and Herve Renard (right) return to the dugout for South Africa and Ivory Coast respectively while Patrick Vieira (centre) starts his first international job with Senegal Just eight months on from the final of the 2025 Africa Cup of Nations (Afcon) - and with the world still waiting to find out the ultimate destination of the title - the road to the 2027 tournament begins in earnest. The 48 sides still in contention will play two rounds of qualifying in this extended international window, which gets under way on Thursday. Two more matches follow in November, with the groups reaching their denouement with the final two fixtures in March. The top two in nine of the 12 groups will progress to the 24-team finals in Kenya, Tanzania and Uganda. Preparations for the tournament in East Africamay be lagging behindbut, with the three hosts all guaranteed qualification, there is only one spot on offer in their respective groups. That means a second-placed finish may potentially not be enough. Several managerial changes have occurred since the last Afcon in Morocco and this year's Fifa World Cup, while several star players have hung up their boots. Here's what to keep an eye on in the first two rounds of action. Senegal appeal date set after Afcon win overturned Among several coaching changes, two in particular have caught the eye. Herve Renard, the only man to win Afcon with two different nations, hasreturned to the Ivory Coast jobsome 11 years after leading the West Africans to the title. The 57-year-old Frenchman starts his second stint with the Elephants at home against Ghana on Thursday in what is the standout match in the first round of fixtures. In the opposing dugout, the experienced Carlos Queiroz isback at the helmafter leading the Black Stars to the last 32 at the World Cup. However, Tottenham's Mohammed Kudus is among a number of players to withdraw from his squad. Patrick Vieira is another high-profile arrival, as the 1998 World Cup champion with France takes charge of Senegal, the country of his birth. The former Arsenal midfielder, 50,describes the role as "an absolute dream"yet he will begin with two away games against Mozambique and Ethiopia because Dakar is getting ready to host the 2026 Youth Olympics. Africa prepares for historic Olympic moment at Dakar 2026 Claude Le Roy, who guided Cameroon to Afcon glory in 1988, returns for another spell with Congo-Brazzaville five years after leaving his most recent international job with Togo Cape Verde wereone of the great stories of the 2026 World Cup,pushing Argentina all the way in the last 32 before the debutants lost 3-2 after extra time. Long-serving coach Bubista has since resigned from the Blue Sharks hotseat, with his former assistantHumberto Bettencourtstepping up. He will begin his reign in Mali on Friday before hosting Rwanda on Tuesday. Algeria, Tunisia and South Africa have also changed coaches since the World Cup. The Tunisians have turned to former Esperance and Renaissance Berkane bossMoin Chaabanas they aim to move on from their disastrous World Cup campaign which sawSabri Lamouchi dismissed after one gameand Renard fail to orchestrate a revival. Pitso Mosimanehasbeen reappointed by South Africasome 14 years on from his last spell in charge - which saw Bafana Bafana miss out on the 2012 Afcon - andBrahim Hemdanihas taken over Algeria after Vladmir Petkovic's departure. Meanwhile, Afcon legendClaude Le Royhas returned at the age of 78 after signing on for a second stint with Congo-Brazzaville. The Red Devils have not appeared at the finals since 2015, while Frenchman Le Roy is aiming to coach at a record-extending 10th edition of the finals. Burkina Faso have turned to ex-Comoros bossAmir Abdouand, after a stint with Libya, 2021 Afcon-winning coachAliou Cissehas his first competitive matches in charge of Angola. The former Senegal boss starts with a tough away assignment in Egypt. Riyad Mahrez is among a number of former Afcon winners who have retired from international duty Some big-name players have called time on their international careers since the World Cup, with several of them former Afcon winners. Senegal are looking for a new number one afterEdouard Mendyhung up his goalkeeping gloves. The 34-year-old helped the Teranga Lions become champions at the 2021 and 2025 tournaments - even if the latter title is stilldisputed at the Court of Arbitration for Sport. Wing wizardRiyad Mahrez,who captained Algeria to the trophy in 2019, has quit international duty while Ivory Coast will have to cope without midfieldersSeko FofanaandJean-Michael Seri. Ellyes Skhirihas also called time on his international career and will not be involved as Tunisia aim to reach a record-extending 18th consecutive Afcon. Meanwhile,Pierre-Emerick Aubameyanghas stepped back from Gabon duty, saying he felt "humiliated" by his treatment after their exit at the previous tournament. The 37-year-old was excluded from the national team set-up after their group-stage exit. Thatsanction was later lifted,but Aubameyang ruled himself out of Sebastien Migne's Panthers squad despite his fine start to the season with Deportivo La Coruna. Sheffield United striker Siem Eyob-Abraha (right) is back in the Eritrea squad after the 18-year-old scored in the preliminary qualifying round victory over Eswatini in March Elsewhere, Eritrea are back in the group stage of Afcon qualifiers - for the first time since the build-up to the 2008 edition - after seeing off Eswatini 4-1 on aggregate in the preliminary round in March. Chad, Djibouti, Mauritius, Sao Tome and Principe and Seychelles are the other five nations already eliminated. However,seven Ertirea players abscondedafter the away leg of their tie which was held in South Africa. Occurrences of Eritrean sportsmen and women failing to return home to what is a one-party state and a highly militarised society has long been an issue, and was part of the reason for the East Africans withdrawing from qualifying for both the 2023 Afcon and2026 World Cup. Yet the Red Sea Camels, who have been drawn alongside Kenya, South Africa and Guinea in Group D, are now largely relying on talent drawn from the diaspora. Just three home-based players have been named in the squad for their opening two fixtures, which see them take on the tournament co-hosts in Nairobi on Saturday before a 'home' game against Bafana Bafana in Cairo on Tuesday. Meanwhile, Somalia have reached the group stage of qualifying for the first ever time but face a very tricky draw alongside Ivory Coast, Ghana and The Gambia. The Ocean Stars are ranked 53rd on the continent but, like Eritrea, can at least dream of reaching Afcon as the tournament returns to East Africa for the first time since 1976.

Headline: Alberta’s self-image as world’s only rat-free region shattered by discovery of rat
Body: Province’s rat patrol called in to investigate as town of Bowden announces discovery of dead vermin For more than seven decades, residents of Alberta have shared something in common withAntarcticaand the high Arctic: all locations are officially free of rats. But on Thursday the Canadian province’s reputation as a firewall against rodent infestation took a hit when the town of Bowden announced the discovery of adead ratand called on the province’s “rat patrol” to investigate. “If you’ve noticed rat droppings or any signs of rats, please contact Rat Patrol Alberta so they can follow up,” the town said in a statement. “Please stay alert and report any sightings.” Officials in Bowden did not say where in the town the rat was found. But as global temperatures increase, rat numbershave surged in major cities. Over the past decade, rats increased by 390% in Washington DC, 300% in San Francisco and 162% in New York, according to researchers, who analysed public sightings and infestation reports. Toronto, Canada’s largest city, is facing a “perfect rat storm”, with numbers up 186% in the last 10 years. Unlike other regions in the world that have been overrun by the wily and adaptable urban mammals, Alberta has actively fought rats from entering at all. “Albertans have enjoyed living without the menace of rats since 1950 when the Rat Control Program was established,” the province says in its rat guide. It cites both the province’s unique geography, with mountain ranges and boreal forest surrounding most of Alberta, and the fact that the Norway rat – “one of the most destructive creatures known to man”, the province claims – cannot survive in vast natural areas and cannot overwinter in cultivated fields. The very lack of the humans and their structures that rats need to survive has given the province a chance to ward off infestation. In the 1950s, suspecting rats might try to enter from the east by way of neighbouring Saskatchewan, Alberta officials created a “rat control zone” – a strip of land measuring 373 miles by 18 miles (600km by 30km) – to monitor incursions that ranges from Cold Lake in the north to the Montana border in the south. In addition, from June 1952 to July 1953, 140,000lb of 73% arsenic trioxide powder was used to treat 8,000 buildings on 2,700 farms to slow the spread of rats. The province also amended the Agricultural Pests Act of Alberta in 1950, obliging “every person and municipality” to destroy rats they found;made posters reminiscent of a national war effort; and hosted a radio show, Call of the Land, to educate residents. Today, there are dedicated telephone lines and an email address to report rats. But while the rat patrol receives hundreds of calls each year, it says the vast majority are not rats but muskrats, voles and field mice. Still, it concedes there are exceptions. “Alberta’s rat-free status means there is no resident population of rats and they are not allowed to establish themselves. It does not mean we never get rats.”

Headline: Call for 'transparency' over £68m flood scheme information
Body: Mike Sutherland called on the council to "reveal all it must reveal" The man behind the freedom of information (FOI) requests where a council response was found to be "entirely unacceptable" has called for someone to be held to account. Mike Sutherland said he believed there had been a "catalogue of errors" in the handling of the £68m Whitesands flood protection scheme in Dumfries. The Scottish Information Commissioner (SIC) recently ruled that Dumfries and Galloway Councilhad "failed at the most basic level" in its response to his requests about the project. The council said it was considering the findings and would respond within the timescales set out. Council's flood scheme request approach 'entirely unacceptable' The street that has flooded more than 200 times Work has now started on the Whitesands flood schemewhich has proved controversial. Opponents say it is too costly, spoils the view and costs car parking spaces. Those in favour argue it will provide defences to an areawhich has flooded hundreds of timesand also help with its regeneration. Sutherland believes the Local Government (Scotland) Act 1973 required the council to seek court approval to use common good land. After an attempt to fund a challenge through the courts raised only a fraction of the funding required, the former council worker from Lockerbie turned to FOIs to raise his concerns about the project. He asked for information about the use of common good land - owned by the council for the benefit of the community - and whether it had petitioned the courts for a change of use. The response from the local authority was severely criticised by Scottish Information Commissioner David Hamilton. What stories would you like BBC News to cover from the south of Scotland? Sutherland said that made him feel vindicated in his persistence to get answers about a scheme "hated by many people". "I've asked them a few more testing questions which they've been very furtive about indeed," he said. "They're quick enough in making other people accountable - what about their accountability? "They're going to try and avoid answering all the same -  because they want this project as far down the line as possible," he said. Sutherland said he accepted that the project would go ahead but he still wanted to pursue answers. "They have no hesitation whatsoever in holding other people to account when they slip up just once," he said. "They've made a catalogue of errors here over a £68m project that a lot of people do not want." He said he would not stop until the council was forced to "reveal all they must reveal". His call received support from MSP Craig Hoy this week. Craig Hoy said the council must "clearly and willingly" explain the legal position of the Whitesands scheme "There are important questions that Dumfries and Galloway Council must now address," he told the Scottish Parliament. "It must clearly and willingly explain the legal position surrounding the use of common good land that is affected by the project and show that the proper processes have been pursued at all stages." He said he would be meeting the council chief executive to ask the council to answer questions about the scheme "fully, openly and transparently". The council said it was still examining the findings on its FOI responses which were issued a week ago. "We are currently considering the SIC's decisions and the requirements set out in them," it said. "We will fully consider and respond within the timescales set out. "It would be inappropriate to comment further until we have had an opportunity to review the decisions in detail." Work begins on Dumfries flood defence scheme

Headline: Catherine Zeta-Jones bases new role on funny Welsh people she knows
Body: Catherine Zeta-Jones plays Jackie Price, a former cocaine dealer who is being targeted by hitmen in a new series Actor Catherine Zeta-Jones says she based her performance in the new series Kill Jackie on people she knows in Wales. The Mumbles star plays Jackie Price, a former cocaine dealer who is being targeted by hitmen, in a new series for Prime. It isthe first time she has played a role using her Swansea accent,externaland the first time she has filmed a drama in Wales. "I played on people I know in Wales, people who are comedic and the accent makes it funny and real and true, but the character comes from a tough side of Swansea, which we do have as well," she said. Óscar Jaenada as Zigor and Zeta-Jones as Jackie Price in Kill Jackie The series is based on a book called The Price You Pay, set in the US, and the central character is a man called Jack. Zeta-Jones said they "flipped it" for her to be a woman with all the quirkiness and craziness that Jack had in the book. She said: "I told my creative team, I want to play her Welsh. And they went OK. "For many reasons. One, I've never played real Welsh Swansea ever, never shot in Wales and I think it would ground me in her character and add nuances that I would know," she told Lucy Owen onBBC Radio Wales. "I'm so glad I did it because she's such a great character and I just wanted her to be Welsh." Zeta-Jones says she "could not believe" how many of her fans noticed the use of her accent in the thriller Zeta-Jones, also an executive producer on the series, said she had an idea for one scene to use a song by Welsh singing legend Tom Jones, and have him help save the day. She said: "Jackie has installed this high-tech security system behind these Andy Warhol style prints of Tom Jones. They lift up and out come very dangerous machine-guns that do the bad guys in. "That was my contribution to the scene." Catherine said she did not know if Jones realised he had such a crucial role and said she needed to text him to tell him about it. "I think because I'm playing such a badass, I think he's going to love that we used his song in that particular moment in the show," she said. Catherine Zeta-Jones on using her real accent in Kill Jackie The actress chats to Lucy Owen about her new drama. Zeta-Jones has been praised by fans for using her Welsh accent in the thriller, which begins on 2 October. One fan said they loved hearing the "queen of Wales sounding Welsh". She has previously spoken abouther strong connection to Wales, adding in her heart she "never really left". One fan commented on an Instagram post of the trailer, saying: "Her Welsh is out and I love it, can't wait". Speaking onBBC Woman's Hour, Zeta-Jones said she "could not believe" how many of her fans noticed the use of her accent and that it had made her "very happy". The Hollywood actress also revisited comments she made recently about the term "nepo baby", whichshe said was a "horrific" phrase. During the interview, she said her husband Michael Douglas - son of Hollywood legend Kirk Douglas - was "the ultimate nepo baby". She also said her children Dylan and Carys had dealt with the "intense attention thrown on them profoundly well". Catherine Zeta-Jones says her husband Michael Douglas is "the ultimate nepo baby" Despite her Welsh pride, Zeta-Jones has also revealed that she turned down an appearance on Welcome To Wrexham, alongside fellow Hollywood stars Ryan Reynolds and Rob Mac. In an interview with Heart Radio she said she was asked several times to feature in the documentary series. "It's really hard to explain to Americans that I'm from Swansea and I was brought up with Swansea City. My uncle Bobby was director of the Swans when John Toshack took us to the premiership. "I was in the front seat of the parade. I have been a lifelong Swansea city fan. I can't go to Wrexham. I can't even go to Wrexham to tell them how much I love Swansea. I think they would throw bricks at me in the street," she joked. Crashed RAF jet steered to 'avoid built-up areas' before pilots ejected What are my children exposed to? Headline: No 'switch' to stop small boats, Lucy Powell tells BBC
Body: This video can not be played Labour deputy leader Lucy Powell spoke to presenters from BBC local radio There is no "switch" to stop small boat crossings and not every migrant boat can be intercepted, Labour's deputy leader has told the BBC. Lucy Powell's comments came after two uncontrolled landings from the Channel in two days, at Folkestone and Samphire Hoe in Kent. The Home Secretary, Shabana Mahmood, has ordered an urgent review by Border Security Command, calling the failure to intercept the two boats "not acceptable". But the Conservatives say Labour has lost control of Britain's borders and a "radically different" approach is needed. A total of 781 people were recorded as arriving in 10 boats on Wednesday, the highest in a single day for far this year. In a round of interviews with BBC local radio ahead of Labour's annual conference, Powell told BBC Radio Solent: "We are taking all steps we can to really bear down on and eradicate the small boat crossings altogether. "This has been a mammoth task across a whole range of different policy areas over the last couple of years, which is now starting to bear fruit, in that small boat crossings are significantly down this year - in fact, significantly lower than at any time in the last six years. "Obviously as we close down some avenues and we close down routes criminal gangs look to find new ways to deliver their terrible business model." Lucy Powell said the government's work to stop small boat crossings was making an difference The thousands of migrants crossing the Channel are usually brought to shore by Border Security Command or RNLI boats. Before Monday, no small boat arrivals to the UK coast without an escort had been officially recorded since September 6, 2025. Uncontrolled landings are so rare that last year's incident was the only other one recorded since the Home Office began keeping data in 2023. Powell told BBC Radio Kent: "It's not easy. If we had a switch that we could switch tomorrow to stop all small boats, we would switch it". Labour's deputy leader and education secretary told Radio 4's Today programme that they "can't stop everything all of the time". She said: "Of course, it's a concern. That's why the Home Secretary has demanded and ordered this urgent review, because this is not what we want to see. This is not acceptable." On Wednesday, British rescue boats were sent to collect a group of migrants who had spent more than 33 hours at sea The Conservative Shadow home secretary Chris Philp said on X: "Labour has lost control of our borders. A radically different approach is needed. "We need to leave the ECHR so anyone entering Britain illegally can be rapidly deported. No hotels. No benefits. No lengthy court process. No asylum claim. Just rapid removal. Then the crossings will soon stop." The Liberal Democrat home affairs spokesperson, Max Wilkinson MP, said closer cooperation with the EU was key to tacking small boat crossings. "Until the government adopts Liberal Democrat proposals to tackle the root cause by entering the EU's landmark Migration and Asylum Pact, these the smugglers will continue to find a way through, lives will be put at risk and taxpayers' money will be wasted," he said.

Headline: Did El Niño turn Hurricane Polo into the most powerful storm of the season?
Body: This video can not be played Hurricane Polo, a large storm off the coast of Mexico, has been downgraded to a category 4 hurricane but remains "very powerful", according to the US National Hurricane Center. The Pacific hurricane, one of the strongest of the season, was projected to head towards the coast of south-western Mexico bringing intense wind and rain, but was not expected to make landfall. The slow-moving storm is being fuelled by extremely warm waters caused by the El Niño climate phenomenon. Headline: Martha's Rule rolled out at every A&E department in England
Body: The rule is named after Martha Mills, who died aged 13 at King's College Hospital in London in 2021 The NHS is expanding Martha's Rule to all hospital emergency departments in England to help patients and families challenge staff and seek a rapid review of their care if they want. It is named after Martha Mills, who died aged 13 in 2021 after developing blood poisoning, or sepsis. Her family's concerns were not listened to, which later prompted her parents, Merope and Paul, to change that culture by creating the rule. Patients, loved ones and staff in A&E units will be able to call a dedicated phone number to trigger an urgent review if a patient's condition is deteriorating and they are concerned this is not being taken on board. The nationwide expansion should be complete by March 2028, after a trial at seven trusts. It is already being rolled out in all inpatient wards. Scotland is beginning to use Martha's Rule and Northern Ireland is considering using it, while Wales has a similar scheme called Call4Concern. Acoroner ruled,externalin 2022 that Martha would probably have survived if she had been transferred earlier to intensive care and given appropriate treatment. She was in King's College Hospital in London after a cycling accident on a family holiday in which she fell heavily onto the handlebars after skidding on some sand. It left her with serious injuries to her pancreas. After a few weeks, she developed an infection and then signs of sepsis - when the body's response to an infection is overwhelming and ends up injuring its own tissues and organs - but this was not managed properly. This video can not be played Watch: The Crown actor Jason Watkins who lost his daughter Maude to sepsis spoke to the BBC about his support of Martha's law. Prof Aidan Fowler, national director of patient safety at NHS England, said the expansion of Martha's Rule would give families and NHS staff "a critical new lifeline" to help improve care and save more lives. He told the BBC that a Martha's Rule call would mean a patient receives an "appropriate response" - for example, a senior nurse or member of the critical care outreach team could conduct a review of the case. Staff can also ask for a review from a different team if they are concerned the appropriate action is not being taken. Elliott Paterson, from Cheltenham, told the BBC he "truly believes" Martha's Rule saved the life of his 67-year-old father, Chris, who was treated at Gloucester Royal Hospital last year after he broke four ribs falling off his bike. Elliott said his father's treatment in the surgical ward was complicated due to his Addison's disease, a rare autoimmune condition affecting the adrenal glands. The family noticed Chris' deterioration in health, Elliott said, and called the critical care team, which was then able to treat both Chris' injuries and his Addison's. "To hear that Martha's Rule is now to be rolled out across the NHS is brilliant news and I hope that for more people it will continue to save lives," Elliott said. "I am incredibly fortunate and grateful to have had Martha's Rule at our disposal at the time." During an eight-month pilot of the scheme at seven emergency departments, 69 calls were made to dedicated Martha's Rule phone numbers, including some calls relating to acute deterioration following an urgent clinical review. In some cases, it led to a patient having immediate surgery or being transferred to intensive care. Fowler told the BBC's Today programme that, while these numbers might seem relatively small, the decision to roll out Martha's Rule further was "on a background of very, very extensive experience in other settings". This included in-patient wards, where he said his teams had received "nearly 20,000 calls" - three quarters of which came from families. Fowler said: "Early testing has shown that Martha's Rule can work well in busy A&Es and builds on the evidence from our adult and children's wards, where thousands of calls have been made by patients, families and staff to date, with many leading to changes in treatment and potentially life-saving interventions." Elliott Paterson said he was "incredibly fortunate and grateful" to have Martha's Rule in the case of his father Chris (pictured) Questioned whether busy A&E staff might struggle with a sudden influx of calls, Fowler said this had not played out in the recent tests. "Actually people have used it very sensibly," he added. "We've tested it through winter and across this busy summer, and therefore I am not concerned that when we roll this out we are going to be overwhelmed with calls." Health minister Baroness Merron said the initiative was part of "wider efforts to put patient safety at the heart of the NHS". Actor Jason Watkins, whose two-and-a-half-year-old daughter Maude died from sepsis in 2011, praised the rollout, saying Martha's Rule was already "making a difference on the wards". "It enables a parent to have a voice and if there is an issue, that is addressed," he told BBC Breakfast, urging parents: "If you're at all worried when you go into A&E, ask for a second opinion." Watkins said the rollout of Martha's law could benefit medical professionals too, explaining: "Those extremely dedicated medical practitioners, nurses, doctors and consultants, it gives them a pause and a thought [of] 'am I doing everything I can to assess this child accurately?'." Before the phased rollout is completed in England, patients and their families can check with their local hospital or NHS trust where Martha's Rule is available by visiting the trust's website or asking hospital staff. Headline: Iranian minister says only negotiation can end conflict after Trump rejects Hormuz deal
Body: Only a "negotiated solution" can end the conflict between the US and Iran, Tehran's foreign minister has said, after President Donald Trump publicly rejected a proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz. Trump told reporters at the White House that Iran's proposal was not "acceptable" and that Tehran wanted to make a deal to open the strait to commercial shipping  within seven days because "they're losing so badly". In a post on Telegram, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi acknowledged Trump's rejection, but said Iran would wait for a "definitive" official US response. He said the president had made contradictory statements in the past. Araghchi said the conditions to open the strait were the same that had been included in amemorandum of understanding (MOU) between the US and Iranthat was signed in June. Iran said it had raised reopening the strait and ending hostilities during negotiations on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York this past week. The vital waterway through which around a fifth of the world's gas and oil supply usually flows has been effectively closed since the outbreak of war in February. "I'm rejecting their deal," Trump said on Saturday, adding that the US already had "total control" of the strait, with "massive amounts of oil" passing through it, causing massive rises in global oil prices and steep fuel cost increases for consumers. Araghchi wrote on Telegram that Trump "has made many good statements, as well as many contradictory ones, which unfortunately we hear frequently". He continued: "We are waiting for the mediators to convey the definitive views to us, and we will make a decision based on them." Separately, Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian, whotravelled to New York for the UN general assembly, told the BBC's US news partner CBS that "distrust created by this war needs to be overcome" in order for talks to be successful. He said the Iranians were open to talks on implementing the MOU in stages in order to end the impasse, but that the "US needs to show it does not intend to overthrow our government". Pezeshkian said Trump had "tore up" the MOU when the US resumed its bombing campaign, adding: "If we don't abide by what we have written down, can we really resolve it by dialogue?" He was also asked about Iran's new Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei, who was injured in the US strike which killed his father in February and has not been seen in public since. Reports have claimed he suffered serious injuries to his legs and face. Pezeshkian said he had met the supreme leader on two occasions, telling CBS he had "no specific ongoing health issues or challenges" and had been well enough to hold seven hours of talks. Oman, which has been acting as a mediator between the US and Iran, called for all parties to continue having open dialogue to resolve the crisis. Oman's foreign minister, Sayyid Badr bin Hamad bin Hamood Albusaidi, told the UN General Debate that "all parties" should cooperate with Oman in efforts to safeguard navigation in the strategic waterway. Trump's rejection of Iran's proposal was backed by US ambassador to Nato Matthew Whitaker. Speaking to Fox News on Saturday, Whitaker said that Iran had offered "half measures" and "illusory deals to make themselves look good on the world stage". "President Trump's right to reject it," he said. Meanwhile, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Saturday that economic sanctions imposed by the USwere taking a toll on Iran. Posting on X, Bessent said Turkey, Oman and the United Arab Emirates had halted flights from various Iranian airlines, and some banks in the UAE and Turkey had stopped transactions with Iran. The Trump administration has dubbed an economic blockade on Iran "Operation Economic Outcast", with the White House attempting to use economic pressure to force Tehran to stop attacks on vessels in the Strait of Hormuz. But some economists have questioned whether the latest sanctions will be effective, as this depends on the reaction from Iran's major trading partners. These include China, the biggest buyer of Iranian oil, which has ignored previous US sanctions and continued to do business with Tehran. Headline: Weekend of mixed UK weather with sunshine before showers arrive for some on Sunday
Body: A deep area of low pressure is forecast to approach from the Atlantic next week bringing a spell of windy weather. This potential storm may also bring heavy rain to places, especially in the west, whilst some places further east could stay dry. Many drought affected parts of England and Wales - where significant rainfall is still needed - may stay largely dry throughout the next week. Before the arrival of wind and rain, though, some bursts of warmth will lift temperatures above average, possibly reaching the low-20s Celsius at times in south-east England. It will be a day of warm sunshine for many on Saturday with rain for some on Sunday After some unseasonable warmth over the past week, especially in the south, a weak weather front ushered in cooler air to Scotland and Northern Ireland on Friday, whilst warm and humid air stayed put in southern England and south Wales. Into the weekend it does look as though most places will return to more typically late September conditions, with UK temperatures ranging between roughly 15 to 21C north to south.. Just how hot and dry was your summer? Use our postcode lookup to find out Summer 2026 was UK's hottest on record, Met Office says Temperatures will again be close to the seasonal average through the weekend and it should feel pleasantly warm in the sunny spells. Saturday will bring the chance of further showers to many western areas, while on Sunday spells of rain will sweep most areas at some point. As we head into next week and the final days of September there are currently no signs of any significant bouts of unseasonable warmth. Some pleasantly warm and sunny days are still possible during the first half of the week, but forecasts show a very changeable pattern overall. As well as occasional rain for most, northern and western areas could see much windier conditions at times. Expected rainfall over the next five days will be focused on northern and western parts of the UK. Some places in central and eastern England may stay completely dry September rainfall so far has been very mixed across the UK. In parts of north-west Scotland, there has already been 146% of expected September rainfall. At Achnagart in Highland, it has rained for the past 27 days. In contrast, it has been very dry in parts of eastern England, with Bridlington in East Yorkshire seeing just 11% of expected September rainfall. Low pressure systems will bring some rain over the next week or so. However, the bulk of the rain will fall in Scotland, Northern Ireland and western parts of England and Wales, with no significant or useful forecast further south and east. Headline: Scam hotel booking sent family to Wetherspoon pub
Body: Wetherspoon staff have been turning away up to 20 tourists on a daily basis as scammers use the address as a fake Booking.com holiday apartment, Which? has found A theatre-goer fell victim to a "sophisticated phishing attack" after booking a "luxury" London apartment, only to discover the address was a Wetherspoon pub. Paul Dawson, from Loughborough in Leicestershire, paid £73 for a one-night stay for his family via Booking.com at The London Crown apartments to watch the musical Hamilton in the West End. Days later, he said, he discovered the address shown in the listing was actually The Liberty Bounds pub, a Wetherspoon near Tower Bridge. Consumer protection organisation Which? said Wetherspoon staff had been turning away up to 20 tourists a day after scammers used the pub's address as a listing for a "block of luxury apartments". Which? said it was also made aware of a property listed as "Apartments near Big Ben", with the address given as Portcullis House, part of the House of Commons estate, where hundreds of MPs work. Booking.com told Which? that in both cases, listings for legitimate properties had been targeted by a "sophisticated phishing attack, allowing criminals to hijack the listings". Wetherspoon said it had informed Booking.com about this scam "as soon as it came to their attention". Paul Dawson said he had to find alternative accommodation for his family Dawson, 55, made his booking in August. Two days later, he said he received an email from The London Crown containing a link to a fake Booking.com page, which asked for his bank details. Dawson told Which? he contacted Booking.com with his suspicions, but said the platform told him that he would need to visit the "fake apartment" and wait until after 7pm before it would relocate him. This was despite Mr Dawson explaining to them that he had since discovered the address shown in the listing was actually The Liberty Bounds pub. He told Which?: "I explained to the support staff that I had autistic children and the idea of turning up at a clearly non-existent property at 10.30pm would have been catastrophic. "This did not change their response, that I needed to go to the property. They said that if it was not possible to check in then I could contact them again and they would find an alternative." Dawson said the family ended up staying in the Premier Inn in Goodge Street. The Liberty Bounds is in Trinity Square, Tower Hill, and near the Tower of London The listing for the London Crown apartments had 250 negative reviews from August and September along with a handful of, likely fake, positive reviews, Which? said. The BBC checked the listing on Thursday. The information was still visible but the page carried the message: "We're sorry, but this property isn't taking reservations on our site right now". Wetherspoon said the listing was removed only for it to reappear, "though it now appears that the ability to book has been blocked". "We have again notified them [Booking.com], asking for the listing to be permanently removed. "It is clearly unacceptable for people to be defrauded in such a flagrant manner. "This is upsetting for the pub team, as there is little they can do to help, but even more so for the people who have been misled and have lost money as a result. "Booking.com urgently needs to adopt more robust procedures to prevent fraudulent listings like this appearing in the first place." The BBC was able to access the listings page on Thursday for The London Crown, but bookings were frozen Many of the reviews from customers said they told Booking.com that it was a scam but had been ignored. One customer said: "I reported it to Booking.com three days before check-in but they refused to do anything." Another customer, from Spain, complained that she and her friend had been left stranded, writing: "Two girls alone in London at two o'clock in the morning with no accommodation." Booking.com also has an AI trip planner called Dot, which allows users to ask questions. On The London Crown listing page a Which? researcher asked: "Is this a real property, or is it a scam?". It replied: "The London Crown is a legitimate property located in the centre of London. It offers various amenities such as free wifi, free bikes, and free private parking. It is conveniently located near Longleat Safari Park and Longleat House, with London City Airport just 10km away. Based on the detailed description and amenities listed, the London Crown appears to be a real and well-equipped property." Dot failed to recognise that Longleat Safari Park was more than 100 miles (160km) from London, in Wiltshire. An AI trip planner called Dot said The London Crown was conveniently located near Longleat Safari Park and Longleat House "Apartments near Big Ben" and The London Crown apartments were both targeted by the phishing attack, said Booking.com. "The attack affected the properties' own computer systems and gave cybercriminals temporary, unauthorised access to the accommodation's Booking.com account," a spokesperson said. "We take incidents like this extremely seriously, and suspended bookings at both properties, as well as supporting affected customers." An Ofcom spokesperson said: "Fraud online can have serious consequences for victims and platforms have clear legal duties to take down illegal content generated by users once they become aware of it. "More broadly, we've shown that we'll use our enforcement powers against platforms that fail to comply with the Online Safety Act, and have already launched investigations into over 100 sites."
