Headline: Indians are discovering the thrill of shopping without paying
Body: FoodNeverComes calls itself a 'dopamine kitchen' You are hungry. Or you are not. It doesn't matter. You open FoodNeverComes, pick from 22 cuisines and start scrolling. Butter chicken looks good. So does bibimbap. You add a few dishes, watch the total climb and hit checkout. A tracker says a rider is on the way. Then you get a dummy AI-generated call from inside the site. He is outside your building, he says, but cannot find your street or door. Except there was never any food in the first place. The order exists only on the screen. "Order the food. Skip the bill," says thesite.,externalIts slogan is blunter: "The food never comes - but the dopamine does." Built by two 26-year-old software developers - Purvansh Parmar and Anshul Sharma - from Udaipur in India's northern state of Rajasthan, FoodNeverComes says it has attracted more than 2.7m visitors since its launch in June. It now offers 22 kitchens, 327 dishes and 319 real recipes, complete with fake prices, a simulated checkout and a fictional delivery experience.  The site offers 22 fake kitchens, 327 dishes and 319 real recipes FoodNeverComes belongs to a new internet genre: "dopamine sites", which recreate the rituals of consumption without the consumption. There are fake shopping sites, fake delivery services and even fake holidays. The genre took off inSouth Korea,externaland has since travelled well beyond, spawning a growing crop of sites -Dopamine Shop,externalorFakehaul,external, for example - that mimic everything from food delivery and shopping to travel. What, exactly, are we enjoying when we enjoy buying something? The idea began with the founders' own shopping habits. Parmar and Sharma met on a computer science diploma course and later started NeuroX AI, which builds software and AI products and makes Instagram content. They noticed it in their own lives: online baskets filling up with things they wanted, but never actually bought. Sharma would browse electronics, fill an online basket and abandon it. Parmar's mother did much the same. "She would add things to the cart and say, 'I will order this later'," he recalls. Parmar's own version ended at food delivery checkouts. During a two-month project in Mumbai, he says, he was spending 5,000-10,000 rupees a week on food, sometimes ordering treats he did not necessarily need: Belgian waffles, ice cream and, once, a large jar of sour cream he barely wanted and gave away to friends. He believes "perhaps the real craving was not always for the food, but for the ritual of ordering it". Purvansh Parmar says he spent a lot of money on a work trip on food and treats he did not necessarily need What begins as genuine hunger, the two argue, can become associated with the pleasure of ordering. Over time, boredom, anxiety or habit can trigger the urge even when the hunger has disappeared. "Sometimes you're not hungry at all. You're bored or busy, and then you realise that ordering food makes you feel good. You start associating the act of ordering with that dopamine hit. Eventually, it's not just the food you want," says Parmar. Ravi Dhar, director of the Yale Center for Customer Insights, calls this "anticipatory utility" - the pleasure of looking forward to consumption. It is especially strong with things that capture the imagination - a new pair of shoes, a holiday, a restaurant meal - because anticipation becomes part of the experience. Sometimes, Dhar says, anticipation can be more pleasurable than ownership: "The thrill is in the chase." Once the object is acquired and the tension resolved, psychological arousal falls. Neuroscience has a name for this gap between the chase and the catch, and it complicates a popular idea. Dopamine is not simply the brain's pleasure chemical, whatever the internet's talk of "dopamine hits" might suggest. Swiggy, a popular food delivery site in India, alone handled roughly 2.5m consumer orders a day in FY2025 Kent Berridge, a University of Michigan neuroscientist who developed the theory of "wanting" and "liking", says they are separate processes. Wanting is the motivational pull towards something; liking is the pleasure of having it. They often travel together, but not always. Dopamine, in his account, drives the first, not the second. Tempting food or products online are likely to activate this wanting system, which Berridge calls "incentive salience". "Some situations can trigger 'wanting' by itself," he says. We can pursue something intensely even when the eventual pleasure is weak - or, in more everyday terms, want something more than we ultimately like it. Dr Anna Lembke, a Stanford University addiction psychiatrist and author of Dopamine Nation, makes a similar distinction. "To call dopamine a chemical of pleasure is an oversimplification," she told me. "Dopamine is the molecule that says 'get more of' or 'do more of', but it doesn't necessarily equate to pleasure." TripNeverLeaves lets users plan a holiday before sending them on a virtual flight that never leaves the runway. What she adds is the role of ritual. Cues and habits attached to a reward can become reinforcing in their own right, she says: in addiction, the routines leading up to drug use can eventually matter as much as the drug itself. "Anticipation of reward can be as reinforcing as the reward itself," she says. Can repeatedly ordering imaginary food satisfy a real craving? Berridge says the ritual could produce a "dopamine hit and strong 'wanting', and also evoke faint conditioned 'liking'". But he would expect the "novelty to soon wear off", and would be "surprised" if many people returned to place more than about 10 imaginary orders. Dhar is more open to the possibility that simulated consumption could serve as a kind of release valve. "While we still need more empirical data to know if simulated shopping can satisfy a consumer urge, evidence from simulated consumption in gaming shows it can be highly effective," he says.  A festive sale of of e-commerce site in India featuring Bollywood star Amitabh Bachchan But there is an equally plausible danger: the ritual may simply rehearse the behaviour it is supposed to replace. Lembke says the evidence is not in yet, and the effect may depend on the person. But her own bet is that, over time, the sites could "reinforce the same addictive neural networks they are trying to simulate". "The one up side, though, is that people using these sites have on some level already admitted to themselves they have a problem, and that admission is often the first step in recovery," says Lembke. Sharma ran an accidental experiment of his own. When his phone screen cracked, he spent a week on Amazon comparing six or seven replacements and adding them to his basket. Then he repaired the handset. "I enjoyed the process of research and putting the phones in the cart," he says. "Eventually I didn't buy a phone." He now catches himself doing the same on food delivery sites, particularly when anxious, filling baskets without checking out. "I realised that I suffer from this problem," he says.  TripNeverLeaves lists 260 places 'you won't go' The site's blog explores the "serious side" of the fake takeaway, from food-delivery addiction and why fake ordering feels good to cravings, guilt and the psychology of the shopping cart. The founders have since taken the idea beyond food. A second site, TripNeverLeaves, lets users plan a holiday - destination, flight, seat, hotel and activities - then sends them on a virtual flight that never leaves the runway. They say it has attracted more than 100,000 visitors. Who those visitors are is harder to establish. But Lembke says younger people may be especially vulnerable to reinforcing digital rewards because the "developing brain is a vulnerable brain". "In childhood and early adolescence, the front lobe, which acts like the brakes on appetite, is not yet fully connected to the emotion centres of the brain. Hence, teens are more likely to take risks without appreciating the negative consequences, and more likely to get addicted to reinforcing substances and behaviours, once exposed," she says. For now, the founders say the sites are not about making money. They plan to keep them free and eventually share the data with neuroscientists and psychologists. What looks like a joke about ordering too much food has stumbled into a bigger question about modern consumption: if so much of the thrill comes before we get the thing, do we need the thing at all?

Headline: How the oil capital of the US welcomed a solar power boom
Body: Farmer Steve Cargil is now paid $200,000 a year for hosting a solar farm on his land Steve Cargil's family has farmed the flat, dry land around Uvalde, a small city in southwest Texas, since 1953. Cargil, 67, had always assumed that one of his three children would eventually take it over, the way he had from his father. But that assumption took a hit one night in 2018 after a violent hailstorm. Cargil and his son, Ryan, had spent months nursing crops of cabbage and onions to harvest. Then a storm rolled through and destroyed them overnight. "I remember my son saying, 'Dad, I just don't know if I can do this. You do everything right, and we work so hard, and you come out one morning and it's all gone'," Cargil says. Cargil's farm was at risk of ending with him, he says, with none of his three children wanting to farm full time. For years, that left him wondering what would happen to the land, and to his own retirement, since farmers rarely have a pension to fall back on. Then in 2001 Cargil signed a deal to lease 600 acres of his land, about a quarter of the total, to a company called OCI Energy which built a vast solar farm. "Never in my wildest dreams did I think that a solar project would be on my farm," Cargil says. Looking back now, he calls it a blessing. The lease, which pays Cargil $200,000 (£150,000) a year, has let him keep his farm running through a punishing drought. He has been able to concentrate his water irrigation allowance on the land he still farms, and he has stopped losing sleep over rises in the price of things such as diesel and fertiliser. "It's changed my life." Texas, which remains the largest oil producer in the US, earlier this year overtook California to become the country'sbiggest generator of electricity from solar farms.,external And in March of last year, more electricity was produced by solar in Texas than from coal for the first time, according to the US Energy Information Administration. Solar farms can stretch out across the flat lands of Texas On hot afternoons, when demand for power peaks, solar is now regularly supplying around a third of the electricity used across Texas, says Mark Stover, executive director of the Texas Solar and Storage Association. He says that the solar boom is being driven by two main things. Firstly, it is cheap and quick to connect solar farms to Texas' power grid, which is separate to the rest of the US. Secondly, Texas has a huge and growing appetite for electricity, driven by a burgeoning population. Between 2015 and 2025, Texas's populationincreased by 15.8%,,externalmaking it one of the fastest-growing states in the nation. "We need a whole lot of power in Texas, and we need it quickly," Stover says. Solar has also become inexpensive. James Scott, vice president of project development at OCI, says the technology has had years of small manufacturing gains that brought the price down to the point where it is now the cheapest way to generate power in the state. "No one would have believed that 20 years ago," Scott says. Once a project is built, he says, the price of the electricity it produces can be fixed for decades, since the fuel, sunlight, is free. "We'll charge you $40 a megawatt hour for the next 25 years," Scott says, adding that large buyers such as Amazon and Apple value being able to lock in a price for that long. By contrast, new coal plants in the US produce power at nearly $90 megawatts per hour, says the Energy Information Administration. Farmers have become central to that growth because solar developers need large stretches of flat land. Stover says the industry is now paying out multigenerational income to families through leases that typically run 25 to 30 years and rise in value each year, letting some retire, set up family trusts, or simply keep a farm solvent. Stover argues solar's footprint is smaller than critics assume. "The industry is utilizing less than 0.15% of Texas land," he says. Texas is now the largest producer of solar farm power in the US Yet solar has its opponents. In Franklin County, in northeast Texas, a small group of residents has spent the past few years fighting its growth. BF Hicks, a local lawyer whose family has owned land in the county since the 1800s, says he watched neighbours sign 30-year leases with solar companies and bulldozers clear centuries-old oak trees near his property. He describes a summer when smoke from burning cleared land hung over his town for weeks. "It got real personal," he says, when a solar farm was built next to his family's cemetery. His relatives have been buried here dating back two centuries. David Truesdale, a retired federal law enforcement agent who moved to the county to get away from city life, says he became involved after learning that a neighbouring solar project would sit near his home. And that under Texan law no environmental review was required. "We're destroying the world as we're trying to save it," Truesdale says of the land clearing he has seen. He also points to the large lithium-ion battery units installed alongside many solar farms, drawing a comparison to fires that have occasionally engulfed similar batteries in electric bikes. "If one of those things catches fire, they go off in series, so each one will progressively cause another one to go off," he says. Lawyer BF Hicks fights the building of new solar farms Both men say their objections are not about politics. Franklin County is solidly conservative, but its residents helped push through one of the state's first county-level moratoriums on new solar construction, before it was later rescinded under legal pressure from developers. Their complaints echo a broader unease that has followed solar's expansion into rural Texas - worries about visual impact, water runoff after land is cleared, and battery storage units that scorch their land. President Trump has called solar and wind power "farmer destroying" and moved to unwind tax credits for renewable projects. Yet Fabrizio Lee and Associates, the polling firm used by President Trump, found back in February that 68% of Republican voters believe the country needs "all forms of electricity generation, including utility solar"to keep costs down.,external Stover says he has found broad support in the Republican-controlled Texas state legislature. "There is an acceptance that these technologies bring reliability benefits to the grid," he says. Back in Uvalde, Steve Cargil says that while he has no plans to retire any time soon, he is more positive that the farm might make it to a fifth generation after all, now that the solar farm has put a floor under its finances. "You're better off being lucky than being smart," Cargil says, echoing something his father used to tell him. "And this was one of those cases where I was just lucky." Headline: PM pledges £210m to regenerate UK's high streets
Body: The prime minister said money would be allocated to rescue buildings at risk of closure The prime minister has announced a £210m package to regenerate the UK's communities and high streets. Empty spaces will be put back into use, Andy Burnham said, turning them into "community hubs, health centres, shared workspaces, cafés and the local services that people actually want to see." The scheme is part of funding earmarked by the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government for high street support and regeneration. It comes ahead of Burnham's first Labour Party conference as prime minister, where he is set to emphasise his plans for the UK will have "making life more affordable" at its core. As part of Burnham's high streets scheme, a £125 million derelict buildings fund will be available to transform mothballed and dilapidated buildings. And an £85m pot will enable communities to take over neglected spaces including pubs, clubs and shops, the government said. There will also be £65m allocated to rescuing businesses and buildings at risk of closure, and a further £20m allocated to help communities set up co-operative businesses and let out empty units. The prime minister said: "People don't measure growth by looking at a spreadsheet. They measure it by looking at their local high street. Are shops opening or are the shutters down? Does the place feel like it's moving forward or being left behind? "Today's funding will help put power back into the hands of locals who know their area best." Communities Secretary Angela Rayner said the scheme showed the government would mean communities see "boarded-up buildings that have been left to rack and ruin turned into places people are proud to visit again". Meanwhile First Secretary of State Louise Haigh said the investment would give local people the resources they need to make change, adding: "This is what devolution means in practice". The move follows Burnham's announcement in the summer that pubs, clubs and social venues would see20% cuts to business ratesfrom April. But Peter Kyle, business secretary to former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer, suggested Burnhamneeds to act with "more urgency" to boost growth, as the PM arrives in Liverpool for Labour's party conference this weekend. The Conservatives' own plan for "stronger high streets" would abolish business rates for thousands of businesses, and would "defend key pillars of the community such as post offices, pubs and pharmacies", according to the party. Headline: Home secretary hits out at 'unacceptable' migrant landings
Body: This video can not be played Watch: Migrant boat arrives on beach near Folkestone The Home Secretary has said migrant landings on UK beaches are "not acceptable", as she ordered an urgent review after two boats reached Kent without being intercepted. Shabana Mahmood told Border Security Command to carry out the review after vessels came ashore at Samphire Hoe, between Dover and Folkestone, on Tuesday, and near Folkestone on Monday. Twenty-one people were detained on Tuesday after the arrival at Samphire Hoe. Five people were also detained on Mondayafter the uncontrolled landing near Folkestone, the first undetected landing for a year. The Home Office has not said whether more people are being sought. Migrants crossing the Channel are usually brought to shore by Border Security Command or RNLI boats. Before Monday, no small boats had been officially recorded as arriving in the UK without an escort since 6 September 2025. Uncontrolled landings of migrants in the UK, as seen on Monday and Tuesday, are so rare that the incident in 2025 was the only other one recorded since the Home Office began keeping data in 2023. The home secretary has ordered an urgent review after the landings Mahmood said the beach landings were "not acceptable". She said: "Our improved monitoring has led to uncontrolled crossings becoming incredibly rare, but even one is one too many. "That is why I have ordered an urgent review by the Border Security Command into how this happened, and what must be done to ensure it doesn't happen again." She said that new tactics adopted by people smugglers, including launching small boats from much further west in France, were "a reminder of two things". The home secretary said: "Firstly, these gangs have no regard for human life. They are putting people on increasingly long and dangerous crossings. "Secondly, our efforts are having an impact. We are making it much harder for gangs to launch vessels, forcing them to change their approach, and as a result we are significantly reducing the numbers coming here by small boat." Early on Wednesday, migrants were brought to Dover after embarking on a crossing from a village near Bayeux in Normandy to Gosport in Hampshire,spending more than 33 hours at sea. Use all powers necessary on anti-migrant protests, home secretary tells police RNLI reviews security after volunteers targeted online Police must review anti-migrant protests, PM says Chris Philp MP, Shadow Home Secretary, called it "a day of despair" for the Labour government. He said: "Our border security has descended into chaos with illegal immigrants crossing at will over ever larger distances and in ever larger boats." Philp said: "This latest fiasco shows that the French are not even trying to stop the illegal immigrants' boats in French waters, instead they are escorting them here." "What's more, there have been two uncontrolled migrant landings in a week. It is a complete free for all – the Labour government have no idea who is coming into the country. "The only way to stop Channel crossings is to deport anyone who arrives illegally to their home country or a safe third country. That's the only way we can end this madness." A boat came ashore near Folkestone in one of two uncontrolled landings in two days Earlier, a government spokesperson said: "Border Security Command officers alongside Kent Police have been responding to an incident in Dover. "Twenty-one individuals have already been detained under a swift enforcement response. "There is a thorough investigation ongoing and it would be inappropriate to comment further." Officials said those who had been detained had been taken to Western Jet Foil for processing. The uncontrolled arrivals come after Border Security Command suggested they were a thing of the past, because of new surveillance technology and improved resources. Earlier this year, Reform UK set outa proposal to call in the Royal Navy to help intercept migrants, but it was rejected. On Tuesday, 154 migrants arrived in three boats, of which one was an uncontrolled landing. It takes the total of migrants to have arrived in the UK this year to 17,784. The total so far this year is down 44.7% compared with figures for 22 September 2025, at which point 32,188 migrants had arrived that year. Headline: NHS to suspend staff suspected of snooping on patient records
Body: NHS staff in England suspected of looking at patient records without a valid reason will be immediately suspended as part of a "zero-tolerance crackdown" on snooping. Those under suspicion will also be locked out of NHS computer systems, preventing any further viewing of confidential records, including from home. NHS England chief executive Sir Jim Mackey has written to every trust, ordering the measures to be introduced immediately to strengthen protection against data breaches. The move follows a series of high-profile incidents involving the records ofNottinghamandSouthport attackvictims anda child who was injured in a crocodile enclosure in Cambridgeshire. This week, Bristol Foundation NHS Trust said it had launched an internal investigation after it emergedthe medical records of an 18-year-old had been accessed years after his death. The boy's mother, Paula McGowan, told the BBC she was "deeply concerned and hurt" and called for the NHS to do more to deal with the problem. Oliver McGowan, pictured here with his mother Paula, died in 2016 after being prescribed anti-psychotic medication at Southmead Hospital in Bristol The NHS said the "hardline" approach is part of a wider crackdown, including the launch of a national campaign to "remind staff of their responsibilities and the serious consequences of unlawful access". "Patient records contain some of the most private information people will ever share," said NHS England's chief executive Sir Jim Mackey. "We have seen too many cases of people abusing that trust, and enough is enough. "Anyone who thinks they can satisfy their curiosity by looking at a patient's record should know this: they will be found out, they may lose their career and could end up with a criminal record." This month, an investigation for the Health Services Journal found that at least 214 NHS staff have lost their jobs and around 2,000 been sanctioned for snooping on sensitive patient data over the past five years. In some cases, it emerged staff were curious about a high-profile patient and wanted to know more about their condition or care. Other staff have been struck off after looking up the medical records of relations, acquaintances and ex-partners without authorisation. In 2023 an NHS consultant in Cambridgeshire was investigated by the General Medical Council (GMC) after accessing the health history of a woman who had started dating the doctor's ex-boyfriend. There is no single NHS-wide electronic record system that every member of staff can access. Instead, organisations including GP practices, hospitals and specialist clinics maintain their own records and determine who can view particular information. IT systems keep an audit trail that should be able to show exactly who accessed a patient's records and when. Paula McGowan, whose autistic son Oliver died in 2016, was told that at least five members of staff at Southmead Hospital may have accessed his records without permission as recently as this year. Bristol NHS Foundation Trust said it was undertaking a "thorough investigation" and it would be "inappropriate to reach conclusions before those enquiries are complete". McGowan said she welcomed the NHS's commitment to tackling the problem but said it must now be followed by "meaningful action". "Medical records contain deeply personal information about people and their families," she said. "Accessing them without a legitimate clinical or professional reason is a serious breach of trust and must have consequences." Headline: Why did an OpenAI system hack Australia's health system - and can it be stopped in the future?
Body: This video can not be played Watch: What you need to know about the OpenAI Australian government hack An OpenAI agent has gone "rogue" and "infiltrated" an Australian government website in what cyber-security experts are calling the first hack of its kind. But why did it take the government months to discover what happened - and could it happen again? The hack was carried out by an AI agent - an autonomous computer program that uses AI to complete a task with minimal human oversight. On 18 June one of OpenAI's agents went rogue during a test exercise - the company has said it was supposed to "look up answers, and available statistics for questions about Australia during an internal evaluation". In the process it "infiltrated" a private statistics portal containing "non-sensitive" data from Australia's universal healthcare scheme Medicare, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said. OpenAI said it only realised the breach had happened at all in August while reviewing "misaligned model activity", and the company sent an email to a generic Australian government inbox some weeks later. That email seems to have gone unnoticed for five days before it was escalated to Australia's cyber-security experts on 10 September. The prime minister described the breach as "obviously unacceptable" and said OpenAI took "way too long" to inform Australian officials. Analysts have also raised concerns over OpenAI's almost three-month delay in noticing and reporting the breach via email. "The way the notice arrived bothers me as much as the delay," chief data and AI officer Simon Liu from cyber-security firm TrustDecision told the BBC. OpenAI is the company behind the popular ChatGPT servie Australia has said this incident is the first of its kind, and experts agree it might be. As far as we know, hacks carried out by AI agents are still quite rare occurrences - but then again, it is largely up to companies themselves to disclose them. Hacks like this have happened before. In July, OpenAI agents went rogue during a test andinfiltrated tech start-up Hugging Face's internal systems. The AI agents decided that ignoring the limits on what should be done to achieve their goal was the best course of action. This is what the industry calls "misalignment" - broadly defined as when AI machines do not act in humanity's best interests, such as by bending the rules. It is a problem that is fundamental to making AI safe, and it is proving challenging. To put it simply, the type of AI models at play here - known as large language models - are designed to predict the likeliest output to a given input, rather than consider the consequences of that output as a human would. Companies attempt to prevent negative consequences by placing "guardrails" on the AI but, as the Australian government found out, that is not always enough. Dr Hammond Pearce, senior lecturer at the University of New South Wales Institute for Cyber Security, told the BBC this sort of hack would likely "grow in severity and in frequency", adding: "I do hope that this incident does start ringing alarm bells in governments around the world." Niusha Shafiabady, professor of computational intelligence at the Australian Catholic University, said this incident had shown the need to "judge autonomous AI by its behaviour under pressure, not by the promises in a product launch". "The deeper technical risk is that autonomous AI does not always know when it is wrong, and humans may not be able to see why it made a decision," she said. "Without strong verification and hard boundaries, probabilistic errors can quietly become operational failures." The explosive rise of AI has left governments scrambling to put protective measures in place, with some calling for companies to be forced to build ways to disable their own tech into its systems. One idea backed by some AI firms andlawmakersis a "kill switch" - a way to simply to turn the tech off in a crisis. OpenAI isreportedly,externalalready working to build automated tools which can shut down its systems if needed. Speaking to BBC Radio 4's Today programme, former deputy prime minister and Facebook executive Sir Nick Clegg said the kill switch remains an unproven idea. "There isn't a room with a little fuse box [where] you just pull out the fuse and everything winds down," he said, with AI tools underpinned by global infrastructure. Cyber-security experts said the systems protecting Australia's Medicare were just not strong enough, and a skilled human hacker could have got around them. But other experts say that is not the point - and that this was the latest case of AI agents ignoring laws around how to safely access online information, and perhaps the most serious yet given the information was under government control. Why are there concerns AI could threaten humanity, and how real are they? How to stop AI agents going rogue As warnings mount about the potentially devastating impact of AI, many in the industry and in governments around the world are openly wondering about what national and international regulations might be needed to keep it in check. Meanwhile some scientists, experts andworkershave dismissed the bleak projections as vague, hypothetical, or an effort by large AI developers to ensure their dominance. As it stands, AI companies largely regulate themselves - but this week, 20 nations, including Australia and Canada, signed a joint statement calling for better safeguards, globally consistent standards, and an international regulator off the back of these concerns. However, the US and China, two nations at the forefront of AI development,have so far resisted calls for greater regulation, raising questions over whether this hack will be the first of many, or the wake up call many experts want it to be. "The immediate harm here appears limited, but the governance lesson is not," says Dr Raffaele Fabio Ciriello, senior lecturer in business information systems at the University of Sydney. "As AI agents become more capable and autonomous, those capabilities need to be matched by proportionate containment, real-time monitoring, clear accountability, independent oversight, and much faster incident reporting." Headline: ‘Hell on earth’: last residents eat weeds to survive in Russian-occupied Oleshky
Body: Ukrainian forces airdrop supplies to city where bodies are left to be eaten by dogs because of deadly risk from drones The phone message sent out of Russian-occupied Oleshky was grimly matter-of-fact: food had finally run out for the 2,000 or so civilians, including 50 children, remaining in the city and its surrounding villages. “We’re in Oleshky [and] we can’t get out. We’re going hungry … Right now, I’ve got absolutely nothing to eat,” read the message from a woman in the besieged city who was waiting to be evacuated by the occupying forces. Before the war, she had weighed 110kg (17st); now she weighed just 67kg, she wrote. “At first I was glad [to lose some weight], but now I realise I’ll die without proper protein-rich food. It’s very hard. The house where we stayed last winter was also destroyed and burned down. Just like our own home … We’re still alive.” Oleshky, across the Dnipro River from the southern city of Kherson, has become “a hell on earth”, according to Ukrainians familiar with conditions there. This weekend, military authorities in Kherson carried out a large-scale airdrop of emergency food, water and medical supplies into the city and surrounding areas, using large drones, after Russia reportedly again rejected a ceasefire to evacuate civilians. The military governor’s office in Kherson said an operation had dropped about four tonnes of food to 100 locations, but it was unclear how much the Russian military had intercepted. The Ukrainian foreign minister, Andrii Sybiha, raised the situation in Oleshky at the UN general assembly in New York this week. A“Save Oleshky” bannerwas lifted at a Ukraine-Hungary Nations League football match on Friday. In a statement published on Monday, Sybiha warned of a “humanitarian catastrophe” and called for an immediate evacuation, accusing Russia of standing as “the only obstacle”. He said in an address during the general assembly: “Russia is deliberately making life there impossible. They are starving them to death.” The Kremlin spokesperson, Dmitry Peskov, this month acknowledged the “critical situation” in Oleshky but accused Ukrainian forces of blocking humanitarian supplies intended for its residents. Until May, food supplies were still getting through to residents of a city that had once been home to 24,000. But since May, as the occupying Russian forces expanded minefields and drone cover, the trickle of supplies has entirely halted. Compounding the issue for civilians is the fact that Ukraine’s highly successful summer drone campaign against Russian supply lines has caused shortages for the invading forces’ frontline troops, who in turn steal what little food Ukrainian civilians have managed to save. In messages shared with the Guardian, residents said they were down to one meal a day: soup without potato, made with courgette grown in what once were the flower boxes of the city’s apartment houses, sometimes with the addition of foraged purslane, an edible weed. “We’re running out of everything,” said a resident early in the summer. “By August, the situation will be critical for us. And come autumn, we’ll definitely die. I’m already dying. I’m getting weaker by the day.” On 1 September, a food convoy heading to the city was attacked. Moscow blamed the Ukrainian armed forces for the attack, while Kyiv blamed Russian troops. Ukrainian officials say attempts to drop food by drones have done little to help: the supplies are seized by Russian soldiers and in at least one case the intended recipient was arrested. Commenting on the airdrop over the weekend, Kherson’s military governor, Oleksandr Prokudin, described it as the largest operation of its kind so far. “Food was delivered directly to 100 distribution points. And now I would like to address the Russians,” he said. “Civilians have absolutely nothing to do with the Ukrainian armed forces. Because of the conditions you have created in Oleshky, people simply have no choice but to take food. Do not deprive people of the chance to survive and avoid starvation. “Russia, as the occupying power, is obliged to provide people with food, medicines and adequate conditions for healthcare and hygiene. If its own resources are insufficient, the occupying authorities must consent to humanitarian operations by international organisations and other states. Instead, we are seeing the opposite.” He continued: “Russian occupying forces are obstructing the provision of aid to the civilian population. They are destroying vehicles attempting to deliver humanitarian supplies. And they are killing people trying to bring in food and medicines. They are also blocking all initiatives and agreements regarding the evacuation of people from Oleshky.” According to Tetiana Hasanenko, a Ukrainian official serving from the western side of the Dnipro as the head of the Oleshky military administration, problems began in earnest late last year as access to the city from the Russian side for Ukrainian civilians became ever more difficult. “The density of the minefields has become very high,” she told the Guardian. “From December onwards, food deliveries became much less frequent because vehicles were hitting mines and being targeted by drones. By winter, supplying food had already become very difficult. “And it’s already been very hard. There’s no other infrastructure, electricity, therefore no ATMs, no cash. Oleshky isn’t functioning. People used to grow food in their vegetable plots before the war. There was not only enough for themselves but they used to sell it to Crimea and Kherson city. Now they cannot even grow it for themselves.” Hasanenko described a reported incident where a 74-year-old man was digging out a cellar that had been flooded with mud after Russiablew up the Kakhovka damin 2023, looking for stored food. Refusing to allow the soldiers into the cellar he was excavating, he was murdered by the soldiers. “Some people have been digging out these cellars looking for canned vegetables, pickled vegetables and canned meat that people were storing up for winter,” she said. Despite the horrific conditions in the city, Ukrainian officials believe the occupying forces are dragging their feet with the evacuation of the remaining civilians in order to discourage a Ukrainian counterattack. Hasanenko said: “The Russians are afraid that an offensive [against Oleshky] will start from Kherson city and they are just keeping people, civilians, as human shields.” She added: “It’s an old city. It has existed for almost a thousand years – and in all this time, people never lived in such horrible conditions, in such a hell like they do now. There are dead bodies not only in the basement of the hospital, but all over the city. They’re just lying there because you cannot pick up the dead body. The drones are flying constantly and then the dogs are eating the bodies.” In a text message, another resident said simply: “All supplies are running out.” Another messaged: “A week ago, the orcs [a Ukrainian term of abuse to describe Russian soldiers] came into people’s yards and dug up all the potatoes, onions, and garlic. “They took all the food supplies from the elderly women. When one of the grandmothers started shouting, they replied that people ‘soon to be living in heaven’ like them should subsist on nothing but water.”

Headline: Inside the FBI hack: Agents fearful and angry after 'dangerous' data breach
Body: Current and former FBI agents have spoken to BBC News of their shock, fear and anger following a hack thatappears to have exposedthe private and personal information of the agency's entire workforce. "This is really bad for our undercover agents," says one former FBI agent, who fears for the safety of his colleagues. The former cyber investigator is in a group chat with current agents who are worried their personal information could soon be freely available online to criminals and hostile nation-state hackers. He says staff fear they could be targeted, or that criminals could use the data to create highly convincing phishing attempts, scams or demands for bribes. The hacking group ShinyHunters is threatening to publish the stolen databases and documents within four days unless its demands are met. Some agents are also concerned about the risk of physical attacks from cyber criminals they have investigated. "One of the things we are discussing in the group chat is 'violence-as-a-service' attacks from young online gangs," says the former worker. "They could use this information to harass an FBI agent who has worked on their cases." Groups similar to ShinyHunters - believed to be an English-speaking gang - have in the past been linked to swatting incidents, and even petrol bomb attacks against law enforcement officers and rivals. Swatting is a phenomenon so-called because perpetrators make calls that prompt armed police units - called Swat teams in the US - to swoop in on victims. The group claims it breached FBI systems on Monday and later posted details of the attack on its darknet site. The FBI has not responded to requests for comment. However, on Wednesday the agency acknowledged the breach - saying it was "aggressively investigating" how it occurred. For Michael McPherson, a former FBI agent who is now senior vice president of security operations at cyber firm ReliaQuest, the hack presents "a security threat which cuts to the core of agent safety, particularly their families". He says agents understand the "inherent risks" that come with the job. "But this incident reportedly includes personal data such as home addresses and contact information, which could expose family members who are normally insulated from the threats associated with such a career," McPherson says. ShinyHunters shared samples of the alleged stolen data with reporters, along with an extortion demand. The samples appear genuine and include names, addresses, phone numbers, badge numbers, job titles and information about spouses. The records appear to relate to thousands of agents, including senior officials such as deputy directors. The criminals also appear to possess highly sensitive medical information relating to thousands of special agents. BBC News has seen samples of stolen "fitness-for-work"medical examinations containing information such as blood and urine test results, along with doctors' notes mentioning conditions including a "shellfish and banana allergy". Agents' full names and addresses, as well as references to medical issues including "blood in the urine" and "high cholesterol" are now in the criminals' hands. Cynthia Kaiser, who was the Deputy Director of Cyber at the FBI and now leads the Research Centre at Halcyon says ShinyHunters appear to already have lost control of some of the data which is circulating in various online groups of cyber researchers and could lead to harm even before the main tranche is published. "A lot of the damage may already be done, and as we have seen in past FBI data breaches, that information continues to circulate the dark web years later," she said. There are also concerns about the breach's national security implications, such as staff becoming targets for recruitment efforts by hostile foreign intelligence services. Alongside fear, many of those who spoke to the BBC expressed anger at the FBI for allowing the data to be stolen. The hack is particularly embarrassing from a technical perspective because ShinyHunters is not generally regarded as a highly sophisticated hacking group. One former cyber agent said FBI staff were furious about the "sloppy and lazy security failures" that allegedly enabled the breach. There is also confusion about how to handle any fallout if data is published next week, as threatened. The FBI appears unlikely to comply with the extortion demands, and the hackers have indicated they intend to post the information on their darknet site. Unusually, the group is not demanding money. Instead, it wants the FBI to retract an advisory published in May, which it claims "offended" them. "The agency leadership is lost," the former cyber investigator tells me. He says staff have been advised to sign up to a service called DeleteMe, which helps remove personal information from data broker websites - a response he feels is inadequate. The hack may raise further questions for FBI director Kash Patel, whose leadership has already faced scrutiny According to another former agent, there is widespread shock that such a breach could happen at one of the world's best-resourced law enforcement agencies. "You would think this information would not be internet-exposed. It's disturbing, actually," he says. There is also embarrassment that a prolific group of young cyber criminals has repeatedly managed to evade law enforcement while carrying out a string of high-profile hacks. ShinyHunters has been linked to numerous extortion attacks, including on Rockstar Games andthe education platform Canvas. The group regularly communicates with reporters via Telegram, where members often boast about their activities. "The bureau doesn't know what to do with teenage cyber criminals," one former agent says. McPherson says there is no doubt the FBI is taking the incident extremely seriously. He expects the agency to draw on its extensive network of partners and resources "to make this group suffer the consequences for this brazen and taunting attack". Kaiser added that the hackers have been "reckless and foolish" and warned them to expect "a significant effort by the FBI to quickly bring them to justice." Headline: Greens aim for first London MP in Holborn race
Body: Camden Town is at the heart of Holborn and St Pancras constituency On 8 October, voters in the Holborn and St Pancras constituency will choose their next MP. A win in this seat, which has returned Labour MPs for decades, would be a feather in the cap of the Green Party after Sir Keir Starmer stood down from the House of Commons at the start of September, shortly after leaving office as prime minister. Labour are confident of holding on, but the Greens also have high hopes of winning their first London seat - and there are 13 other candidates in the mix all hoping to take this central London constituency. BBC London spoke to five of the leading candidates. Zack Polanski says people in the constituency want change Zack Polanski, the Green Party candidate, told BBC London he was "feeling confident or I wouldn't have put my hat in the ring in the first place, but I'm not complacent". He said he would "work with the Labour government constructively on the things we agree with". He added: "But where they're letting us down on things like housing, on nationalising Thames Water, on tackling the climate crisis - they're talking about drilling for new oil and gas - voting Green and sending me to Parliament is a way to keep this Labour government in check." Polanski, who is a member of the London Assembly and leader of the Green Party in England and Wales, said people in the constituency "desperately need change". "People are telling me over and over again they can't afford the cost of housing, they need more council housing. "Renters who need rent control, leaseholders who need justice for leaseholders. The government said they'd end this feudal system of leasehold and then haven't taken the action." When asked about the last time he ran in Camden, as a Liberal Democrat candidate for the council, he said: "I think in politics we need less politicians who treat political parties like football teams. "Someone picks a team and they have to stick with it for life no matter what they do. "Actually, there's lots of people including Liberal Democrats in this constituency that will recognise I'm the only person in this constituency who can beat Labour." Sagal Abdi-Wali has been the leader of Camden Council since May Sagal Abdi-Wali, Labour's candidate, said the campaign had been "really good" so far. She told BBC London: "It's quite a big deal politically, absolutely, "Andy Burnham's first by-election, standing against the Green Party leader; yeah, quite a big test for the party... you have the responsibility to deliver." Abdi-Wali, whose family came to London from Somalia as refugees in the 1990s when she was a child, has been the leader of Camden Council since May. She told BBC London: "For me, I'm just so excited. "We've got an opportunity to make sure that we send a Labour member of Parliament that would be really local and really visible and committed to this area, someone who comes from this area. "I grew up in this area my whole life. It's made me, Camden made me who I am, and to be able to now represent us in Parliament will be such a major thing." Abdi-Wali acknowledged there were problems with housing and crime in the constituency. "I want to make sure that particularly with housing, for instance, it's an issue. It's a crisis here in Camden. It's a crisis in London. It's a crisis all over the country and it needs a national response." Abdi-Wali praised the former MP, Sir Keir. "The work that Keir did as the member of Parliament for here for 11 years and before that the 30 years that he gave to social justice. "Now with Andy Burnham, we have an opportunity to really work on a lot of those issues." Reform UK's Peter Newman says voters are worried about crime Peter Newman, the Reform UK candidate, said he served in the Metropolitan Police for 31 years from 1978 to 2009. He told BBC London: "I had a good and varied career, but you know the time has come when, you know, woke leadership was getting too far into the Met." Newman said he was standing because "I couldn't walk by any more". "The chaos of the Conservatives and Labour that have left this country in, I had to do something. "Reform is the only option for the people of Holborn and St Pancras, the only option in fact for the country." He said the party was "picking up votes all the time in local elections". "We're improving our percentages in London all the time, and we've got a tough election. And the people of Holborn and St Pancras, they want change. "They've been let down by Keir Starmer, who clearly used it as a stepping stone just to become prime minister." He says on the doorstep, voters are telling him "they're fed up with the crime, disorder. This borough is crime-ridden. It's soaked in crime." If elected, Newman said he would be "relentless in pursuing the police chiefs and the mayor of London and his policing advisers in finding out what's gone wrong with policing in London". Liberal Democrat candidate Patrick Stillman says the party are community champions Lib Dem candidate Patrick Stillman said his party's ground game in the by-election was helping it reintroduce itself. He told BBC London: "We've got a really good liberal message: we care about the things you care about, and we're going to work really hard for you." Stillman is a Camden councillor, representing West Hampstead in the north of the borough. The party led a joint Conservative-Lib Dem administration when the council was under no overall control from 2006 to 2010. He said the by-election "is our opportunity really to sort of re-represent ourselves and say, 'Actually, you know, look at the great work our team are doing, look at the great things we're saying in Parliament - wouldn't you like a bit of that here?'" Stillman added: "We find community champions, we get leaflets through doors, we talk to people on their doorstep about what matters to them. "That revolves around a lot of good activists, and sometimes it's a case of if you don't do something in an area for a while those people fade away and move away and then you find yourself a bit more boxed in. "For us that's what I'm really excited about. With Holborn and St Pancras is a chance to get back on the doors, to get back into communities, to get back picking up issues of local people and saying, 'We'll champion them for you.'" Conservative candidate Ewan Cameron says the constituency is no longer family-friendly Ewan Cameron, the Conservative candidate, said he was the only candidate in the by-election talking about the housing crisis. He told BBC London: "My opponents, what are they doing? They're talking about segregation. They're on the ballot paper, they want to have religion. Religion's not what we should be discussing. "We should be in a position where every day, whether you're Jewish, whether you're Muslim, whether you have no faith, we all have the same issues. And again and again those issues are, what? "Holborn and St Pancras is no longer family-friendly, there's not enough family homes." Cameron, who was a Camden councillor for the Belsize ward from 1998 to 2002 and sat on the council's development control committee, said crime was another priority in his campaign. "If you come out of work at night and walk home and you don't feel safe, who do you blame? I blame Labour. Labour has been the local MP, they have control of the local council, you've got Sadiq Khan who's the local Labour mayor; again and again London's not safe. "The fact that the police sometimes come, but not always. But the blatant, the blatantness of the theft, it leaves you speechless." Cameron added: "Camden [Council] sits on its hands and my biggest concern is the fact that if Labour win Holborn and St Pancras, they'll just be complacent." The Holborn and St Pancras by-election will be held on Thursday 8 October. A full list of all the candidates can be found here. Headline: 105-year-old investigated for crimes at Nazi PoW camp in Germany
Body: Thirty thousand Soviet prisoners of war are buried at Stalag 326 in Senne German prosecutors are investigating a man aged 105 over allegations that he was an accessory to multiple counts of murder at a Nazi prisoner of war camp in World War Two. The suspect is alleged to have been a camp guard at Stalag 326 VI K in Senne in northwestern Germany. A similar case had also been under way involving a second former camp guard at Senne, Dortmund public prosecutor Sonja Frodermann said in a statement. That suspect died a few months ago at the age of 99, she said. No further details about the two former guards have been made public, however the two cases highlight the difficulties faced by prosecutors who continue to investigate Nazi-era crimes, with most of the remaining suspects already dead. More than 5.3 million soldiers from the Soviet Red Army were held in German captivity during World War Two and half are thought to have died. Many of those who did survive were treated as traitors on their return home. But the PoW camp, or Stalag, at Senne was one of the biggest. One in three Soviet PoWs entering Nazi Germany between 1941 and 1945 went through the complex at Senne, according to the memorial site, and they often ended up doing forced labour in the wider region. Living conditions at Stalag were horrific, and prisoners faced appalling mistreatment and malnutrition. Of the 180,000-200,000 Soviet prisoners of war registered there, many died and tens of thousands are buried there. PoWs from France, Poland, Serbia and Belgium were also held at Senne. More than 9,000 Soviet prisoners of war were alive in the camp at the time of liberation in 1945 The prosecutor made clear the investigation surrounding the 105-year-old was still under way and that the allegations of being an accessory to multiple murders related to his activities at Stalag 36. There has been no statute of limitations in Germany for either murder or accessory to murder since 1979, to enable the prosecution of Nazi-era crimes. Another centenarian camp guard from the Hemer Stalag VI A camp is also said to be under investigation. However, bringing perpetrators to justice more than 80 years after the war is now fraught with difficulty. Four years ago a 101-year-old concentration camp guard was given a five-year jail term for complicity in murder at Sachsenhausen. Josef Schütz was the oldest Nazi criminal ever brought to justice. He never served time in jail and died in 2023while appealing his sentence. A former Nazi concentration camp secretary was convicted in 2022 of abetting murder and given a suspended jail term. She died last year aged 99. Although prosecution of Nazi crimes is handled by the public prosecutors in the western city of Dortmund, cases are initially taken on by the central office for Nazi crime investigations in Ludwigsburg in the south-west. Headline: The young women guiding tourists through India's night sky
Body: Padma Chamchot, Tsering Yangdol, Tsering Dolker and Palzes Angmo (left to right) - Hanle's astro-ambassadors, trained to guide visitors through the night sky It's 10pm and bitterly cold in Hanle. Strong winds sweep across this remote village in India's Himalayan Ladakh region, but no one seems to mind. Dinner is over, yet, instead of bed, many people are gathering outside. The reason is above them. At 14,764ft (4,500m) above sea level, Hanle is known for itsexceptionally clear, dark skies. Wrapped in thick jackets, woollen caps and gloves, tourists and visitors gather to see the Milky Way and look through telescopes at planets, the Moon and distant stars. Among them are four young women: Palzes Angmo, Tsering Dolker, Tsering Yangdol and Padma Chamchot. They are Hanle's astro-ambassadors, trained to guide visitors through the night sky. By day, they cook meals, clean rooms and look after guests at their family-run homestays. By night, they set up telescopes, trace constellations with laser pointers and explain what visitors are seeing in the dark skies. These women - all in their late 20s - grew up watching these stars, but it was only a few years ago that they learnt to study them through a telescope. "The sky here has always been twinkling like this," 28-year-old Dolker says. The difference today is thatpeople travel hundredsof kilometres to see what locals have long regarded as an ordinary part of life. The Indian Astronomical Observatory is one of the world's highest sites for astronomical observation Hanle's remote, high-altitude location, dry air and lack of light pollution make its skies prized by astronomers. The cold desert offers suitable observing conditions on around 260 nights a year. Hanle is also home to the Indian Astronomical Observatory, run by the Indian Institute of Astrophysics, and is a major centre for astronomical research. In 2022, it became India's first Dark Sky Reserve, helping protect its pristine skies from artificial light and putting Hanle on the astronomy tourism map. Visitor numbers have since surged: from about 3,000 a year five years ago to nearly 30,000 in 2024-25, according to government figures. As visitors grew, so did opportunities for locals. In 2022, the Ladakh administration and Indian Institute of Astrophysics trained 24 young people from Hanle and nearby villages in astronomy. These four women were among them. Over 15 days, they learnt to identify stars, planets and constellations, navigate the night sky, operate telescopes and photograph the Milky Way on their phones. Becoming astronomy guides was never part of their plans. They were nervous when they first handled the equipment, fearing they might break something. Gradually, they learnt how it worked and grew confident using it. Hanle was designated as India's first dark sky reserve in 2022 Four years on, they are confident astronomers, with evenings beginning around 9pm. They position telescopes for the night's planets and constellations before guiding visitors from local homestays. They show them the Moon's craters, Saturn's rings, Vega - the brightest star in the night sky - and other planets, using laser pointers to trace constellations and objects visible to the naked eye. Then comes the Milky Way. At 11pm each night, the village switches off its lights, plunging Hanle into darkness as visitors scramble to photograph the now-brilliant galaxy. "When people look through the telescope and capture a photo alongside the Milky Way, they experience immense joy. We also help them with their mobile phone settings so they can capture the Milky Way," Padma Chamchot says. It often starts with helping one visitor take a picture and ends with a long queue. The women take pictures for their own social media too, comparing notes on the stars and other sights they captured that night. The women also point laser at the sky to help visitors spot stars visible to the naked eye But by day, life is more ordinary. Hanle has few hotels and no resorts, so visitors mostly stay in family-run homestays, often extensions of their homes. Chamchot's family runs one too. "Taking care of guests, cooking meals, cleaning rooms, and managing household chores fills our day," she says. "From nine in the evening, we begin setting up the telescopes for the night's stargazing sessions." Their families' homestays remain the main income source, but the women earn about 25,000 rupees ($260; £193) a month from astronomy, charging 200 rupees a session. Income dips during the harsh winter, when few tourists visit, but the earnings have given them greater financial independence: they no longer need to ask their parents for money. "We can save our earnings and spend them on things we want - including new phones," Padma says. For the astro-ambassadors, the transformation has been personal as much as financial. "Before taking on this work, we lacked confidence," they say. However, the growing popularity of Hanle comes with risks. The same tourism that supports local livelihoods could also threaten the darkness that makes Hanle unique. Rapid construction and rising tourism also poses a threat to Hanle's dark skies Visitor numbers have surged, fuelled partly by social media posts about Hanle's night skies and its location on the route to Umling La, which is among the world's highest motorable mountain passes. But more tourists also mean more traffic, construction and artificial light - all threats to the darkness they come to see. Sonam Jorphail, a senior engineer and head of outreach at the IAO, says tourism is creating jobs and driving development in Hanle, but growth must be managed to protect its dark skies. "They bridge the gap between the science community and common people - locals and visitors," Jorphail adds. But longtime residents say Hanle's night sky is already changing. Padma's father, Dhuntup Chamchot, in his 70s, remembers when the skies were even darker. "Back then, when the weather was good, people would often sleep outdoors under the open sky," he says. The young women often take their families stargazing too. "We frequently show the night sky to our families through the telescope. They enjoy looking at it now," says Yangdol, one of the astro-ambassadors. "If one of us takes even a single day off, the families ask why the telescope was not set up," she jokes. The women say they have no desire to leave Hanle or its dark skies. They hope for advanced training and better telescopes and eyepieces to enhance visitors' experience. Four years ago, the equipment was unfamiliar; now, they are building a future around the stars.

Headline: Hurricane Polo downgraded but remains 'very powerful' off coast of Mexico
Body: This video can not be played Did El Niño turn Hurricane Polo into the most powerful storm of the season? Hurricane Polo, a large storm off the coast of Mexico, has been downgraded to category 4 but remains "very powerful", the US National Hurricane Center said. The Pacific hurricane, one of the strongest of the season, was projected to head towards the coast of south-western Mexico, bringing intense wind and rain, though was not expected to make landfall. A Hurricane Hunter aircraft, operated by the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (Noaa), flew into the storm on Tuesday and recorded sustained wind speeds near 180 mph (285 km/h), with stronger gusts. The slow-moving storm is being fuelled by extremely warm waters caused by the El Niño climate phenomenon. It was previously a category 5 storm - the highest level on the scale - but was downgraded to category 4 on Wednesday morning. Forecasters said that the storm was expected to fluctuate in intensity over the next few days. As it slowly drifts north west, Polo will drive torrential rainfall in parts of Mexico's south-west coast, and "may produce life-threatening flooding and mudslides, especially in areas of steep terrain," the forecaster said. Forecasters said heavy rainfall associated with Polo could impact coastal regions in southwest Mexico through Thursday. A tropical storm warning remains in effect for portions of southwest Mexico and a tropical storm watch is in effect west of Playa Perula, the National Hurricane Center said. The hurricane centre said people under a tropical storm warning should expect conditions to develop on Wednesday, and those in the watch areas can expect conditions to develop by Thursday. Rainfall totals of up to 6in (15cm) are forecast, with 8in possible in some areas. Residents have also been warned of large ocean swells and life-threatening surf conditions for the next few days. "So far, the information we have is that (Polo) will not make a direct landfall on the coast," Mexico's President Claudia Sheinbaum said on Tuesday, but she warned residents along the Pacific coast to be vigilant. Sheinbaum highlighted the states of Jalisco, Colima and Michoacan as being at risk. So far this season, the Pacific has seen 15 storms, all in early September. Polo is the strongest of a batch of three storms currently swirling between Hawaii and the North American mainland. Data from the Hurricane Hunter aircraft indicated that Polo could still strengthen, because of what NOAA called a "very conducive" environment of extremely warm ocean waters feeding the storm. Members of the National Guard patrol a beach as Mexico prepares for Hurricane Polo Scientists monitoring the ocean temperatures say the current El Niño climate phenomenon is now the strongest on record. Daily sea surface temperatures in a key region of the central-eastern Pacific were 3.05C above average on 19 September - exceeding the previous record of 3.02C set during the very strong El Niño of 2015. Some longer-term measures of El Niño have not yet hit record levels but this is likely to change, with the peak not expected until later this year. Warmer ocean waters mean storms can pick up more energy, leading to higher wind speeds. El Niño is a naturally-occurring pattern, which happens about every two to seven years and tends to last for around a year. Trade winds that typically blow from east to west across the Pacific Ocean can weaken or even reverse, allowing warm water to spread eastwards. Heat is then released from the ocean into the atmosphere which can boost global temperatures and drive changes in weather patterns around the world. Headline: Yemenis flee across Red Sea as Houthis and Saudi-backed forces escalate war
Body: This video can not be played Watch: Inside a camp for Yemeni refugees in Djibouti Ibrahim Issa, 50, is from the Yemeni coastal town of Dhubab, right on the front lines of the war between Yemen's Houthis and the Saudi-backed pro-government forces fighting them. Today he sits, surrounded by his family, on a tarpaulin spread over a sandy floor inside a vast open-sided warehouse at Markazi camp in Obock, northern Djibouti, packed with Yemeni families who have fled by boat across the narrow Bab al-Mandab Strait. After their sea crossing, Yemeni refugees have made their way by truck and on foot to this camp, jointly administered by the government and the UN. "How could I just sit there when my kids are screaming and shaking in terror?" says Ibrahim Issa. "When the sound of the planes start, and the kids hear the planes, they begin shouting and screaming. As parents it is our responsibility, what can you do when you see this? That is why we fled, to save them." UK to provide Saudi Arabia with 'defensive' military support, says Burnham Lightning Houthi advance in Yemen may bring dangerous new dimension to Iran war Ibrahim Issa escaped on his fishing boat with family and several goats As a fisherman, Ibrahim Issa already owned a boat large enough to bring out his family from Yemen. He even brought several of the family's goats which I can now see nibbling at scraps nearby, foraging amidst the discarded canisters of cooking gas and empty plastic bottles. Some families have been able to bring small bundles of possessions with them from Yemen – one family has even brought a "jeraak", a tall metal shisha pipe – but others have arrived, exhausted, in just the clothes they left in. In just the last few days more than 3,000 refugees have arrived here from Yemen, many entire families. The UN estimates that in all, more than 120,000 Yemenis have been displaced by the sudden surge in fighting along Yemen's Red Sea coast. This month, the country's Houthis, who had already seized most of the populated parts of Yemen years ago,made a lightning dashdown the coast towards Bab al-Mandab, the narrow, maritime chokepoint where the southern Red Sea flows into the Gulf of Aden and the wider Indian Ocean. Saudi Arabia, which backs the internationally recognised government of Yemen, has responded with hundreds of air strikes along the flat, coastal plain where the Houthis are now digging in. The Houthis have also launched hundreds of drones and missiles at cities and infrastructure in south-western Saudi Arabia. "We don't care which side it is that's attacking," is the message I got loud and clear in Arabic from everyone here I spoke to. "It's the bombs falling all around us that have caused us to flee." Djibouti, a tiny former French colony that sits just across the water from Yemen, has made it clear it has no intention of involving itself in the war between the Houthis and the Saudi-backed Yemeni government. And yet Djibouti is one of the most militarised nations in Africa. Since 2003, the US has run a huge multinational base here, Camp Lemonnier, once home to the French Foreign Legion. China too has a major base here, its largest military presence on the Indian Ocean and recently upgraded. Back in Markazi camp, one of those I spoke to is Qassim Abraham Abssy. Once also a fisherman, his identity card shows him to be 100 years old. "What led us to come here?" he asks rhetorically. "It was the planes. The sounds of the planes, boom! That's what made us flee, for the sake of our children. It burns ours hearts. We don't know which side they are from. They are bombing everywhere, because the Houthis are everywhere, in the mountains, in the roads. A plane comes, bombs everywhere." More than 120,000 Yemenis are estimated to have been displaced by the sudden surge in fighting Outside in the blazing 37C heat, close to the neat lines of tents supplied by the UN refugee agency, UNHCR, I met Mohammed Abdullarim from Aden, a 63-year-old former tour guide old enough to have been born when Aden was still a British protectorate. Unlike the new arrivals, Mohammed has been here since 2015. He fled to Djibouti soon after the fighting first flared up between the Houthis and the government of the now-ousted President Abdrabbuh Mansour Hadi. He has been at the camp ever since but suddenly, as we were talking, the sadness of what is happening to his country overwhelmed him and he turned his head away, choking back tears. "Most of the people here are in the worst condition, inside the tents here. I am very touched, I'm crying for these people, for my people, for their suffering. I want our voices to be heard by the NGOs and the Djibouti government. And I'm thankful to them for accepting us." How long will they have to stay here? That depends, of course, on the fighting. Yemen has been wracked by a horrific civil war that has killed tens of thousands of people and displaced millions since 2014. A shaky, UN-brokered 2022 truce between the Saudis and the Houthis has broken down spectacularly in recent months, with the two sides trading missiles, drones and air strikes. "We are willing to go back in peace if peace returns to our country," says Aisha Abdulkadir Mohammed Yemen's war may be a remote one to most people but the effect of choking off Saudi Arabia's oil exports through the Bab al-Mandab Strait are well publicised. But as ever, it is often the human cost that goes unnoticed. Sitting beside his wife on their tarpaulin, amid the cacophony all around them, Qassim Abssy the fisherman is wary of leaving the safety of Djibouti: "If the war continues then we're not going back because we have peace here." His wife, Aisha Abdulkadir Mohammed, agrees. "We are willing to go back in peace if peace returns to our country, and we are praying to God that peace does return. All we need is peace, even for our children's future, they get safety first, then food, water and an education. "As you see we just fled with our clothes, and left everything behind, because [in Yemen] there is no peace." Headline: More than 170,000 respiratory cases recorded in haze-choked Indonesia
Body: More than 40,000 cases – which range from mild coughs to pneumonia – involve toddlers Some 175,000 people in Indonesia have suffered from respiratory illness since August, its health ministry said, as it continues to battle wildfires that haveraged for weeks. More than 40,000 cases – which range from coughs to bronchitis and more serious conditions like pneumonia – involve toddlers. Forest fires have blanketed parts of the country as well as neighbouring Malaysia and Singapore in toxic smog, pushing air quality indices into "unhealthy" territory. Indonesia has deployed more than 54,000 officials and dozens of jets to the islands of Borneo and Sumatra for water bombing, but the vast territory and challenging peatland conditions make it hard to put out the fires, authorities say. "From the air to the ground, all forces continue to move," Indonesia's Cabinet Secretary Teddy Indra Wijaya said on Monday. "Everything is being done to extinguish the fires, reduce the impact of the smoke, and, most importantly, protect the public from the threat of forest and land fires." Indonesia regularly battles wildfires during its annual dry season, which usually runs from July through October. This year, however, the fires and haze have been turbocharged by a so-called"Godzilla" El Nino, which has fuelled extremely dry conditions. The independent forest monitoring platform Nusantara Atlas has detected around 734,000 hotspots across the country as of Wednesday - a figure that is more than 30% higher than that of 2019, one of Indonesia's worst wildfire seasons. Since January, at least 895,657 hectares of land – nearly six times the size of Greater London – have been burned. The wildfires have led to school closures and a surge in hospital admissions across Indonesia. The number of people suffering wildfire-related respiratory illnesses had more than doubled to 113,336 by 9 September, up from 50,891 on 1 September, according to figures from the health ministry. The toxic smog has also taken a toll on wildlife, including critically endangered orangutans. Late last month, an Indonesia-based wildlife foundation shared footage showing an orangutan writhing on the ground on a palm oil plantation in West Kalimantan, one of Indonesia's hardest-hit provinces. The great ape, which was discovered by a farmer, was rescued and given emergency treatment for hypoxia, but later died. This video can not be played Orangutans in danger as wildfires blaze through Borneo Indigenous and civil society groups in West Kalimantan filed a class action suit last week against the central government and local administrations, accusing them of deliberate negligence for failing to properly tackle the wildfires scorching the province. "This is a disaster that occurs every year. This recurring pattern proves our view that the defendants knew about the potential haze disaster and the risks of disaster from forest and land fires," the group's lawyer Glorio Sanen said in a statement at the time. Indonesia has carried out several rounds of cloud-seeding operations in recent weeks, some conducted together with members of Japan's Self-Defense Forces who arrived in Borneo earlier this month to help with firefighting efforts. Cloud seeding involves manipulating existing clouds, such as by dropping salt crystals or silver iodide into them, to help produce more rain. Meteorologists, however, are divided over the effectiveness of the practice. In the Malaysian state of Sarawak, one of the worst-affected areas outside Indonesia, authorities launched a five-day cloud-seeding operation earlier this month. Apart from tackling the ongoing haze, this exercise was aimed at boosting declining water levels at several hydropower dams ahead of a severe dry spell forecast for October. "October might be hotter and drier," Sarawak's Deputy Premier Douglas Uggah Embas told reporters. "We want to increase the water levels as much as possible while we still can." The haze has reached as far as parts of the Philippines, where local officials have urged residents to stay indoors as much as possible, and Singapore, where authorities have begun issuing daily haze advisories.
