Headline: Iran's president tells Trump it will never 'bend the knee'
Body: President Masoud Pezeshkian has said Iran will never "bend the knee" after almost seven months of war with the US and Israel, but is ready for a diplomatic solution to the conflict. Responding to US President Donald Trump's threat to "annihilate" the Islamic Republic if a deal is not reached soon, he told the UN General Assembly: "The resistance of the Iranian people will only increase in the face of sanctions, increased pressure, increased bullying." Pezeshkian also insisted any deal would have to include an end to the US blockade stopping Iranian ships from using a key Gulf waterway. "It cannot be the case that everyone benefits from the Strait of Hormuz while we are denied access," he said. There was no immediate comment from the US, whose delegation walked out of the chamber at the start of Pezeshkian's address. US and Iran hold first talks since June after Trump's 'annihilation' threat American power, AI and a walkout - key moments from Trump's UN speech UN experts say grounds to believe US committed war crimes in Iran strikes "The US president described us as terrorists. We have been the victims of terrorism," Iran's president told the UN in New York. He then held up a photo of the country's late Supreme Leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, who was killed in a strike on his residence when the US and Israel launched a joint attack in late February. He also presented pictures of some of the more than 175 civilians, two thirds of them children, who Iranian authorities say were killed in missile strikes on a primary school in Minab and a sports complex in Lamerd that day. The US has denied striking Lamerd and said it is still investigating what happened in Minab. "Our innocent people have been the targets of cowardly attacks and aggressions imposed on our country. And we defended ourselves with utmost strength," Pezeshkian said. Also on Wednesday, an attack on a cargo ship in the Strait of Hormuz killed an Indian sailor, the Agence France-Presse news agency reported, citing Omani and Indian authorities. The attack was condemned by India's foreign ministry, which called for unimpeded passage through the Strait to be restored. In February, Iran retaliated for the massive US-Israeli air campaign by launching deadly missile and drone attacks on Israel and neighbouring Gulf Arab states which host US military bases. It also effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of global oil and gas shipments usually pass, by attacking commercial vessels in the Gulf, the Gulf of Oman and the Arabian Sea. The US responded by imposing a blockade of Iranian ports and ships in April. In June, the US and Iran reached a preliminary agreement to end the war and reopen the strait, but it collapsed within weeks after the Iranian attacks on shipping resumed and the US reinstated its blockade. Iran wants to retain some measure of control over the strait and collect fees from vessels that use it, which the US has rejected. This video can not be played Watch: Trump threatens to 'annihilate' Iran if no deal reached In his address to the UN General Assembly on Tuesday, Trump said he faced a "big decision" - either negotiate a deal that would allow Iranians to rebuild their country, or "annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly". Pezeshkian said the threat was "a sign of a bullying mentality". "[Trump] must know that the resistance of the Iranian people will only increase in the face of sanctions, increased pressure, increased bullying. We will never bow our head or bend the knee," he said. But he added: "We are ready for dialogue and diplomacy and negotiations without accepting the language of force." Pezeshkian made clear that the US blockade would have to end as part of any deal. "It cannot be the case that everyone benefits from the Strait of Hormuz while we are denied access to shipping through this waterway," he said. He also reiterated that Iran would not give up its right to have a civilian nuclear programme and that it would not seek to develop nuclear weapons. "We say it clearly: no nuclear weapons and no limitations on peaceful nuclear technology." Trump argued in his speech that the war had prevented Iran from obtaining a nuclear bomb and demanded that its leaders "relinquish their nuclear ambitions". On Tuesday, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi and US envoy Steve Witkoff held indirect talks brokered by Qatari mediators on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York. Witkoff said he hoped the discussions – the first since June – would "prove constructive and promising", adding that the mediators would continue their work. But Iran's foreign ministry spokesman Esmail Baqai said the talks were "not anything new" and that Araghchi had maintained Iran's conditions, including the end of the US blockade and the release of frozen Iranian assets.

Headline: China's new youth idol isn't a pop star - he's an academic
Body: Young Chinese people are anxious about their future in a rapdily changing country "A star sent from the heavens," is how Zihan Han describes the man she's become a huge fan of recently, a man who young Chinese people call an "idol". Except this is no pop singer or movie star, but a 54-year old anthropologist. Professor Biao Xiang has become an unlikely guide for an increasingly disillusioned generation. And it's because of what he talks about: anxiety and how to navigate it. China's economy and tech have grown at breakneck speed, but there is plenty worrying its Gen Z, from jobs to romantic prospects to the sheer pressure of keeping up. "The transition from school to the real world brings a lot of uncertainty now, and people often feel anxious because they don't know how to face it," says a 23-year-old Chinese graduate who didn't want to reveal her name because she was worried speaking to foreign media might affect her chances of finding a job back home. "People need an anchor in their life. And his words make us feel there is someone that gets me." She and Zihan were among some 500 people - mostly Chinese diaspora - who piled into an auditorium recently in Singapore. Xiang spoke for more than an hour in Mandarin before he took questions. When it ended, dozens queued to meet and take photos with him. The Chinese grad called it "an academic fan meeting". Xiang has been interviewed by major Chinese outlets and has travelled to top Chinese campuses to talk, including at his alma mater, the prestigious Peking University – one talk earlier this year was live-streamed because the auditorium was full.  "When in doubt, ask Biao Xiang," has become a saying, according to Chinese media. About 500 people heard Biao Xiang speak in Singapore recently In Singapore, Xiang spoke of the recognition young people seek in today's China, where they often look to systems for approval - from competitive exams to secure jobs - and how that approval becomes a measure of self-worth, which can be exhausting and damaging. It is healthier, he suggested, to seek meaning and understanding from others and use that to understand ourselves better. These are hardly quick fixes. But in a country where discontent can be politically sensitive and heavily censored, he is a rare public figure who addresses what he calls the "pain point of the times". "Everyone knows where the issue is, but they are reluctant to look at it. Sometimes it is too painful to look at, or they don't have a way," he tells the BBC over tea in Singapore. "But as an academic, it is not terrifying if you can describe it – that's how you analyse and manage it." He now lives in Germany, where he is the director of the Max Planck Institute for Social Anthropology, and studies social change in China and other parts of Asia. Xiang believes Chinese society is at a "turning point", where people are searching for meaning while making sense of rapid social and economic change. He sees contradictions – uncertain youth in a powerful, assertive country; disillusionment despite huge advancement – and his job, he says, is to unpack what is driving it. China's leader Xi Jinping has acknowledged it too: he said the "principal contradiction" was "between the people's ever-growing needs for a better life and unbalanced and inadequate development". Young people are seeking a new narrative in a highly competitive China, Xiang says Xiang has catchy names for what is causing this. "Floating" is how he describes people working relentlessly just to survive, like a hummingbird that keeps flapping its wings to stay mid-air. "The nearby" refers to what is immediately around us. Xiang argues that people are preoccupied by the "very near" (themselves) and the very far (the world) while the space in between - "the nearby" - is neglected. This, he says, leaves them feeling disconnected. This seems to be resonating deeply with young people looking for answers. One user on RedNote writes, "He consistently views issues from the perspective of the vulnerable, attributes personal stress to macro-level causes, and encourages people to actively engage with life - it's truly wonderful." Another says, "He never spouts empty, feel-good platitudes; instead, he crouches down to face real-life dilemmas alongside us." Zihan says it boils down to Xiang's willingness to talk openly about these things: "Those who have said similar things aren't as kick-ass as Teacher Xiang, yet people who are as kick-ass as him haven't said such things." Xiang has become famous among Chinese people for his candid lectures Born in 1972, Xiang came of age during another turning point, as China emerged from the brutal chaos of Mao Zedong's rule to trade with the world. It urbanised, ordinary people turned into entrepreneurs and businesses took off for the first time in the Communist nation. Growing up in Wenzhou, which transformed into an industrial port, Xiang witnessed this first-hand. "It was a vast landscape of small business owners," he recalls. "Most people didn't care too much about education, the focus was on practical matters - specifically, how to make money." And many of them did. Their children grew up in a glorious era of double-digit economic growth. But the economy slowed during Covid and hasn't bounced back. The old equation - hard work = secure job - no longer works, and they want a new narrative, Xiang says. Youth unemployment hit 21.3%, before the government stopped publishing the data in mid-2023. Those with "good jobs" - civil servants, corporate employees, engineers - are anxious about losing them. They constantly complain online about long, exhausting working hours and a toxic office culture and their fear of the "curse of 35" - a cutoff age for job advertisements, after which it is harder to find a new job. Because of censorship, it's hard to know the true extent of this mood. But that feeling of being squeezed seeps into public discourse in other ways. That anxiety quickly turns into anger in online debates, be it about university entrance exams or bride price or food safety scandals. Young people praying at monastery in Beijing for bright job and marriage prospects Terms associated with this mood have been trending for years. The most famous are "lying flat", when people opt out of the rat race entirely, and "involution", a rather clunky term now commonly used to describe intense competition which generates little meaningful reward. Xiang believes two forces have amplified this anxiety - the property market and the higher education system. The property boom, fuelled by local government's reliance on land sales, tied families' sense of security and success to the values of their homes. And a rapid expansion in university enrolment raised the bar for achievement, intensifying competition. The result, he says, is a universal playbook: get a good degree, find a stable job, marry and buy a home. "When 1.4 billion people are all in the same race, that is involution." About three years ago, when he learned that a camp for digital nomads where he spoke raised prices after his visit, he "realised I was no longer only known in the academic circles". Many of his peers, he said, prioritise publishing research and are "quite cold" to his methods. Some warned him about "cherishing your feathers", a Chinese expression for protecting one's reputation. But Xiang is encouraged by his popularity. "If someone calls me an influencer I'll take it as a compliment. Because the real influence I can have is to make people think for themselves." Headline: Burberry closes London Fashion Week 2026 with signature check print and celeb-filled front row
Body: Burberry closed London Fashion Week on Monday evening, with the British fashion house's chief designer Daniel Lee pairing their signature check print with clashing florals and soft leather. The show was put together with the help of textile designer Celia Birtwell, who hand-painted some of the runway designs, including check print trenches and smiley-face emblazoned jumpers. Burberry, which this summer reported a growth in revenue for the first time in three years, often attracts some of the biggest names in British culture to its shows, rivalling fashion weeks in New York and Paris. Monday night was no exception, with Central Cee making an appearance on the catwalk as Romeo Beckham, Skepta, Jonathan Bailey and Rosie Huntington-Whiteley looked on from the front row. Burberry's most striking looks: puffed pink bubble-hem trench, 3D floral embellishments, Celia Birtwell smiley-face print coat, vivid pool-blue & sunset-orange outerwear - plus Central Cee's surprise denim debut Leo Wu, Jorja Smith, Romeo Beckham and Kim Turnbull among the guests on the front row at Burberry's SS27 show Rosie Huntington-Whiteley, Chiwetel Ejiofor and Jason Statham join the star-studded front row, for the show closing London Fashion Week The latest fashion week has been about return and renewal - as two of Britain's biggest designers showcased their spring/summer 2027 designs. The first was Alexander McQueen, which as a brand moved to London after 25 years  of showing in Paris - something Laura Weir, CEO of the British Fashion Council, told the BBC was "quite a big deal for us". Creative director Seán McGirr brought the brand back to its roots, with a runway of devil horns, lace corsets and chainmail skull dresses. Mulberry was the second designer to make its big return, this time after a nine-year absence, with Christopher Kane's debut collection centring around the brand's Baywater bag, while going big on leather in the form of coats, skirts and loafers. Weir says the "big mission" for her and her team this season was to "re-platform London Fashion Week as not only a home for British design, but an engine for creativity and commercial growth". Alexander McQueen made a historic return to London Fashion Week after 25 years, staging a homecoming show that fused severe tailoring with dark romanticism Amy Taylor of Amyl & The Sniffers, Siouxsie Sioux, Florence Welch, Emma Corrin and Jamie Campbell Bower attend the McQueen show Lashana Lynch, Ruth Wilson and Hayley Atwell attend the ERDEM show Here are some of the major trends to come out of London Fashion Week 2026: Rejecting "quiet luxury" uniforms, Chopova Lowena, Sinead Gorey, and Conner Ives led London Fashion Week's embrace of the "messy girl" aesthetic by championing deliberate chaos, pairing intentionally undone tailoring and messy updos "The number one trend for this season is messy girl," says Elektra Kotsoni, deputy director for Vogue Business and Vogue Runway, whose team predicts the trends ahead of each season. She tells the BBC: "We're going to be having a messy girl summer" and says "it's a reaction to the clean girl and quiet luxury aesthetics that took over our Instagram feeds," last year. Kotsoni says as "the world is quite messy" this form of dressing is a sign of "resilience" and rebellion. She says if you are looking to replicate this trend, mix pastel colours, dreamy florals, and tactile materials to form "unexpected clashes" that "look really messy". This form of what Kotsoni calls "crazy styling" was on display at London Fashion Week - with the noisy clashes at Chopova Lowena, Sinead Gorey and Conner Ives. Erdem, Yuhan Wang, and Bora Aksu channelled a "gardencore" vibe, trading quiet luxury for unpolished, allotment-ready chaos - pairing parkas and structured trench outerwear with kitchen-garden details According to Kotsoni - gardening is officially cool in the fashion world. A new twist on the cottage-core looks that emerged post-pandemic, instead of gingham, wicker bags and sourdough starters, it's all about looking like you're fresh from planting seeds or operating a lawnmower. "There are lots of gardening appropriate silhouettes on the runways," she says, including aprons, waterproof materials and trench coats. It started with Spanish fashion house Loewe launching a watering can-shaped handbag a couple of months ago and has now translated on the runway with Erdem, Yuhan Wang and Bora Aksu. Kotsoni says "fashion is always a reflection of what's happening in the world" and likes how designers have been able to "take an interest like gardening and present it as something" tangible in a fashion show. Dujancourt's free-spirited aesthetic, organic draping, trailing ribbons, and delicately hitched slip skirts Whilst some designers have been taking cues from the great outdoors - others have been inspired by film. Another key trend identified by Kotsoni's team is the idea of the modern goddess - a take on the styles of Ancient Greece and a nod to Christopher Nolan's hit film The Odyssey this summer. Kotsoni says the items to look out for are "draped garments, breezy materials and lots of bohemian and flowy silhouettes". Pauline Dujancourt's London Fashion Week show epitomised this style - focusing on maximum volume and billowing fabrics. Kotsoni says these looks are in opposition to how guests themselves have been dressing at this fashion week, suggesting a turning of the tide. "Everybody has been dressed really minimalist in a specific quiet luxury way and I think people are tired of that," she notes. Mulberry, Justin Cassin, Enny Atelier and Vin + Omi showcased some orange Whether your preference is melon, tangerine, ginger or coral - orange appears to be the big colour trend for next year. Kotsoni says she is hedging her bets on whether a shade of orange will be Pantone's colour of the year for 2027 as it has already been making its way into celebrity styling (it's not too late to replicate Kylie Jenner and Timothée Chalamet'smatching neon outfits,externalat the Marty Supreme premiere for Halloween) and on the runway. Mulberry, Justin Cassin, Enny Atelier and Vin + Omi all featured orange in their London shows and presentations over the last couple of days. A school sports hall is transformed into a ballet stage for Edeline Lee's latest collection which drew inspiration from the intense discipline, repetition, and physical toll of classical dance Ever the fashion muse, Chalamet is once again at the centre of another trend for 2027 - ballet. After he said "no one cares" about the discipline in May this year, Kotsoni says she "thinks it's interesting" that it's now being forged as a clear trend for next year. Edeline Lee put on a striking show in London - complete with models taking to the runway en pointe in a transformed school sports hall. "Ballet is very much in fashion," she says, noting that this month's Vogue Italia has La Scala's principle dancer Roberto Bolle on the cover, whilst Royal Ballet dancer Francesca Hayward has recently been modelling for Armani and Chanel. "Ballet flats are massive and still will be [next year] and small silhouettes for shoes are going to be prevalent next season," Kotsoni adds - encouraging fans of the style to seek out items in charity and vintage shops if they want to replicate the look.

Headline: Texas ICE shooting leaves Venezuelan DoorDash driver with bullet in his back, says lawyer
Body: This video can not be played Watch: 'I am frustrated' - Protesters take to the streets after Austin ICE shooting A Venezuelan DoorDash delivery driver who was shot by ICE agents returned to hospital after being sent to a detention centre with a bullet still in his back, his lawyer has said. The shooting of Wilber Rafael Garcés Perez, 28, triggered protests in Austin, Texas, on Sunday. The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) said in a statement to the BBC it was investigating the shooting of a man in the Texan capital who had entered the country illegally. It was unclear what led to the shooting with the local mayor and police demanding an investigation. It comes months after a man in Houston was shot dead by an ICE officer. Wilber Rafael Garcés Perez was shot and injured by an ICE officer Attorney Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch told the BBC that after being unable to move his  arm in the detention facility, Garcés Perez was transported back to hospital on Monday evening. He was treated there and has since been returned to the detention facility. "He reports that during the transfer he was handcuffed, shackled at the ankles, placed in a waist chain, and handled roughly despite his gunshot injury,"  Lincoln-Goldfinch said. She added that detention personnel have revoked his communication privileges and have since moved him from an infirmary into an isolated room with a flat, non-adjustable bed. The BBC has contacted the Department of Homeland Security for comment. The gunshot fractured Garcés Perez's clavicle and he still has "significant swelling and pain", and wears a sling, his lawyer also said. The cause or extent of the loss of movement he experienced has not yet been determined, she added. Texas lawmaker Joaquin Castro, a Democrat, on Tuesday has demanded his release from detention. He said  Garcés Perez was in the US legally, had work permits and was seeking asylum. Garcés Perez'sfederal case remains pending and a hearing is scheduled for next week, his lawyer said.  The Trump administration has ramped up immigration enforcement efforts and arrests during Trump's second term, sparking unrest across several US cities. The administration has defended its policies and the agency's controversial tactics as necessary for public safety and to enact Trump's campaign promise to secure the border and carry out mass deportations. The shooting in Austin on Sunday occurred just before 1300 local time, although details remain scarce. Dozens of protesters, some waving the flags of Mexico and Guatemala, gathered at the scene carrying signs demanding that ICE leave Austin. Local television outlets showed the demonstrators gathering across the street from ​a blue Toyota Corolla that ⁠sustained damage to the passenger-side door, as ICE agents stood nearby, Reuters news agency reported. Mayor Kirk Watson, a Democrat, said that Austinites have a right to know what happened and "a right to feel safe in their city" during a media briefing on Sunday. "They should know the truth," he said, adding that he is pleased that the city will also be involved in the investigation. He added that ICE operations have surged in Austin in recent weeks. ICE has faced intense scrutiny after a number of deadly shootings, including the death of Houston resident Lorenzo Salgado Araujo. Salgado Araujo had not been a target of an ICE investigation, but was shot during an ICE traffic stop,according to DHS. Texas Congressman Greg Casar, a Democrat, has demanded a full and immediate independent investigation into the latest shooting and the release of body camera footage. He also demanded "accountability for any ICE officer who broke the law". Activists say that the administration has violated due process as it carries out the crackdown. Democrats have demanded reforms at the agency, including requiring immigration enforcement agents to wear body cameras and not conceal their faces. Earlier this month the US Department of Justicecharged an ICE agent with lyingabout the non-fatal shooting of a Venezuelan migrant in Minnesota - a rare instance in which the current justice department accused a federal agent of breaking the law on the job. Earlier this week, Florida lawmaker Maria Elvira Salazar, a Republican who has spoken out against the immigration crackdown, released an advert criticising the targeting and detaining of individuals who have no criminal record. Salazar appeared on the CBS programme Face the Nation on Sunday and said that she has since spoken to the president, and believes he will keep the country on the right track. "He gets it more than anybody," she said.  What is ICE and what powers do its agents have to use force? Headline: Marra claims Scottish government 'hoarding power' in conference speech
Body: Michael Marra made his first speech to the UK Labour conference in Liverpool The new leader of Scottish Labour has claimed the Scottish government has "hoarded money and control" at Holyrood and called for the decentralisation of powers to local regions. Michael Marra called on the Scottish government to put "power and money" in the hands of "councils, colleges and industries" across the country to grow local economies. In his inaugural speech to the UK Labour conference in Liverpool, Marra urged members not to mistake the SNP's "progressive posturing" for progressive politics. He said it was his job to remind the people of Scotland what Labour stood for after the party's worst ever Holyrood election result in May. Marra said: "Had our regions grown at the same pace as Manchester in the last decade, the Scottish economy would be £30bn larger. "Too much power is centralised in Scotland. The Scottish government has hoarded money and control at the expense of Scotland's communities." He attacked the SNP's record on education and child poverty, as well as the SNP administrations announcement that itwould sack and re-hire 23,000 workersat Glasgow City Council. Michael Marra announced as new Scottish Labour leader Who is new Scottish Labour leader Michael Marra? Marra used his conference speech to highlight Scotland's shipbuilding history as an example of failure in the government's skills policy. He said Scotland has a reliance on foreign workers due to a lack of available, skilled Scottish equivalents. "Shipbuilding – Scotland is famous for it," he said. "We're world class at it. There should be a sense of national pride that the ships being built in Scotland are providing opportunity and security for Scottish workers. "So, my message to Bute House is put control and money in the hands of the councils, colleges and industries who know what their local economies need better than any bureaucrat in Edinburgh." Marra was speaking just a week after defeating Joe Fagan in a leadership election. He replaced Anas Sarwar, who stood down to take up a a role in theHouse of Lordsas part of Prime Minister Andy Burnham's government. Marra said Burnham was the first person to phone him after his victory was announced. He joked they may not agree on everything, including "dancing to The Smiths," but different "approaches and ideas" were welcome. Scottish Labour's return of 17 MSPs saw them tied with Reform UK as the second-largest party in the Scottish Parliament. He admitted the results of the May election "hurt" and the party had some "difficult truths to face up to". Marra said he and Burnham did agree on the need for an "antidote" to a political "poison of hate, anger and fear". He said the next UK election would be a straight fight between Labour and Reform. Marra, whofirst joined Labour as a teenager, also spoke about his upbringing in Dundee in a family of ardent trade unionists. He said he made his first leaflet run ahead of the 1987 general election at the age of eight, supporting Ernie Ross MP in Dundee West. Marra said his grandmother Margaret, one of seven children, slept in a single room and was the only member of her family lucky enough to go to college while the others worked six days a week at the city's jute mills. He said he was "forever grateful" for their sacrifice as the opportunity "changed her life" and her education changed Marra's, two generations later. He said "not enough lives" in Scotland were being changed by education, and pledged to put Scottish education back among the world's best. "It's no longer the SNP's priority, if it ever was," he said. "I will make Scottish education the best in the world again. Not just steady, not just average, the best in the world again."

Headline: New policies, election speculation: What to expect from Burnham's first Labour conference as PM
Body: Andy Burnham is gearing up to deliver his first conference speech as Labour leader Andy Burnham had plenty to say about where the government - and the country - was going wrong at last year's Labour conference in Liverpool. But that was at a fringe meeting on the sidelines of the main event. Now, as Labour leader and prime minister, he is the main event - and it is down to him to show party members and the wider public that he has some answers. Earlier this week, he said his debut leader's speech would leave nobody in any doubt about "what I'm trying to do in this role". "People are going to know the direction I want to take this country and I will set it down quite clearly," he told reporters en route to the UN General Assembly in New York. An internal No 10 note has set out the broad themes he will explore when he takes to the stage in Liverpool on Tuesday - including setting out long-term solutions to build a belief that the future can be brighter. The slogan for this year's conference is "Hope Again". So in his speech he is likely to point to his forthcoming 10 Year Plan for the UK – which, he says, will have "making life more affordable" at its core. As for the specifics of what he will say, some of it will be very familiar to anyone who was listening to his conference fringe speech 12 months ago. Back then, he declared then that the country had "lost control" of "the essentials" following the Thatcher-era sell off of utilities and that we were all "overpaying for  water, housing  energy, transport". He called for a renewed emphasis on technical education and wanted to see a decade of council house building on the scale of the post-war Labour government. For a politician frequently denounced for "flip flopping" he has been remarkably consistent in recent times. He is likely to re-alight on themes from his Labour leadership campaign – saying more about his commitment to greater "public control" – though not necessarily public ownership - of life's necessities; building national resilience in an unstable world; and investing political capital in the reform of social care. A potential crowd pleaser would be to tell Labour activists from the main stage what he told them as Greater Manchester mayor from the fringe last year – that he will set up a commission to examine electoral reform. A quarter of his own MPs signed a parliamentary amendment calling for this, and the Labour conference has previously given its backing to changing the voting system, though this was not taken forward in government. But it may now be a way of demonstrating Burnham's commitment to a "new politics". We are also likely to hear more about getting young people into work or training, with the conclusions of the review by the former Labour cabinet minister Alan Milburn likely to be published soon. And there is certain to be plenty about his efforts to devolve power away from Whitehall to England's mayors and the new No 10 North. The task for Burnham is to meld these snapshots into a compelling and coherent narrative, culminating in a vision of the Britain he wants to see a decade from now. But there are already worries that this might become a fictional narrative unless he also focuses even more on the here and now. After all, Sir Keir Starmer's "decade of national renewal" was binned after just two bumpy years in office. Unite's Sharon Graham is calling for more help with the cost of living We are told there will be policy announcements on each day of the conference – starting on Saturday. Each announcement will have to fit in with the PM's priorities – "putting power in people's hands" - in other words more devolved powers;  "growth in every postcode" – such as investment decisions around the country; and help with cost of living. Party insiders say measures such as removing VAT from electricity bills are just the start of that assistance. But Labour's biggest union funder, Unite, wants to see much more robust action on living costs sooner rather than later.  The union does not want the promise of jam tomorrow, but some instant sweeteners. Its leader, Sharon Graham, has called for a "winter fuel in reverse" – a policy from Burnham next week which would be as popular as Starmer's early removal of payments from many pensioners was unpopular. The union has put forward a motion which gives the PM plenty of options such as a cap on energy prices and unfreezing tax thresholds – an issue Burnham himself said had come up on the doorsteps when he was campaigning to be the MP for Makerfield. The union has said revenue can be raised through a windfall tax on banks. The umbrella body for unions, the TUC, has called for an increase in the bank surcharge to subsidise energy bills. All eyes will be on John Healey's first conference speech as chancellor on Monday. With borrowing costs for last monthsoaring to their second highest level, his room for manoeuvre is limited and he will not scoop his own Budget next month by announcing what is in it. But Labour activists will be keen to know from his language whether Healey's Treasury will opt for continuity or will represent a break from the past two years under Rachel Reeves, not just in rhetoric but reality. Some in Labour's ranks believe Burnham is planning for an early election, with party HQ recently launching "operation second term", to beef up its campaigning and organising strength. Burnham does not have to call an election until August 2029 - but going to the country early - perhaps as early as next spring - could deliver him a mandate of his own and free him from the constraints of Sir Keir Starmer's 2024 manifesto. Recent polling has suggested that a "Burnham bounce"  is real, though not dramatic. The party has moved from just under 20% in the polls at the end of the Starmer era to around the mid-twenties now. Ipsosputs its standing as high as 28%,external, while YouGovregisters a more modest 23%,external. Labour strategists will be pleased that Reform UK's share – 21% in YouGov - is the lowest since January 2025,  and that Nigel Farage's party is now neck-and-neck with Kemi Badenoch's Conservatives. One Labour insider told me that Burnham is happy to see a resilient Badenoch, as this blunts Reform support and could point to a split vote on the right at an election. Andnew research from YouGov,externalsuggests that at the all important constituency level, 63-68% of Lib Dem and Green voters would tactically vote for Labour to stop Reform UK winning their seat. Burnham of course also faces a challenge on the left. How much of a threat Zack Polanski's Greens can be in some traditional Labour seats will betested in the Holborn and St Pancras by-electionjust a week after the Labour conference concludes. Downing Street insists that an early election is not being planned. To say anything else, though, would be to repeat the uncertainty of Gordon Brown's early months in No 10 when election speculation wasn't doused - and had become so rife that he was reputationally damaged when he decided not to go to the polls. But some who have been in regular touch with No 10 tell me they have seen no serious signs that an early election is in the offing. Burnham appears determined to give his government enough time in office to present tangible achievements to a sceptical electorate. And with Labour still well below the 34% vote share it captured in 2024, many Labour MPs will be pushing the PM not to cut and run. So don't expect the centre point of Burnham's conference speech to be a message to his MPs to go back to their constituencies and prepare for a loss of some of their seats. But equally don't expect election speculation to subside at this conference. Environmental campaigners are firmly opposed to Rosebank and Jackdaw The Labour Party has tried and trusted methods of managing dissent at party conferences, when it comes to votes on party policy. But the coming week could see a concerted effort by some on the left to push for a complete ban on arms sales to Israel and for Israel's actions in Gaza to be described by Labour as a genocide. Those close to Burnham believe he has gained considerable credit by sanctioning the illegal Israeli settlements on the West Bank and won't need to go further. There is also some frustration that his government has not yet revised proposals to make migrants wait much longer to gain permanent residency rights, and there are genuine differences over whether the Rosebank and Jackdaw oil and gas fields should go ahead. But while Burnham is facing some difficult calls, this is not a leader facing a restless party in revolt. He has offered to give the hard-pressed public "breathing space" amid a cost of living crisis. And his own party is so far giving him breathing space as leader – largely sighing with relief that it is not Sir Keir Starmer who will be delivering the main address this year. Senior Labour officials have hailed the forthcoming conference as an opportunity to "show voters a party that is boldly, confidently, and authentically Labour". But not too far below the political radar, there are already demands from some in the wider Labour movement to prove it. Do you have any views, comments or questions about this story? Headline: The ecstasy of buying our first home was short-lived after we found 150 faults
Body: Charles and Georgina Barnes bought a new build home in February 2026 It was the day Georgina and Charles Barnes had waited three years for, as they picked up the keys to their first home. But when the brand new property was inspected days later by a Welsh snagging company,  the final quality check by independent inspectors, they found 150 defects. These included incorrectly installed fire barriers, signs of a previous leak and what they called "exceptionally poor" workmanship. Swansea-based New Home Quality Control was set up by John Cooper, who became fed up of being asked to hide things from customers on building sites. It is the responsibility of developers to make sure new-builds meet regulations, according to theNational House Building Council,external(NHBC). The couple are far from alone when it comes to issues with new houses. Written evidence submitted by the New Homes Ombudsman Service said the Home Builders Federation national new homes customer satisfaction survey, published in March 2025, showed93.7% of new-build buyers reporting defects or snags to their developer after moving in,external. Just over a quarter of buyers also found more than 15 problems in their new-build home. Charles and Georgina were excited to move into their new home "We just wouldn't have known," said Georgina. "If there had been a fire, that's one thing that could have happened and been very detrimental." Georgina, 36, and her husband saved for three years to buy a house, before falling in love with the development in south Leicestershire. As moving day approached, social media began serving her a steady stream of new-build horror stories After paying £299,995 for the house, she said getting it snagged was "non-negotiable". "It just felt unbelievable that we'd finally done it," she added. "We actually finally got our own place. This is ours. This is ours to do what we want with. It just felt great." But the report also identified improperly roofing defects, low water pressure and what inspectors described as "exceptionally poor" installation of the gas meter cabinet and gas pipe. More than a dozen of additional cosmetic and finishing defects were also recorded throughout the property As they had a two-year warranty from the developer, it meant they fixed the issues. This video can not be played John Cooper describes how he came to set up a snagging company "I would say for any new-build buyer, 100% no doubt, I recommend a snagger," Georgina said. Vistry, responsible for the housing developer Countryside, which built Charles and Georgina's house, said it supported "appropriately conducted independent inspections as an additional source of reassurance about build quality". It said each home is checked by its teams and independent inspections take place and, two to three weeks after customers move in, the build team meets to discuss and agree any snagging work. Such issues are not new to John Cooper, 50, co-founder of New Home Quality Control. He said, while working as a contracts manager in 2018: "The site manager asked me to hide something from a customer that was moving in the next day." This was the tip of the iceberg after he had seen poor quality workmanship over about six years. "From that moment on, I thought to myself 'I've got to make a change in this industry somehow. This can't continue'," he said. Cooper spoke to his supervisor at the time, Lee Challenger, 42, and the two men quit their jobs and started New Homes Quality Control. "We've never inspected a house and found absolutely nothing wrong with it," he said. John Cooper was asked to hide issues in new build homes so he created a company to fight back The most common defects involve brickwork, carpentry and roofing, he said. "I just think that there's not enough quality bricklayers to build the amount of properties that the developers are building across the UK on a yearly basis." The team also regularly identifies missing or incorrectly installed weep vents - which are installed in exterior walls to let moisture escape. Cooper said some developments had even featured "fake" weep vents, where decorative plastic pieces had been fitted instead of functioning openings. "They thought they could get away with it," he said. Cooper said before new owners get the keys, the NHBC inspects the property and sign it off. "I'm sick of hearing every property being signed off, because if that was the case, then we wouldn't have a company," he said. Many of Cooper's clients get emotional when they see how many issues there are with their new houses. "We've had people cry," he said. "There were some quite serious issues in their new property and they had spent all their life savings on it." Cooper said his long-term goal was for every new-build home to undergo an independent inspection before its owners moved in. "If someone's spending their life savings on a house, they deserve to get what they paid for," he said. The inspections take between two and four hours, depending on the size of the house, and usually cost between £349 and £499. Among the arsenal of tools the snaggers use are drones, GoPro cameras, cavity cameras, thermal imaging equipment and laser levels. But not everyone can afford their services as they spend all their money on the house. "Money is tight for a lot of people." Georgina and Charles' home had 150 issues when they moved in NHBC said it was the responsibility of the builders to ensure they meet building regulations and homeowners must raise any issues with the house builder within two years. If they are not fixed can seek resolution via NHBC. The organisation said it carries out inspections at "key stages of the build" and "provide feedback" on the quality. Home Builders Federation (HBF), which represents the building industry said: "New homes are not made in a factory. "They are bespoke products, built by numerous tradespeople, often on sites exposed to all weathers, and it is inevitable that on occasions there are some snags." It said the "vast majority of snagging issues are minor" and there was no evidence that quality standards were not keeping pace with the rate of housebuilding. While there is a need for more homes, house-building levels are flatlining due to "major barriers" preventing their construction, it said. But "quality and service levels remain extremely high" and there is "no evidence" that labour shortages are affecting the new homes. "Although the industry does face skills challenges in some areas, as does the wider construction industry, we are currently building around 200,000 homes a year versus a need to deliver around 300,000 with no sign of output increasing," it said. HBF said it would support statutory registration for builders with the New Homes Quality Board but warned that snagging inspectors were not regulated. "Customers need to take care that any inspector they use is suitably qualified and accredited by a professional body, such as RICS," it added. "We do not believe additional blanket inspections are necessary. There is already a comprehensive framework of regulation, building control, warranties and builder quality assurance in place." Property developers Taylor Wimpey refused to comment, and Watkin Jones, Barratt Redrow and Persimmon Homes did not respond for comment. The Welsh government said it was committed to making sure homebuyers get high quality and are protected if things go wrong. The UK government said it was investing £39bn in affordable housing and pledged £625m to train up to 60,000 construction workers. Headline: Pope warns against 'losing humanity' to AI machines
Body: This video can not be played Watch: Pope Leo XIV arrives in Paris for four-day visit Pope Leo XIV has issued a warning about the dangers of artificial intelligence (AI) at the start of his four-day visit to France. The pontiff cautioned against "losing our humanity amid a paradise of machines" in wide-ranging remarks to Church and state officials at the Élysée Palace, following an hour of talks with President Emmanuel Macron. Leo made a similar warning earlier this year when he spoke of the need for AI to be "disarmed" in thefirst major teaching document of his papacy. In his May appeal, he mentioned the slave trade in relation to AI, suggesting that the world was in danger of normalising the exploitation of people once again. The highpoint of Leo's visit to France is set to be a giant Mass attended by more than half a million people in Paris on Saturday, for which an altar has been built on the Place de la Concorde and a large area around the Champs-Élysées sealed off by police. Large crowds are expected throughout the trip, reflecting an enthusiasm that the Church attributes to growing spirituality among the French and other Europeans. He was greeted at Orly airport early on Friday by Macron, with the pair expected to deliver a speech later in the day in Metz. Crowds were meanwhile gathering along a route to the Notre Dame, where the pontiff will later be driven in his popemobile. The president will not be at any of the Pope's Masses, largely to avoid breaching France's strict separation of state and religion. On Friday, Macron hailed Pope Leo's visit to France as a "great honour", stressing that French secularism "in no way negates religion". Leo said that "authentic secularity" should not exclude religion "from the public sphere or from education". In recent years, French politicians have often invoked France's brand of secularism to justify bans on religious symbols, including Muslim women's attire, in public spaces and schools. The Pope was welcomed at the Elysee Palace after landing on Friday The Champs-Élysées Mass will be attended by Macron's wife Brigitte and Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu. Several candidates for next year's presidential election are also due, including Marine Le Pen of the nationalist right, centrists Edouard Philippe and Gabriel Attal, and conservative Bruno Retailleau. There were reports of tensions between Macron and the Vatican team sent to make arrangements, with the president allegedly frustrated in his wish for a more ceremonial aspect to the visit. This was dismissed this week by Élysée officials, who said it was customary to offer a visiting head of state – which the Pope is – a range of high-profile events, such as a cavalry escort down the Champs-Élysées. But they said it was never expected that the Pope would actually take the offer up. They did confirm that Pope Leo turned down Macron's idea of a meeting with artisans who helped rebuild the fire-devastated Notre-Dame cathedral. This was because his agenda was too tight, they said. After a Popemobile ride through crowds to Notre-Dame cathedral on Friday afternoon, Pope Leo XIV will be joined in the evening by 80,000 young people at the Stade de France in northern Paris. On Sunday 150,000 have signed up to attend mass in the Pyrenean sanctuary of Lourdes. Preparations are taking place in Lourdes ahead of the visit On Monday the Pope will be in Metz, in northeast France, where he will pay tribute to Robert Schuman (1886-1963), a founding father of the European Union and a fervent Catholic who is today a candidate for beatification. The Pope will also meet a group of migrants in Paris, and in Lourdes some victims of sexual abuse by members of the Catholic clergy. Born in Chicago in 1955, Pope Leo XIV was originally called Robert Prevost – a French name. In fact his paternal grandmother was born in Le Havre in Normandy in 1894. When she married in the US many years later she and her Italian husband took the name Prevost, which had been her mother's maiden-name. France has a historically complex relationship with the Catholic Church of Rome.  The country was long known as the "Eldest Daughter of the Church" because supposedly, but inaccurately, it was the first kingdom to convert to Christianity. Actually Armenia, Georgia and Ethiopia preceded it. In the 14th Century the papacy came in exile to Avignon in southern France, and over following centuries French armies periodically intervened in Italian politics, wherepopeswere secular rulers as well as heads of the Church. Napoleon held two popes in captivity. Recent popes have all come to France, most notably John-Paul II, who came several times between 1980 and 2004, and Pope Francis who came three times, but avoided Paris, going instead to Strasbourg, Marseilles and Corsica. Pope John Paul II, pictured here in Paris in 1980, visited many times Today France has secularised with the rest of Europe, and less than half of the population identifies as Catholic. The number of regular worshippers has fallen from 35% of the population in 1960 to less than 5% today, while the number of priests has shrunk by two-thirds from 25,000 in 1990 to fewer than 9,000. But in recent years there have been signs of a growing interest in religious tradition, with the number of adult baptisms more than doubling in five years to hit 10,000 in 2025. "France has indeed secularised, but there is a void where God and values used to be," said Cardinal François Bustillo, Bishop of Ajaccio. "People are searching for something. Maybe they go to India or Tibet or the Amazon. And now the Pope comes here from Rome, bringing a reminder to people of their own roots. "It was John-Paul II who awoke the East. Now Leo XIV will awake the West," he said. Get our flagship newsletter with all the headlines you need to start the day.Sign up here. Headline: Sir David Beckham nets £38.5m after World Cup ad deals
Body: Sir David Beckham has netted a £38.5m payout from his sports, fashion, and media business after the 2026 Men's Football World Cup helped it bring in record profits. The former England star's DRJB Holdings, which includes the Beckham brand, reported an almost £50m profit in 2025, a 46% jump compared to a year earlier. Sales rose from £72.2m to £84m. The rise was driven by a slew of advertising partnerships struck in the runup to the tournament, including with Bank of America, McDonald's, Verizon, and PepsiCo Lay's. Sir David,Britain's first billionaire sportsman, was commonly seen in adverts during the summer's World Cup. In the US, it was difficult for fans to watch a gamewithout coming across Beckhamin adverts for Stella Artois, Home Depot and Lay's crisps - known as Walkers in the UK. Sir David also launched menswear collections for Hugo Boss last year, as well as a pair of Adidas Predator football boots and an eyewear range with Italian glasses maker Safilo. Revenues at DRJB, of which Beckham owns almost half, were boosted by growth in Beckham's health supplements business too. DRJB paid its shareholders £38.9m, followed by a special £46.6m payment after the end of the financial year. Sir David's share of those dividends would have been around £38.5m due to how much of the company he owns. The remainder of DRJB is owned by New York-based Authentic Brands Group, which also owns Reebok, as well as the rights to other celebrity brands such as comedian and actor Kevin Hart. Authentic's entertainment chief executive Corey Salter said the performance showed Sir David's name is "one of the most powerful global brands in sport, lifestyle, entertainment and much more". "It's been an outstanding year, from new partnerships to important philanthropic campaigns and overall brand growth," he said. Sir Davidpreviously drew criticismfor associating himself with a country where same-sex relationships are illegal by acting as an ambassador for the 2022 Men's Football World Cup in Qatar. "It was an important competition and one I was proud to be part of," he said at the time, adding that he had engaged with the LGBTQ community during the tournament. Headline: Are claims of a white genocide in South Africa real?
Body: This video can not be played An Afrikaner lobby group has displayed thousands of white crosses on the National Mall in Washington DC, saying they represent the victims of a genocide of white people in South Africa. But South Africa's new ambassador to the US, Roelf Meyer, says that the notion of a mass attack on the white Afrikaner minority in South Africa does not exist. Meanwhile, the Trump administration is planning to admit up to 17,500 additional white Afrikaners as refugees over the next 12 months, according to a notice sent to Congress on Tuesday. Headline: Greek PM urges Burnham to return Elgin Marbles permanently
Body: The Greek prime minister has called on Andy Burnham to find the "political will" to send the Parthenon sculptures back to Greece. Kyriakos Mitsotakis wrote in the Guardian that returning the classical treasures, also known as the Elgin Marbles in the UK, would "send a powerful signal" but would require "courage". The sculptures have been on display in the British Museum since the 19th Century, though Greece has long disputed the legality of their removal. Mitsotakis and his government have previously held talks with the British Museum about the sculptures, but the two have so far failed to reach an agreement, with Greek authorities seeking their permanent return. The Greek PM used the recent fanfare generated by the loan of the Bayeux Tapestry to the British Museum to restate his country's claim to the Elgin Marbles. "Nobody would seriously contemplate cutting what survives of the tapestry in two and displaying half in London and half in Bayeux, and claiming this was an adequate way to understand it,"he wrote on Thursday,external. "Yet that is exactly what happened to the Parthenon sculptures." His comments come after British Museum director Nicholas Cullinan suggested that the recent arrangement struck between the UK and France, after decades of rejected requests to borrow the medieval embroidery, offered hope of a deal with Greece over the Elgin Marbles. Mitsotakis said he was "surprised at the recent suggestion from the museum that the Bayeux Tapestry loan might provide a template for an agreement over the Parthenon sculptures", adding: "I do not believe it does." "Greece cannot accept any arrangement that would require it to recognise the British Museum's ownership of the sculptures, or a scheme that would mean we 'borrow' parts of our own monument," he wrote. Instead, he urged Burnham to stand by his previous comments on the sculptures and find a way of returning them for good. This would be a "decisive step", Mitsotakis said, that would "reunite the sculptures and transform a historic dispute into a unique act of cultural friendship". Back in 2023, several years before he returned to government and became prime minister, Burnham said the sculptures should be returned to Greece with "no strings attached". For years, he supported a change in the law to allow for this. But last month, he told the Financial Times that "ultimately it's an issue for the British Museum", adding that "legally that's where that issue rests". Many of the Elgin Marbles originate from the Parthenon in Athens British ambassador Lord Elgin was granted permission by the Ottoman Empire, the governing authority in Athens at the time, to remove some of the marble statues in the early 19th Century. They were created between 447BC and 432BC to decorate the Temple of Athena - what is now known as the Parthenon, in the Acropolis in Athens. After an 1816 parliamentary select committee deemed Elgin's actions legal, the sculptures entered the British Museum collection by an act of Parliament. The Greeks dispute their removal was lawful and the demands to return the statues have been vocal. The Parthenon gallery in the Acropolis Museum in the Greek capital was deliberately designed with spaces left for the sculptures in the British Museum. Back in 2023, George Osborne, then the museum chair, told the BBC he was looking for a "more co-operative arrangement" after "quite a bitter disagreement" with the Greeks for more than 200 years. Mitsotakis's latest comments appear to suggest a ramping up of rhetoric around the thorny issue once again. Last month, Greece's health minister told Breitbart News he would like to see US President Donald Trump pressure the British to return the Parthenon pieces. The British Museum's position - and that of the UK government - is that the law prevents the permanent return of items held in its collection, though loan agreements are common. Campaigners point out that the British Museum Act could be amended. However, the UK government has not signalled that this is a priority. Elgin Marbles: What are the Parthenon Sculptures?

Headline: British celebrities beat AI companies lobbying to get free use of their work. They have a warning for Australia
Body: ‘People care about the songs, books and pictures that influence the critical moments in their lives,’ says the architect of the fightback in the UK Get ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcast If you want to state the case against copyright reform in Australia, get Kylie Minogue’s phone number. If there is one lesson to be learned from a similar battle in the UK, high-profile members of the creative industries make a difference. They get your argument on the front of newspapers, in the news bulletins and on social media. In the face of this onslaught, the UK government backtracked on plans to let AI firmsuse copyright-protected work without permission. The many artists who put their name to various letters and protests against the reforms to create a virtual red carpet, included: Sir Elton John, Sir Paul McCartney,Abba’s Björn Ulvaeus, the actor Julianne Moore and the Radiohead singer Thom Yorke. John had one of the most memorable soundbites,calling the government “absolute losers”who were on course to “rob young people of their legacy and their income”. Overall, the campaign was more sophisticated than just rounding up irritated celebrities. Beeban Kidron, a member of the upper house of the UK parliament and an award-winning film director, marshalled an effective political campaign against the proposals by pushing legislative amendments thatwould have spiked the plans. She also helped organise celebrity opposition. Kidron says the campaign struck a chord with the public. “People care about the songs, books and pictures that influence the critical moments in their lives,” she says. Polling backed this up, withseven out of 10 adultsin the UK supporting the payment of royalties to copyright holders whose work had been used to train AI models. The Australian prime minister should take heed, Kidron says. “Albanese has been a leader in standing up to tech. He should not squander his reputation by selling Australian creatives down the river.” The campaign against copyright reform also benefited from the ingenuity of an industry that knows how to grab people’s attention. One of the most prominent figures in the movement against the proposals, Ed Newton-Rex, organised a “silent” album and an “empty” book, to warn of the consequences of watering down copyright law. “There is no one out there, who does not work for an AI company, who thinks AI companies should not pay for the content they use,” he says. “What we did in the UK was make the government understand that was the case.” Newton-Rex, a composer and former AI executive,put together an albumfeaturing recordings of dormant music studios and performance spaces, called Is This What We Want? It was backed by more than 1,000 musicians, including Damon Albarn, Kate Bush andAnnie Lennox. The author stunt, called Don’t Steal This Book, involved 10,000 writers listing their names in an otherwise empty paperback. Contributors included Kazuo Ishiguro,Philippa Gregoryand Richard Osman. “The only way the government gets something like this copyright proposal through is if no one notices what they are doing. It will take just a moment for people to understand this is not fair,” says Newton-Rex. Albanese’s government needs to be wary of committing the same mistake as its centre-left UK counterpart, says Pierre Andrews, a former adviser on culture policy under Rishi Sunak’s Conservative government in 2023-2024.“The [UK] Labour government’s mistake was that it thought it could convince the creative industries to go along with it,” he says.Instead, the nation’s assembled artists and authors recoiled at a perceived betrayal by a party they thought would be on their side.“There was a strong sense of surprise within the creative community that Labour would even consider changing copyright to their detriment,” he says, adding that he foresees another government U-turn, but in Australia this time. The tech industry still believes in the win-win argument; that the UK could get behind a policy where domestic AI companies are able to train models on British shores using copyright-protected content, while the holders receive adequate compensation for their work. “The government recognised that it didn’t frame the initial consultation very well,” says Antony Walker, deputy chief executive of trade association techUK. “But I also think rights holders were extremely effective at shouting down the debate. It was a one-sided argument.” In March the then UK technology secretary, Liz Kendall said the key proposal to let tech companies train on copyright protected material unless artists “opt out” of the process beforehand was no longer the government’s preferred option. The new prime minister, Smiths-loving Andy Burnham, has yet to set out a new policy on copyright but would face a battle-hardened opposition if he took the unlikely step of taking on the creatives again. Over to you, Kylie,BazandHugh.

Headline: Fifteen new members in Isle of Man general election
Body: First-time MHK Kirrie Jenkins (second right) topped the poll in Arbory, Castletown, and Malew Fifteen new members have been elected in the 2026 general election, with three members of the council of ministers losing their seats. The outgoing enterprise minister Tim Johnston, education, sport and culture minister Daphne Caine and environment, food and agriculture minister Clare Barber have all lost their seats in the House of Keys. Former infrastructure minister Michelle Haywood, former health and social care minister Lawrie Hooper, former education, sport and culture minister Julie Edge, and deputy speaker of the house Ann Corlett were also among the seven outgoing MHks that were not re-elected. In the western constituency of Glenfaba and Peel, Daniel Davison said it was "surreal" to be the youngest ever MHK to be elected in Manx politics at the age of 18. Chief Minister Alfred Cannan kept his seat in Ayre and Michael There were 82 candidates contesting the election for the 24 seats available in the House of Keys. The poll saw 15 new Members of the House of Keys selected, eight of whom are women - down from 10 in 2021. The new House of Keys had been guaranteed to have eight new faces following the retirement from politics of six members, the election of Juan Watterson as President of Tynwald, and the death of John Wannenburgh in August. The results have seen the re-election of two members of the Manx Labour Party - Sarah Maltby and Joney Faragher. However Liberal Vannin Party leader Lawrie Hooper losing his seat in Ramsey means that party has no elected MHKs for the first time since it was established. Party founder Peter Karran failed to make a political comeback in Onchan after 10 years away from politics. Neither of the newly created parties - Change and Transform Isle of Man - secured seats. Sarah Maltby topped the poll in Douglas South Stephen Broad and Alfred Cannan have been elected for Ayre and Michael In Ayre and Michael, Stephen Broad topped the poll while Chief Minister Alfred Cannan has kept his seat. Broad told Manx Radio he would "give it my best shot". Cannan said the election period had been a "humbling experience" but thanked constituents for taking the time to speak to him. He said he needed to shape things in a way to try to address some of the "critical problems that have been raised on the doorstep and that "we all know we are facing". The result meant former Enterprise Minister Tim Johnston was ousted from his seat. Katryna Baptist and Daniel Davison have been elected in Glenfaba and Peel In Glenfaba and Peel, Katryna Baptist came out on top, with Daniel Davison becoming the youngest ever person to be elected to the House of Keys. Baptist told Manx Radio she was "really excited" although there was a "lot of work to do". Davison, who is 18, said it was "such a surreal experience," adding that "it brings a generation to government who have never been there before". Jane Poole-Wilson and James Cochrane have been elected for Middle Deputy Chief Minister Jane Poole-Wilson attracted the most votes in Middle, with James Cochraine taking the other seat. Poole-Wilson told Manx Radio that she was "honoured" to be re-elected and to have served over the past five years. James Cochrane said he was "really proud" to have stood next to the other candidates in Middle. In Douglas East, Andy Saunders and Joney Faragher have been elected In Douglas East, Andy Saunders came out on top of the poll while Joney Faragher kept her seat. But Environment, Food and Agriculture Minister Clare Barber was out after 10 years in the House of Keys. Richard Henthorn and Victoria Hewison have been elected for Garff Richard Henthorn and Victoria Hewison have been elected for Garff. Reacting to the results, Hewison said she was "shocked" as she "really didn't expect to get in". Kirrie Jenkins and Jason Moorhouse will represent Arbory, Castletown and Malew Kirrie Jenkins and Jason Moorhouse will represent Arbory, Castletown and Malew. Jenkins said she was feeling "elation" to be elected and she was "speechless". And Moorhouse said it was a "privilege" to be elected for a third term. Juan McGuinness topped the poll followed by Robert Cowell Juan McGuinness topped the poll in Ramsey followed by Robert Cowell. McGuinness told Manx Radio that the "hard work starts now," and Robert Cowell said he was "overwhelmed" and "very grateful" to be elected. Lawrie Hooper, who lost his seat after 10 years in the House of Keys, said that although he was "disappointed" McGuinness and Cowell would do a "fantastic job". Hooper, who is a former health minister, said he was proud of his work to reduce waiting lists, and would now go back to being a chartered accountant. David Ashford and Damian Ciappelli will represent Douglas North In Douglas North, David Ashford topped the poll for the third time, while Damian Ciappelli was elected to the seat previously held by John Wannenburgh, who died suddenly in August. Ciappelli told Manx Radio that he was "delighted" to be elected and was "ready to get stuck in." Peter Shimmin tops the poll in Douglas Central followed by Chris Thomas Peter Shimmin, who secured the highest number of votes in Douglas Central, said he was "overwhelmed" and "incredibly grateful". When asked about his priorities, he said the economy, affordable housing and "anything that supports younger people and families and makes the Isle of Man a great place to build your future". Current Treasury Minister Chris Thomas – who kept his seat – said he was "very pleased" to be elected in a "difficult constituency". He said there were "many, many important challenges and we need to rise to them", citing issues with transport, public finances, healthcare and food security. "Compromise is a good thing, consensus is a good thing, but we can't afford a fudge," he added. Meanwhile, Ann Corlett, who lost her seat, said it was "a little disappointing" but she had "a strange sense of relief" that she could "get back" to her life and "do some of the things I've been planning to do". She said her highlights included bringing through social legislation and being Deputy Speaker of the House of Keys. Mark Kemp and Michael Crowe have been elected in Rushen Michael Crowe and Mark Kemp were elected in Rushen, while former infrastructure minister Michelle Haywood lost her seat. Crowe, who topped the poll, said he was "grateful" to be elected and was "looking forward to getting stuck in". Kemp told Manx Radio: "I think people are just sick of what we've had," adding that he wanted to focus on diversifying the economy. Rachel Glover topped the poll in Onchan, with Rob Callister second In Onchan, Rachel Glover topped the poll at her first attempt to gain a seat in the House of Keys. Rob Callister, who retained his seat by coming second in the vote, said on Facebook that he was "deeply grateful and honoured" to have been re-elected, adding, "tomorrow, I get back to work". Julie Edge, who failed to get re-elected, told Manx Radio: "I have worked really hard for the people of Onchan, and I have delivered, but the results are what they are." Edge, who served a spell as education minister during the outgoing administration, said she would continue with her work on whistleblowing. Sarah Maltby and Claire Christian have both been re-elected in Douglas South In Douglas South, Claire Christian said she was "really thrilled"  with the "really wonderful" result. Christian, who is the current health minister, added: "I want to thank the electorate." Sarah Maltby, who topped the poll for a second time, said on social media: "Thank you for trusting me to represent Douglas South. "I am completely overwhelmed with the support." Peter Shimmin topped the poll in Douglas Central, followed by Chris Thomas Those who have been elected will be sworn in as MHKs on Tuesday by the first and second deemsters. The House of Keys will then sit on 13 October to nominate a chief minister and speaker of the House of Keys. Headline: 'A tumour the size of a football saved my life'
Body: Lisa Carroll was only 41 was she was diagnosed with the rare form of ovarian cancer A mum-of-three who was diagnosed with a rare cancer has urged other women not to dismiss their symptoms. When Lisa Carroll, 47, from Coventry, returned from a family holiday in August 2021, she thought she was suffering from irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), a kidney infection or something minor. Instead, she was told it was mucinous ovarian cancer (MOC), one of the rarest forms of ovarian cancer in the UK. "I thought I had possibly a bit of IBS or a kidney problem or something like that. I was in quite a lot of pain," she said. Next year, Carroll and her husband are looking forward to celebrating their 20th wedding anniversary After calling NHS 111, Carroll was sent to hospital in Coventry where medics discovered a 12cm cyst on her right ovary. She was told it did not appear particularly sinister and was placed on a waiting list for surgery. "Within a month, a cyst the size of a fist had grown to the point that I could feel it like a football in my stomach. Pain and discomfort got worse and I felt shattered emotionally and physically", she said. By December, scans revealed the tumour had grown to 20cm and was beginning to rupture, so three days later she underwent an emergency procedure to remove the tumour, a fallopian tube, her appendix and surrounding tissue. Two weeks later, doctors gave her the diagnosis. Following surgeries and chemotherapy, Carroll is approaching her five-year anniversary of being cancer free The cancer is exceptionally rare, with only around 200 cases diagnosed annually in the UK, said Ovacome, an ovarian cancer charity. "Some ovarian cancers are really sneaky, hang around for years and you've got no sign of any symptoms at all", said Carroll, who works as the CEO of Lifespace Trust, a Warwickshire-based charity for young people. "The fact that mine grew so quickly was what alerted them as early as they did." Yet despite losing her hair and enduring months of treatment, she says the biggest challenge was something she had not been prepared for. "I got chucked into early menopause and that was the bit I massively struggled with. I didn't know what was depression and what was menopause." The Ovacome charity is hosting a fundraising walk in Cannon Hill Park, Birmingham on Saturday "I didn't know what was a cancer symptom and what was a menopause symptom. I couldn't open the washing machine, the dishwasher or the oven. I couldn't cook anything on the hob because I'd just have this awful hot flush. I was forgetting words. I was incredibly emotional." Today, Carroll is cancer-free and approaching the five-year milestone that will see her formally discharged from oncology care. "I do not underestimate how fortunate I am that my long-term outlook is a lot brighter than for many," she said. "That brings with it a kind of survivor's guilt." She has since became involved with Ovacome, which connected her with others facing the same fears. "They became my safe space," she said. "They helped me to connect with other people who understood what I was going through. They made an incredibly scary and isolating time feel far more manageable." Now preparing to take part in the charity's annual fundraising walk, Carroll hopes sharing her story will encourage others to trust their instincts and seek help when something feels wrong. The fundraising walk takes place at Cannon Hill Park in Birmingham on Saturday.
