Headline: India is producing more green energy - but wasting a lot of it
Body: Renewables make up for 54% of India's total 552GW installed power capacity On a hot July afternoon this year, electricity generated from renewable energy briefly met over half of India's peak power demand - only the second time this happened. The first instance was around the same period a year ago. While it was only briefly that power generated from solar, wind, hydro and nuclear sources collectively outstripped coal-based output, it was a milestone moment reflecting the astonishing growth of non-fossil fuels to the country's electricity mix over the last decade. "It showed that renewable energy is no longer a marginal source sitting at the edge of the power system," Sumant Sinha, CEO of ReNew Power, one of India's largest Nasdaq-listed clean energy companies, told the BBC. To be sure, coal-based power plants still continue to generate 70% of India's electricity on average because they run on a higher load factor, or for more hours than solar or wind. Yet, the country's push for clean energy appears to have reached a crucial inflection point. A decade ago India's installed renewable energy capacity was barely 4GW. It now makes up 300GW or 54% of its total 552GW installedcapacity,external- a target that's been achieved five years ahead of schedule. For a nation long seen as the poster child for dirty coal dependence, this rapid transition points to a remarkable achievement in decarbonising its grid. Yet, the gains are tempered by some serious challenges. Electricity generated from renewable energy briefly met over half of India's peak power demand in July Foremost among them is a shortage of grid capacity. The renewables' build out has significantly outpaced transmission infrastructure, a point of major concern for policymakers. "In the first quarter of 2026, transmission constraints accounted for nearly two-thirds of all renewable energy curtailment at 300 gigawatt-hours (GWh)," according to Ember, a global energy think-tank. Put simply, that means a bulk of the clean energy that was produced in India was wasted because the country's transmission lines have been dogged by missed targets, with one out of four inter-state projects facing delays of over a year. The difficulty lies in matching the speed of generation projects with the grid build-out, says Sinha. "Generation projects can be constructed in 18-24 months… Transmission can take much longer because they involve right-of-way, land acquisition, approvals and coordination across many agencies. It is an execution issue that becomes more important as the system gets larger," he adds. Vibhuti Garg of the Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis also blames "poor planning" for the problem. The grid was able to absorb new capacity as long as India was generating 10-15GW annually, she told the BBC. But that pace has dramatically increased, reaching a record 51GW last year, and the infrastructure is no longer able to cope. The concentration of renewables projects in the north-western states of Gujarat and Rajasthan has also compounded the challenge of evacuating power in the face of such grid shortages. Analysts at Ember now believe this growing mismatch between fast-moving generation projects and slower-moving transmission infrastructure, is the "most critical operational risk to the country's 2030 target of 500 gigawatts (GW) of non-fossil electricity". A quick solution to addressing this gap would have been to build battery storage systems at renewable pooling stations to integrate the power into the grid. "Had that been the case, India could have stored the energy and used it during evening hours rather than wasting it," says Garg. But storage capacity has not grown because of a huge jump in the price of batteries, raw material shortages due to the war in the Middle East and a fall in the value of the Indian currency which has jacked up financing costs for Indian companies. "Many storage projects that were meant to come up fell through as a result," Garg adds. Indian renewables projects are concentrated in the north-western states of Gujarat and Rajasthan Yet, finance isn't a constraint merely for storage projects but an industry wide problem. While ample global capital is available for green transition across the developed world, getting access to it remains a persistent struggle for Indian clean energy companies, despite the strides that the country has made in its renewables commitments. Estimates suggest the country will require $400-$500bn to meet its 500GW renewables target by2030,external. But currently, around 83% of India's finance for climate mitigation is sourced domestically, according to the government's economic survey.  While the Paris Agreement clearly mandated developed countries to provide financial resources to the tune of $100bn annually up to 2025 to developing countries for their climate action, that money has been hard to get. "Emerging and developing economies outside China receive only around 15% of global clean-energy investment, despite accounting for roughly two-thirds of the world's population," says Sinha. According to him, while India does not necessarily need developed countries to finance its entire transition, help is needed in the form of cheaper loans, guarantees and protection against currency losses so that  private investors are encouraged to put in more money into the space. Plugging these critical gaps in finance, transmission infrastructure and storage will be critical given this transition is under way at a pivotal moment, say experts. Transmission shortages are said to be the most critical operational risk to India's renewables build-up India is the world's third largest emitter of greenhouse gases and facing a sharp rise in electricity demand, which has grown at a compounded rate of  over 7% every year. It is expected to further accelerate with the expansion of industries like data centres and chip manufacturing. TheInternational Energy Agency,externalpredicts India's electricity demand will increase by 80% by 2035, the sharpest jump among emerging economies. It also credits the country's robust expansion of its renewables as a major contributor for slowing emissions in the developed world this year, even as energy related CO2 emissions rose more strongly in advanced economies for the first time since the 1990s. How successful India is in achieving its targets on time will thus have an outsized impact on the world's ability to meet its climate goals. Headline: Celebrity Traitors 2 cast: Who are this year's 'big dogs' and dark horses?
Body: The winning celeb will score £100,000 for their chosen charity Celebrity Traitors returns next week for a second round of deception and amateur detective work. Hosted by Claudia Winkleman, the Traitors castle will welcome 21 new celebrities on Thursday, as a group of famous "faithfuls" attempts to work out which among them are - and perhaps, always have been - "traitors", secretly murdering contestants each night. Last year's show provided Bafta's most memorable TV moment - an award voted for by the British public - when traitor Alan Carr broke down in tears at the end of the final having bluffed his way to a win by hiding in plain sight. Let's have a stab in the dark, then, at who might follow in Jonathan Ross's footsteps as this year's "big dog", and who, like singer Cat Burns, could fly under the radar? If Carr was the star of last year's show, then perhaps his fellow TV funnymen could be the ones to watch this time around. Naturally good readers of a room and skilled at misdirection, comedians can inject some comic relief into those tense roundtable moments. It worked for Carr, who was considered to be less of a threat and more out of his depth by the other sleuths. This time around, stand-up starJoe Lycett, 38,is one of the leading candidates for the role of class clown. Known for his quick wit and political stunts, Lycett told the BBC he asked Carr for advice on "how to spot a rotten little traitor like you". Last year's winner replied: "Just anyone that's sweating and giggling." With his brightly coloured outfits, Lycett will bring some glamour to the castle, if and when he's not donning the famous dark cloak. "There's a lot of variety and silly stuff that I might not get to wear at all if I end up doing a Paloma," he noted, with reference to Paloma Faith, who was brutally killed off early doors last year by her supposed friend, Carr. If laughing all the way to the winning line is to work again, then it's hard to look beyondJames Acaster. Anyone who has seen his Netflix special Repertoire or heard his podcast Off Menu will know his deadpan, absurdist humour and whimsical flights of fancy could make it difficult to tell whether he is telling the truth or not. A "huge fan" of the show since the first non-celebrity edition in 2022, Acaster, 41, said he would prefer to be a faithful as he wasn't good at lying - though Carr did previously say something similar... Romesh Ranganathan's dry humour and wry presenting style saw him succeed Anne Robinson as the host of The Weakest Link revival in 2021. Could it help him to become a more believable traitor or faithful? The former maths teacher and now comedy podcaster, 48, blamed his youngest son, who was "desperate for me to come on", for his reluctant participation this year. One of his best friends on the comedy circuit, Parenting Hell podcasterRob Beckett, is another of this year's funniest contestants. A decade's worth of friendship with the 8 Out of 10 Cats and Mock the Week panellist could count for nothing in the castle, Ranganathan said. He believes Beckett, 40, is "just as easily going to be on my side as he is going to twist the knife in my back given the opportunity". One of the nation's other most celebrated comics,Miranda Hartwill no doubt be a big personality among the group. In her self-titled sitcom, she starred as an awkward, accident-prone shopkeeper. Her apparent clumsiness and warm, self-deprecating persona might make her seem more trustworthy (rightly or wrongly). After a spell of ill-health, Hart, 53, hopes "the joy of mucking about on television again will hopefully outweigh some of the challenges". Irish comedianJoanne McNally, 43, could also be the joker of the pack this year. Her popular podcast My Therapist Ghosted Me is full of gossip, oversharing and comic bickering - music to the ears of the Traitors producers, no doubt. Her stand-up is confessional and brutally honest. But honesty gets you nowhere in this game - or does it? The "Big Dog Theory" was a piece of gameplay logic proposed by ex-rugby union star Joe Marler during roundtable discussions last year. His reasoning was that one of the most famous contestants, AKA the big dogs, would have been chosen as a traitor to cause mass confusion (and, presumably, strong viewing figures). Marler wondered out loud whether the big dog traitor in question was Sir Stephen Fry (no) or Jonathan Ross (yes). For the new series, a glut of huge names and personalities from across the worlds of film, TV, music, modelling and broadcasting have also been selected. Michael Sheen,the award-winning Welsh actor and campaigner, is perhaps the biggest dog in the fight, so will come under real scrutiny. Sheen, 57, is acclaimed for his ability to convincingly portray a range of different personalities on screen, from Tony Blair to Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor via Brian Clough. But in real life, he's seen more as a loveable golden retriever than a Rottweiler, despite his success. Which version of him we shall see on the show remains to be seen. Fellow big screen charmerRichard E. Grant, 69, who starred in films such as Withnail and I, may also leave some of the less well-known celebrities star-struck at first, as might American-British supermodel/actressJerry Hall. Hall, 70, shares four children with ex-partner Mick Jagger and has also been married to media mogul Rupert Murdoch. Love Island presenterMaya Jama, 32, and University Challenge host, journalist and YouTuberAmol Rajanare also powerhouses in the world of broadcasting. Speaking ahead of the show, 43-year-old Rajan, who is in it to win it, said : "I don't want to go in there and at round table number one be Mr Forensic Investigator! "However, I do interview politicians for a living, and I really have to pursue answers to questions." He's conscious of putting "a target" on his back too soon, so plans to form alliances. "To begin with, I want to try and make friends and keep my head down," he added. EastEnders hardman turned hard-hitting documentarianRoss Kemp, 62, might prove popular once the tasks get physical. And we don't know yet whether to expect the soppy You're Beautiful balladeerJames Blunt, 52,or the prolific (and hilarious) online troll of the same name. Either way,ifthe Big Dog Theory holds true, then one of the above will surely find themselves in the traitors' turret before long. Little Mix and solo singing starLeigh-Anne Pinnock, 34, may be a big dog in the world of pop music, but she comes across as a down-to-earth family woman these days. Don't be fooled, though, as she has a wealth of experience of managing relationships under intense public pressure from her girl group days. Meanwhile, another potential dark horse,Bella Ramsey, revealed they had been playing a version of The Traitors since they were 10 years old, even hosting events at home - so should be well-prepared. Now 22, the Last of Us star, who also featured in Game of Thrones, is the youngest of this year's contestants but should not be underestimated. The Traitors castle should be a cakewalk compared with the apocalypse or the Battle of Winterfell, right? The plan is to be "instinctive, measured, and perceptive", Ramsey said. "I will be keeping my opinions to myself until I feel it's absolutely the right time to share them." King Kenny, a member of popular British YouTube collective Beta Squad, is known for pranks, vlogs and more recently (and briefly), boxing. The 29-year-old will be hoping the class of 2026 has more faith in online influencers than last year, when his Beta Squadmate Niko Omilana was the first player banished from the castle. Omilana's early exit also sparked a discussion among some critics about non-white contestants being voted off UK/US reality game shows at an early stage, and whether unconscious bias may play a role. Mathematician and broadcaster,Hannah Fry, who co-hosts The Rest is Science podcast, could fill David Olusoga's intellectual shoes this year. Historian Olusoga quietly made it to the final last year despite having repeatedly voted out faithfuls thinking they were traitors. Fry, 42, said she was "here to fulfil the nerd quota" and was taking the responsibility "extremely seriously". She added: "I would say people tend to think I'm smarter than I actually am, bluntly, and I don't think that's going to serve me particularly well as I may be seen as a bit of a threat." If the comedians are aiming to be the next Carr, then who could be the new Cat Burns and fly under the radar all the way to the final? US actressMyha'la, 30, who plays Harper Stern in banking bonkbuster series Industry, may be top pick. Unlike her ruthless character on the show, she said she was more of a "kill them with kindness kind of girl rather than a blatantly bullish bulldog". She added: "All that said, I want to be a Traitor. Obviously!" She's deliberately planned her look - clothes, hair and jewellery - to separate herself from Stern and "be seen as me and not that character". Julie Hesmondhalgh, will be known to audiences Up North especially as Roy Cropper's wife Hayley in the soap Coronation Street, between 1998 and 2014. Hesmondhalgh, 56, who also appeared in Broadchurch and Mr Bates vs the Post Office, won't struggle to make friends with her warm personality. But they'd be wise not to forget she is, after all, a talented and experienced actress. Sharon Rooney, star of My Mad Fat Diary and the Barbie film, is another contestant likely to keep a low profile, which, as we've seen, can work well up to a point. But will it trigger suspicion of the Scottish Lawyer Barbie actress, 37, eventually? And last but not least,Sebastian Croft,star of the recent Netflix coming-of-age hit Heartstopper, rounds off our list. Younger viewers will know all about Croft, 24, already, but will the older contestants? Some names are bigger than others right now, but as three of last year's finalists - Burns, Olusoga and Nick Mohammed - discovered, that could change quickly over the coming episodes. Headline: UK to review Chagos Islands deal over lack of US support, Streeting tells BBC
Body: This video can not be played  The UK is reviewing its deal to hand over the Chagos Islands to Mauritius, the defence secretary has said. Wes Streeting confirmed the deal was being looked at again after US President Donald Trump called it "terrible" at the UN General Assembly on Tuesday. The original agreement would see the UK cede sovereignty of the territory to Mauritius and pay an average of £101m ($136m) per year to lease back a joint UK-US military base there, prized for its strategic location in the Indian Ocean. In April the deal, agreed under Sir Keir Starmer, waspaused indefinitelybecause Trump pulled his support. Streeting said "we have to" review the deal "because the United States doesn't support it". "What President Trump said yesterday wasn't new but I think it does provide absolute clarity that his position on this Chagos deal as currently drafted is not changing," he told BBC Breakfast. "So we have to do more work with our American allies, with President Trump and his administration, to get the deal to a place where he can support it." Streeting said the focus now would be to secure a long-term certainty for the base on Diego Garcia, the Chagos archipelago's largest island. He said it had been the view of every UK prime minister since Boris Johnson that an ongoing legal process - as Mauritius argues it was illegally forced to give away the islands in 1965 to gain independence - risks the security of the base. During Trump's first face-to-face meetingwith Prime Minister Andy Burnham at the UN General Assembly in New York, the US president criticised the "terrible deal" and said the UK was "going to be looking" at it. Burnham replied: "Yep." He later told broadcasters he has "inherited the situation and we need a resolution". Burnham added: "It's critical to safeguard the future of the base, and that matters to us for security reasons, but also clearly to the United States as well. "What I said in the meeting is that we will work to find that resolution between the different sides, and we'll work hard to find it." The prime minister had spoken to his Mauritian counterpart, Navin Ramgoolam, ahead of his trip to New York, and an official readout from that meeting said Burnham "reiterated his commitment to continue doing everything possible" along with the US to ratify the deal. The "review" is not expected to constitute a formal process operating to a specific timeframe. Government sources are insisting that Burnham and Streeting's comments do not represent a major shift from the previous position, which was that any deal would require American support. However Streeting's comments were notable for their explicit acknowledgement that without changes the deal is not going to attract Trump's support. Prior to the pause in April, the UK and Mauritius had signed an agreement in May 2025 and a final draft of the bill to hand over sovereignty of the islands had not passed Parliament. Under the terms ofthe deal agreed in 2025, Britain would hand sovereignty over the archipelago to Mauritius but lease back the Diego Garcia base for 99 years, which the UK government said would be a net overall cost of £3.4bn. However, Sir Keir, who was then prime minister, came under heavy criticism from opponents who said the real cost of the deal could amount to £35bn, adjusting for inflation, and risked allowing China to establish a presence on the archipelago. Trump, who originally backed the deal, has been a frequent critic of the move, previously branding it a "a blight on our great ally" and an "act of total weakness". Reacting to the review, Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch called on Burnham to "just scrap this terrible deal". Reform UK leader Nigel Farage said: "The Chagos deal is dead. Thank God." In 2019, the International Court of Justice (ICJ) gave an advisory opinion that Britain's separation of the Chagos Islands from Mauritius was unlawful and stated the UK must end its administration as rapidly as possible. While non-binding, the ICJ advisory opinion - which was endorsed by the United Nations General Assembly - emboldened Mauritian assertions of sovereignty and led to theUK opening negotiations in 2022. Streeting told BBC Radio 4's Today programme on Wednesday that no money would be handed over to Mauritius "at this stage" while officials review the deal. Describing the Diego Garcia base as "one of the most sensitive and valuable national security assets", he said work was underway to find a deal "that maybe not everyone loves, but everyone can live with". Headline: Rolls-Royce signs 'multi-million' engine deal
Body: The order includes both the engines and a maintenance package Rolls-Royce has moved forward with a deal to power a new fleet of Airbus long-haul jets for Philippine Airlines. The FTSE-100 firm will provide 18 engines for nine new Airbus A350-1000 aircraft in a deal worth "hundreds of millions of pounds". The agreement, once finalised, also includes a maintenance package, meaning Rolls-Royce will continue servicing and monitoring the engines throughout their operational life, officials said. The government welcomed the deal, saying it would bring "good quality jobs" to the  company's Derby base. The order was first announced as a memorandum of understanding at the Farnborough International Airshow in July. At the time, Rob Watson, president of civil airspace at Rolls-Royce, said the company was "proud to continue strengthening our long-standing relationship with Philippine Airlines". While the deal is described as being worth "hundreds of millions", the precise value has not been confirmed. Airbus designs and manufactures wings for all its commercial aircraft at its Broughton site in North Wales. Minister for trade Anas Sarwar said: "This news shows British engineering is flying high with world-class innovation that puts our companies at the front of the pack. "Building these engines and wings brings good quality jobs to Derby and Broughton, and means UK expertise is at the heart of thousands of flights by one of the fastest-growing airlines around the world." The engine involved, the Trent XWB-97, can operate using a 50% sustainable aviation fuel blend, with plans for it to run on 100% sustainable aviation fuel in the future. This order follows Philippine Airlines's previous order for nine Trent XWB-97-powered Airbus A350-1000 in 2023. Headline: Just how hot and dry was your summer? Use our postcode lookup to find out
Body: The UK faced its hottest summer on record this year, with much of the country experiencing drought and repeated heatwaves. But temperatures and rainfall were not the same everywhere. Type in your postcode to see what summer 2026 was like in your area. A modern browser with JavaScript and a stable internet connection is required to view this interactive. As a result, we can't show information for your location, but data for the entire UK is available below. Data up to August 2026 In the UK summer temperatures have beenabove average. The maximum daily temperature was21.3Con average, which is2.4C abovewhat it was for summer between 1991 and 2020. Virtually all of the UK experiencedabove averagetemperatures, driven by repeated heatwaves. Southern England and Wales saw heat far above usual. Temperatures were closer to normal across Scotland and Northern Ireland. Colder: blue Warmer: red -4C: deepest blue No Change: white +4C: deepest red Rainfall in the UK has beenbelow averagethis summer. Across the country a total of195mmof rain fell on average, which is23% belowwhat it was for summer between 1991 and 2020. Summer months tend to be drier, but this year was exceptional. Only north-western Scotland saw more summer rain than usual, as droughts were declared across much of the rest of the UK. Drier: brown Wetter: blue -100%: deepest brown No Change: white +100%: deepest blue This lookup uses data from theHadUK Grid dataset(opens in new tab), which is produced by the Met Office Hadley Centre. HadUK Grid is one of the main products used by scientists to monitor and research the UK’s changing climate. The HadUK dataset displays temperature and rainfall data across a uniform grid covering the entire landmass of the UK. The data does not cover the Channel Islands. Every value on the grid is an estimate for the centre point of a 1km by 1km grid box, the most detailed climate data publicly available for the UK. The values are created using observations from land-based weather stations across the country, and by taking into account additional factors such as altitude, terrain and distance from the coast to scientifically “fill in the gaps” between weather stations. The results displayed for each grid area represents a mean average of that grid cell and its nearest grid cells. For most areas, this represents a 5km square centred on the primary grid cell. Along irregular coastlines and on small islands, the nearest grid cells are chosen to match the shape of the coastline or island, but no cells are further than 7km away. This approach aims to avoid sharp jumps between neighbouring locations which may occasionally arise due to uncertainties in the data, while still making use of the most detailed dataset available to capture local weather conditions across the UK's varied geography. The data for 2026 is provisional, with fewer observations feeding into calculations due to lags in data availability. As such, the precise values could change slightly in future as more data comes available. The historical averages are calculated over a 30-year period from 1991-2020, which matches the standard period used by the UN’s World Meteorological Organization. The average temperature represents the mean average of the selection of grid cells across the month or season. The maximum temperature is the mean average of the daily maximums recorded across all nearest grid cells for the month or season; the minimum temperature is the mean average of the daily minimums. The rainfall is the total amount of rain for the month or season, averaged across the selection of grid cells. Methodology support from Dan Hollis, Amy Doherty and Oli Claydon, UK Met Office. HadUK Grid is one of the main products used by scientists to monitor and research the UK’s changing climate. The data for 2026 is provisional, with fewer observations feeding into calculations due to lags in data availability. As such, the precise values could change slightly in future as more data comes available. The historical averages are calculated over a 30-year period from 1991-2020, which matches the standard period used by the UN’s World Meteorological Organization. The HadUK dataset displays temperature and rainfall data across a uniform grid covering the entire landmass of the UK. The data does not cover the Channel Islands. Every value on the grid is an estimate for the centre point of a 1km by 1km grid box, the most detailed climate data publicly available for the UK. The values are created using observations from land-based weather stations across the country, and by taking into account additional factors such as altitude, terrain and distance from the coast to scientifically “fill in the gaps” between weather stations. We’ve matched every active postcode in the UK to its nearest 1km by 1km grid cell in the HadUK dataset. The results displayed for your area represent a mean average of that grid cell and the surrounding grid cells to your location. For most areas, this represents a 5km square centred on your postcode. Along irregular coastlines and on small islands, the nearest grid cells are chosen to match the shape of the coastline or island, but no cells are further than 7km away. This approach aims to avoid sharp jumps between neighbouring locations which may occasionally arise due to uncertainties in the data, while still making use of the most detailed dataset available to capture local weather conditions across the UK's varied geography. The average temperature represents the mean average of the selection of grid cells across the month or season. The maximum temperature is the mean average of the daily maximums recorded across all nearest grid cells for the month or season; the minimum temperature is the mean average of the daily minimums. The rainfall is the total amount of rain for the month or season, averaged across the selection of grid cells. To calculate the number of days above the heatwave threshold, we first averaged the daily maximum temperature for each grid cell with its nearest grid cells on every day. Using the Met Office’sheatwave thresholds(opens in new tab), we determined how many maximum daily temperatures exceeded the threshold for your location, based on the centre of your grid cell. Your area’s heatwave threshold may be approximate if your postcode is near a county boundary. This is not the same as the number of days spent in an official heatwave, where the threshold has to be met or exceeded for at least three consecutive days. Methodology support from Dan Hollis, Amy Doherty and Oli Claydon, UK Met Office. High-pressure weather systems sat over the UK for much of the summer, bringing clear, sunny skies for many parts of the country and creating warm, dry conditions. But global warming - mainly the result of the burning of fossil fuels - israising average temperatures in the UK. This means that any warm spells can reach higher temperatures than the same weather systems of the past. The Met Office estimates that this summer's average temperature was made about130 times more likely by human-caused climate change. Rising temperatures also mean that our vegetation and soils dry out more quickly - which can worsen the effects of low rainfall. UK summers are expected to become drier on average due to climate change - although when there is heavy rain it could fall in more intense bursts. Not every summer will be as hot or dry as this one, as weather patterns vary from year to year. But scientists warn that average temperatures will keep increasing while countries keep adding greenhouse gases to the atmosphere. Headline: Burnham brands ban on football fans drinking alcohol in stands as 'discrimination'
Body: Andy Burnham has branded a ban on fans being allowed to drink alcohol in the stands during men's football matches as "discrimination". The prime minister told reporters that "I don't think it's fair for football fans to be singled out", as he suggested a change could be trialled. Laws are in place which prevent drinking in view of the pitch at stadiums for clubs in the top five tiers of men's football in England. Other sports do not face such a restriction. The Football Supporters' Association (FSA) said the "outdated" legislation should be reviewed, but police chiefs have warned against relaxing the law and would like to meet the PM to "explain the challenges". The legislation was introduced in 1985 by Margaret Thatcher's government for English and Welsh football grounds. At the time, then-Home Secretary Leon Brittan said that alcohol was a "major contributory factor in violent and disorderly behaviour" in football grounds. Burnham is a keen football fan and a season-ticket holder at Premier League team Everton. Shortly before he became prime minister, he criticised the restriction on football fans as he attended a rugby league game at Everton's Hill Dickinson Stadium where it was possible for supporters to have a drink in the stands. Speaking to reporters on his trip to the United Nations in New York, Burnham was asked if it was still his view now he is in Downing Street. Burnham replied: "I think that legislation dates to an era where football was very different. "And I do believe there is a case to remove that discrimination. There are different ways it could be done. It could happen on a trial basis. "But I'm not going to back away from what's been a long held view of mine. I don't see how it can be fair that some supporters of one sport can be treated differently." Government sources have stressed that Burnham was restating an opinion that he has long held, rather than making any sort of policy announcement. The prime minister's comments are not being seen inside government as an indication that he is looking to change the law in the area. A trial or pilot scheme to look at whether a change would be possible is not being ruled out but any wider move would require extensive consultation involving football clubs, fans and the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport - none of which is currently planned. A UK Football Policing Unit (UKFPU) spokesman warned that changes to the law would pose "challenges" to policing and the "safety of staff and fans at football games". He said: "Other sports simply don't see the violence and criminal behaviour from their supporters that football does, albeit a minority, with alcohol often playing a significant part in violent and disorderly behaviour. "It would be irresponsible to fuel this by allowing greater alcohol consumption during games." He added it would be "incredibly rash to make fundamental changes without a full examination of the evidence and meaningful consultation with police practitioners who have the expertise in this area". FSA chairman Tom Greatrex said it was "unfair to criminalise football fans for having a pint while watching the match - especially since you can sit in the same seat drinking alcohol whilst watching an Oasis gig or rugby league". He said "many clubs" were in favour of a change, adding: "We welcome the prime minister's comments and totally agree that the legislation is outdated and deserves to be reviewed." A fan-led review of football governance in 2021 called for the law to be re-examined. The rules have been relaxed this season withall Women's Super League (WSL) clubs allowed to offer alcoholto supporters in the stands following two seasons of successful trials. The law is more restrictive in Scotland, where the general sale of alcohol has been prohibited in Scottish football stadiums since 1981, but trial sales have been taking place recently andfans can now buy alcohol at Hampden Park games. Headline: One Nation boss called David Farley an ‘asshole’ in lead-up to Farrer byelection, text messages reveal
Body: Exclusive:Documents seen by Guardian Australia show that Kelvin Morton has also clashed with party HQ staff and Brisbane volunteers Get ournew political email,free appordaily news podcast One Nation’s general manager, Kelvin Morton – brought in by the party to improve its vetting processes – referred to David Farley as an “asshole” just days beforeFarley’s historic Farrer byelection winfor the party in May. In a series of text messages seen by Guardian Australia, Morton responds to anews article published in the Sydney Morning Heraldabout infighting among senior party figures over Farley’s previously undeclared support for the Labor party. “Shit stirring,” he writes. “We need to do way better with our candidate selection – we need to stop finding these assholes … or letting them find us. “I guess this might nail David’s colours to us a little more. He’s sworn allegiance in the face of all the concerns being raised – he’d look like a completely untrustworthy snake if he jumped ship after the election – he’d be ruined forever.” AOne Nationparty spokesperson said that Farley was “a dedicated One Nation MP”. “The comments made do not reflect the view of the party. “The only untrustworthy snake is the person who leaked the text messages.” Tensions between Farley and other One Nation MPs and staff have reportedly been high since he was elected to parliament, with the party having topublicly criticise himafter he claimed One Nation’s migration policy was not dissimilar to the Labor government’s. Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here Morton, who claims on his LinkedIn to be a “strategic business transformation leader” with vast experience with some of the world’s biggest companies, was appointed as general manager in February. At the time, he said the party’s national executive had wanted him to build a “professional, scalable, and legally robust organisation capable of outright victory at the next general election”. He claimed to be introducing a new vetting process and was in his position when Farley was preselected. But while his appointment was heralded as a turning point for the professionalisation of the party, the Guardian can reveal that Morton has since clashed with staff at the party’sBrisbaneheadquarters and officials at one of the party’s most active branches. He was recently appointed to the One Nation national executive, replacing former treasurer Alex Jones. Documents seen by the Guardian show he wrote to the Lilley branch in Brisbane advising it of federal intervention, which included removing the entire committee of volunteers. This came after a dispute about access to promotional materials and a local fundraiser that raised $12,000 for the party. The dispute arose after Morton and the Lilley branch coordinator, Mark McGuire, clashed over access to promotional materials for a different event, which prompted Morton to suspend him. “Your membership will continue to remain suspended until a formal written apology is received by you,” Morton said, accusing him of removing promotional materials from head office and clashing with a staff member. McGuire told the Guardian he had accessed policy flyers to take to an event being run by the party’s Brisbane branch. Other volunteer branch members and the president, Deb Dalton, complained about McGuire’s treatment, advising head office that the branch committee would cease volunteering in protest. Sign up toPolitics, really Our political team brings you up to speed on the stories that really matter and what they mean for you after newsletter promotion The letter from Morton sent in response stated that he accepted the board’s “resignation”, despite the branch members only advising they would cease volunteering. “The Federal Executive is now intervening in the management of the Lilley branch as its functioning and compliance are in question,” he writes. “All branch decisions and actions are now subject to direct review and management by the Federal Executive, which reserves the right to overturn any local decision which is not in the best interest of the Party.” Morton also accused the branch of not handing over $12,000 raised at a branch fundraising dinner last year and demanded it be transferred to party headquarters where it would be controlled by the party’s national executive. “You are reminded that … branches are strictly prohibited from maintaining independent bank accounts,” Morton said in a letter to the branch president. “All branch funds – including the $12,000 referred to by Mark McGuire in his phone call to me – must be managed centrally.” He said he would revoke the membership of all branch committee members, and that “ongoing membership is contingent upon the full and transparent return of all party property, financial records, and the $12,000 in raised funds”. McGuire told the Guardian that he believed the party’s volunteers had been treated unfairly and the $12,000 had already been paid automatically to central office when people bought tickets. “They were treated with no procedural fairness and total disrespect,” McGuire said. “They all put their own time in, they make a sacrifice for their own family. “The fact is that he’s got it wrong, the question is, where’s the 12 grand? Who’s had their sticky fingers in the pie? He needs to stand up and be accountable to show the whole of the branch where the 12 grand is.” A One Nation spokesperson said the party “does not provide comment on internal disciplinary actions”. “All branch donations are managed through a microsite that tags funds with the corresponding branch. Branch funds are quarantined for localised campaigns.”

Headline: Trump reveals millions of dollars' worth of share deals in big tech and AI
Body: US President Donald Trump US President Donald Trump has disclosed millions of dollars' worth of stock market trades made during July, including in firms from Elon Musk's SpaceX to tech and AI giants such as Microsoft. According to official documents, between $6.5m (£4.8m) and $31m worth of stock in Microsoft was sold on behalf of Trump, while they show purchases of between $165,000 and $400,000. Across more than 1,000 trades, shares were bought and sold in AI company Nvidia and software firm Palantir, a contractor with the US defence department and Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), the filing shows. A White House spokesperson said Trump's stock and bond portfolio is independently managed by third parties. The spokesperson told the BBC: "Neither President Trump nor any member of his family has any ability to direct, influence or provide input regarding how the portfolio is invested or when investments are bought or sold. "There are no conflicts of interest." According to the filing, thousands of dollars' worth of stock was also bought and sold in SpaceX, the rocket, satellite and AI company led by Musk - who was once in charge of the US Department of Government Efficiency. SpaceX listed its shares on the US-based Nasdaq stock market in June. Its share price has fluctuated since then, sharply declining in July and August, but it is currently trading 14% higher than its stock market debut. Shares were also bought and sold in Tesla, Musk's electric vehicle-maker, on behalf of Trump. Trump has previously publicly disclosed thousands of stock market trades since he returned to the White House in January last year. The disclosure of the July trades made on behalf of Trump emerged against a backdrop of renewed focus on AI and how safe it is. Trump has rejected calls for safety-driven slowdowns, warning that restrictions risk the US slipping behind China. He told an audience of world leaders at the United Nations General Assembly on Tuesday that he wants torebrand AI as "super intelligence" to project American dominance. Trump has previously argued that the US must come out on top in the AI development race, stating last week: "Whoever wins AI, wins." He is firmly against government regulation or introducing new guardrails, putting him at odds with many of those gathered at the UN, including Secretary General António Guterres who continues to advocate for binding international safeguards. The president is set to meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping this week during a state visit to Washington. While Trumpframes a rebrand as an instrument of national competition, his administration is simultaneously proposing an emergency AI "hotline" with Beijing to managepotential cyber risksorrogue AI incidents. Headline: Heathrow Airport warns third runway could be delayed by four years
Body: The UK's busiest airport, Heathrow serves more than 80 million travellers a year with its two runways and four passenger terminals in west London Heathrow Airport has warned that its planned third runway might be delayed by four years due to planning and regulatory issues. The government had hoped the new runway at the UK's busiest airport, estimated to cost £33bn, would open by 2035. But Heathrow sees this deadline as increasingly difficult to deliver without further steps to simplify the planning process. It said on Saturday that it hoped to secure planning permission by 2029 and then open the runway "within a decade". The Department for Transport (DfT) said the project's timeline had "always been ambitious" and that it would continue to work with stakeholders "at pace" on the matter. The airport said its "core scenario" had always been to open a new runway within a decade of securing planning permission. It said it was encouraged by the chancellor's efforts to streamline infrastructure and remove regulatory bottlenecks, and promised to continue to work with ministers, airlines and stakeholders to "progress the planning application with pace". Former chancellor Rachel Reeves announced the government's support for the project in January 2025 as a means to grow the economy, and Prime Minister Andy Burnham - who was previously critical - said he was "open-minded" about the scheme when he came to office. Despite attracting wide opposition from environmental campaigners and local resident groups, the project is expected to create around 100,000 jobs and provide a major boost to the economy as part of a wider £49bn modernisation of the airport. The expansion would mean demolishing hundreds of homes, diverting rivers, and rerouting the M25 motorway between junctions 14 and 15 through a tunnel under the new runway. The number of flights from the site, currently capped at 480,000 a year, could go up to 720,000 - or nearly 2,000 a day on average. An artist's impression showing three runways at Heathrow Airport London Mayor Sadiq Khan has always opposed the new runway, warning of the impact on noise, air pollution and climate change. The government's climate advisers warned last week that the expansion should only go ahead if airlines were required to pay for cleaner flying,which could push up the cost of flights. Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander said the advisers had set out "one view" but there was "more than one pathway to meeting our climate change obligations", in an interview with the Daily Telegraph published on Friday. A draft of the planning framework for the expansion was published in June this year for consultation. Once finalised, it then needs to be put to a parliamentary vote, which could reportedly be delayed until 2027. What's the plan for a third runway at Heathrow Airport? Third Heathrow runway should only go ahead if airlines pay for cleaner flying, say advisers Heathrow expansion an 'outdated' risk, mayor says A DfT spokesperson said: "There is currently no live planning application for a third runway, and we cannot comment on ongoing consultation processes or prejudice them in a way that will only delay progress. "The timeline has always been ambitious. We'll continue to work with promoters, including Heathrow, and all other stakeholders at pace to ensure the right framework is in place for which a planning application for a third runway could be considered." A spokesperson for Heathrow said: "It's right that ambitious targets were set; the sooner expansion begins, the sooner the whole UK will benefit." They said the benefits would involve "at least 108,000 new jobs and billions of pounds invested in supply chains in every part of the country". "This is a national project, 100% privately financed which will support growth today and secure the UK's position in the global economy once the runway opens." Heathrow is the UK's busiest airport, serving more than 80 million travellers a year with its four passenger terminals and two runways. Correction 26 September: An earlier version of this story said the runway was estimated to cost £49bn. It has been updated to reflect that this figure is the total amount of investment planned for the airport, including £33bn for the runway.

Headline: Big Bang wins over fans old and new at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium
Body: Taeyang, G-Dragon and Daesung of BigBang perform during the 2026 Coachella Valley Music and Arts Festival A sea of glowing yellow crowns. Thousands of voices chanting in Korean. An explosive surge of energy as the opening synth riffs of Fantastic Baby shatter the stadium air. Big Bang is back. Fourteen years after their first major European shows, and after a decade marked by military service, member departures and legal scandals, the South Korean group played at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium in London on Saturday as part of their 20th anniversary world tour. Inside the near-capacity venue, the crowd did not just watch a concert - they stepped into a significant moment in K-pop history. As the band emerged in their trademark high-fashion, glittering outfits, the crowd danced freely, setting the tone for an evening that felt less like a routine tour stop and more like a homecoming. Inside Tottenham Hotspur Stadium For fans, it is a long-awaited reunion. But the significance of Big Bang's return extends beyond nostalgia. Years before BTS were selling out Wembley Stadium and Blackpink were headlining Hyde Park, Big Bang were already proving Korean pop could succeed far beyond Asia. The group filled arenas across the West, collaborated with major American artists, experimented with hip-hop and electronic music, and turned their own fashion and creative identities into part of their appeal. Having attended their European debut at Wembley Arena in 2012, the shift in atmosphere on Saturday was striking. Where their original UK shows were driven by a hunger to prove themselves and promote a new album, this return as a trio, comprising G-Dragon, Taeyang and Daesung, felt entirely crafted for their dedicated community. By reworking classic tracks and cleverly remixing songs to accommodate absent members, the group relied on pyrotechnics, their signature live band and sheer stage presence rather than elaborate staging. The result was a reunion that felt celebratory, grounded and playful. G-Dragon, Taeyang and Daesung on stage with dancers In 2011, Big Bang became the first K-pop group to win a major Western music award when they took home the newly created Worldwide Act prize at the MTV Europe Music Awards. When they made their European debut at Wembley Arena in December 2012, a second show was added after the first sold out in under two hours. They were leading a pioneering generation that proved global crossover was genuinely possible. Then in 2016, Forbes estimated Big Bang had earned $44m (£33.2m) over the previous year, making them the first K-pop act to appear on its Celebrity 100 List. "When it comes to the global market for K-pop, there is no doubt Big Bang made a huge contribution," says Dr Haekyung Um, senior lecturer in music at the University of Liverpool. "Earlier acts were popular within Asian markets, but Big Bang were true international stars. I would call them the Kings of K-pop, just as we call Michael Jackson the King of Pop," Um adds. "Big Bang's success really was an early signal of how successful a K-pop stadium tour in the West could truly be." G-Dragon, Taeyang, and Daesung celebrating their 20th anniversary during the XX: Cosmos World Tour Before Big Bang, K-pop groups were often viewed as heavily manufactured by entertainment agencies. But music critics say Big Bang broke the mould. They wrote and produced their own songs, shaped their own streetwear image and blended genres ranging from hip-hop and R&B to trot, a traditional South Korean folk genre. For many attending on Saturday, the show served as a direct lesson in K-pop's lineage - a chance to see "the idols' idols" perform live. "They were different because they didn't follow the uniform K-pop cookie-cutter pretty boy phase," explains Sharon, who was visiting London from Singapore. "They went harder on their music, a bit more hip-hop. They did what they had to do, and they are the absolute OGs for me." The shift set them apart across Asia and helped establish the blueprint for modern self-produced acts such as BTS. Fans arrived kitted out with Big Bang merchandise And then there is the yellow crown. At Big Bang concerts, it is impossible to miss the group's crown-shaped lightstick, known as the Bang Bong. In early K-pop, fans supported artists by waving coloured balloons or generic glow sticks. But seeking a distinct, permanent identity for their fandom, dubbed "VIPs", band leader G-Dragon proposed a handheld yellow crown, setting the template for custom concert merchandise. "Fan engagement and coordinated chants have deep roots in Korean music history," explains Um. "But Big Bang helped modernise the physical technology." The Bang Bong established a model for custom-designed fandom lightsticks and merchandise that modern K-pop groups now follow. Outside the venue, that same fan-led energy spilled into the streets, with attendees trading handmade gifts and photo cards - a ritual that has spread to Western arena tours in recent years. Volunteer fan groups distributed roughly 35,000 custom-printed banners across the stadium, co-ordinating a massive crowd-wide salute to be raised in unison during select performances. Fans exchanging handmade gifts outside the stadium Big Bang's story, however, is far from a straightforward tale of success. South Korea requires able-bodied men to complete mandatory military service, and Big Bang's members served at different points during the group's hiatus. Then came the scandals. In 2017, former band member T.O.P was convicted of marijuana use, an offence heavily criminalised and socially taboo in South Korea, and received a suspended prison sentence while serving his mandatory military duty. He later formally departed from the group. Then in 2019, the group's youngest member, Seungri, permanently retired from entertainment amid the "Burning Sun" scandal. It was a high-profile police investigation into a Seoul nightclub of the same name which exposed a network of sex trafficking, bribery, and illicit filming involving several male K-pop stars. South Korea's Supreme Court later upheld an 18-month prison sentence for Seungri in 2022 on charges including prostitution mediation, overseas gambling, and embezzlement. Fans with their merchandise, holding up free banners ahead of the show Although the band didn't openly acknowledge the departure of two of their former members from the stage, their absence was obvious to long-time fans in the audience. Though it did not matter to fans like Annie, who flew from New York to see the show with friends. She said Big Bang's perseverance through hardship made their music mean even more. "Big Bang was my starter," she says. "I love how they move through the obstacles - it gives me hope. After years of hiatus, it's amazing they're coming back. They are the OGs." The crowd erupted as the opening chant of Bang Bang Bang echoed before the band even walked out, while their iconic 2008 ballad Haru Haru produced a massive stadium-wide singalong. Fans meeting up ahead of the concert The K-pop industry Big Bang helped build has changed almost beyond recognition. Yet their return has drawn a striking mix of original second-generation fans and younger Gen Z listeners who were barely born when the group debuted. While many veteran followers grew up alongside the band, a whole new generation discovered them through digital archives or cross-media appearances. Gemma and her daughter Casey travelled from Edinburgh wearing handmade custom jackets. "I found out about them through T.O.P in Squid Game and then fell down a rabbit hole," Gemma says. "I've converted so many of my friends to K-pop now. It's all about the energy." For Korean diaspora fans, the show carried an even deeper cultural resonance. "I got into Big Bang when their Alive EP (in 2012) was released because I felt they were quite ground-breaking," says Kevin. "Before, I felt there was a lot of mimicking by Korean artists on what was happening in the West, but here they took full ownership of their unique identity. It's very rare in K-pop that you have a band around for 20 years, and they definitely played a part in making K-pop mainstream." Nicole and her son Arthur attended the concert to celebrate his 8th birthday Much of this multi-generational pull is driven by archival concert footage, TV appearances, and classic music videos circulating across social media platforms like TikTok and YouTube. "Nostalgia can be built upon something people didn't even experience personally at the time," notes Um. "It comes through shared digital memory. YG Entertainment was early in leveraging digital platforms like YouTube, which built a lasting global fan foundation that has accumulated across two generations." While the band refrained from directly addressing their past on stage, the emotional weight of their history peaked during the finale Still Life. As T.O.P's unmistakable baritone echoed through the stadium via recorded vocals, a visible wave of emotion swept across the crowd. Addressing the venue during the encore, G-Dragon appeared clearly moved, admitting they never expected their music to leave such an enduring global mark 14 years after their London debut. As fireworks lit up the night sky, the three members linked hands and bowed deeply - a triumphant moment for the group widely credited with helping reshape modern K-pop. ‘My heart still hurts’: The personal sacrifice of revealing a K-pop scandal Pop megastars BTS electrify historic centre of Seoul with comeback concert Japanese pop group XG went from brutal five year training to global pop stars

Headline: Internet restricted after fighting breaks out in Ethiopia's Tigray region
Body: The internet was cut in Tigray during the two-year civil war which ended in 2022 (file photo) Internet and call services have been disrupted in Ethiopia's northern region of Tigray following the outbreak of fighting this week between regional forces and the national army. Services provided by state-owned telecoms operator Ethio Telecom have been completely cut, although those from the smaller private firm Safaricom remain operational. Internet monitoring group NetBlocks earlier posted on X that network data indicated a sub-national internet shutdown in northern Tigray. "Last night telecommunications got knocked out," Duke Burbridge, an American humanitarian worker in Tigray's capital, Mekelle, told the BBC's Newsday programme. The BBC has contacted Ethiopia's authorities for comment. Sources have told the Reuters news agency that the group which controls Tigray, the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), ordered the communications blackout, with one suggesting it was to disrupt government drones. The TPLF has not commented. The BBC is unable to report from Tigray and surrounding areas. Even before the current disruption, finding video and images to establish what is happening on the ground has been a challenge. So far, other than footage from Mekelle, most of what has been shared online has been from outside the region. The young women who fought in Ethiopia's last civil war and don't want to see another one Burbridge said there had been a scarcity of cash in Tigray for the past eight months, with people unable to access ATMs so the lack of internet services would be "devastating for everybody". Many people rely on banking and mobile money applications for transactions, with the majority using Ethio Telecom and Safaricom's networks to access these services. On Thursday a Mekelle resident who we are only identifying as Fitsum made a similar point. He told the BBC "there is almost no cash" in the city. With the outbreak of war, people were limiting their movements and the city was all quiet - "it's like a curfew has been placed," he said. This video can not be played Tigray capital 'out of cash' as fighting escalates Clashes between Tigrayan forces and their allies and Ethiopia's federal troops broke out on Wednesday, prompting fears of a return to a full scale civil war and reports of panic buying. A humanitarian source in the neighbouring region of Afar told the AFP news agency there was "heavy fighting overnight", including drone strikes, around the town of Abala in the mountains between Afar and Tigray, as "federal forces pushed the rebels from entering the town". There have also been reports of fighting near the town of Lalibela in the Amhara region, which is home to churches hewn out of rock, recognised as a UN World Heritage site. The US has warned against travel to all three regions. During the two-year conflict which ended in 2022, Tigray was totally cut off from the outside world. Limited access to cash, food and medicine pushed hundreds of thousands into famine-like conditions. It was one of the most deadly conflicts this century - with estimates that some 600,000 people died as the fighting drove the region to the precipice of famine. On Sunday, the TPLF announced an alliance with six other armed groups to oust the government. On Wednesday, its forces seized control of three airports from federal police. Following the seizure of the airports, Ethiopian Airlines has cancelled all flights to Tigray. Headline: Trump says he can do business with Burnham but criticises 'terrible' Chagos deal
Body: This video can not be played Burnham "gets it" says Trump, as the two leaders meet for first time US President Donald Trump has said Andy Burnham is a man he can do business with, after the two leaders met in person for the first time. Trump said UK-US relations are "more up now" that Burnham is in power, following their meeting on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York. Speaking to reporters, Burnham said he had "established a good connection" with Trump and they had "taken that further today" following discussions on issues such as trade and immigration. But the US president made clear his opposition to the UK's "terrible" deal to hand over the Chagos Islands to Mauritius and pay to lease back a joint UK-US military base on the archipelago's largest island, Diego Garcia. Burnham, asked by broadcasters if the deal is "dead", later said the UK will "work hard" to find a resolution between the different sides and he is "confident we can find it working with our US partners". Trump and Burnham met on Tuesday as they attended the United Nations for the annual gathering of world leaders. Following bilateral talks, Burnham sat alongside Trump and used his opening remarks to say: "You and I have established a good connection in our early discussions and we've taken that further today." The two men then faced questions shouted from the assembled press pack. Asked by the BBC if Burnham was a man he could do business with, Trump said: "Yeah I do, I think he's a natural businessperson, we've had a lot of discussions even before this meeting we've spoken to each other numerous times on the phone. "Yeah, I think so, he gets it, he understands what he has to do." Burnham later said he had explained to Trump that Britain has been in "too much turbulence" in recent times but it is time to "turn the story" about the country into a positive one. The US president added that the UK is a country with "great patriotism", and he thinks it is "waiting for good leadership, waiting for success". Relations between Sir Keir and Trump also began well before becomingincreasingly strainedearlier this year when the then-prime minister refused to permit the use of UK bases for the initial US-Israel strikes on Iran. Trump reiterated his criticism of the Chagos Islands deal and stressed how a joint UK-US military base on Diego Garcia is "strategically very important", particularly in relation to US operations in Iran. The agreement would see the UK cede sovereignty of the territory to Mauritius and pay an average of £101m ($136m) per year to lease back the military base - but in April thedeal was paused indefinitelybecause Trump pulled his support. Speaking on Tuesday, Trump said: "I think the prime minister is going to be looking at [the deal]." Burnham replied: "Yep." He later told broadcasters he has "inherited the situation and we need a resolution". Burnham added: "It's critical to safeguard the future of the base, and that matters to us for security reasons, but also clearly to the United States as well. "What I said in the meeting is that we will work to find that resolution between the different sides, and we'll work hard to find it." The prime minister had spoken to his Mauritian counterpart, Navin Ramgoolam, ahead of his trip to New York. Reform UK leader Nigel Farage, who has long been a critic of the deal, posted on X: "The Chagos deal is dead. Thank God." Burnham also referenced that his private discussions with Trump included the Falkland Islands, which have been the subject of comments by the US president and Argentina's president Javier Milei. The Falklands, in the south-west Atlantic Ocean, remain the subject of a sovereignty dispute between Britain and Argentina, more than 40 years on from an armed conflict over the territory. Earlier this month,Trump hinted he would not come to the UK's aidin a potential future conflict with Argentina over the British overseas territory. He had previously said theUS could revise its neutral position on the islands' sovereigntyif the UK failed to increase defence spending. Milei heightened tensions with the UK after hewarned he would impose economic sanctions on firms which exploit oil close to the Falklands. During a national address in early September, Milei also said: "The Falklands are our future, we need to recover these islands which are nationally relevant. There is no other path forward". Burnham told broadcasters: "We will stand firm in the face of any threats, we will defend the right of the Falkland Islanders to self-determination and to remain British. "And I just wanted the [US] president to know directly from me, that's the clear British position, and he very much understood what I was saying." One of the areas Burnham has been keen to focus on during his trip to the UN is artificial intelligence (AI). The prime minister met business leaders, including Apple's executive chairman Tim Cook, on Tuesday. He told them he wants a "single set of global principles and standards that are very much about unlocking the full potential whilst guarding against the risks". Burnham's approach could cause friction with Trump, with the president using his address to the UN General Assembly to say that the US "totally rejects any attempt to construct a globalist scheme" to control AI. Trump dubbed AI as "super intelligence" and said the US will "encourage it, not rein it in". Burnham later met European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, with the PM apologising for arriving around 10 minutes late due to his bilateral with Trump running over. Von der Leyen reassured the PM, saying: "These things are understandable." Sign up for our Politics Essential newsletterto keep up with the inner workings of Westminster and beyond. Headline: FBI investigating claim hackers have stolen details of all its agents
Body: The FBI is investigating a claim by a cyber-crime group that it has stolen sensitive information on all bureau staff - around 38,000 people. The group, Shiny Hunters, says it has every agent's name, role, badge number and personal details including home address, phone numbers and spouse information. Professor Ciaran Martin, the former head of the UK's National Cyber Security Centre, said - if confirmed - it was "as serious as it gets when it comes to data breaches." In a statement posted on X, the FBI said it was aware of the claim and the agency was  "actively and aggressively investigating the matter". The criminals claim to have breached the FBI's servers on Monday night and began contacting reporters on Tuesday sharing samples and screenshots of the stolen data. The BBC has seen a small portion of the data, which appears to be genuine. According to Reuters, some of the data contains details about officials' ​job assignments, including sensitive work against Chinese spies, Russian intelligence and drug cartels. ShinyHunters is an international collective of hackers, believed to have originally started in France. It has been behind a number of high-profile breachesincluding on Rockstar Games in Apriland a highly disruptive hack on education platform Canvas in May. The group claims to have found a vulnerability in the Oracle cloud storage system used by the FBI to breach multiple systems including FBIJOBS, FBI BEAST, which does background checks on employees and applicants, FBI MedLink, which holds agent's medical records and FBI BICS, which holds investigation information. In its message on the dark web, the group said it did not hack the FBI system for money. Instead, the cyber-criminals are asking the agency to retract an advisory that it issued in May about the gang, saying it was "offended" by its characterisation. That FBI'spublic service announcement,externaldescribed ShinyHunters as "threat actors" who often "use their real or exaggerated claims of access to sensitive or personal information to prompt payment from victims". "They target major companies across tech, finance, and retail, often stealing millions of customer records at once," the advisory said. ShinyHunters said it would give the bureau one week to correct or remove what it says are false allegations or they would publish the full databases. The FBI did not respond to multiple requests for comment from the BBC. In its statement on X, the agency said it was trying to determine whether or not the hackers had breached its systems or a third party. "We are actively and aggressively investigating this matter and working closely with those third-party providers that support FBIJobs.gov to mitigate any and all risk," the post said. In a statement to the BBC, a cyber-security expert said it was a "retaliation attack", which demonstrated that "no organisation is safe from the group". "The group clearly wants to control the narrative around their activities, ensuring nothing is said that could dent their reputation," said William Wright of Closed Door Security. Meanwhile Andrew Brandt of cyber-security firm Huntress said it may provoke the FBI to track down and prosecute members of the hacking group. "ShinyHunters must feel pretty confident they won't get caught to threaten a government agency like this," he said.

Headline: US rejects pleas from OpenAI, Anthropic for global AI standards
Body: Sam Altman of OpenAI has become a key figure in the AI technology development. The heads of OpenAI, Anthropic, and Hugging Face have told the UN that the current pace of artificial intelligence (AI) development, and the risks it poses to society, demands international coordination. Altman called for common risk evaluation standards, as did Dario Amodei of Anthropic, a main rival of OpenAI, and Clement Delangue of Hugging Face. Earlier this month, Amodei wrote an essay welcomed by Altman and others calling an AI development slowdown in response to fears about the technology's threat to humanity. However, at the same UN conference, a key technology advisor to US President Donald Trump, rejected the idea any new form of AI regulation. Michael Kratsios, a former Scale AI executive, admitted that the speed of AI development is increasing and that there are risks presented by the technology, but told the UN this was not reason enough "to pause development or constrain it with new global governance structures". "International dialogue in this forum and others cannot be allowed to drift toward global governance," Kratsios added. Kratsios's comments echoed similar statements made by Trump in recent weeks. Trump told the UN on Tuesday hewanted to rebrand it "super intelligence"and has strongly opposed any idea of an AI slowdown because of the US's competitive advantage in the sector. "We're leading China on AI... and, frankly, I want to keep it that waybecause whoever wins AI, wins," he said earlier this month. Sam Altman of OpenAI and other AI chief executives expressed a different view in their talks to the UN on Wednesday. "If AI is to be democratic, the most important decisions cannot be made by labs in San Francisco alone," said Altman. He told the UN that he wanted countries to start working together toward "the collective good in the face of powerful new technology". He called for "national and international" AI standards on measuring the capabilities of an AI tool, assessing related risks, AI safeguards, and the degree to which human oversight over such tools is maintained. He also called for "speedy incident reporting, classification, and reporting protocols so the world can learn from failures before they become catastrophes". "We need common standards so countries can compare evidence, verify compliance, and have a shared language and understanding what is happening," Altman added. Not all AI workers think the tech could kill everyone AI 'kill switch' may need to be mandatory, Anthropic co-founder tells BBC AI staff 'genuinely frightened' for humanity's future, ex-Anthropic researcher tells BBC Anthropic's Amodei and Hugging Face's Delangue made similar comments in their speeches. Amodei said that AI "if managed poorly... could be a risk to humanity as a whole". He added that further development of AI tools calls for "even more stringent standards of safety". "We will slow down as much as necessary in order to make sure that every successive AI technology that we release is actually safe," Amodei added. "But regardless of what we do, managing these risks is ultimately bigger than any one company, and it has an industry-wide and global scale." Hugging Face's Delangue said: "The global community needs stronger standards for monitoring and incident disclosure." All three of the executives are based in the US and directly involved in the development of AI technology. Hugging Face, a platform for AI developers, more recently rose to prominence after it admitted tobeing hacked by AI agents, or AI bots that operate somewhat autonomously, that came out of OpenAI. Hugging Face has since been acquired by AI chipmaker Nvidia. The Hugging Face hackhas been treated as a 'wake-up call' within the industryfor the ways in which AI technology has advanced and could hypothetically act in ways that could harm humanity.

Headline: Lula bans fixed-odds sports betting a week before Brazilian elections
Body: President’s ‘hard, drastic and necessary measure’, likely to attract widespread public support, polls suggest The Brazilian president,Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, has signed an order banning fixed-odds sports betting just over a week before the first round of the presidential election, in a move he said was designed to tackle the pervasive problem of families falling into debt. The decision ends the operation, offering, intermediation and advertising of betting. The provisional executive order comes into force immediately but will need congressional approval within 120 days to remain in effect. It prohibits new deposits into accounts and gives users of betting platforms until 5 October to withdraw their funds. Lula’s government has also drafted a bill to establish criminal offences related to fixed-odds betting – the most common and dominant type of online sports betting – such as promoting them and using personal data to solicit punters. “I made the decision to take a hard, drastic and necessary measure,” he told journalists in São Paulo. “It’s like cancer, you take out the tumour, or the tumour will kill us.” Lula had also criticised the betting industry earlier this week at the UN general assembly, accusing it of “transforming addiction into profit” and of “destroying homes”. Polls suggest a ban enjoys widespread support among Brazilians. Flávio Bolsonaro, Lula’s main rival in the coming election, accused the current leader of an “electoral measure”. Brazil’s president has sharply criticised online betting at least since April, when he called for a ban. The public backlash against it grew during the Fifa World Cup when advertisements were ubiquitous and the number of people betting surged. Betting and gambling are estimated to cost Brazilian society 38.8bn reais (£5.6bn) annually and increases suicide and depression, according to a 2025 study by the nonprofit Institute of Studies for Health Policies. The country’s central bank estimated last year that Brazilians spend about 30bn reais on bets each month. That figure included spending by beneficiaries of the cash-transfer federal welfare programme Bolsa Familia (family grant), which was blocked from those platforms last year. Lawmakers, including many from Flávio Bolsonaro’s Liberal party, struck down a Lula order for tax hikes on online betting and virtual casinos in October last year. Gambling is illegal in Brazil, but the country opened the gates to online betting in 2018 during the presidency of Michel Temer. The phenomenon snowballed under the watch of the former president, Jair Bolsonaro, Flávio Bolsonaro’s father. In December 2023, Lula signed a law to regulate and tax betting companies for the first time. Months later, his administration blocked more than 2,000 online betting websites that were designated as irregular, including some linked to criminal organisations such as the First Capital Command from São Paulo and the Red Command of Rio de Janeiro. It was part of a national push to regulate the sector. Lula and members of his administration have spoken about banning online betting as necessary to close a drain to the country’s economy and to tackle a public health issue, as many Brazilians are addicted and in financial difficulties due to spending their money on these platforms. Business analysts say that revenues for sports betting, one of the betting models banned on Friday, are estimated at more than $4bn (£3bn) per year in Brazil, one of the biggest markets in the world. Before Friday’s move, Brazil’s main football clubs sounded the alarm after betting companies reportedly warned that their sponsorships would end immediately if the government banned betting. They said the move could lead to the end of Brazilian football, a claim mocked by some social media users in the football-mad country.
