Headline: Tory ex-ministers face serious questions over migrant centre chaos, inquiry hears
Body: The Manston centre in Kent, used to hold thousands of migrants, became overcrowded in 2022 An overcrowded migrant reception centre, where a man died, raises "very serious questions" for ministers in the former Conservative government, including two home secretaries and former prime ministers, an inquiry has heard. The Manston centre in Kent became overwhelmed in November 2022 at the height of the small boats crisis, with around 4,000 people held there. Home Office officials knew conditions were unlawful and children were at risk of harm, but had no alternative plan for where to accommodate them, the inquiry heard on Friday. Former Home Secretaries Dame Priti Patel and Suella Braverman shared in preliminary evidence that Number 10 was involved in decisions made at the time. The Manston centre, a former military site near Dover, was converted into an emergency holding facility for cross-channel migrants in early 2022, as small boat crossings began to soar. It was designed to hold up to around 1,000 people at any one time and for no longer than a legal limit of 24 hours. But by November 2022, thousands of people were sleeping in marquees and it was apparent that there was disease, illness and no adequate care for children traumatised by crossing the English Channel. During this critical period, the government was hoping that it could eventually send asylum seekers to Rwanda. As the number of detainees grew, doctors identified diphtheria was present - and that 31-year-old Iraqi Hussein Haseeb Ahmed was suspected of suffering from the highly dangerous disease, the preparatory inquiry hearing heard on Friday. He was not immediately taken to hospital, but died on 19 November at 05:30 after he was admitted to hospital as his condition deteriorated. "He was handcuffed until around 2am," Claire Dobbin KC, the inquiry's lead lawyer, said. "His handcuffing in hospital at a point when he must have been close to death, all require separate examination." At one stage, some 81 families were sharing one toilet with babies, children, teenagers and adults sharing the same space despite clear safety concerns, she said. Some detainees had visible wounds. One person, who was not given medical care, was using a plastic croissant wrapper as a dressing. "The position of children is a matter of great concern," said Dobbin. "Generally the circumstances in which children can be detained in England are very limited indeed." Dobbin added that one senior official at the Home Office told colleagues that the conditions were the worst he had seen in 20 years. He wrote in an email: "Political decisions have forced hard-working officials and suppliers into an impossible position. This will end up as a public inquiry and rightly." Other witnesses have said there was racism, hostility and aggression towards the detainees from some staff, with some accused of threatening to withhold meals from people who wanted to use the toilet. "The body of evidence raises very serious questions for senior officials and ministers as to how the detention of children in these conditions was tolerated on humanitarian or legal grounds," said Dobbin. Two former home secretaries involved in the Manston decision-making - Dame Priti and Braverman - have already provided evidence that will be examined in depth in future hearings. Braverman's personal legal representative - who is paid for by the government - gave no statement on her behalf during Friday's session. But the inquiry heard she had already explained in written submissions that Number 10 had been aware of the situation at Manston and that the decision to pause using hotels had led to the overcrowding. It was also told there had been "prolonged periods of disengagement" from Robert Jenrick, the immigration minister in late 2022, although he had provided a statement. It is not clear yet whether former Prime Ministers Boris Johnson or Rishi Sunak will be asked to give evidence about their roles. The inquiry team will now continue gathering evidence with the date for full hearings yet to be fixed.

Headline: US backs Elon Musk's bid to overturn €120m EU fine against X
Body: The US government is seeking to join Elon Musk's legal challenge to overturn a €120m (£105m) EU fine against X over its blue tick badges. In December 2025, the European Commissionsaid the platform"deceives users" by allowing people to pay for a blue verified check mark, because it is not "meaningfully verifying" who is behind the account. But US Assistant Attorney General Brett A. Shumate said on Thursday that the commission had "inappropriately attempted" to expand its reach to American companies outside its control. Musk, who spent millions helping elect Donald Trump and other Republicans, has previously claimed EU tech regulation "inhibits progress" for companies. The US Department of Justice (DOJ)has filed an application,externalwith the EU's General Court in support of Musk's and X's attempts to dismiss ​the case. It claims that under a section of law in the Statute of the Court of Justice of the EU, a state may intervene in disputes before the court if it "can establish an interest in the result of the case to the court". The DOJ said the US "has a clear interest" in ensuring any decision by the commission was applied consistently with "how territorial jurisdiction is generally understood in international law". It also wants to make sure it would not "otherwise prejudice" US-headquartered digital services that "contribute significantly" to its economy. Ina press briefing on Friday,external, European Commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier said it was "ready to defend" its position in court. He added that the commission had an "solid case" at its disposal, due to the alleged breach of its Digital Services Act. In addition to its use of blue ticks, EU regulators had accused X of failing to provide transparency around its adverts and denying researchers access to public data. Henna Virkkunen, the regulator's executive vice-president for tech sovereignty, said at the time of the fine's issue it was "holding X responsible for undermining users' rights and evading accountability". "Deceiving users with blue checkmarks, obscuring information on ads and shutting out researchers have no place online in the EU," she said. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio and the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) had criticised the EU regulator, accusing it of attacking and censoring US firms. "The European Commission's fine isn't just an attack on X, it's an attack on all American tech platforms and the American people by foreign governments," Rubio wrote in a post on X. "The days of censoring Americans online are over." His remarks were reposted by Musk, who added "absolutely". The European Commission denied targeting any specific nationality, stating it is simply protecting its digital and democratic standards to maintain its role as a global benchmark. The action marked the Commission's first official non-compliance decision under the Digital Services Act (DSA), one of two mandatory rulebooks governing online platforms in the EU. However, the EU is also conducting several other investigations into the platform, includingone into its integrated AI assistant Grokover concerns it was used to create sexualised images of real people. Headline: German town bans 'stumbling stone' memorials to Nazi victims
Body: "Stumbling stone" memorials - like the one pictured in the Netherlands - are often placed in memory of Jews and other victims of the Holocaust There has been a wave of criticism in Germany after the town of Heidenau, near Dresden in Saxony, decided to ban "stumbling stone" memorials to victims of the Nazis. Germany's Education Minister Karin Prien told newspaper Bild that the ban was a "scandal". Since the 1990s, many towns in countries across Europe, including in Germany and Austria,have embedded small brass plaques in the streets in memory of Jews and other victims of Nazi atrocities. The plaques, called Stolpersteine in German, are often placed outside the houses where the victims used to live or work. They are frequently funded by donations. But now councillors from the Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) party and the conservative CDU in Heidenau have voted to ban stumbling stones in their town. The AfD in Saxony has been classified as extreme-right by German intelligence, a designation the party rejects. The motion in the town council said that many citizens felt that this form of commemoration of Nazi victims was inappropriate. Memorials should in future be placed at the city's Nordfriedhof cemetery to make it "impossible to step directly onto the memorial elements", the motion stated. Stumbling stones placed near the Reichstag in Berlin However, Karin Prien, a member of the CDU, criticised the decision. "Anyone who banishes Stolpersteine and memorial sites commemorating Jewish life from public spaces to the cemetery is prioritising death over life and rendering Jewish people invisible once again," she told Bild. She said her own CDU party in Saxony also bore responsibility for the decision. Charlotte Knobloch, a Holocaust survivor and president of the Jewish Community in Munich, said that removing memorials from the cityscape was "completely the wrong approach". She told the Funke Media Group that she was "appalled that a democratic party would stoop to supporting such a transparent manoeuvre by the extremists of the AfD". Knobloch said that she was not a supporter of the stumbling stones, but added that "decentralised remembrance – which is not banished from public space but, on the contrary, permeates and shapes it" was crucial to a genuine culture of remembrance. In her own city of Munich, there are no Stolpersteine on municipal land. Instead, the city allows memorial plaques on public buildings. As the name suggests, Stolpersteine are intended as memorials people stumble upon, making them reflect on the history of their location. Gunter Demnig, the artist who initiated the Stolperstein project, said that given the recent electoral successes of the AfD "it was certainly to be expected that something like this would happen". The AfD recently secured major victories in state elections in Saxony-Anhalt and Mecklenburg-Vorpommern. Some branches of the populist AfD are classed as right-wing extremist by domestic intelligence, a designation the party strongly rejects. Its anti-immigration, "Germany first" and Russian-friendly agenda has found fertile ground in the country's former communist east. Headline: OpenAI bots meddled with multiple US government agency sites
Body: OpenAI has been at the centre of new concerns over uncontrolled AI activity OpenAI has acknowledged that it alerted "dozens" of global institutions that their websites may have been meddled with by its AI bots acting improperly. AI agents attempted to get information from "governments, universities, public agencies, and other institutions", including the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), Census Bureau and Education Department, the company said. The disclosures come days after Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese announced thatOpenAI agents had breached non-public files on the websiteof its government-run health care scheme. Since August, public fears have grown over the potentially serious, even life-threatening, impacts of AI tools falling outside of human control. OpenAI said that some of the data was accessed by AI agents, essentially bots that are designed and trained to operate somewhat autonomously, which were working to find "authoritative sources of public information". But the company noted that some of the bots went beyond that and worked to bypass security measures on websites. When attempting to get information from the Census Bureau, for instance, AI agents used tools reserved for software developers to access it, the company said. OpenAI said all of the government data accessed by bots was public. However, it noted that information that its bots accessed from the SEC, which regulates the US stock market and protects investors, was later published by AI agents on another website. OpenAI says this action was not intended. In other instances that OpenAI disclosed on Friday, its AI agents transferred data when it should not have. Such activity resulted in at least 53 incidents where an OpenAI agent took an image from ChatGPT user activity and transferred it elsewhere. The company said that in each instance of a user image being used and transferred by an AI agent, the user had opted in to allow OpenAI to train models using their data. Nevertheless, OpenAI admitted: "This is not an appropriate use of this data." It added that the leak of user images occurred before it had put in place new safeguards on AI training, and it was working to get all the user images transferred to any third-party removed. Reuters first reported the expanded investigations. OpenAI also published details to its public blog. In certain instances of the agent activity, OpenAI said the tools "bypassed" security controls of some websites. In other instances, the AI agents showed "misalignment" in attempts to get at information from websites. Misalignment is a term used by AI companies and researchers to describe instances where an AI tool did something that it was not trained to do or was otherwise unintended. OpenAI said that it was limiting identifying what entities were impacted because many had asked the company to not disclose details. "Our goal is to give each organization the facts and defer to them on if and when to make the incident public," it said. Not all of the instances involved in this incident were being considered a significant security breach, the company noted. "Some organizations may review what we share and conclude that the information was intentionally public or that the model's interaction was not concerning," it explained. "Others may identify a design issue or security weakness they want to address." Why are there concerns AI could threaten humanity, and how real are they? Could AI wipe out humans and how might it do it? The company said many of the incidents are being referred to as "agent spam", which it described as "unexpected or concerning" AI agent activity, like posting information to the internet. OpenAI began taking such incidents more seriously after an incident in July where a group, or "swarm," of its AI agentshacked the AI developer platform Hugging Facewithout being prompted to do so. Hugging Face was first to go public with the incident, with OpenAI publicly taking responsibility for it later. Clement Delangue, the head of Hugging Face, during a United Nations Security Council session on AI on Wednesday: "I often wonder what would have happened had I decided not to disclose this attack publicly." "Especially now that we know similar incidents had been happening months earlier in secret at a handful of frontier labs without monitoring," Delangue added. During that same UN meeting, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Dario Amodei, the head of rival firm Anthropic, asked for international leaders to formglobal standards for AI safetyand ways to monitor and report such incidents. This video can not be played Watch: What you need to know about the OpenAI Australian government hack While OpenAI and Anthropic have both said in recent weeks that they will bring third-party evaluators inside their companies to do real-time safety evaluations of AI tools and models, such evaluators have not yet arrived, asthe BBC has reported. OpenAI said on Friday that it is currently reviewing training activity by its AI agents and going back on a "month by month" basis from when the Hugging Face hack occurred. "Most cases identified so far have been low severity, with limited or no evidence of meaningful impact," the company said. "Given the scale of the review required, and the need to verify each case, this work will take months to complete." David Krueger, a professor of machine learning at University of Montreal and the founder of AI safety group Evitable, said on Friday that he was "deeply troubled" by the increasing number of AI-related safety incidents. He called for "an immediate, indefinite, international moratorium" on AI development. "We have yet to understand the extent of existing incidents, and future rogue AI scenarios could be catastrophic," Krueger said. Are we back in big tech's 'move fast and break things' era? Headline: Lidl banned from selling copycat Birkenstock sandals, Dutch court rules
Body: Lidl must stop selling Birkenstock copies, including sandals based on the "Arizona" worn here by actor Jason Mamoa Lidl must stop selling copycat versions of Birkenstock's famous sandals in the Netherlands, a Dutch court has ruled. The discount supermarket chain faces a fine of €5,000 (£4,200) per day if it fails to comply and must also hand over sales data to Birkenstock, according to the ruling. Lidl must also compensate Birkenstock and pay its legal fees, with the amount to be decided in separate court decisions. Birkenstock said the judgement sent a clear message that "copycats must not be allowed to free-ride on [our] creativity and innovation". The BBC has contacted Lidl for comment. The ruling, which can still be appealed against, means Lidl cannot sell its copycat versions of Birkenstock's Arizona, Madrid, Gizeh, Boston, and Florida models across the Netherlands, after the court found the discount grocer infringed on the brand's trademark "footbed design". It is the latest in a string of court decisions on Birkenstock designs. In November 2025, a Dutch court order stopped retailer Scapino from selling similar lookalikes in a judgment which is being appealed against. And in December 2025, Europe's highest court ruled everyday commercial products can hold copyright if they represent creative design choices, a decision which Birkenstock said was relevant to its "iconic" sandals. However, Birkenstock also faced a setback in Germany's highest court in early 2025. The sandals may have been cool enough for Margot Robbie to wear in the Barbie film, but the German judges ruled they werepractical products rather than works of art– an outcome Birkenstock called a "missed opportunity" at the time. Following Wednesday's ruling, Birkenstock said it will "continue to defend its rights vigorously and will use all available legal means to combat imitations of its iconic products". "To protect its retail partners and consumers, Birkenstock will continue to take decisive action against copycats seeking to profit from the company's creative ideas and innovations," it added. Birkenstock is far from the only fashion brand locked in battles with mass retailers over design mimicry. Footwear giants like Dr. Martens have repeatedly taken online big-box sellers to court over boot designs, while luxury house Christian Louboutin spent years in global litigation defending its signature red soles against high-street copycats. Birkenstock sandals are not art, says German court

Headline: Rogue OpenAI agent 'infiltrated' Australian government website in world first
Body: This video can not be played Watch: What you need to know about the OpenAI Australian government hack A rogue OpenAI agent hacked an Australian government website in June and accessed private data in what experts say is the first known case of its kind in the world. The agent "infiltrated" a statistics portal containing "non-sensitive" data from Australia's universal healthcare scheme Medicare, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said in New York on Wednesday, local time. He had a "very frank discussion" with OpenAI boss Sam Altman for taking "too long" to disclose the breach and said there would be "legal consequences". OpenAI said it only learnt of the breach in August while reviewing "misaligned model activity" and emailed a general inbox of an Australian government agency on 10 September. Five days later, that government agency, Services Australia, escalated the email to Australia's cybersecurity centre before a government minister was notified and the prime minister alerted. Albanese said he spoke to Altman and raised "Australia's extreme concern about this incident" as well as his "disappointment" that the company had taken months to reveal the breach and "the nature of the way" it did so. The Australian leader said Altman had acknowledged there were "issues with protocols" at OpenAI. A "forensic investigation" led by the country's cybersecurity agency would aim to find out if other government systems were affected, Albanese said. The probe would also assess if the matter needed to be dealt with by police, he said, noting there "will obviously be legal consequences". Detailing the breach, Albanese said it had involved "public and non-public files" on the Medicare Statistics Reporting Service portal, home to "non-sensitive" data and statistics. Three other government systems "may" also have been affected: the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare and two state-based agencies - the New South Wales Bureau of Crime Statistics and Research and the Victorian Department of Health. "No personal information is believed to have been accessed at this stage, but investigations are ongoing," Albanese said. "Nonetheless this situation is obviously unacceptable," he said. Albanese said it took "too long" for OpenAI to inform Australian officials of the breach in June OpenAI, in a statement, said it had "identified activity involving several Australian government websites and services as our models attempted to look up answers, and available statistics for questions about Australia during an internal evaluation". "In the course of that, our models took actions we did not intend," the statement said. It has also emerged that OpenAI's systems tried, and failed, to hack a digital library at the University of New Mexico in May, according to Transluce, a not-for-profit AI research lab. It said the systems also attempted to hack Data USA, a repository of public government data that same month. This also failed. Albanese declined to answer whether he raised the matter with US President Donald Trump during their face-to-face meeting on Tuesday night in New York, where world leaders have gathered for the UN General Assembly. Australia was one of 22 countries that earlier this week signed a joint statement calling for global oversight and guardrails for the development of AI. Cybersecurity experts told the BBC the incident is a wake up call for regulators, given that AI agents are becoming more widely available for individual and commercial use. Dr Hammond Pearce, senior lecturer at the University of NSW Institute for Cyber Security, told the BBC that though this is the first known incident where AI agents have chosen to breach a government body of their own volition, there'll be more to come. "I expect that these kinds of attacks will keep occurring," he said, adding that they would likely "grow in severity and in frequency". "I do hope that this incident does start ringing alarm bells in governments around the world." Earlier this year,OpenAI revealed a group of AI agents it had been testing had escaped from their controls and secretly worked together to hack another tech firmnamed Hugging Face. And a string of other rogue AI incidents have also been made public this year, including a case where a digital assistant - without instruction -booted someone off a pilates class waiting list in a bid to get an Australian man in. Several AI firm leaders themselves - including Altman, Anthropic's Dario Amodei, and Elon Musk - have said the speed at which AI is developing is dangerous to humanity and needs to be reined in. But the US and China, who are vying for AI supremacy, are roadblocks. Both are hostile to greater regulation, wanting the economic and technological spoils of AI, and have downplayed safety concerns. Headline: 'I lost my love for swimming' - Smith comes out of retirement
Body: Tatjana Smith was the only South African to win a gold medal at the 2024 Olympic Games in Paris Having ended a two-year exile from competitive swimming, South Africa's most successful Olympian Tatjana Smith has revealed she "lost the love" for her sport before stepping away from the pool in 2024. The 29-year-old's decision to retire straight after the Paris Games came as a surprise, given she had justwon 200m breaststroke goldin the French capital to add to her100m title from Tokyo 2020. But after two years away, which included several months in which she did not swim at all, Smith says she is now "free from the things that made me hate swimming". "My whole life, I was kind of a robot towards swimming," she told Newsday on the BBC World Service. "You're so zoned in, you're obsessed with something, so there isn't actually time for you to think about things outside of the pool that you potentially have a passion for. "I think probably everyone would think that the timing [of retirement] was the worst. But I absolutely 100% believe it was the best decision at that time, and I still have so much peace about it." Having also picked up a silver medal in both Tokyo and Paris, Smith's total of four Olympic medals for South Africa is matched only by fellow swimmer Chad le Clos, who claimed one gold and three silvers across the London 2012 and Rio 2016 Games. Smith on retirement and becoming South Africa’s most decorated Olympian But despite making history for her country, Smith says financial worries, which included a dispute with Swimming South Africa over prize money, also contributed to her decision to retire. "The financial burden on any athlete is so tough," she explained. "I relied on my parents funding me until I broke the world record at the Olympics. And then, all of a sudden, now people are interested in maybe sponsoring you. "But the majority of sponsorships for athletes are based on performance. So then you have that pressure and expectation to always have to perform, otherwise you're not going to get paid. "I think the financial side, and also being in a system where they're not really putting the athletes first, made it really difficult." Smith won her first Olympic title under her maiden name Schoenmaker, before changing her surname when she married sports agent Joel Smith in 2023. The marriage made her part of a wider South African sporting dynasty, given that her sister-in-law is Rachel Smith, whowas married to Springboks captain Siya Kolisi before their split. Tatjana Smith admits her own marriage changed the way she thought about her future. "Thinking about families as a woman, you have to time it perfectly, because if you're pregnant, it's not like you can still compete." While children are not yet part of her journey, Smith says working out what to do next was far from easy. "I definitely understand what athletes mean from the post-Olympic depression," said the 2023 200m breaststroke world champion, who also counts Commonwealth and African titles among her achievements. "It was such an emptiness in my life, because my whole life revolved around swimming. "I don't have to eat at a certain time, I don't have to sleep at a certain time, I don't have to think about travelling or not spending time with family anymore. "The world is so overwhelming. It's like, in which direction to go? "It was definitely the toughest season that I had to go through. I think it's probably why it's made me a stronger person." Smith married her husband Joel in November 2023 and says family life was one of the reasons behind her decision to retire Initially, Smith took on speaking engagements to pay the bills. She smiles when she admits: "I hate public speaking. I hate being in front of people." The same cannot be said of her love for competition. Having returned to the pool in order to keep fit, she decided to have a crack at triathlon, something she describes as a "crazy idea". "The training was so intense, and I was like, 'OK, I might as well just go back to swimming if I'm going to train this hard'," she said. "Every time I went back to the swimming pool and I dived in, I was like, 'Yeah, this is a feeling that I really miss so much'. "I think slowly over the year and a half, I just realised 'Wow, I really do love swimming'." Having made her decision to come out of retirement, Smith now wants to freshen things up and "try something new". That means a change to the 50m breaststroke, an event which has just been added to the Olympic schedule for the first time ahead of the 2028 Games in Los Angeles. "I thought, 'Why don't I try? Why don't I give myself that challenge? Reinvent myself'," said Smith. "I always try and describe it to someone that maybe doesn't understand swimming; it's like a 400m runner and a 100m [runner]. It's two different body types, two different trainings, and that's where I'm going." It means she has more than halved her training volume, with three sessions a week instead of eight - a change she believes will help her retain her love for her sport and live a more balanced life. "I feel like I'm being so lazy because I used to do 12km per day and now the focus is on taking time to be as explosive as possible. "Now I'm doing 12km over a whole week. "I have 20 years of endurance in my pocket, but I can definitely see I don't have those fast twitch [muscle] fibres. It's a whole different way of teaching my body how to swim." Those initial 20 years in the pool left Smith feeling burned out. Now she says she has earned the right to do things on her terms. "Swimming was an opportunity given to me by my parents and I believe I took it on full heartedly. "But, for the first time, it's my decision whether I want to come back. I'm choosing swimming. "I've achieved way more than I ever dreamed in my whole life, so I have nothing to prove." BBC African Sports Personality of the Year 2021: Tatjana Schoenmaker profile. Headline: They were labelled 'pervert glasses'. Will a camera-free version transform their image?
Body: They were labelled 'pervert glasses'. Will a camera-free version transform their image? When Meta first launched its AI-powered smart glasses in 2023, in collaboration with the sunglasses brand Ray-Ban, it unleashed a storm of controversy. There have been multiple reports of the devicesbeing used to harass women and girls in particular, filming them without their consent, then sharing the footage. The image problem doesn't seem to have been cured by Meta's enlistment this summer of Kylie Jenner, Kim Kardashian's sister, as their prime model. The devices have been dubbed "pervert" or "creepy" glasses. In the UK,  JD Wetherspoon pubs, a handful of major theatres, Comic-Con, some schools, and Faslane, home of the UK's nuclear submarines, have all chosen to ban them. On Thursday, Meta is unveiling a new version which does not contain a camera at all, called Ray-Ban Meta Audio. They will have the audio functions of the original glasses - including the ability to make phone calls or play music, with the sound funnelled directly into your ear - but with fewer implications for privacy. To some in the industry, it looks like an interesting pivot - a response, perhaps, to the backlash over privacy. Mark Zuckerberg - who wore a set at an event in California last year - predicts that smart glasses will replace mobile phones The tech giant denies that the new glasses have been rushed out in response to public anger. They say the product has been in development for two years. The audio-only version is cheaper than its camera-enabled cousins, and Meta says it has a lighter frame and better battery life. When I put it to Meta Glasses' head of product Ankit Brahmbhatt that I thought they might overtake the original camera-enabled glasses in sales, there was a pregnant pause. "We have, I think, something for everyone," he said, choosing his words very carefully. Does the release of a camera-free option represent a shift in how tech companies see the future of smart glasses? And is Meta's original vision getting further away? Or should we see camera-free glasses as a niche side-product that serves a small market - a bit like how some mobile manufacturers are now releasing internet-disabled "brick" phones for people who are tired of social media? There's no doubt that smart glasses have become controversial. I was lent a pair of Meta Ray-Bans – with cameras - to try out. I was initially nervous about wearing them in public, in case someone got physical: I have heard of people knocking them off wearers' heads and smashing them in the street. The reality was that I wore them on public transport and on foot in several cities including London, Glasgow and Portsmouth, and nobody batted an eyelid. It made me wonder whether awareness of them is really as high as both Meta and anti-glasses campaigners believe. That said, some people quietly told me they would not be confident enough to approach someone wearing them even if they did spot them, for fear of the interaction being filmed and uploaded. The glasses are designed to work as an extension of your phone. They use Bluetooth to sync with a handset via Meta's AI app. They are voice-activated, with open speakers in the arms funnelling sound into your ears. The result is a bit like wearing headphones without the addition of noise-cancelling features, so you can still hear the world around you. My potentially cancellable opinion is that I found many of the glasses' features useful. Interestingly, none of them included the camera. Listening to music and podcasts on the move without having earbuds stuffed into my ears felt safer.  I felt more confident about avoiding the gamut of e-bike-riding phone thieves in central London without my phone physically in my hand. Left: Meta's demonstration of a user making a phone call, with an image of the person they're talking to displayed inside their glasses. Right: Zoe Kleinman wearing a set on her commute And as someone with a pitiful sense of direction, I rely a lot on map apps. It was handy to have the directions spoken in my ears. The pay-off for this, however, was having to accept allowing the Meta AI app to know exactly where I was at all times. Meta is notorious for its hunger for personal data. When I posted about using the Meta Ray-Bans on social media, I got a bit of a hard time. Less so when I showed them to people in my everyday life. My hairdresser loved the idea of using them to record her clients' hair transformations. A builder I chatted to at the gym reckoned they would be useful on sites for recording what he was doing, either in the event of an accident or even to teach others new skills. My friend who runs said he would like to wear them on a jog. Plenty of content creators are big fans. My son borrowed them to wash my car, and was proud of his film showing me how he delicately chipped away at a stubborn bit of bird poo without damaging the paintwork (I was pleased, and happy to take his word for it). More broadly, smart glasses have been welcomed by the blind community. One user described them to the BBC as a "game-changer" because they can give audio descriptions of current locations and read out visible text like restaurant menu options. Earlier this year Meta donated 15,000 pairs to a charity for the blind in Ireland. But still, anger over privacy has grown. The glasses have a blinking white LED that switches on when the camera is active, but a whole industry has sprung up around finding technical workarounds to disable that light, some of which involve taking the glasses apart. Meta says less than 0.1% of the frames it has sold worldwide have been physically tampered with. Exact sales figures are unknown, but Ray-Ban's parent company EssilorLuxottica has reported that it sold seven million last year. Liz Hunter, a tech founder and parent who launched the "Stop Smart Glasses" campaign, and has set up a petition calling for urgent new regulation of the technology, is furious. "They should never, ever have left the lab at Meta," she told me. "It's a real travesty of public trust, and of women's equality, and it's rolled back our privacy rights right before our very eyes." Hunter thinks smart glasses should remain available for blind people, but not for the general population. "We don't need them, we don't want them," she says. Tech founder Liz Hunter is campaigning for tighter regulation of smart glasses A Polish developer has released an app called ZuckOff which uses Bluetooth to identify nearby smart glasses. It's been downloaded thousands of times, reports Wired magazine. Ben Wood, from tech research firm CCS Insight, remembers first reading the phrase "pervert glasses" in the usually strait-laced Financial Times - a sign, he says, that it had prompted a "significant public backlash". The furore has not deterred other companies from eyeing the market, however. Samsung is reported to be working on a collaboration with the upmarket glasses brand Warby Parker. Google is also said to be working on a set. Snap, the firm behind Snapchat, has just launched Specs, which are retailing in the US for $2,195 (and £1,995 in the UK). Users can see data inside the glass, and snap their fingers to take a photo. Snap founder Evan Spiegel says he thinks smart glasses will eventually replace phones, and he's not alone. When Meta launched smart glasses in 2021, they were geared in part around what the user could see. The firm promised they would allow users to "easily record the world as you see it", and to "capture life's moments as they happen from a unique first-person perspective". So Meta's latest announcement - glasses without a camera - is notable. Janusz Swierczynski, a researcher at Oxford University's Saïd Business School, who is worried about smart glasses, says the release of a camera-free version is a "positive sign" that Meta seems to have listened to privacy concerns. "They're thinking about it and that they're responding," he says, though he thinks it's "not a perfect" response because the camera-enabled glasses are still on the market. Others are less sure it represents a real shift. "It's certainly not the end of cameras in glasses," says Wood, from CCS Insight. He thinks that smart glasses are largely about capturing information; the glasses collect as much data as they can from your surroundings and then use AI to tell you about it. And glasses armed with a camera - trained on whatever you can see - are an "extremely good" source of that information. "That is an invaluable data stream to an AI platform, which can then interpret that data and provide you with the best possible information related to it," Wood says. "So having the vision parts of it with the cameras is a key pillar for getting the best experience." How the social media ban could reshape how all of us use the internet AI 'slop' is transforming social media - and a backlash is brewing Tech billionaires seem to be doom prepping. Should we all be worried? He imagines Meta has been working on the camera-free glasses for several years, and the current backlash over privacy provides "fantastic timing" for their release. Indeed, Meta doesn't yet show any signs of slowing down its development of camera-enabled glasses. The company is bringing its third generation of the glasses to the UK next month. These can visually display data inside the specs' lenses. (As a live broadcast journalist who has talked openly about brain fog, I can see the appeal of glasses that can discreetly display a script). Kate Winick, a tech analyst at the research firm Forrester, says it's not a step back from camera-enabled glasses but more of a "half step to the side, where they give users time to get comfortable with the technology… so that users themselves start to say, 'Oh, this would be so much more useful if it had a camera'." And she says, paradoxically, the existence of camera-free glasses might help "take the heat" off people who wear camera-enabled glasses in public. "It's now clear that out in the market some glasses have cameras and some don't," she says. "You can't automatically get mad at everybody wearing Meta's glasses, because you may not know whether or not they have a camera." And other companies are trying to address privacy concerns in different ways - without getting rid of the camera. The Taiwanese firm HTC recently launched Vive Eagle glasses, which cost less than a quarter of Snap's. Thomas Dexmier, a vice president at HTC Vive, says that if anyone near an Eagle specs wearer says "stop filming" or "stop recording", and it is picked up by one of the four microphones, the camera will deactivate. And he adds that all recordings captured by the glasses are encrypted, and the firm itself cannot see them -  though this also means HTC cannot flag harmful content. "We acknowledge that there are some challenges, potentially becoming a real problem, especially for women," he said. He said HTC Vive was working to make it as difficult as possible for the tech to be misused but said it was "too early to comment" on whether the firm would consider a version without cameras. Ultimately, Wood thinks that camera-enabled glasses are "not going away". He says the current moment reminds him of the 2000s, when some people said that mobile phone companies couldn't install cameras in their devices because of similar concerns over privacy. "There's an inevitability there," he says. "We will have to find a societal norm, a framework for the use of these products." Top image credit: Getty. Headline: How long can Labour's feel-good factor last?
Body: How long can Labour's feel-good factor last? "He just loves being prime minister," a government insider observes. Andy Burnham might not yet have delivered his all-important conference speech, but he has been preparing for this moment for years. He'll lap up the inevitable whoops and cheers – not just as Labour's leader, but the kind of leader who chimes with the party's rank and file, who puts social justice at the top of his list, who is not averse to cranking up the greatest hits – whether taking a pop at Mrs Thatcher, privatisation, or the divides between north and south. Speaking to MPs, ministers and advisers inside the party, there is no doubt whatsoever that Labour is in a much, much happier place than this time last year. There is a very simple reason, according to one cabinet minister, fans of Sir Keir Starmer, look away now, "people like the new prime minister more than they liked the old one – that's the truth of it". Another minister tells me: "There is no appetite for destruction – very little naysaying." But Labour is in a position that's been all too rare for all our political parties in the last few years – there are no whispers about chucking out the leader, no-one stirring revolt. And even those who don't like the direction of travel are labelling their opinions as a desire to be helpful, they're not trying to criticise the boss. "The mood's good – everyone is going into conference with their ears open," one MP said, keen to hear more from the prime minister. The feel-good factor is also driven by the party inching up a little in the polls – one senior figure says: "We're all witnessing the Burnham bounce – whether that's how you feel when you see the polls, or how we all feel when we have meetings together." And those who work inside government also credit a more effective political operation around the prime minister. "The system's better, you get clearer decisions, better steers when you need them," says a minister. Another government source also credits the new Downing Street operation but notes wryly, "it's unfair to compare the end of a regime which is always pretty nasty, with the arrival of a new one which is always more hopeful… these things can change". There are whispers of announcements in the next few days on housing and defence. Some MPs also want to hear Burnham expand on themes they, and the country, have heard plenty about but that aren't specifically defined – "public control" and "re-industrialisation". And frankly, the happy prime minister would probably be only too glad to talk for as long as necessary about those favourite subjects. But however much he loves being PM there are also less tempting realities he'll have to confront. "It's a new front man," says a minister, "but the song hasn't changed." And the soundtrack to this autumn might prove to be downright miserable. While Andy Burnham will be pressing the flesh at dozens of party events in the next few days, his Chancellor John Healey will be spending a lot of time holed up in his hotel room making decisions about the Budget which is only a month away. The pressure on public cash is intense as the budget approaches – the choice for the chancellor doing the rounds is, "10 billion of cuts or 10 billion of tax rises," according to a well-connected senior figure. Treasury sources say they don't recognise that simple number. However the figures shake down, the increasing cost of paying the interest on the country's debts weighs heavily. Don't forget the rising welfare bill, demands for more defence spending. It's unusual that a party conference is happening with a budget just weeks away, and it looms over the conference, just as the state of the economy looms over Labour's current feel-good factor. The UK can't force the US and Iran to find peace, to get traffic flowing freely through the Strait of Hormuz, to bring the oil price down. Nor can the prime minister make Putin bring his war on Ukraine to an end, with pressure on European gas supply as we enter another winter. There are already predictions of our annual energy bills going up by £500 early next year. You know the script – higher energy costs raise the spectre of price rises everywhere. "We're really suffering at the hands of energy prices," says an insider. One influential figure predicts an array of grim economic consequences, unconvinced that Burnham and his team have grasped what might be coming down the track and planned accordingly. "The big economic challenges coming – rising housing costs, rising inflation, downward pressure on public spending because of the cost of borrowing, 500 quid on energy from January  - I just don't see what the game plan is." And there are nerves about whether the new No 10 is concentrating on getting the economy growing. Many of Burham's priorities so far are about spending money, not helping people make it. One of his own advisors publicly described the administration as a "traditional tax and spend socialist government with better TikTok". Ouch. Now, the former business secretary, Peter Kyle, has very politely, but firmly, expressed concern that Burnham and his team are not thinking hard enough about helping the country make money, perhaps more focused on how to spend it.You can read more about his comments here. He told me: "We must act with more urgency, and we must feel the need for economic growth as acutely as we do about tackling things like rough sleeping and about social care, and some of the social reforms that we want because they are inextricably linked." Kyle is not the only person in the Labour Party who worries Burnham and Healey are more interested in spending money than helping business generate it. And budget speculation is full of chatter around increasing taxes on property or other assets like stocks and shares. At the other end of the spectrum there are demands on the left for the prime minister to ease the pressure on less well-paid workers. One prominent figure warned: "Labour has a second hearing. One shot to get this right. It is beyond doubt that if they do not keep to the promises made to everyday people - workers and communities will turn their back." Expect union leaders to renew calls for tax cuts for workers and more investment. It's a tug of war. In the next few days, Labour are likely to look like a happy political tribe. The new chief delighted to be in charge. The rank and file relieved to have a leader they can cheer. But one senior figure warns that what's coming could turn things sour. "The budget looks like a disaster – by Halloween we'll be looking at something else," predicting a big change in mood. That portent of doom doesn't match the overall atmosphere around Labour right now, but there is a quiet creeping concern about whether Burnham's rhetoric of hope, and change, the classic political mantras, can be matched with people's experience. A senior source says: "His political will needs to be more bold than the machine around him – don't write cheques you can't cash." One minister niggles that it's easier to talk in broad terms about your long-term ambitions than to grapple with problems affecting people today, "there is comfort in dealing with some of the largest possible questions because it's a way off delivering them. But the cost of getting to work, or getting across town is expensive, going out or staying in – that's right now". Conferences are a chance for political parties to enjoy each other's company, but also to show off to the country. But the reality of paying the bills is, of course, more present in most people's lives, one minister tells me: "If you go into Tesco and the cereal you buy is noticeably more expensive, that has more cut through than any political clip you see on telly or Facebook." Labour's spirits have been transformed by Burnham's soft coup that saw off Starmer. But the minister says: "The contrast is not between now and hard times, but between the new regime and the old regime." The question that beckons beyond the conference hall – can that carry on if hard times hit? Headline: Why India's Election Commission is in the eye of a storm - again
Body: India's opposition parties have demanded that Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar resign from office India's Election Commission (ECI) is facing yet another crisis of credibility after a series of fresh allegations of irregularities against its chief. One of the most trusted public institutions in the world's largest democracy, the three-member commission is headed by the Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar and includes Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi as commissioners. The latest row broke out after a report in theIndian Express newspaper,externalsaid that in the past few months, CEC Kumar had been repeatedly questioned by his two colleagues over the integrity of the voter database, changes to the way new voters are enrolled and the security of the electoral rolls itself. The report said that Commissioners Sandhu and Joshi objected to several decisions which were taken without their knowledge. There were at least 14 times in the past 10 months when Commissioners Sandhu and Joshi were kept in the dark, it added. In one instance, the report says, the two commissioners even wrote a letter complaining to the cabinet secretary, the top bureaucrat in the Indian government. The revelations have created a furore, with opposition leaders demanding Kumar's resignation. Sandhu and Joshi have not publicly commented on the report but the ECI said in a statement that "differing views" were part of the "decision-making process". The report comes at a time when the commission is carrying out a controversial country-wide revision of the electoral database. The Election Commission says the aim of this Special Intensive Revision - better known by its acronym SIR - is to ensure that no ineligible name remains on the rolls. It says the last revision was done nearly a quarter of a century ago and the voters' list needs to be updated to account for those who have died, left the country or are registered in more than one place as they've moved to a new address. But the exercise has been mired in controversy from the start with the opposition parties accusing CEC Kumar of manipulating voters' list to favour Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) during elections. Both the BJP and the Election Commission have rejected the accusations. But the latest revelations are being seen as much more serious as they are about questions being raised from within the Election Commission about the way its chief is functioning. The Indian Express report says that CEC Kumar has been repeatedly questioned by his two colleagues over the integrity of the voter database in recent months From the start, questions have lingered over the robustness of the revision, which has seen 130 million names from across India struck off the voters' list. Millions of voters have also complained to the authorities that their names are missing, saying the new process set by SIR to register as voters is too cumbersome and involves furnishing documents that many don't have. Former CEC SY Quraishi, who says he has "been a critic of the SIR from the beginning", told news agency PTI that he always wondered why Commissioners Sandhu and Joshi had been "keeping quiet". "[Now] I realised that very silently and quietly they were protesting, they were writing notes. That is a good thing, they have gone up in my esteem," he said. How a Brazilian woman became the face of India vote fraud row New voters list in Indian state includes wrong photos and dead people The row over 'vote theft' that has shaken Indian politics The revelations have also provided fresh ammunition to the opposition parties and critics who have repeatedly claimed that SIR is being used to exclude their voters for the BJP's benefit and that elections in India are no longer free and fair. On Wednesday, angry opposition politicians once again questioned the sanctity of India's election process and demanded that CEC Kumar resign, saying he had no right to continue in office, with some even calling for his arrest. The charge was led by MP and senior Congress party leader Rahul Gandhi who has repeatedly accused the Commission of "stealing votes from the opposition". On Wednesday, he also accused the Commission and its officers of "treason". "Vote chori [theft] is a crime against the Indian people and a direct attack on our constitution. The BJP, RSS [Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh] and EC who organised it have committed an act of treason. Justice will be served,"he posted on X,external.  He also shared a 15-second video telling the commission and its officers that "your time will come. You cannot get away". Mamata Banerjee, leader of the regional Mamata All India Trinamool Congress, called for Kumar's arrest and demanded fresh polls with the pre-SIR voters' list in the state of West Bengal which she lost to the BJP in the recent elections. At least 2.7million voters were removed in the state during SIR - Banerjee and her supporters say that cost them dozens of seats and the election win. Congress leader Rahul Gandhi has repeatedly accused the commission of "stealing votes from the opposition" Within hours of the Indian Express report and statements from opposition leaders, the Election Commission put out astatement,externaldefending its way of working. "Differing views and observations are a normal part of deliberation in any institution. They are a part of the decision-making process before a final decision is taken. "Not only the three Commissioners, but every officer of the Commission is fully authorised to give his suggestions to the Commission for improving the electoral system," the statement said. The note said that highlighting "certain specific internal notes and observations spread over the period of 10 months while overlooking the much larger body of approvals, decisions, instructions and initiatives" give only part of the picture. And that in recent months, the commission has "introduced around 40 new initiatives and undertaken many electoral reforms including the conduct of electoral roll revision (including SIR) across the country. All these decisions are an outcome of the unanimous decisions of the full commission in the past one year". The BJP has also defended CEC Kumar, calling the opposition criticism a "smear campaign" and that dissent was "a sign of a vibrant democracy". Party spokesperson Sambit Patra told a press conference that "ever since the Modi government came to power in 2014, opposition parties have been collapsing one after the other". And because they cannot win elections, they are trying to "undermine the institutions of the country", he said. Indian journalists condemn 'denial' of voting and passport rights of prominent editor Why India's Election Commission is facing a test of credibility But the row over the election database is likely to intensify. Banerjee has already said opposition parties will hold protests until Kumar remains CEC. And India's influential Gen Z-led Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), which recently forced the education minister to resign, has also said it will protest against the "hijacking of India's democracy". Analysts say the defence of the Election Commission is unlikely to satisfy many, with some pointing out that its statement doesn't address all the issues raised in the newspaper report and that "CEC Kumarneeds to clear the air,externalif we are to view the Commission as an impartial body". Headline: Indian billionaire’s payments firm plots biggest London flotation in years
Body: Sunil Bharti Mittal’s Airtel Money targets $9bn IPO in boost for ailing UK stock market Nils Pratley: Does this mark the end of London’s listing drought? Not yet A payments business that operates across Africa and is ultimately controlled by an Indian billionaire has announced its intention to float on the strugglingLondon Stock Exchange. Airtel Money, the mobile money arm of Airtel Africa, is planning one of the biggest UK listings in years, in a boost for the shrinking London market that hasfaced a string of recent departures. The company is understood to be hoping to raise about $800m (£601m) from the initial public offering (IPO) and is targeting a valuation of $8bn to $9bn, which would make it one of London’s largest listings in recent years. Airtel Money has 53 million monthly active users across 13 countries in sub-SaharanAfrica, including Uganda, Zambia and the Democratic Republic of Congo. It operates through a network of branches and kiosks, which enable customers to load money on to their phones, withdraw cash and access other money services, and the company generated revenues of just under $1.4bn in the last financial year. Airtel Money’s parent company is Airtel Africa, a telecoms provider that is part of the Indian conglomerate Bharti Enterprises, which is ultimately controlled by the billionaire Sunil Bharti Mittal. Airtel Africa is already listed on the FTSE 100 but said it wanted Airtel Money to be listed separately. “From a company perspective, [the listing] gives us flexibility for the future,” said Airtel Money’s chief executive, Ian Ferrao. “We evaluated multiple [stock] exchanges, including the Middle East because we’ve got a headquarters in Dubai, along with European and North American exchanges. Ultimately, shareholders felt that London was the right choice. We still believe there is deep capital available … all the global institutional investors are here.” Ferrao added: “Most importantly there’s a deep understanding of emerging markets in the London market and Africa specifically.” Airtel Money said it would announce more details about the float in early October, including the indicative price range and number of shares to be offered, with final pricing to follow later in the month. Airtel Africa had originally targeted a listing in the first six months of 2026 butdelayed itto the second half of the year, blaming unfavourable market conditions as a result of the US-Israeli war on Iran. Several other companies also pushed back planned IPOs amid the market volatility caused by the conflict. Sign up toBusiness Today Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning after newsletter promotion Airtel Africa owns just under 78% of Airtel Money and will remain a long-term investor after the IPO. Minority stakes are held by TPG, ​Mastercard, the Qatar Investment Authority and Chimetech Holding. Revenue in Airtel Money’s most recent quarter to 30 June climbed 38% to £399m, according to Airtel Africa. The decision to float Airtel Money in the UK could mark a turning point for the City, which has struggled to attract listings in recent times and has also been hit by departures, partly as a result ofoverseas takeovers of UK companies. Airtel Money’s planned listing could be one of the biggest debuts since the international payments company Wisefloated in 2021with a valuation of £8.75bn. Wise has since moved its main listing from Londonto New York.

Headline: Liam Neeson involved in new movie revealing story behind Tuam babies
Body: Catherine Corless is played by English actor Monica Dolan in the film The story of the amateur historian whose research helped uncover the Tuam babies scandal is being brought to the big screen, with the help of actor Liam Neeson. The Bon Secours Mother and Baby Homeinstitution for unmarried mothers and their childrenwas in operation from 1925 until 1961. It came to international attention in 2014, after local historianCatherine Corless discovered there were 796 death certificates for children and babies who died there, but no burial records. A 2017 article in theNew York Times,externalabout Corless' journey left Neeson in a "quiet rage", he told RTÉ'sLate Late Show,external, prompting him to use his standing in the film industry to bring the story to life, and be a co-producer. "I thought if my standing in the film business is anything at all I'd love this to become a film so more people could see it and we could share this atrocity," Neeson said. Irish filmmaker Frank Berry, Monica Dolan and Liam Neeson at the Toronto Film Festival From there, Corless said she received a call from the New York Times writer Dan Barry, who said: "Listen, Liam Neeson may be giving you a call and he'd like to speak to you and get permission to do the film." Nine years later, the film - The Lost Children of Tuam - is now in cinemas. The film tells of the story of how Corless began researching a former institution for unmarried mothers and their children in Tuam, County Galway, and uncovers the hidden history of neglect and loss. It examines how Corless was faced with the silence of church and state as she embarked on a campaign for justice. Catherine Corless discovered there were 796 death certificates for children and babies who died at the institution "The way the film is done, it's just true to life," Corless told BBC Radio Ulster'sGood Morning Ulsterprogramme, describing it as "fantastic". Corless said the film's director, Frank Berry, "really wanted" the film "to be true and they stuck to the truth". "It shows the diversity between people in power and ordinary people like myself struggling to get a story out there that I knew was true, I had all the evidence," she said. A team is currently excavating the site of the former institution. In June, it was reported that they had found a further eight sets of infant remains,bringing the total number recovered to 77. "I really had to fight for it to come to this stage, not for the film exactly, also the excavation in Tuam is going ahead and the exhumation. I fought years with the denial from authorities that anything wrong happened," Corless said. "It's something I had to keep working on and that's portrayed very, very well in the film." English actor Dolan had to develop a Galway accent for the role Catherine Corless is played by English actor Monica Dolan in the film. Corless noted that Dolan had to develop a Galway accent for the role, which she said the actress did "very well". "She wanted to actually become me, to get into the knitty gritty of the efforts that I had to put in," Corless said of Dolan. "She portrayed me just as myself. I was amazed at what she was able to do," she said. "She went to the extremes, really, to get the feeling and the emotion I went through and the struggle." Corless added: "She did it so, so well, I must say that, she really did." The film was awarded Best Irish Film Award at the 38th Galway Film Fleadh in July. The Lost Children of Tuam opened in cinemas in Ireland on 25 September and it is scheduled for UK release on 9 October. Headline: Uproar in France over award-winning author accused of using AI
Body: Thélyson Orélien has denied allegations he used AI in his work The French book scene is in uproar after a Canadian-Haitian author billed as a sensation was accused of using artificial intelligence (AI) to write his first novel. Thélyson Orélien, 38, has just been awarded the Prix du Roman Fnac – the first of the literary season's prizes – forC'était ça ou mourir(It was either that or die). He is also a finalist for the most prestigious annual French language awards, the Goncourt and the Renaudot, set to be issued soon. But on Tuesday a little-known group calledBalance ton Claude(Denounce your Claude, in reference to Anthropic's AI assistant) claimed the book was "almost totally" written by AI - a charge the author denied. "We tested several passages, from different bits of the manuscript, to come up with the identical result: 100 percent AI," the group said on X. According to the group – whose membership is unclear – the detection was carried out by a programme called Pangram, which it said was "by far the most accurate", with an almost negligible chance of making a mistake. Orélien, who was born in Haiti and moved to Montreal in 2010, immediately denied the accusation. "I have always loved creation and literature. I can't see why I would feel compelled to use a machine," he told Libération newspaper. He said he was "compiling a dossier" with his editor to prove that he authentically wrote the book. "My traditions are Haitian and Caribbean. The images, the repetitions and the rhythms are the living word, they are my own," he said. The publishing house Grasset also came to his defence, saying the allegations "are atrociously injurious to a writer with an exceptional life-story" whose "work of creation is original and powerful." The novel tells the story of a teacher who flees gang violence in Haiti and his adventures before he finally makes it to Canada, where he re-discovers "the right to breathe without fear". The row recalls the controversy over Trinidadian writer Jamir Nazir's The Serpent in the Grove, whose Commonwealth Short Story prize was initially withdrawn in July over allegations that it was written with generative AI. The prize was subsequently re-awarded, after the organisers said they were satisfied the writing was genuine. Critics of Pangram and other AI-detectors say they are unreliable – with different programmes often giving different results after analysing the same texts. Thélyson Orélien's book won the Prix du Roman Fnac this week These tools do not actually know who, or what, wrote a piece of text. Instead, they look for patterns commonly found in AI-generated writing, but those patterns can also appear in human work. Research has found that AI-detectors can wrongly flag human writing as AI-generated and miss text that was produced by artificial intelligence, particularly if it has been edited or paraphrased. Some also say that the programmes are built around the use of standardised language - English or French - and so cannot accurately interpret texts that use dialect from places like the Caribbean. But the writers behindBalance ton Claudesaid that Pangram had been shown to make a wrong call about an AI-generated text only one time in every 24,400. The latest detectors no longer compare text with text, to see if there has been plagiarism. Instead they analyse probabilities and statistics, to see if certain linguistic patterns betray the use of AI. With AI becoming increasingly normalised, the row overC'etait ça ou mourirwill feed the debate over what mix of human and AI creativity is deemed acceptable – it being perfectly possible for writers to generate AI then adapt it, or conversely write an original text then ask AI to review it. Orélien was born in 1988 in the northern Haitian city of Gonaives. His first work – before leaving his homeland – consisted of mainly poetic texts, and later in Canada he worked as a journalist. The novel, described by his Canadian publisher as its biggest seller in 60 years, is due to be translated into around 20 languages. Orélien toldLibérationthat the first draft of the book was written in 2019 – well before AI programmes to generate text became generally available. Headline: Man charged with murdering woman in Darlington
Body: Leanne Park was pronounced dead at the scene in Darlington A man has been charged with murdering a woman who was found dead by police. Andrew Bell, 44, of Darlington, is accused of killing Leanne Park, 44, in the town on Wednesday. Durham Police said she was pronounced dead at an address in Parkgate at about 21:15 BST. Her family said she was the "best mam, nana, daughter and friend we could wish for". Bell is due to appear at Newton Aycliffe Magistrates' Court on Monday. A 27-year-old man arrested on suspicion of assisting an offender has been released on bail, the force said. A spokesperson said crime scene investigators would continue to work at the scene and a police cordon was "expected to remain in place for some time". Headline: Turner Prize gallery 'centre of creative universe'
Body: Work by four artists nominated for the Turner Prize will go on display at the Middlesbrough Institute of Modern Art Turner Prize nominated artworks are going on display at a gallery in what its director has called a "prestigious opportunity". Work by four artists in the running for the prize - Simeon Barclay, Kira Freije, Marguerite Humeau and Tanoa Sasraku - will go on display at Teesside University's Middlesbrough Institute of Modern Art (MIMA) from 26 September. Dr Laura Sillars, director of MIMA and dean of culture and creativity at the niversity, said of the exhibition: "While it's here, at a certain level, we are the centre of the creative universe." The Turner Prize is awarded each year to a British artist for an outstanding exhibition or other presentation of their work. Middlesbrough Mayor Chris Cooke said the exhibition, which includes works of mixed media, sculpture and spoken word, would provide residents with an "incredible opportunity" to see cutting-edge art in their home town". He said: "I hope it inspires our young people to dream about what's possible. "Why shouldn't it be them in a few years' time? "Hosting the Turner Prize gives us a chance to show off what we have to offer to people across the country." Established in 1984 and named after English Romantic painter Joseph Mallord William Turner, the prize is one of the most prestigious awards for visual arts. The winner, who will be announced on 10 December, will be awarded £25,000, with £10,000 given to the other shortlisted artists. Headline: Inside iconic horror game Silent Hill's Scottish makeover
Body: This video can not be played Watch: Take a look at clips from Silent Hill: Townfall As I creep through the heavy fog of Silent Hill: Townfall, I'm met by an oddly familiar sight amid the terror - a sign for a Sunday roast. For the first time, one of gaming's biggest horror franchises - created in Japan but traditionally set in the US - has come to the UK, set on a fictional Scottish island. Jon McKellan, director at Glaswegian developers Screen Burn, told me taking on the mega brand was an "absolutely terrifying" prospect for the relatively small team. As a fan of the games, I was keen to find out what one of the most iconic survival horror series looks like in Scotland - and whether it can live up to its legacy. Sadly there's no option to go inside The Mariner, have a nice cold pint, and wait for all this to blow over I played Silent Hill: Townfall, which was released on Thursday, on my PlayStation 5, and it ran well, though there have beensome reports,externalfrom others of performance issues. Set in 1996, the game follows the plight of an American man called Simon Ordell, who washes up on St Amelia with a red hospital ID band around his wrist and an IV drip in his arm. As is to be expected from the Silent Hill games, the real reasons why you're there and what's going on are teased as you progress through the story in a typically vague fashion. Simon Ordell arrives on the island of St Amelia, with no memory of who he is or why he's there The team took inspiration for the setting from the tiny fishing village of St Monans in Fife. For those concerned the game might lean into any typical Scottish stereotypes, McKellan told me he wanted it to feel "authentic and natural". "It's not tartan everywhere, but if you grew up in a working-class town in the 90s, you will get a lot of the references," he said. In Townfall I walked past film-quality models of red pillar boxes, 20 mph speed limit signs and charity collection boxes shaped like guide dogs. Not since 2006, when I had to storm Manchester Cathedral in Resistance: Fall of Man, have I felt an oddly patriotic attachment to game areas or objects. To save the game, I had to use a phone, which often meant stepping inside a "coins and card" telephone box - a sight instantly familiar to anyone old enough to remember them on British streets. Meanwhile, a level set in a council estate leans into the concrete starkness of the area's looming grey buildings. While some may question why the main character is American rather than Scottish given the setting, there are narrative reasons why Simon is more of an outsider to this community, which are slowly drip-fed into cutscenes and in-game documents. For the most part I was intrigued by the story, which, like many of the previous games, explores themes of trauma and guilt sensitively. This edition also touches on ideas around the impact of big corporations on small communities, which brought added relevance to the setting of an isolated seaside town. Even everyday objects like electricity meters appear as part of the game's puzzles and missions I soon had to face the island's monsters - gnarled, fleshy beings with axe-like heads or mangled faces. While St Amelia's inhabitants might not quite live up to the heights of Silent Hill 2's mannequins for sudden frights, their speed and general nastiness were still enough to make me want to run away as fast as possible. Even when I picked up weapons such as a plank of wood or a steel pipe, a series staple, there was never much sense that I had the upper hand. These all degrade over time, and though I did eventually get a gun, bullets are scarce, meaning I still had to sneak around rather than face threats head-on. If you do end up going the wrong way down a one-way street, the game has a few weapons you can use, like this plank "We don't do jump scares, really," said McKellan - although I can think of a few alarming times playing the game I vehemently disagreed with that statement. The fear is dialled up an extra notch by Byron Bullock's rich sound design, with the music swelling almost unbearably intensely when spluttering nasties stumbled closer. Composer Pilotpriest, also known as Anthony Scott Burns, deserves recognition too for his hauntingly bleak soundtrack. I think it says a lot that I closed every door I opened behind me in the game, in the naive hope it might stop monsters following - even at moments when there were none around. The CRT monitor is just one example of the retro tech used to avoid getting attacked Simon soon picks up a handheld CRT device to help with sneaking - a clever updated version of another staple of the Silent Hill series: the crackling radio. This piece of retro tech - basically a small portable TV - gives you a fuzzy image of nearby monsters on its screen, so you have some idea of where they are in order to avoid them, though it can get a little fiddly if there are several nearby. "I think it lends itself well to horror when the technology is a bit frail, a bit outdated," said McKellan. "You don't feel safe when those kinds of things are fragile." Later sections where you rely on even cruder tech to spot enemies ratchet up the tension further, at the expense of making the gameplay much slower. Thankfully, there are often other cues as to the whereabouts of your fleshy foes, such as flickering lights and their awful, gurgling cries. Reviews of the game have championed its atmosphere, with IGN's Tristan Ogilvie calling it "oppressively ominous". Silent Hill: Townfall has three difficulty settings for combat - easy, normal and nightmare (there are also two settings for puzzles, with one giving more hints). I played on normal, though there were one or two sections with a new, super-strong and fast single enemy where I considered changing to easy. These were the most aggravating parts of the game for me, despite having played and loved Alien: Isolation, a game McKellan also worked on, which has a lot of challenging bits where you have to avoid the powerful Alien. Chris Scullion, deputy editor at Video Games Chronicle said these moments were "deeply frustrating" and caused the game, which he otherwise found "outstanding", to come "grinding to a halt". Unfortunately for Simon, 20 is rarely plenty for the monsters of St Amelia Townfall is not the first time the series has strayed away from the original game's location in America, 2025's Silent Hill f was set in 1960s rural Japan. This sparked a conversation about whether a game can be part of the series yet not be set in or around the fictional eponymous town. The series' lead producer at Konami Motoi Okamoto told me the team were looking at various areas to potentially set the next games, from "other parts of Europe" to "Latin America". Games journalist and self-proclaimed "Silent Hillian" Vikki Blake told me the latest game exceeded her expectations, though she's still not convinced these newer games truly fit under the Silent Hill name. After my playthrough, I can see why Konami are pushing ahead with the idea to let other studios breathe new life into the franchise and take it to different destinations. Townfall is a brutal, grim journey - uneven in parts, but clever - and full of immense tension and inventive game design, the kind that is needed to push a nearly 30-year-old franchise forward. Okamoto has alsoexpressed his desire,externalto release a Silent Hill game every year - whether that be a remaster, remake, or entirely new material. If more new studios can keep the games feeling as fresh as this, we may eventually become like one of the series' many troubled protagonists – forgetting why we ever needed the titular town at all.
