Headline: Burnham announces scheme to help first-time buyers onto housing ladder
Body: Prime Minister Andy Burnham is to introduce a new scheme to try to help people "who have given up hope of ever having a home to call their own" get on the property ladder. The "Your First Home" scheme would be open to first-time buyers in England with a deposit of 2.5%. It would provide them with a loan worth 20% of their new build property's value to help pay for the purchase. On Sunday, the government also shared plans it said would make it simpler for councils to take over empty homes to provide housing for those in need. The announcements come as the prime minister prepares for his first Labour conference as leader. With the "Your First Home" scheme, which was first announced on Saturday, there would be an initial interest-free period for the equity loan - more details on how it would work are expected in next month's Budget. The Conservatives warned the policy would leave first-time buyers taking on more debt and risks "pushing up the price of new homes" - the prime minister said those who do not have support from the "bank of mum and dad" are among those who it would aim to help. Burnham said: "Too many young people are struggling with the cost of housing, with many giving up hope of ever having a home to call their own. "So we will step in to help more first-time buyers on to the housing ladder." The PM added he believes the scheme will give builders the "confidence to deliver the high-quality new homes the country needs". Funding for the scheme is expected to come from reprioritising existing budgets, but housing developers will pay towards the running costs. Ministers have not yet confirmed whether there is an age restriction on the scheme, or a cap on the price on the value of the property. On Sunday morning, the government also announced plans to strengthen council powers to take over empty homes to meet the need for council houses. It would, Labour said, make it simpler for councils to bring some of the more than 300,000 empty dwellings into use for essential housing. The plans were unveiled by Housing Secretary Angela Rayner ahead of the party's conference in Liverpool. Conservative shadow minister for state housing and planning Gareth Bacon accused her of "desperately reaching for any lever she can find" to hit "Labour's 1.5 million homes target". Housing Secretary Angela Rayner, pictured arriving at the annual Labour conference, said the government will "explore further changes to protect local authorities from absorbing the costs they face in taking over empty homes" The "Your First Home" policy is similar to initiatives from previous governments, including the coalition's Help To Buy scheme, introduced in 2013 by then-Chancellor George Osborne. It expanded a previous scheme, known as FirstBuy, which was aimed solely at first-time buyers. Help to Buy initially enabled all purchasers to put down a 5% deposit on a newly built home, with a value of up to £600,000. Up to 20% of the cost of the home was funded by a shared equity loan, which was interest-free for the first five years. The first version of the programme was active until 2021. A second iteration of the scheme, which ran until 2023, restricted access to first-time buyers and applied regional-level price caps to the properties that could be bought. An evaluation of the scheme,externalfound more than 387,000 properties were purchased through it, of which 328,000 were by first-time buyers. In its conclusion, the report noted Help to Buy was "effective in supporting people into home ownership in some areas, but did not remove affordability barriers for first-time buyers in areas that were already relatively expensive". Rayner said "Your First Home" would "build on the lessons learned from previous schemes, while retaining the benefits". The Home Builders Federation welcomed the proposals, saying it had "long called for action to improve access to home ownership". "Our analysis shows a well-designed scheme can make a meaningful difference for households struggling to get on to the property ladder," it added. Conservative shadow housing secretary Katie Lam accused Labour of wanting first-time buyers to "take on even more debt to afford the few homes that have been built". She added taxpayers would take a "stake in their homes" and be "picking up the bill for months". Lam said: "Slapping another levy on developers risks pushing up the price of new homes too. "This is a colossal admission of failure. This Labour government is making homes harder to build, then asking buyers to borrow more to pay for them." Lam said the Conservatives want to scrap stamp duty, "back British house builders" and ensure that houses are "built in the places that people actually want to live". Rayner told the BBC earlier this month that there wasonly a "slim chance" the government would meet its target of building 1.5m homesin England by the next election, but said she was "not giving it up". Data up to June this year suggested the government wasbehind on the rate of construction needed to meet the goal, which housebuilders have previously warned was too optimistic. BBC Verify analysis showed a decline in the number of new houses being built during Labour's first year in power - continuing a fall that began under the Conservatives. The housing policy announcements come as Burnham arrives in Liverpool ahead of his first Labour Party conference since becoming prime minister. The PM said he wanted to make it a "really important week where we set out a new direction for the country". He added: "We've had a decade since Brexit and it's been a decade of too much drift, too much division, and we need to draw a line on that." In an interview with the Guardian,external, the prime minister said he can deliver on his promise of radical change for the country. "There's always things you can do; it's just whether you're prepared to do them," he said. "The public would have more respect for us if we go and grab something difficult… and say, 'Right, we're going to do something here', rather than constantly playing the political game before fixing the problems." He also criticised previous governments for failing to tackle difficult issues - including housing supply - saying there are no "easy or quick wins" and longer-term reform is needed. Another pre-conference announcement included a pledge to offer quicker access of a guaranteed job to young people receiving health or disability support. The offer would be made three months after they start claiming benefits. This approach would be introduced from next April. Labour said the government would cover 100% of wage costs for up to 25 hours a week for six months. Currently, jobless young people aged 18 to 24 must have been on universal credit for 18 months before receiving an offer under the government's job guarantee scheme. Conservative shadow work and pensions secretary Helen Whately said Labour should have cut "burdens" on businesses to help ensure disabled people are employed. She said: "Instead, they are bringing back a Conservative post-pandemic scheme. Andy Burnham clearly has no new ideas." Whately also questioned how the change would be funded. Headline: Miliband tells Iran minister UK will not tolerate 'hostile activity' on British soil
Body: Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband has told Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi that the UK will "not tolerate intimidation, threats or hostile activity on UK soil". The ministers met face-to-face at the UN General Assembly in New York City. The Foreign Office said Miliband spoke to his counterpart about "the UK's unwavering resolve to combat threats from Iranian-linked groups in UK soil, including attacks on the British Jewish community". They also discussed war in the Middle East and a British couple detained in Iran, it said. There was no immediate comment from Araghchi. Iranian news agency Irna reported that the men "discussed bilateral ties and international developments during their talks". Miliband's comments followan arson attack on four Jewish community ambulancesin Golders Green in March and other incidents. The BBC understands that UK intelligence chiefs were initially keeping an open mind as to whether the Iranian state or organisations working for it played a role in the Hatzola ambulance attack and other attacks against Jewish communities during 2026. They later concluded that intelligence pointed to Iran or its proxies being involved in the attack. A small power plant in the UKwas also shut downin July due to a cyber attack, whichthe Telegraph reported,externalwas carried out by hackers affiliated with the Iranian regime. The Foreign Office said Miliband also spoke to his counterpart about the country's war with the US, telling Araghchi that Iran should choose "de-escalation and diplomacy instead of prolonging the war" while stressing the importance of reopening the Strait of Hormuz. In February, the US and Israel attacked Iran, killing the country's supreme leader. Iran responded by launching strikes on Israel and neighbouring Gulf Arab states that host US military bases. It also effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of global oil and gas shipments usually pass, impacting the global economy. Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian told the UN General Assembly on Wednesday that any peace deal would have to include an end to the US blockade preventing Iranian ships from using the waterway. Responding to US President Donald Trump's threat to "annihilate" the Islamic Republic if a deal was not reached soon, Pezeshkian saidhis country will never "bend the knee". "The resistance of the Iranian people will only increase in the face of sanctions, increased pressure, increased bullying," he said. There was no immediate comment from the US, whose delegation walked out of the chamber at the start of Pezeshkian's address. The Foreign Office said Miliband also used Thursday's meeting to raisethe detention of British couple Lindsay and Craig Foreman. The couple, from East Sussex, have been detained in Iran for more than 20 months after being arrested while passing through the country on a motorcycle journey. The Foremans were each sentenced to 10 years in jail in February on espionage charges, which they deny. In Miliband's discussion with the Iranian foreign minister, he reiterated the call for them to be immediately released and stressed that their welfare remained a priority for the government, the Foreign Office said.

Headline: Why Trump gave Xi an ornate bald eagle statue at the state dinner
Body: President Trump said he and First Lady Melania helped design the statue US President Donald Trump has presented Chinese President Xi Jinping with a sculpture of a bald eagle, a bird native to North America and his country's national symbol, during a lavish state dinner in Washington. The gift, which was unveiled before VIP guests at the Thursday dinner,embodies "the free and soaring spirit of America", said Trump. He said that he and First Lady Melania Trump participated in its design. The statue is part of a valuable - but sometimes tricky - aspect of international diplomacy: gift-giving. Such gifts are a small but meaningful element of the larger aim of Xi and Trump's three-day summit – forging personal relationships between heads of two global superpowers. "They're going to discuss all of these complicated issues," Daniel Kritenbrink, partner at The Asia Group says. "But at the end of the day, these are still two human beings. "So that personal relationship means something," he says. "I think the gift exchange is one key part of that." Kritenbrink, who spent over 30 years as a US diplomat, mostly in Asia, says personal relationships are of particular importance to Xi. He believes the direct Trump-Xi bond is the glue that is holding together "the most complex and the most consequential relationship in the world". He says Trump, too, values what Kritenbrink calls "leader-level diplomacy". Gifts have had a unique presence in the Trump presidency. The US president has received a luxury jumbo jet, an engraved gold bar, a diamond-and-jewel encrusted gold ring, and more. Ole Jacob Sending from the Norwegian Institute of International Affairs says: "You think about the Trump presidency in that way, I think gift giving, certainly broadly defined, is very much part of how he operates." On Thursday morning, Xi announced a gift of two Chinese pandas to a zoo in Atlanta - and a new student exchange programme, which will welcome 100,000 US students to study in China over five years. "The giant panda have been an envoy of friendship between the Chinese and the Americans," Xi said. "In a few days, two pandas - Ping Ping and Fu Shuang - will come to their new home in Zoo Atlanta and meet with the American people." It's unclear if he gave any further presents. The BBC has contacted the White House. This video can not be played Watch: The world’s two most powerful men just met. How did it go? Today, the practice of giving lavish gifts mostly exists in Gulf states and autocratic governments. "Autocracies like China give much more expensive gifts," says Morten Skumsrud Andersen, who co-authored a study on diplomacy and gifts with Sending. In the West, Andersen says, the tradition has been watered down by democratic guardrails and restrictions. For example, the US Constitution has an emoluments clause that puts a dollar-value limit on gifts a president can receive from a foreign government. Currently, the limit is $525 (£397). Anything higher and it becomes federal property, unless the president chooses to buy it back with his own money. Also, when giving a gift beyond a certain amount, a US president would have to go through Congress, unless he was paying for it personally. "There are a lot of rules and protocols involved," Sending says, "A lot of thought and process relating to what type of gift to to give, where should the gift exchange happen? How should it happen? When? "All of this is highly scripted, and involves negotiation at lower levels that goes on for weeks and weeks in advance," Sending says. Anderson adds: "This is not a last-minute purchase at the airport." The bald eagle has become an American icon  During Xi's state visit to the US in 2013, then-President Barack Obama gifted him an inscribed bench made of redwood, native to California where the two had met. They sat on it together afterwards, smiling for cameras. It was a more shining example than in 2009, when then-British Prime Minister Gordon Brown gifted Obama an ornamental desk pen holder made from the timbers of a historic anti-slave ship; while Obama gave Brown a set of DVDs, which reportedly were not formatted for UK DVD players. "That's one example of a kind of an embarrassing exchange," Sending says. Fortunately, Brown and Obama were allied leaders and not deep rivals looking to resolve seemingly intractable differences. "You don't want to mess up," Sending says, adding that the wrong gift could potentially derail any larger objectives. In this case, there is potentially a lot at stake between Trump and Xi. Their third face-to-face encounter since the start of Trump's second term, this summit is happening amid growing fears of an AI-led apocalypse as both countries race for dominance in the quickly growing industry. It's also taking place in the wake of a bitter US-China trade war that has only been resolved by a temporary truce, extended on this trip. The present exchange helps smooth over the differences and should be seen in the same way as the military flyovers, the pageantry and the state dinner, Kritenbrink says. "It's protocol and it's optics and it's gift giving all as a means to an end, which is stable US-China relations. "I'll take a fragile truce over a white-hot trade war any day of the week." Headline: Haiti extradites 18 suspects in assassination of president to US
Body: Haiti has been engulfed in a wave of gang violence since the assassination of Haitian President Jovenel Moise Eighteen people have been flown from Haiti to the US state of Florida to stand trial for their alleged involvement in the assassination of Haitian President Jovenel Moise five years ago. Moise was shot dead at his home in the capital, Port-au-Prince, in July 2021, allegedly by a group of mainly Colombian mercenaries. Previous Haitian investigations into the assassination have stalled due to widespread gang control and lawlessness in the country. The extradition was "the next major phase in our pursuit of accountability" over the presidential assassination, US Attorney for the Southern District of Florida, Jason Reding Quiñones, said in a post on X. "Five years later, we are still bringing defendants before American courts, and we are not finished," Quiñones said on X. He said that 30 suspects had been indicted over the killing so far. US prosecutors allege that the planning and financing of Moise's killing was orchestrated from Florida, as well as the Dominican Republic and Haiti itself. Given the dire state of the justice system in Haiti, the onus has been on US prosecutors to bring the detainees to Florida to try the cases there. When gunmen strode into Moise's residence andmurdered him in his bedroom, it shook the Caribbean nation to its core. It shocked many Haitians that the 53-year-old president was assassinated with such apparent ease. Those extradited on Sunday included a group of 17 Colombian ex-soldiers and a senior member of the then-Haitian Government, Joseph Badio, who worked in an anti-corruption unit at the country's justice ministry. A Miami-based security firm is accused of playing a key role in the hiring of the Colombian ex-soldiers. "Today's multi-location and international arrests underscore the FBI's continued commitment to bringing all participants in this plot to justice," FBI special agent Brett Skiles said on X. Several men allegedly connected to the murderwere killed by police at the time. Four people were convicted in a Miami court in May for their part in the conspiracy, which prosecutors have long said was planned and financed in Miami, as well as the Dominican Republic. The men, whose charges included conspiracy to kill or kidnap Moise and conspiracy to provide material support over the killing, face possible sentences of life in prison. The Colombian former soldiers have claimed they were mercenaries who had been convinced they were taking part in a coup but that they had been unaware of the intention to murder Moise. Haiti has been engulfedin a wave of gang violencesince the assassination of Moise. At least 1,408 people were killed and 656 injured from April through to June this year, according to the UN Integrated Office in Haiti. The country is preparing to hold its first presidential and legislative election since 2016 on December 13 - if the security situation allows. Headline: Treadmills to deadlifts: Why Gen Z are swapping cardio for strength training
Body: When Antonia Duffin, 34, started going to the gym, she wanted to lose weight and tone up. It became such a big part of her life that she decided to become a personal trainer alongside her day job in operations for a supermarket chain - and now runs her own women's gym in Manchester. "Some of my clients want to feel stronger, some want to get in shape for a baby and some are struggling with other conditions like endometriosis and want to feel better," she says. Hybrid training, like Hyrox, which is sociable and competitive, seems to have taken over from running on a treadmill or general cardio on a bike, she explains. Antonia also notes an appetite for more strength training workouts among younger clients, adding: "I think people are now realising the importance of it - we're preventing osteoporosis and things like that." Do numbers bear that out? And how are workouts across the UK changing? This video can not be played Why more young people are switching from cardio to weights According to Sport England, more young adults are going to the gym, using exercise machines and weights to keep fit compared to nine years ago. "Gyms offer broader types of exercise, like resistance training, which can improve body composition and shape more quickly than aerobic exercise training," explains exercise expert Dr Andrew Scott, from the University of Portsmouth. He says social media is having an impact too. "Lots of people are largely learning from influencers, suggesting 'I can do it, this is what I did and so can you'." Student Will Seward, 19, started going to the gym when he was at secondary school because he wanted to "get stronger and build up his physique". His workouts - usually three a week - have changed over time, from using running machines and exercise bikes initially to more explosive training using weights, to help build athleticism. "It's had a real impact on my day to day life," he says, "improving my mood and making me feel generally healthier." Barbells, kettlebells, dumbbells and cable machines are all part of the strength training Antonia offers in her gym space, located in a shipping container. Recent researchsuggests doing the recommended two hours of strength training each week may offer many of the same benefits as regular aerobic exercise, such as lowering the risk of dying from heart disease or stroke while also protecting the brain and boosting self-esteem. These benefits are not the only appeal of exercise though. Many say they feel a sense of connection when exercising with other people. Dr Hussain Al-Zubaidi, a GP, personal trainer and triathlete, says there is now "an enormous ecosystem" for those who are already active, featuring gyms, running clubs, fitness apps, social media and wearable tech. How different age groups meet overall exercise targets varies. Among nearly 2 million participants in Our Future Health - a health and lifestyle questionnaire - younger age groups were more likely to do shorter bursts of vigorous activity every week like fitness classes, aerobics or football. While running has fallen in popularity overall, it is still the most common form of exercise for young men and women - and in the top two activities for adults overall. And organised, social running is thriving, with children, 20-somethings and over 50s accounting for a growing share of participants in parkruns, which are free to everyone and have over 1,400 events taking place across the UK every weekend. Prof Esther van Sluijs, professor of behavioural epidemiology from Loughborough University, says community exercise offers social connection. When working from home is so common, particularly for young people, "easy access to community clubs close to home is very important", she adds. So how much is keeping active costing exercise goers, at a time when budgeting is tight? More than a quarter of 16-34 year olds say paying for gym membership and keeping fit is a top spending priority, over holidays and eating out, data from UK Active shows - up from a fifth in 2024. A 2026 survey by the Gym Group found a third of Gen Z spent £26-50 per month on health and fitness, with a quarter spending more than £50. Events manager Cordelia Sheridan, 27, who exercises four to five times a week at her gym in Battersea, says she treats her £45 gym membership "like an essential utility bill". "If you go to the pub and you're with a group of mates, you can buy a few pints and easily spend that on a night out," she says. Living just five minutes walk from her gym makes it easy to get there for 6.30am and exercise before work. Cordelia has changed her gym routine to incorporate more strength training At the gym, she spends 10 minutes on a stair-climbing machine then 35 minutes using weights and machines to strengthen the thighs, hips and lower back. Before, her routine was all about cardio - but she didn't feel she was getting better or stronger. Now, she says, it's really nice being able to hit targets and lift heavier weights. "I want to go into my 30s being strong." "And it's also weirdly more sociable," she says. Persuading people to exercise is about making it the easy, social and enjoyable thing to do, even if it costs, says Dr Al-Zubaidi. "I think that's why activities like the gym, running clubs and padel have been successful - not because they prevent disease but because they are fun and sociable." Headline: Burnham not doing enough to boost growth, says former business secretary
Body: Peter Kyle served as business secretary during Sir Keir Starmer's premiership A cabinet minister under Sir Keir Starmer has said Andy Burnham's government is not focused enough on boosting economic growth and needs to act with "more urgency". Speaking to the BBC two months after being sacked in Burnham's cabinet reshuffle upon entering office, Peter Kyle said he wasn't making a "criticism" but "pointing to the potential that we have as a country and as a government". "If the destination means prosperity, it means freedom for people to do new things, and it means security for people and families, then why wouldn't we put our foot down and get there quicker," the former business secretary said. It comes as Labour prepares to gather in Liverpool for its annual conference. Burnham will address the conference on Tuesday and has said his speech would leave nobody in any doubt about "what I'm trying to do in this role." He has previously said his time as Greater Manchester mayor had given him"a clear theory of growth"stressing his belief in the importance of devolving powers to local areas. Giving regions and nations more control would, he has argued, create the conditions for "good growth in every postcode". Kyle served as science secretary and later business secretary in the Starmer government, but has now returned to the backbenches as the MP for Hove and Portslade. In an interview with the BBC's Laura Kuenssberg, he said the government should be willing to take decisions that involve "short-term" pain in order to deliver economic growth, suggesting a delay to expanding workers' rights. "We might need to look and have honest conversations with unions about how we sequence some of the rights going forward in order to make sure that we get growth into the economy in the shorter term," he said. The government'sEmployment Rights Act was passed in December 2025but some of the changes are not due to come into force until next year. The former minister also suggested introducing a "tax growth test" which would measure the impact of each tax on the economy and asking government experts to review "obstacles" to growth. Asked if there was enough focus on growth in the government, Kyle replied: "I don't think there is and that isn't a criticism - it is pointing to the potential that we have as a country and as a government. "I think we need to up our ambition, I think that we need to act with more urgency when it comes to economic growth." Chancellor John Healey is due to give his first Budget on 28 October,but faces rising debt costsand warnings of slower economic growth. According to the Organisation of Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), the UK economy is expected to grow by 1%, slightly less than the 1.1% previously forecast. Responding to Kyle's comments that the government needed to act with more urgency on economic growth, Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy suggested that the prime minister was moving faster than his predecessor, Sir Keir Starmer. She told BBC Radio 4's Today programme: "I think the the reason, frankly, that we had a change of leadership at the start of this year is because we all felt that people need to feel the change in their lives that we promised in 2024 much more quickly." She added that she believed Burnham was "impatient for change, and he thinks big about the sort of change that the country needs". Henry Zeffman: Andy Burnham and his chancellor have a battle on their hands as the Budget approaches Burnham has big ideas - but what will they cost? Earlier this week, Starmer ally Darren Jones toldthe New Statesman,externalhe thought Sir Keir should have been given more time in office and criticised "this modern approach of getting queasy and then just changing [leader] too rapidly". "In the past it was normal for governments to be unpopular midterm because you've got to take difficult structural long-term decisions." The former chief secretary to the prime minister added: "Irrespective of what's happened and how, we want it to be successful, and we have a collective responsibility to help make that the case. "We, as backbenchers in the PLP [Parliamentary Labour Party], are looking to… Andy and his team to get that right. We want them to get it right." Headline: Swiss voters reject stricter neutrality rules that would curb Nato cooperation
Body: 70% vote against tightening centuries-old neutrality, which far right said was being eroded by sanctions against Russia Swiss voters have decisively rejected a proposal for a strict definition of neutrality that would have requiredSwitzerlandto curb cooperation with Nato and abandon sanctions against Russia. All cantons and about 70% of voters rejected the proposal for a strictly defined version of neutrality to be ⁠written into the Swiss constitution, final results from the Federal Statistical Office showed. The motion had been promoted by the far-right Swiss People’s party (SVP). Although the defeat was expected, it will be a relief across Europe, amidincreasing strains in maintaining EU unity on sanctions against Russia. Switzerland’s centuries-old neutrality was formally recognised after the end of the Napoleonic wars in 1815. Critics of current government policy claim that status has been eroded by Switzerland’sdecision to mirror EU sanctionsagainst Russia, after the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Voters were asked to decide on enshrining the principle of “perpetual and armed neutrality” in the constitution and barring Switzerland from joining any military alliances or imposing sanctions on warring states, unless mandated by the United Nations. The outcome is a heavy defeat for the SVP’s billionaire backer, Christoph Blocher, who was a prominent supporter of the initiative, reported by Bloomberg to have spent 2 million francs (€2.1m, £1.8m) on the campaign Opponents welcomed the results. “Voters understood what the SVP wanted: it wanted Switzerland to isolate itself internationally and shirk its responsibilities when international law is being trampled on,” said Sibel Arslan, a lawmaker for the Green party. The Swiss government, along with most political parties, opposed the measure, arguing “Switzerland would cease to be a reliable partner in international security policy” leaving the country less secure in the event of an attack and heavily restricting its ability to cooperate withNato. Although not a member of Nato, Switzerland has cooperated with the transatlantic military alliance for 30 years. Analysts said the result showed Swiss people were content with how the government interpreted Swiss neutrality. “The people have spoken: they accept that neutrality is an instrument that can evolve,leaving the government with room for manoeuvre to adapt its application faced with geopolitical upheavals,” wrote Katy Romy, a correspondent for SwissInfo, the online service of the Swiss Broadcasting Corporation. Sign up toThis is Europe The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment after newsletter promotion She also wrote that the yes campaign was unable to shed perceptions it was acting in Russian interests. Russia’s foreign ministry had praised the initiative, while criticising Switzerland’s adoption of EU sanctions and claiming the country was abandoning neutrality. The SVP accepted the defeat and said it had no current plans for further action.

Headline: Dramatic eviction of woman aged 87 highlights Spain's housing shortage
Body: Maricarmen had to leave the flat she had lived in for 70 years on Wednesday The dramatic eviction of an 87-year-old woman from the home in Madrid where she lived for seven decades has drawn attention to the depth of Spain's housing crisis. The tenant of the flat in the Retiro area of central Madrid, Maricarmen, was unable to pay the rent set by the investment firm that owns it. Maricarmen's father first rented the property in 1956 and she continued as the tenant after her parents died, during which time there was a cap on the rent. However, the company that bought the property in 2018, Urbagestión, cited a legal glitch allowing it to raise her rent from €500 (£428; $572) to €2,650. It subsequently lowered the new rent to €1,650 but Maricarmen was still unable to pay it with her monthly pension of €1,350. Three previous attempts to evict her were blocked by the courts and the case has received increasing media attention. Supporters of Maricarmen camped outside the building on Tuesday night, joined by celebrities including Javier Bardem's brother, Carlos, and the singer Ana Belén, who read out the poemDesahucio(Eviction) by Rafael Alberti. Several hundred people, mostly youngsters, had gathered by the morning in a bid to prevent the eviction from taking place, chanting "Maricarmen stays". Some activists blocked the stairs inside the building. In a video posted on social media, a tearful Maricarmen thanked those who had come out to support her against "this cruel struggle by someone who wants to earn money". The hard men removing squatters in Spain Taking back Barcelona's apartments 'Sometimes I want to cry': Eviction in a pandemic Police cordoned off a section of the street and removed people from the entrance to the building, including members of the media, striking some protesters with batons. A representative of tenants' organisationSindicato de Inquilinasshouted at the police through a megaphone: "Think for 10 seconds about Maricarmen, who could be your own grandmother." "There is a police deployment as if this were a military operation," said Beatriz Duro, Maricarmen's lawyer. "This is the fourth time [they've tried to evict her] but the first time they've come right to the door of the property. It's completely disproportionate." In June, the UN Committee on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights called for the pensioner's eviction to be halted and for her to be offered affordable alternative accommodation. The local government said she had declined its offer of a place in an elderly care home. The central government said Urbagestión had refused its repeated attempts to negotiate Maricarmen's situation. The BBC has attempted to contact the company. Volunteers helped pack up Maricarmen's belongings Protesters had gathered outside the building on Tuesday under the slogan "Maricarmen is staying" Maricarmen emerged from the house in a wheelchair to greet her supporters Overcome with emotion at the gathering, the elderly woman broke into tears The possibility of a last-minute reprieve for Maricarmen appeared when an anonymous donor offered to pay most of her rent. However, Urbagestión reportedly rejected the offer and the eviction went ahead. "Today is a very sad day, a very dramatic day, when it's plain to see the effects of unbridled speculation, of not wanting to control the market, of putting out the red carpet for the vultures and the speculators," said Housing Minister Teresa Rodríguez. A shortage of available housing has been blamed for soaring rental costs in recent years, which have left millions of Spaniards struggling to find affordable homes. In Madrid, rentals have increased by more than 100% over the last decade, according to property site Idealista, with a 10% rise over the last year. The Socialist-led government of Pedro Sánchez has frequently targeted companies whose investment pushes up housing costs. In January, the prime minister said he aimed to "protect those who are most exposed to that speculation and that greed". However, some critics of the government say it needs to work harder to build new homes, and others warn that its rhetoric discourages many owners from placing their properties on the rental market.

Headline: Netanyahu defends Israeli military action as delegates walk out before UN speech
Body: This video can not be played Nada Tawfik in New York explains what happened when Netanyahu spoke Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has fiercely defended his country's military campaigns in Iran, Gaza and elsewhere in the Middle East in a speech to the UN General Assembly. After dozens of delegates walked out in protest as he took to the stage, Netanyahu vowed to continue fighting: "We're going to win. We have no other choice." In response to the walkout, he said: "If there are any other moral cowards who haven't left the hall, please do so now." The Israeli leader also rejected accusations that Israel is committing genocide in Gaza. Hours earlier, in a recorded message Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas told the UN that Israeli policies - in particular the illegal expansion of Jewish settlements in the occupied West Bank - threatened "the very life and existence of the Palestinian people on their homeland". He also said it jeopardised the two-state solution, which is an internationally backed formula for peace between Israel and the Palestinians. Abbas said that Palestinians were being subjected to "killing, destruction, starvation and attempts at displacement, as well as a genocidal war" in Gaza by the Israeli military. The Palestinian leader was addressing the annual gathering via a video link because he had been denied a US entry visa. Reconstruction has yet to begin in Gaza almost a year after a ceasefire came into force Netanyahu, who is subject to an International Criminal Court arrest warrant for alleged war crimes, launched scathing attacks on nations and leaders who have criticised him. "They accuse Israel, tiny Israel, of colonialism - some colonialism. And who's accusing us? Among them are people in Britain and in France. For God's sake, they invented the term," he said. Netanyahu also accused the media of misrepresenting violence by Jewish settlers in the occupied West Bank and said "maybe two or three" people are killed a year. But, according to figures published by the UN, 23 Palestinians have been killed in the context of settler attacks this year - and 72 since the beginning of 2023. Netanyahu went on to label Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan a "tyrant", accusing him of supporting the Palestinian armed group Hamas. Erdogan told the UN on Tuesday that the injustices faced by those in Gaza and the West Bank "deeply offends the conscience of humanity". Netanyahu's comments drew a sharp response from the Turkish presidency's communications director Burhanettin Duran. The Israeli PM's use of the UN General Assembly podium to level "baseless accusations" against Turkey and Erdogan was incompatible with the UN's "ideals of peace, law and dialogue", Duran said, according to state-run news agency Anadolu. New York City's left-wing mayor Zohran Mamdani - who had previously vowed to arrest Netanyahu but later said he did not have the authority to do so - was also criticised by the Israeli leader. "Since you were elected mayor of this city, many Jews no longer feel safe in New York," the Israeli prime minister said. In a statement, Mamdani's office said Netanyahu "used his speech to repeat baseless lies meant to sanitize his genocide of Palestinians". Netanyahu also thanked US President Donald Trump for his "bold leadership", referring to the air strikes the US and Israel jointly launched against Tehran in February. "Israel and America acted together not only to protect ourselves, but to save civilisation," he said.  Much of Netanyahu's speech was pitched at the two audiences he needs to convince the most: Israelis as he faces a critical election at home next month, and Americans as Israel faces growing isolation and fractures in support abroad. In Israel, Netanyahu's once unrivalled image as "Mr Security" has come under increasing scrutiny in what is the first election since the 7 October 2023 attacks. Some political opponents have argued he is unfit for office following Israeli media reports, firmly denied by Netanyahu, that he did not heed warnings of a potential attack by Hamas. His characteristic defiance at the UN podium will be replayed in a campaign seeing his religious-right wing coalition trailing in the polls. Netanyahu appeared to have pre-scripted his comments about "moral cowards" as he faced a mass walkout. It will likely be used as he tries once again to burnish an image as being the only Israeli politician that can truly take on Israel's growing number of global critics. There were also clearly marked references meant for American audiences, including the joint US-Israeli strikes on Iran and his praise for Trump. Netanyahu, who was born in Israel but spent his formative years in Pennsylvania, has always tried to present himself as having a unique ability to pitch Israel's case in the US. Despite continued weapons supply from Washington, he faces an increasingly sceptical public. Polls suggest plummeting support for Israel among Democrats, and a fracture in historically high levels of backing among Republicans which has spread to Trump's Maga base. A number of people protesting against Netanyahu's visit were detained in New York City. Among them were the Oscar-winning actress Susan Sarandon and Emmy-winning Hacks actress Hannah Einbinder. Also detained were Democratic congressional candidate Darializa Avila Chevalier and New York City council member Chi Osse. A spokesperson for the NYPD said officers had responded to reports of an "unscheduled demonstration" where protesters were blocking a junction. Actress Susan Sarandon was among demonstrators detained near the UN The Israeli military launched a ground offensive in the Gaza Strip after the 7 October 2023 Hamas attack against Israel, in which about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others taken hostages. During the Israeli military campaign more than 73,920 people have been killed in Gaza, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry. Last year,the world's leading association of genocide scholars declared that Israel was committing genocide in Gaza. A resolution passed by the International Association of Genocide Scholars (IAGS) stated that Israel's conduct meets the legal definition as laid out in the UN convention on genocide. Israel has regularly denied its actions in Gaza amount to genocide and says they are justified as a means of self-defence. On 28 February, Israel and the US started launching massive air strikes on Iran, suspecting it of secretly building a nuclear weapon - a claim denied by Tehran. Iran retaliated by carrying out missile and drone attacks on Israel and neighbouring Gulf Arab states which host US military bases. Headline: Teenagers to be offered new vocational GCSE subjects in school
Body: New vocational GCSEs will be introduced from 2029 for 14-year-olds alongside existing core academic subjects in England. The new subjects could include building and construction, business management and finance, and child development. Education Secretary Lucy Powell said there was "no question" that academic learning was at "the core of any education system", but said there was "huge demand" for subjects with more practical elements too. Education unions said the ideas were welcome, but a clear strategy was needed to make them happen. The Conservatives said the plans risked "throwing away" progress made in recent years. Standards for the new qualifications will be set nationally by the regulator Ofqual to ensure grades are in line with other GCSEs, and will gradually replace other qualifications at this level such as BTec tech awards. The vocational GCSEs will be designed to allow teenagers to progress at 16 to studying similar courses at college, including the newV-levels, which schools and colleges are teaching from autumn 2027, andT-levels. The idea is to create a clear pathway for teenagers into different types of work through a ladder of qualifications. But the Liberal Democrats warned the new vocational GCSEs should not become a "pipeline" directing disadvantaged pupils away from more academic subjects. Powell told the BBC she was "not going to oversee a two-tier education system". "I want working class, disadvantaged young people to have every opportunity to achieve highly academically," she said. "And I also want every child to have the opportunity to take on more vocational and technical subjects." Powell told BBC Breakfast schools would be able to specialise in subjects relevant to the jobs available in their local areas, adding that she wanted to improve the "esteem, respect and recognition" of the current qualifications. Asked whether there would be dedicated funding to help schools cover the cost of the new qualifications, she said the government would "work with the sector to make sure this is absolutely deliverable", and that ministers would "make sure any funding needed is made available". A new national target for employers to help create 200,000 work experience opportunities for under-16s is also being set by Prime Minister Andy Burnham, as part of reforms to shake-up the education system to better prepare young people for the world of work. VCSEs,external, a new style of vocational qualification unique to Wales, will be taught in schools and colleges from September 2027. Learners in Wales can choose from 15 VCSE subjects including Animal Care​, Nature Restoration​ and Motor Vehicle Maintenance​. Daisy is taking business studies at BTec Level 2 - this is the kind of subject that could be replaced by a new Vocational GCSE Vocational subjects at 16 currently make up 7% of the entries for qualifications in England and it is up to each school how many subjects with hands-on learning they offer. Wright Robinson College in Gorton, East Manchester, already offers 10 practical or vocational subjects for study in Year 10. Daisy, in Year 11, is taking business studies as a BTec Level 2 which she said is giving her "practical experience" and building her confidence to progress to an A-level in the subject. This is the kind of subject that may be replaced by one of the new vocational GCSEs. Many of these existing tech awards have their standards set by the examining organisations, not the regulator.  The standards for the new vocational GCSEs will be national. Sarjo, also Year 11, already knows she wants to be a flight attendant so she is taking hospitality and catering as a BTec Level 2 alongside GCSEs. She said she "learns faster" in the practical subject and most teenagers want to do something they enjoy alongside core academic subjects. Martin Haworth, executive head teacher at Wright Robinson College, said any new qualifications had to "add value" to what was already on offer and labelling them as GCSEs might help with credibility. He said schools would need to recruit specialist staff if the courses and exams were going to be "robust", and it would cost schools money to convert existing classrooms for practical learning. Sarjo enjoys the practical elements of her hospitality and catering BTec New analysis of school funding by the independent Institute for Fiscal Studies shows the budget per pupil is growing faster than expected, by 9% in real terms between 2025-26 and 2028-29. This is partly because of various government top-ups to the budget and falling pupil numbers in some areas. Economist Luke Sibieta said asking schools to offer more vocational routes would be a "big change" on top of the significant reforms to support for pupils with special educational needs and disabilities. He said there was a "big question mark" over whether there were enough people to teach technical and vocational subjects, with further education colleges already struggling to recruit. The Association of Colleges (AoC) suggested schools worked with them because they could offer "industry standard facilities" and qualified staff. David Hughes, from the AoC, said this would help ensure learning was "authentically different to school and properly employment focused". Daniel Kebede, from the National Education Union, said "sustained investment and resources" was needed to make a success of the new qualifications. While Pepe Di'Iasio, of the Association of School and College Leaders, described the government's plans as "well-intentioned", but not making sure schools had the staffing and resources would not remove barriers to young people. He welcomed the national push for work experience and said with placements "extremely difficult" to secure, more support was needed from employers. The existing statutory career guidelines for secondary schools in England already require "meaningful" work experience for 14 to 16-year-olds. Employers are now being asked to contact their local careers hub to offer placements. Laura Trott MP, who is the Conservative Party's shadow education secretary, said she was concerned the changes risked losing the progress England had made in improving standards, and "ripping up the system" could mean "sabotaging young people's futures". "Better schools will continue to protect rigorous subjects but disadvantaged children will be steered towards easier routes, lowering expectations for the very pupils who need high standards most," she said. Headline: Venezuela releases dozens of political prisoners as election calls grow
Body: Prisoner releases and free elections were two key pledges made to the US by the new administration Venezuelan authorities have released a slew of political prisoners, human rights groups say, days after the nation's interim leader met US President Donald Trump in New York. Among those released in the early hours of Saturday morning was Wilder Vasquez, who was handed a five-year sentence in 2018 over claims he was plotting to kill former President Nicolás Maduro. Opposition figures have renewed calls for free elections after interim President Delcy Rodriguez held talks with Trump, who captured Maduro earlier this year, at the UN General Assembly on Tuesday. Her administration previously released hundreds of prisoners as part of a reconciliation effort following Maduro's seizure. However, these releases slowed to a trickle in April after Rodriguez said the scheme was "coming to an end". Venezuela's government has not made any statement concerning the latest releases, nor has it indicated whether they were the result of her conversation with the US president. Gonzalo Himiob, vice-president of rights group Foro Penal, said "a significant number" of political prisoners had been released on Saturday morning from several of Venezuela's detention centres. Rights groups critical as Venezuela prisoner release scheme 'coming to an end' US lifts sanctions on Venezuelan interim leader Delcy Rodríguez Venezuelan prison director sacked as inmates allege mistreatment Foro Penal confirmed the release of Miguel Castillo Cedeño, who it said had been arbitrarily detained since June 2019. Also released was Frank Cabañas, who rights groups say had been held in prison for nine years after being linked to the death of a police officer. Foro Penal said he was the only suspect who remained detained, despite family members reporting that he was suffering health problems last year. Opposition and human rights groups have said Maduro's government used the detention of political prisoners to stamp out dissent and silence critics for years. Rodriguez has sought to frame her interim government as more permissive of political dissent while currying favour with the US. The prisoner release scheme was a key concession by her administration to the US. However, her decision to end the scheme attracted criticism from opposition and rights groups. Foro Penal said it was stopped with less than half of the nation's political prisoners released. Rodriguez's government continues to deny dissidents are jailed. It has cast the release of prisoners as a gesture of goodwill and reconciliation. Delcy Rodríguez's meeting with Donald Trump in New York has brought renewed calls for elections in Venezuela Venezuelan Interior Minister Diosdado Cabello, a minister closely associated with Maduro's authoritarian rule, called the interim president's meeting with Trump "a great triumph of the diplomacy of peace". But opposition voices expressed their disapproval over the meeting, viewing it as a snub of their calls – that the US has previously endorsed – for swift elections. Pedro Mario Burelli, a former Venezuelan state oil company executive and opposition commentator, called the two world leaders "the shameless puppet and her unscrupulous and undignified puppet-master", adding: "Little has changed in Venezuela under Washington's clumsy and selective oversight." Venezuela's last elections, held in 2024, in which Maduro was declared the winner, were widely disputed as rigged. Opposition tallies suggested their candidate, who stood after Machado was barred from running, had won by 70% of the vote. Despite this, the Trump administration backed Rodriguez, Maduro's former vice-president, as his successor rather than opposition leader María Corina Machado after Maduro was seized and put on trial on drug charges in January. Analysts at the time cast this decision as the US choosing short-term stability in Venezuela until elections could be held. Rodriguez used her UN General Assembly speech on Thursday to reiterate that there "will be elections in Venezuela", without specifying when. Headline: Drinking at football matches - would fans welcome it?
Body: The law permits supporters at stadiums from the Premier League to National League to drink alcohol outside the ground and in concourses, but not in their seats When UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham embarked on his trip to the United Nations in New York, he might not have been expecting a question about football fans drinking alcohol in grounds. Burnham firmly believes the law that prevents supporters from having a beer at their seat during a match is outdated. It's a position theEvertonsupporter has long held, and when asked was happy to reaffirm. "I do believe there is a case to remove that discrimination,"said Burnham,who feels football fans are singled out compared to those of other sports and events. There is no suggestion this is about to become official government policy, and last year MPsrejected a Conservative amendmentto the Football Governance Bill that would have forced ministers to launch a formal consultation on scrapping the rule. That was, of course, before Burnham returned to Downing Street. It is a complicated and divisive issue, about not just safety. But is it something that match-going supporters actually want? Drinking alcohol at football grounds in England and Wales has been strictly controlled since the Sporting Events Control of Alcohol Act was introduced in 1985. It was brought in to counter escalating hooliganism through the 1970s and into the 1980s. The ban impacts clubs in the Premier League down to the National League. While beer can be sold, it must be consumed in areas that do not have a view of the pitch. Yet fans who support teams in the National League North and South and below can drink alcohol around the pitch. The ban is more strict in Scotland, with a law in place since 1981 that alcohol is only available in hospitality areas and not for other fans. It was initially imposed following a riot during the 1980 Scottish Cup final between Rangers and Celtic at Hampden. However, attitudes have been changing in recent seasons. It was lifted aspart of a pilot schemelast year, with several Scottish clubs selling alcohol in clearly defined, monitored areas of the stadiums. It started with lower-level clubs, eventually being extended to the Premiership. The Scotland national team joined the trial for the friendlies against Japan and Curacao earlier this year. Ithas been extendedto games against Switzerland on 29 September and Slovenia next month. The Women's Super League in England has just completed two seasons of successful trials and the rule preventing drinking in the standshas now been removedby the league's governing company, WSL Football. The women's game is not governed by the Sporting Events Control of Alcohol Act, enabling the competition organiser to make the change. Is there support for the move within English football's corridors of power? Premier League chief executive Richard Masters said in August the competition had not "got a specific view" and "we'd need to give it some really careful thought". The English Football League, however, issued a statement on Thursday that said it would be "receptive to discussions around reviewing the current legislation". It added member clubs had already provided "a mandate to lobby for appropriate reform" which had "not kept pace with significant developments in stadium management, safety and stewarding". This video can not be played Should alcohol be allowed in football stands? The Football Supporters' Association has for some time backed changing the law. Like the prime minister, it considers it to be unfair on football fans. "I think it is outdated," FSA chairman Tom Greatrex told the BBC Radio 4 Today programme. "If you go to watch football in Germany or in other places around the world, then it's perfectly acceptable. "It is civilised and appropriate. There's no reason why that shouldn't be the case for football fans, as it is for fans of rugby league, watching Oasis, or anything else that happens often in the same stadiums in the same seats." The FSA's position is that clubs should have the choice, in consultation with supporters, to sell alcohol. Clubs might want to offer it in all stands, others in designated areas, while a few might choose not to do so at all. Other sports offer designated alcohol-free sections, something that football clubs may wish to copy for some families and supporters who do not consume alcohol because of their religion. The FSA acknowledges this, but believes having the option to make such decisions is important. It believes relaxing the law would be more popular the further down the leagues you go, where alcohol sales could potentially provide a crucial additional income stream. The UK Football Policing Unit rejected the suggestion, arguing alcohol plays "a significant part in violent and disorderly behaviour" and that "other sports simply don't see the violence and criminal behaviour" that football does. Yet for Greatrex, there is already proof police are not open to ideas through their previous opposition to safe standing. Before it was introduced four years ago, Mark Roberts, who has been the national lead for football policing since 2014,told the BBC it would make it "easier to throw missiles, engage in hate chanting, racism, sneak alcohol in, take cocaine". "[The police] were telling everybody that we couldn't have standing at football again, that it would jeopardise safety, " Greatrex said. "Actually, what we saw then was a controlled, managed pilot projects to get that re-established. "There hasn't been the level of disorder that some of the police sources were saying there would be. I think  the police should have more of an open mind and engage in this in a sensible and mature way." Scottish football has slowly started to relax the ban of alcohol sales at matches but fans continue to protest for this to move at a faster pace. For many match-going fans, however, the prospect of beer being thrown and potential anti-social behaviour outweighs the opportunity to watch a game with a pint. Dave, aChelseafan from Twickenham, told Nicky Campbell on BBC Radio 5 Live, that he was "100% against it". "Have a look at some of the footage you see on social media at Boxpark, for instance. A goal goes in and there is beer and lager thrown everywhere," he said. "I don't want to go round stinking of other people's beer and there is a fashion among certain supporters to throw their beer everywhere. "If people can't go without drink for a 45-minute period there is something the matter with them." Adrian, from Leicester, claimed it would be the "worst idea you could come up with". "There is enough trouble with other things in football, with the flares, drug taking and other things," he added. "You throw the alcohol in as well. Football is tribal whereas other sports they aren't." But Ryan, a Wolves fan in Banbury, said "a solution that suits everybody" is to provide designated areas for drinking in stands. Football is in the only sport in the UK which faces restrictions on the consumption of alcohol. Some of these sports have issues with alcohol-related and anti-social behaviour, but none have the same reputation as football. The restrictions differ around Europe. There is a strict ban in the top two divisions of Spanish football, where only alcohol-free beer can be sold outside of hospitality areas. It can, however, be taken to seats. In the German Bundesliga, there is no ban on drinking at your seat. So relaxed is the approach to alcohol at games that you will even find people selling bottles of beer from shopping trolleys outside grounds. In the Italian Serie A it is similarly as relaxed, though to a limit of 5% ABV. Some games which are designated "high risk" have sales suspended in and around the stadium. In France, the Evin Law was introduced in 1991 which is pretty much in line with Scotland, as far as football is concerned. Alcohol cannot be sold at any sports event, other than in VIP areas. Headline: Rebel offensive against Ethiopian army stokes fears of return to civil war
Body: Fighting escalates after Tigrayan rebels form new coalition aimed at overthrowing Abiy Ahmed government There are growing fears of a return to civil war inEthiopiaafter an offensive by fighters from Tigray into the neighbouring states of Afar and Amhara and the formation of a new rebel alliance aimed at overthrowing the government of the prime minister, Abiy Ahmed. About 600,000 people died between 2020 and 2022 duringa devastating warbetween the Ethiopian army and the political party and paramilitary group the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF). Both sides are now accusing the other of triggering a return to open conflict. On Sunday, seven armed groups from around the country, including the TPLF, announced the formation of the Ethiopian Peoples’ Forces Alliance for Survival, aimed at deposing the government in Addis Ababa. Then, on Wednesday, the TPLF seized control of three airports from federal police. The state-owned carrier, Ethiopian Airlines, said it had suspended flights to the region “due to the current situation”. The TPLF also launched attacks into Afar and Amhara. A humanitarian source in Afar told Agence France-Presse there were heavy artillery attacks by the group on Thursday as they attempted to take control of the town of Yallo, near the Tigrayan border. Flights to the historic Ethiopian town of Lalibela were also suspended on Thursday because of nearby fighting, while people in Tigray stocked up ⁠on food and cash, with one resident telling Reuters that people there feared they could face siege conditions similar to those during the previous war. A resident of Adigrat, a city close to the Eritrean border, ‌described panic-buying and shops emptying. “Food shortages are worsening as market shelves sit empty … Essential medicines remain scarce and astronomically expensive,” he told Reuters. “Daily survival has become a constant calculation.” The TPLF’s vice-president, Amanuel Assefa, told AFP: “We are in the situation of full-blown war now.” He confirmed Tigrayan forces were fighting alongside local armed groups in Afar and Amhara. The group took control of Abala, also on the Tigray-Afar border, on Wednesday, a foreign security source based in Ethiopia told AFP, while a TPLF source said they had seized several other towns in Afar. The foreign security source also said there was fighting around the Amhara town of Weldiya – one of the few routes to the capital. In its first public comments on the fighting, Ethiopia’s army said on ⁠Thursday it had foiled the attacks and killed, wounded or captured more than 500 enemy fighters. Analysts say the TPLF has support from Ethiopia’s​ neighbour and historic adversary Eritrea, which fears landlocked Ethiopia is planning to invade its territory to gain access to the Red Sea. The TPLF’s Assefa told AFP “we have no information about Eritrea’s plan”. Asked if they would request Eritrean intervention, he said: “Not yet.” The current fighting reflects shifting dynamics from the civil war, whenEritreaand Fano, an insurgent group that is now part of the new alliance, both fought with the government against the Tigrayans. Speaking at the UN general assembly on Wednesday, the Ethiopian president, Taye Atske-Selassie Amde, decried “the forces of destruction and mayhem” and “interference in our internal affairs by adversarial elements”. He said Ethiopia had exercised “immense restraint” and made progress with its neighbours. Abiy’s spokesperson, Billene Seyoum, said members of the alliance had been collaborating for a while ​with the financial backing of Eritrea. Eritrea ​has repeatedly denied similar accusations. The TPLF ruled Ethiopiafrom 1991 to 2018 before being sidelined by the rise of Abiy, eventually triggering the civil war. The renewed fighting marks the most serious challenge ​yet tothe 2022 Pretoria agreement, which ended the civil war and maintained an uneasy calm until late last year, when clashes resumed. It raises fears of a broader regional conflict that could draw in armed groups from across and further destabilise a region already strained by war in neighbouring Sudan and tensions along the Red Sea. On Wednesday, the African Union chair, Mahmoud Ali Youssouf,urged“utmost restraint” from the warring parties and resumption of direct talks. An EU spokespersoncalled for“immediate de-escalation” and a recommitment to the Pretoria agreement. In the 2020-22 war, Tigray was largely cut off from the outside world as communications were severed, and access to food, cash and medicines was severely restricted, pushing hundreds of thousands of people into famine-like conditions. AFP and Reuters contributed reporting

Headline: Burnham proposes NHS-style social care system for England
Body: This video can not be played 'Broken social care will in the end break the NHS,' says Burnham Andy Burnham wants to offer access to free social care services to everyone in England, and will put his plans before voters at the next general election. The prime minister told the BBC that it would be a system in which "everyone contributes, everyone is covered". He did not rule out tax rises, acknowledging it may be "difficult or unpopular" with some. Burnham said he wants to set out his "vision" on Tuesday and Whitehall troubleshooter Baroness Casey, who is conducting a review, will advise on the "best way of doing it". Shadow home secretary Chris Philp said the PM was suggesting Labour wanted "more tax rises" to pay for the reforms, adding the Conservatives would not support this. Burnham has made reforming social care one of his flagship policies and has spoken of the experience of his father Roy, who had Alzheimer's anddied earlier this month. While he has been clear on his ambition to make changes to the system, he has yet to explain how any changes would be funded. Adult social care provides state support to help people live more independently, including assistance at home. Unlike the NHS, social care is not free at the point of use. In England and Northern Ireland, people with savings worth more than £23,250 are not entitled to help with care costs from their council. In Wales and Scotland, different rules apply in terms of eligibility. Speaking to the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg, the prime minister said: "I am talking about a system that works on NHS principles because that is the only way you can make it work. "There is free personal care elsewhere in the UK. I don't think it's right that people in England don't get the same and it's not something we're going to rush." Personal care offered in Scotland is available to all adults who are assessed as needing help with tasks including eating and bathing. Burnham said the changes would have to be "done carefully, without putting extra strain on the public purse". But he said that "nothing is off the table at this moment in time" in terms of how the proposals would be funded. When he was told it had been estimated that a system for everyone in England that is free at the point of use could cost taxpayers £18bn a year, Burnham replied: "It's not that high." He said people already face a "huge cost" at the moment and that social care in England is "as unfair as American healthcare, where the most vulnerable in society can lose everything, they can be wiped out". Burnham added there is also a cost to the NHS due to the "huge number" of people in hospitals across England who cannot be discharged home "because the social care isn't there". Asked whether everyone will have to contribute to his proposed system, Burnham replied: "It will be a system of that kind – so everyone contributes, everyone is covered but not precisely necessarily in the same way that we currently pay for the NHS." He said the details developed by Baroness Casey would be subject to cross-party talks in a bid to "build consensus". Baroness Casey was originally tasked by former PM Sir Keir Starmer to deliver her review of social care in 2028, but Burnham asked her to bring that forward to next summer. On the timeline, Burnham added: "I'm going to say that we stick to the manifesto because I have to keep people's trust, and there are commitments in the manifesto that would make it hard to do in this Parliament." The Labour manifesto in 2024 made clear commitments on tax, including not to increase national insurance, income tax or VAT. Burnham added: "I don't think you can reform this system without consensus. I will develop a very clear plan and I will put that plan to the public at a general election and that will be where the plan gets tested and people will then be able to decide." Philp said tax increases would be a "red line" for the Conservatives and they would "not under any circumstances" support more of them. He said the country is "already taxed too highly", telling the BBC: "If more money is needed, for example, for social care or indeed for defence we would find that money through savings elsewhere, particularly in the welfare budget." Labour MP Darren Jones, who served as a cabinet minister in Sir Keir's government, said Burnham was being "very bold and brave" on social care. He said: "Politics is about prioritisation and these things do cost money and so we'll need to see the detail of that policy." He told Laura Kuenssberg that scrapping the pensions triple lock was an "option that the government should consider alongside others" in order to fund social care reforms. The triple lock pension policy guarantees that the state pension will increase by either average wage growth, inflation or 2.5% - whichever is highest. Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey said Burnham can show he is "serious about fixing care" by getting on with the cross-party talks that began in July. He added: "This can't just be a series of No 10 headlines with no real action." Reform UK's economic spokesman Robert Jenrick said: "Andy Burnham refuses to rule out his universal death tax. "He's too weak to cut the benefits bill so he's coming for your home instead." Burnham accused previous generations of politicians of "cowardice" for failing to reform social care, although his push for change is not without jeopardy. He previously produced a plan for a national care service while serving as health secretary in Gordon Brown's Labour government. It was suggested this would be paid for through a compulsory contribution, including from people's estates after they had died. The idea was branded a "death tax" by Labour's opponents and the proposals went no further after the party lost the 2010 general election. At the 2017 general election, then-Conservative Prime Minister Theresa May was accused of trying to introduce a "dementia tax" by proposing that people receiving care at home pay for the full costs if they were worth at least £100,000. The policy sparked a political outcry and the Conservatives lost their majority in the House of Commons at the election. Andy Burnham wants to fix social care - what are the options? Headline: Two mass shootings in South Africa leave 27 dead
Body: Gunmen torched vehicles as they fled the scene of a mass shooting at bar near Johannesburg Twenty-seven people have been killed in two mass shootings hours apart in South Africa, the latest gun violence to hit the country. Seventeen people were killed when eight gunmen stormed a bar close to Johannesburg on Saturday evening, with 15 more injured. In a separate shooting in the early hours of Sunday morning, 10 people were killed outside an entertainment venue in a township near Cape Town and a further 11 were injured. South Africa has one of the highest murder rates in the world and has struggled to contain gang-related gun violence in recent years. Police have not given a definitive motive for either of the latest attacks. In Johannesburg, gunmen opened fire on customers outside the bar before continuing the attack inside and torching two vehicles before fleeing. Police said thirteen men and four women were killed. Gauteng Police Commissioner Lt Gen Tommy Mthombeni said people from Ethiopia and Lesotho were among those caught up in the shooting, but that the vast majority were South African. He also said police believed the motive behind the shooting was robbery, as personal belongings had been taken, but that they could not rule out turf wars between illegal mining groups. In Johannesburg, gunmen torched two vehicles after opened fire on customers at a bar. Mining without permission in abandoned shafts or dump sites is a persistent problem in South Africa, causing numerous deaths from unsafe conditions. Authorities say the miners are typically undocumented migrants recruited by organised crime gangs. Earlier, deputy provincial police commissioner Maj Gen Fred Kekana said the attack may have been a retaliation for an incident last month, in which one person was killed and another wounded, according to news agency AFP. He said at the scene that police had clear pictures and in some cases names for the suspects. In Cape Town, five victims died at the scene and a further five people died in hospital. No arrests had been made in either case on Sunday morning. The two mass shootings camedays after 11 people were killed in the city of Durbanwhen gunmen stormed a house in the KwaMakhutha township. Armed security forces were deployed to the scene of a mass shooting in Cape Town on Sunday morning Illegal weapons are prevalent in South Africa and gun violence has been a persistent problem for decades, with about 60 murders recorded every day in the country of 62 million. But a recent spate of mass shootings has raised fears that the problem is deepening, with violence often linked to turf wars between gangs engaged in drug trafficking and illegal mining. In February, President Cyril Ramaphosa called organised crime "the most immediate threat to our democracy, our society and our economic development". Earlier this year, themilitary was deployed alongside police in areas with the highest murder ratesin an effort to reduce armed violence. On Saturday,a tenth woman's body was found in Ekurhuleni, to the east of Johannesburg, with local police saying they were unable to rule out a serial killer operating in the area with similarities between the deaths.

Headline: White House bars CNN from travelling with Trump on Air Force One
Body: CNN had been scheduled to fly with Trump on Air Force One Broadcaster CNN has been barred from travelling with US President Donald Trump on Air Force One for a trip to Tennessee on Saturday. The move is the latest in a battle between the White House and the mediaafter it was forced to lift its banon some news outlets. CNN was scheduled to fly with Trump for his trip to Tennessee for a college American football game until a note released on Friday night by the White House did not list the broadcaster on the media schedule. The BBC has requested comment from the White House. CNN has reported that no other outlet was listed as replacing them in the president's tentative schedule. Last week, Trump banned CNN, Politico and MS NOW journalists from the White House after accusing them of writing "fiction or lies" about his administration. All three media outlets saidthey were pursuing legal actionand accused Trump of violating their constitutional rights to free speech and freedom of the press. Four television networks that have a daily rotation of White House coverage alongside CNN - ABC, CBS, Fox News and NBC - had paused their broadcasts of the president in solidarity with the banned outlets. The White House then launched its own streaming channel, Trump TV, ahead of the UN General Assembly in New York. A federal judge has since ruled that Trump barring news outlets from the White House was likely unconstitutional and that the administration had to let them back in, at least for now. However, the White House still denied entry to some CNN and MS NOW reporters assigned to cover arrivals at a state dinner for Chinese leader Xi Jinping on Thursday. In a series of online posts on Saturday, Trump criticised the CNN and other media outlets dubbing them "fake news". "FAKE NEWS SHOULD NOT BE ALLOWED IN THE WHITE HOUSE," he said. A White House communications account earlier posted on X that "contrary to what the Fake News wants you to believe, they don't just get to have free rein into every part of the White House, every event and every press call". Regular US television coverageresumed on Fridayafter White House officials allowed reporters entry. The president is set to attend a football game between University of Tennessee vs University of Texas College at Neyland Stadium in Knoxville from midday local time on Saturday.
