Headline: Open wounds and eyes that can't close - women warn about cheap bleph eyelid surgery
Body: Nikita had stitches in her upper eyelids. This photo was taken seven days after her bleph procedure  Warning: Graphic images and descriptions of surgery "Everyone made it out to be so easy, but my face felt like it was on fire and there was a horrible smell of burning skin," says Nikita Morgan, as she describes her eyelid surgery. She decided to get a blepharoplasty, or a "bleph", removing skin from just above the eyes - after seeing videos about it on social media. Even though she was given a local anaesthetic, Nikita felt extreme pain. Oculoplastic surgeons - doctors specialising in surgery around the eyes - say a concerning number of patients are reporting problems from cheap bleph surgery, typically carried out abroad. This video can not be played Watch: 'My eyelids split open and became infected - I was scared to sleep' They have told the BBC the demand for this procedure, which normally costs thousands of pounds in the UK, has increased as part of a wider aesthetic trend to tighten, smooth and lift the face. Surgeons say complications have been linked to clinics across mainland Europe, Africa and Asia, and, when they occur, the lack of aftercare puts a burden on the NHS. As well as Nikita, we have spoken to dozens of people who have experienced problems - including one woman who had to tape her eyes shut to sleep because too much eyelid skin had been removed, while another feared she was losing her sight. UK surgeons have also told us they have seen patients unable to close their eyes properly after treatment abroad. Nikita, from Dublin, wanted to make her eyes more defined, but could not afford upper eyelid surgery in Ireland that she was told would cost more than €4,000 (£3,400). Then the 31-year-old discovered on TikTok that she could get a bleph with Dutch company, Faceland for €750 (£650). She described its clinic in Düsseldorf as "like a conveyor belt, just one in, one out constantly". The company says it has performed more than 2,950 bleph procedures on UK patients at its clinics in the Netherlands, Germany and Switzerland since October 2024. It says it offers "safe and quality" treatments and told us "less than 1% of procedures have led to a complaint", although this does not include everyone who needed revision surgery. The majority of patients who spoke to the BBC about problems with their blephs had been to the company's clinics - but we do not know how many complications in total have occurred at Faceland. Nikita, who went for her bleph in November 2025, says she did not realise how invasive the procedure would be, believing it to be like "getting your lips or Botox done", she says. She was injected with local anaesthetic, but when the doctor began cutting delicate eyelid skin, she felt pain she had never experienced before. "I went into shell shock, it was horrible," Nikita says. "When she was stitching me I could feel the needle going through my skin." Nikita's eye before the bleph (L) and six days after the surgery (R) Faceland says all patients have consultations and sign consent forms before procedures, to ensure they are "well informed and well prepared". It added that Nikita's doctor had said Nikita was "very anxious and uncertain" during her procedure "which can influence the perception of pain". Within hours, a "traumatised" Nikita was boarding a plane home. Flying on the same day of surgery is not advised by medical experts as well as Faceland, but she saw lots of people doing it on social media. "I was struggling to see," says Nikita, "if I looked up, my stitches would bleed so it was like I was crying blood." She really regrets flying on the same day as her surgery and advises others not to. In the past three years, videos about blephs posted by UK social media accounts on four leading platforms were viewed nearly 150 million times, BBC analysis has found. This figure is five times greater than the previous three years. Many people report positive results in their posts, and a lot have been treated at Faceland. One woman told us her droopy eyelids had been restricting her vision and causing her headaches. She was not eligible for NHS treatment and could not afford to go private in the UK, but now she says, after going to Faceland, her issues have been resolved. The company's website claims it is changing the market by focusing on "affordable, accessible and high quality care". Treatments are carried out by accredited medical doctors who receive internal training by Faceland in surgical procedures, it says. Surgeons in the UK told us upper eyelid surgery typically takes about three hours, including preparation, surgery and post-operation care. But Faceland patients we have spoken to say they spent less than an hour at the clinics. Faceland says allowing practitioners to perform a higher volume of treatments helps significantly lower costs. Eight days after her Faceland bleph surgery, Laura, not her real name, made her first of four visits to A&E because her eyelid wounds had reopened. Her procedure at the company's Amsterdam clinic in June had seemingly gone smoothly, but problems began when she took her stitches out back home in the UK, something many patients do when they have treatment abroad. The crescent shaped cuts above her eyes which had been held together by the stitches came apart, exposing raw, red wounds which became infected. This should hardly ever happen if a practitioner has been properly trained, UK surgeons told us. The first time this happened, Laura, who is in her early 40s, says she called Faceland's emergency helpline several times, but could not get through. Desperate, she rushed to A&E. "When I closed my eyes for too long the tension would cause my wounds to open up again," she says. "I was scared to go to sleep and was in constant agony." Laura's eye before treatment (L) and eight days after her surgery (R) In the days after, Laura was communicating with her doctor from Faceland and, on several occasions, she offered to fly back for assessment. "I was crying, literally begging: 'You can't leave me like this'," she says. But Faceland told her the best course of action was seeking treatment local to her. Laura was referred to an NHS eye specialist who said "excessive skin" had been removed. How did Laura feel about the NHS picking up the cost of fixing her cheap surgery? "I feel guilty... People will think 'it's your own fault', but I would never have gone had I known what could happen." Laura says if she closed her eyes the tension would open up the wounds in her eyelids Faceland says it cannot comment in detail about Laura's case because she is pursuing legal action against the company. As a goodwill gesture an independent complaints committee that works with Faceland offered Laura €175 (£150), which she has rejected. UK surgeons tell us that, when they have seen patients with blepharoplasty complications over the past 12 months, those people have, in most cases, been treated abroad. The most common issue following overseas procedures has been people not being able to close their eyes properly, according to a survey for the BBC, to which 63 members of the British Oculoplastic Surgery Society (Bopss) in the UK and Ireland responded. A woman in her early 30s who didn't want to be identified. Her eye pictured three weeks after surgery (L) and about six weeks after the surgery (R) "Removing too much skin from the eyelid is dangerous because it leaves the eye exposed to the elements," explains consultant ocuplastic surgeon, Colin Vize, who is on the Bopss executive committee. "Correction can be difficult and expensive." He likens eyelids to "a pair of curtains". When you open them there needs to be a pleat, so when you close them there is enough skin to cover the eyeball. Other issues from overseas procedures reported by the Bopss members include scarring, uneven eyes and wounds opening up. Surgeons say they also saw patients with complications after having been treated by unregistered UK practitioners, including blepharoplasties that had been carried out in living rooms. On Christmas Day 2024, Caryn Harte woke up struggling to see. It was days after her bleph surgery at Faceland's Amsterdam clinic, her swollen left eye was weeping blood, and the wounds above both eyes had started to open. "I was terrified I was going to lose my sight over a bit of excess skin," she says. Caryn went straight to A&E, seeing no point in calling Faceland because it was too far away. Doctors later reassured her she would keep her vision, but her face was badly infected. She was prescribed antibiotics and required hospital check-ups. Caryn before the eyelid surgery (L) and 20 days after (R) The BBC has seen emails that show Caryn contacted Faceland twice, to report what had happened, and that she received a short reply 12 days later. A few further emails followed, but Caryn says she has not heard from the company since. Faceland maintains it "did not leave her without support or follow-up during the aftercare process". It says it is sorry if patients felt insufficiently supported by its teams or experienced complications. Like Caryn, Laura and Nikita, patients we have spoken to who have had cheap eyelid surgery abroad say limited aftercare is their biggest complaint. "Aftercare for the typical bleph should be available to a patient 24/7," says Vize. "If your surgeon is hundreds of miles away, the ability to provide care with a sense of immediacy is impossible." He also warns that patients should be aware that in some cases lower costs may mean lower standards. A week after her surgery, Nikita removed her own stitches. She worked out what to do by watching TikTok videos. "It makes you feel weak, like you're pulling something out of your skin," she says. Faceland says patients are advised to consult its doctors about when to remove their stitches and are given information on how to do so. Nikita says she did not receive an aftercare pack or instructions. Nikita as she is now The company also says patients can come back to a Faceland clinic to have stitches removed, but no-one we spoke to had done that. Patients removing their own stitches is "a recipe for disaster", according to Vize, who says stitches should be taken out by a surgeon or a nurse to reduce the infection risk and the chance of wounds splitting open. Nikita is mostly happy with her results, aside from a small scar, but she wants other people to learn from her experiences and fully understand the risks. "If I'd had the money or if I hadn't listened to the spin on TikTok, I probably would have gone somewhere closer to home and not rushed into it," she says. Nearly two years on, Caryn still has issues with her left eye, including some blurry vision and scarring. Meanwhile, Laura fears she may have scars above both of her eyes for life. "I tried to fix a problem that didn't really need fixing, and I've come back with a bigger problem that I need surgery for, and I can't afford that," she says. "It's pretty devastating." Have you had a similar experience, or have you been affected by similar issues? Sign up for our morning newsletterand get BBC News in your inbox.

Headline: Why Australia chose the world's biggest political stage to reveal OpenAI hack
Body: This video can not be played  Australia made a dramatic revelation on Wednesday during the United Nations General Assembly. Rogue AI agents hadhacked one of its government bodies- the first known incident of its kind in the world. Private data, but not sensitive information, was taken from Medicare, Australia's universal healthcare scheme. The breach happened in June, but OpenAI says it only became aware of it in August - and then took until 10 September to alert Australia's government, by sending an email to an address used by researchers and academics to alert authorities to concerns of vulnerabilities. While worrying, the timing of the incident is somewhat of a gift for Australia. A middle power that doesn't usually get as much of a platform as its influential allies, the country wants to be seen as punching above its weight on one of the most defining issues of our time - big tech regulation. In the past year alone, it has implemented the world's strictestsocial media ban, announced what it says are the world'sstrongest algorithm controls, floated the possibility of "world-leading"limits on smart glasses, and is now the first government to confront AI firms over a rogue attack on its data. The Australian prime minister says he'd had a "frank" discussion with OpenAI CEO Sam Altman about the breach It's entirely possible other governments have been the victim of rogue AI agents. Former Australian government cybersecurity adviser Alastair MacGibbon told the BBC he'd heard whispers that several others have been notified of similar recent breaches by OpenAI agents. "Some have chosen to not be public – that's every government's choice on how it wants to handle these things," he said. "The [Australian] government chose a time to release this to gain maximum publicity which is their wont to do." Revealing a data breach can of course be a risky strategy for governments - it leaves them vulnerable to criticism that their security systems aren't up to scratch. But the fact that no sensitive information was leaked put Australia in a stronger position to use the incident. "Nobody has died," says the University of Queensland's associate professor Michael Noetel, who studies AI risks. "This is another canary in the coal mine. This sort of loss-of-control incident, even though it's minor now, is what CEOs are worried about getting worse over time." Though Australia has made a name for itself by taking a stand against social media companies, taking up the AI mantle now is another way for Australia to rein in big tech, says Tama Leaver, professor of internet studies at Curtin University in Perth. "It's impossible to say for sure, but it seems incredibly likely that this was very carefully planned." All smiles in their selfie but Trump doesn't agree with the Australian prime minister's approach to AI The fact that leaders were all together in New York this week has probably helped. Albanese says he had a "frank" discussion with OpenAI CEO Sam Altman to express Australia's "extreme concern" about what happened. Altman acknowledged "issues with protocols" at OpenAI, he said. The Australian leader also posed with Donald Trump for a selfie - and the two may have had face-to-face talks. But Australia risks the ire of the US president, who wants to encourage AI, "not rein it in", and evenrename it "super intelligence". Earlier this week, Albanese had to deflect criticism from the Trump administration over his government's proposal to give users the ability to opt out of social media algorithms. The US said it amounted to "censorship of protected speech". US criticises Australia's proposed algorithm opt-out laws as 'censorship' Australia to double maximum penalty for platforms in breach of social media ban Back home,Australia's very own eSafety commissionis currently arming itself with lawyers, preparing to take on social media platforms objecting to its social media law for under 16s. Australia isn't popular with big tech. But its bold policies on social media and internet safety have been largely supported among Australians themselves, especially parents. The government is taking advantage of the hack to position itself as a leader on one of the biggest talking points of our time. And it's wasting no time in using the incident to advance the country's broader crusade. Within hours of the announcement, Communications Minister Anika Wells told reporters: "This is an example of an unregulated industry where big tech clearly feels like they can do whatever they like, and that's not going to wash here in Australia." Headline: Jay-Z rape accuser says her allegation was false
Body: Jay-Z, pictured at the Met Gala in May 2026, previously hit out at the "frivolous, fictitious and appalling allegations" A woman who accused Jay-Z of raping her when she was 13 has formally said her allegation was untrue. The unnamed woman filed a lawsuit in 2024 claiming she had been drugged and raped by Jay-Z, real name Shawn Carter, and Sean "Diddy" Combs at a party after the MTV Video Music Awards in 2000. The stars denied the allegation and she dropped the lawsuit last year. Carter then sued her and her lawyers. In a statement filed in that case on Thursday, she wrote: "Shawn 'Jay-Z' Carter never raped me. I have never met or spoken to Mr. Carter. Mr. Carter never engaged in any inappropriate conduct toward me whatsoever." The woman, known in court documents by the pseudonym Jane Doe, also said: "My claims that Mr Carter and Mr Combs raped me while a third celebrity, [name redacted] watched are false. There is no truth to any of my claims against Mr Carter. "I understand my false accusations have caused Mr Carter immense pain, suffering, and damage that can never be fully undone." Carter had vehemently denied the accusations, saying they were a "blackmail attempt" and describing them as "frivolous, fictitious and appalling allegations". When the accuser dropped her case in February 2025, the rapper, who is married to singer Beyoncé, said: "The trauma that my wife, my children, loved ones and I have endured can never be dismissed." The woman, from Alabama, has now been removed from Carter's lawsuit. She said she had not received any money from the rap superstar or anyone acting on his behalf, and had not been paid to make her latest declaration. The rapper is still suing the woman's former lawyers, led by Tony Buzbee. In a statement toRolling Stone,external, which first reported Jane Doe's new declaration, Buzbee said he had not seen it. He said: "We have multiple lawyers (at least four) who dealt with Ms Doe long before she met me. She gave the exact same story to each. If for some reason now she is claiming she lied to us and the court, that's new information." When Carter filed his lawsuit against the woman and her lawyers in February 2025, Buzbee claimed at the time that Carter's investigators had "repeatedly harassed, threatened and harangued this poor woman for weeks, trying to intimidate her and make her recant her story". In her new declaration, the woman said: "I never received any threat from Mr Carter or anyone acting on his behalf." Setting out the events that led to her allegation, the woman said she saw an advert on Facebook in September or October 2024 looking for people who might have sexual assault claims against Combs. "The ad triggered memories of being raped when I was 13 years old," she said. She was contacted by a law firm but was not provided with a draft of the lawsuit containing her allegations and did not authorise it before it was filed in October 2024, she said. She also said Buzbee and other lawyers acting on her behalf filed it "without conducting any independent investigation, background inquiry, or due diligence, and without obtaining any corroboration of the allegations". She said: "The October Complaint alleges that Mr Carter and Mr Combs raped me when I was a minor while an unnamed celebrity watched. As discussed above, these allegations were false." Buzbee also represents numerous other people who have made allegations against Combs. Combs denied Jane Doe's claims, which his lawyer described at the time as one of a number of civil cases "pushed forward by an attorney more focused on media headlines than legal merit". The BBC has contacted Buzbee for comment. In July 2025, Combs was convicted by a criminal court on prostitution-related charges involving his two ex-girlfriends, and is currently serving a four-year prison sentence. Headline: Killer Christa Pike is to be executed within days, but her defence say she's a victim too
Body: Christa Pike's lawyers have filed a clemency petition seeking to commute her sentence ahead of the 30 September execution date Ashlee Sellars last heard from her friend Christa Pike earlier this week, when Pike texted her from her cell on death row as she prepares to be killed by lethal injection by the US state of Tennessee. Pike told Sellars she does not want any of her loved ones to be present on Wednesday when she is executed. "She doesn't want us to experience that," Sellars says. Sellars finds it hard to reconcile this woman, whom she has only known to be kind and protective, with the person who committed a heinous crime 31 years ago. Pike, now 50, was 18 when she and her boyfriend at the time, Tadaryl Shipp, beat, tortured and murdered Colleen Slemmer, a 19-year-old they met at a job training camp for troubled teens. The murder created a media frenzy in Knoxville, Tennessee in 1995 when Colleen was found with a pentagram, a symbol of Satanic ritual, carved into her chest. Pike had accused Colleen of insulting her and trying to steal her boyfriend. Two other residents at the camp later testified that Pike had bragged about the murder before and after, and showed them a piece of Colleen's skull. A year later she was sentenced to death, while Shipp - who was 17 at the time - was given a life sentence with the possibility of parole. Now, after years of failed appeals, Pike's execution has been set for Wednesday. If it goes ahead, she will be the first woman put to death in Tennessee in more than 200 years. Only 18 women have been executed in the US since the 1970s, compared to 1,663 men. Colleen's mother has said she wants Pike's execution to happen so that her daughter "finally can be resting". Student Colleen Slemmer was tortured and brutally killed in the 1995 murder But Pike's lawyers, who filed a 226-page clemency petition, are still hoping for a last-minute reprieve, and UN human rights expertshave also called for the execution to be stopped.,external Pike has a documented history of childhood sexual abuse, abandonment and neglect. Her lawyers believe that if she was found guilty of the same crime today as a teenager she would not receive a death sentence. In the years since her sentencing, her defence team have uncovered details about her childhood that they say the jury never had the chance to consider. "It is mind-boggling that they did not present any of her history of abuse and rape, even though they knew about it," says Sandra Babcock, an expert in gender and the death penalty at Cornell Law School, who has worked on Pike's defence. "Her case is so uniquely compelling, not just because of her really incomprehensible history of sexual violence but the combination of that with her youth and her mental illness." Christa Pike suffered neglect and was abused by her parents In 1995, forensic psychologist Dr Diana McCoy was hired by Pike's defence team and found she was severely neglected by both of her parents. McCoy's report found Pike was physically and sexually abused by several of her mother's husbands and boyfriends, and raped several times, once when she was 11 and again aged 17. Later it was discovered that she was repeatedly raped as a toddler by her grandmother's boyfriend. McCoy said Pike's mother didn't believe her that these rapes happened. But Pike's trial lawyer did not put McCoy on the stand or call many of the witnesses she recommended. These details emerged more than a decade later in a court hearing reviewing her case, when a new team of lawyers claimed ineffective assistance of counsel, a claim that was denied by the judge. In 2021 Pike was diagnosed with bipolar disorder in prison and has been medicated since. Later, another forensic psychologist working for Pike's defence, Dr Bethany Brand, who assessed Pike in 2023, said her case was extremely rare because she was abused by so many people who should have protected her. "Her childhood was replete with physical, sexual, and emotional abuse. She was sexually violated by a number of men, starting before she was school age," she says. Brand says Pike had untreated manic episodes due to bipolar disorder and untreated PTSD. "Both of those things together absolutely influenced how threatened she felt by the girl she ended up killing and her lack of emotional control in that situation." Babcock adds: "If they let her be executed, then what it tells us is that the death penalty in this country is just a joke. It's not for the worst of the worst. It is for the people who receive the worst legal representation and who are the most damaged and vulnerable." Pike, pictured as a teenager, killed Slemmer in January 1995 after telling a friend she "just felt mean that day", court documents say Last year, Tennessee's Supreme Court ruled Pike had not shown circumstances that would justify commuting her sentence. Her appeals process had been exhausted and a date was set for her execution. A federal appeals court had earlier ruled that the jury had already heard about her difficult childhood during testimony from her mother, father, and aunt during her trial. And that new evidence of bipolar disorder, PTSD, and brain damage "mostly repeated" what the jury had heard and would not have changed the verdict. The row has some parallels with the high-profile case of murderer Lisa Montgomery, whose lawyers also argued she was a mentally ill victim of abuse who deserved mercy. Montgomery's legal challenges failed to commute her sentence, and shewas executed by lethal injection in Indiana in 2021. Unless she is granted clemency by Tennessee Governor Bill Lee, Pike will be executed on 30 September. That decision is unlikely to come until the last moment, and Lee has never granted clemency in a death penalty case before. The Tennessee Supreme Court this week denied Pike's request to halt the execution. Her counsel say they have been discussing next steps. On her execution day, Pike has requested an all-female team. She says being held down by a group of men will exacerbate her trauma. The state of Tennessee has said the goal is that female guards will transfer Pike to the prison where she will be executed but hasn't guaranteed it. Colleen's mother May Martinez supports Christa's execution. "She did the crime. I think she should pay for it," she said on Knoxville TV station WBIR in 2021, and told the BBC this week she still stands by those comments. Pike should suffer before she dies, Martinez told WBIR. "I would feel better that she felt the same pain that Colleen did." May Martinez, mother of Colleen Slemmer, and a retired Knoxville Police department detective outside a courtroom for a post-conviction hearing in 2006 "My heart breaks every single day because I keep reliving it and reliving it, and I can't no more, and I want this to happen before I die," she added. "There's not a day goes by that I don't think about Colleen or how she died and how rough it was. I just want Christa down so I can end it, relieve my daughter, so she finally can be resting." The Justice Coalition, a victims' rights advocacy group, has raised money to help Martinez travel to Tennessee to watch the execution. The group's executive director, Robert Bracewell, said this sentence was determined by a jury of Pike's peers and it is what Colleen's family want. "We stand firm with the family that on the 30 September her execution ought to proceed." Ashlee Sellars grapples with two seemingly conflicting beliefs: that Colleen's mother has a right to feel justice has been served and that everyone, including her friend Christa, deserves a chance at redemption. "When I think about reconciling who you see on TV or the horrible tragedy that happened with Colleen, the only thing that makes sense to me is around mental health and trauma and the way that people process stuff in a moment when they don't have the things that they need," Sellars says. "These horrible things happen in your youth and then those traumas moved through you, in our community, and you cause harm to somebody else." Sellars met Pike in prison while serving a 25-year sentence for her involvement in a robbery-murder. They spoke to each other through the meal flaps in their doors on the high security unit. Now, Sellars works as an advocate for justice reform and victims of crime. "People want to know that everyone's life matters, right? They want to know that Colleen's life mattered," she says. "Christa in this moment, I think she is fighting much more for her life to matter than she is to actually live." Headline: How the bare nails trend became a class issue
Body: In recent months, Paloma Buddemeier has watched a stream of people walk into her nail salon with the goal of looking as if they'd never been there at all. "It's crazy," the owner of Wumman Spa in London says. These customers still get their nails filed, buffed, and trimmed. "You still do the cuticle, you do the soaking and hydrate everything," says Buddemeier, "but you just put no polish on." Driving this, she says, is a viral craze for bare-looking nails. In recent months, artsy shots of glossy naked nails have been flooding social media and taking over fashion runways and red carpets, which some are viewing as the latest symbol of "quiet luxury". But critics argue the bare nails trend actually says something about class, the hamster wheel of beauty standards, and who gets to define what is considered tasteful. Paloma Buddemeier has seen a shift in what customers are looking for at her London nail salon Nail art's historical and creative roots are linked back to black, Latino, and Asian communities and the suggestion that bare nails are now a sign of high status could stigmatise bold manicures, they say. "That trend really promotes blankness and this kind of sameness and erasure of culture and identity that is so important to black and brown communities," beauty journalist Kristina Rodulfo tells the BBC. "They are often called elegant or tasteful, and these are often usually euphemisms that perpetuate white supremacist standards of beauty." For some, though, the choice is less about a dislike of bold nails and more about simplifying their routine. Some converts say they're ditching polish as a way of rebelling against an entrenched female beauty standard or to save time and money. Others just love the look. Then, there are some women who've long left their nails alone, amused to find their routine – or lack thereof – suddenly in vogue. For years, Irish TV presenter Angela Scanlon marched herself to a nail salon every fortnight, a routine that started when she was living in New York in the 2000s. There, she says, manicures were so universal they felt like a uniform. But it soon became a chore. Scanlon would have everything from thin, shiny shellac to sturdier "Builder In A Bottle" gel manicures layered onto her nails every other week without fail. "It wasn't like I was in my head going: 'I must go because Dave from Hull is going to be disgusted if I'm on This Morning next week without a full set'," the Radio 2 presenter says. "I just added it to the list of things that we must do... in the way you would wash your hair." Eventually, in a moment of clarity, Scanlon decided to stop going, in a bid to free up time and mental bandwidth. "I heard myself saying to people: 'Ugh, my god, I have to go and get my nails done.' "And I thought: 'I probably don't need to do this anymore'." Scanlon's posts about her decision to ditch the continuous manicure blew up on Substack and Instagram earlier this year. She seemed to have tapped into a vein.  Angela Scanlon recently decided to abandon her manicure habit Simple nails were in the spotlight at New York Fashion Week in February, with Marc Jacobs among those sending his models out polish-less, though some fashionistas argue this is not new. But beauty magazines have declared "All The Cool Girls Are Quietly Quitting Manicures,external", that "Bare Nails Are the New Status Symbol,external" of "Polished Women" and that "Manicures Are No Longer Classy,external". And there's a never-ending stream of posts on Insta and TikTok promoting shiny, natural-looking nails, and detailing how you can get them yourself. The look has become so hyped some have gone full circle, booking in salon appointments to mimic it. At the Wumman Spa nail salon, some of Buddemeier's clients sit in the chair for hours, as nail artists build them hyper-realistic fake nails in sheer, glossy neutrals, à la Zoe Kravitz and Zendaya. Londoner Khadija says she was once a fan of elaborate nail art but pivoted to bare nails earlier this year. "It's just really chic. And I love less is more, I love minimalism... less consumerism and just self-care things that you could probably do at home." Reluctantly joining the bandwagon thanks to the rising cost of living is her friend Emmanuella. "It's just too expensive now," she says. "I think getting [your] nails done is tacky now, because who's got an hour to waste?" one 25-year-old tells the BBC, adding, "also, I lift weights in the gym, so I don't want to snap a nail and waste money." But there are those who think the trend - or the way it's being discussed by some - belies something more sinister. Manicures have been whispering messages about the wearer's position in society for as long as they have existed, according to fashion journalist Suzanne E. Shapiro. "Women's bodies - and sense of self-presentation - have always held huge political and cultural significance," Shapiro, who wrote Nails: The Story of The Modern Manicure, tells the BBC. Even back in 13th century Imperial China, the lengthy talons grown by nobility and the delicately carved brass nail shields which usually guarded them were a symbol of a life unmarred by manual labour. A single layer of the rose-tinted waxy salves which were popular in the 1800s was a sign of vigour and health, but two layers - in an era when cosmetics and artificial beauty were tied to virtue - was the mark of a vain or "loose" woman. And the red at-home nail lacquer, released by Revlon in the early 1930s, was a badge of honour for modern women rebelling against that kind of oppressive judgement. But it was women of colour who really made manicures an accessible and fashionable form of self-expression, historians say. Entertainer Josephine Baker, disco icons Diana Ross and Donna Summer, and Olympic gold-medal-winning sprinter Florence Griffith-Joyner - whose dramatic acrylic sets often distracted headline writers from her record-setting performances - have all pioneered nail art. Florence Griffith-Joyner shows off her medal at the 1988 Olympics in Seoul "These were times that it was hard for black women to be able to express themselves," celebrity nail artist Celeste Hampton told the BBC. "[Nail art] allowed black women to express our form of softness, our form of femininity, our form of beauty." And when waves of Vietnamese refugees gave rise to the nail bar in the 1970s, professional manicures were no longer the preserve of the rich. But, like many luxuries, as they became more popular and more accessible to the masses, the wealthy began pivoting – a textbook example of behaviour known as "counter signalling", Rudolfo says. "The same way that logo bags are considered gauche or quiet luxury is more aspirational, bare nails are considered the trend now. "The examples are almost always white women or celebrities... [and] they'll often conflate class and taste with that bareness." Others point out bare nails often demand their own time-consuming and costly routine. "The irony in all this is these natural nails are not natural either," Shapiro says. "They also require a lot of grooming and sometimes pretty premiere services." Few would argue there aren't valid feminist questions for the beauty industry to answer, around unrealistic standards for example, but the largely female-run nail sector also feels empowering for many women. "I feel like nail care has very much had a 'for women, by women' sort of ethos around it," Shapiro says. "The first salon opened in New York City was owned by a woman, and she was a remarkably independent one... a lot of the first entrepreneurs offering product lines, opening salons were women." Hampton admits she's saddened by the way trends have been – and continue to be - weaponised. "We're taking the fun out of nails... Anyone should be able to wear what they like - nail polish or bare nails," she says. "Why is there an argument? Why is there beef?" Scanlon too is a little baffled. "For me, it's like, just stop judging ourselves and everybody else," she says. "Some people like to have the nails done, some people don't. "I suppose the question that I was posing was, is it doing anything for you? "The truth of it is: it's not that deep." Supermarket skincare dupes could save you hundreds. Headline: US criticises Australia's proposed algorithm opt-out laws as 'censorship'
Body: This video can not be played "Good to have choice": Australians on opting-out of social media algorithms The US has criticised Australia's proposal to give users the ability to opt out of social media algorithms, saying it amounts to "censorship of protected speech". Under Australia's draft digital duty of care laws, tech firms risk hefty fines if they fail to give users the option to turn off algorithms in a bid to protect them from harmful content. In a rare submission to the proposed laws, the US embassy in Canberra said it had "serious concerns" and allowing the government to "enforce vague definitions of 'harm'" would lead to "viewpoint-based censorship". Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said the legislation was not about giving governments control but giving it back to individuals. "We ask that Australia clarify how exactly 'harm' and 'risks' shall be determined... ensuring these definitions do not encroach on protected speech," the US said in its submission. The US also claimed that theproposed lawsmay risk "reducing the reach of independent journalists or other voices whose content touches on sensitive or controversial topics" if tech firms had to "pre-emptively demote" them. An opt-out option would "allow regulators to impose rigid, one-size-fits-all platform design requirements" on tech firms and this could affect users outside of Australia, it said. "Mandated platform design features, especially when applied to algorithms, may affect what users see, say, and hear not just in or from Australia, but globally." The US also called on Australia to address industry concerns that the "biases and preferences" of government officials do not "disadvantage independent or minority-viewpoint speech". Another worry was that the proposed laws could affect Australia's "reputation as a jurisdiction that enables innovation," the submission said. The criticism comes during Albanese's visit to the US to speak at the UN's General Assembly about his government's tech policies. On Tuesday, local time in New York, Albanese responded to the criticism and claims of the proposed laws being government overreach. "It's not about giving government control," he told the media in New York. "It's about giving people back control over what they receive on their devices." US President Donald Trump meanwhile usedhis speech at the UNto play down fears about AI, rejecting proposals for guardrails on it and arguing it should be renamed "super intelligence" as "the use of the word artificial makes it sound fake". This latest move by Australia to protect its online users from harm comes less than a year after the country introduced asocial media banfor children under 16 last December. Australians will be able to switch off social media algorithms under planned legislation Australia has banned social media for kids under 16. How does it work? Headline: Security lapses at Utah campus where Charlie Kirk was killed, review says
Body: Kirk's Utah Valley University event was held in a courtyard surrounded by tall buildings An independent review has pointed to a number of security shortcomings at the Utah campus where conservative activist Charlie Kirk was shot dead last year. The report said Utah Valley University (UVU) did not carry out a proper written security assessment nor prepare an event action plan, deferring key decision-making about the event to Kirk's conservative organisation Turning Point USA. It also said that Kirk's aides had insisted on a outdoor venue, overriding security concerns from campus officials, who then failed to properly assess the dangers. The 31-year-old activist had been addressing thousands of people in an Orem campus courtyard when he was shot from a nearby rooftop on 10 September 2025. Kirk's family said the report reinforced their concerns about how the event was managed. University officials had raised concerns in August 2025 about holding the event at a location surrounded by tall buildings and had suggested alternative venues, including some indoors,the report,external- published by UVU - says. "But a Turning Point representative insisted that Kirk speak at a campus courtyard because he had been there previously and the organisation was familiar with the location," it adds. Despite the "significant protective operations considerations", no line-of-sight assessment was documented in the planning process, the external consultants note. They also identified shortcomings in the co-ordination between university police and Kirk's private security team. A proposed meeting between the university's police chief and Turning Point security shortly before the event did not take place, the report said. The reviewers described the absence of a joint security briefing and walk-through as a missed opportunity to have identified risks, clarified responsibilities and considered additional security measures. However, the review concluded that no university employee or representative had acted in bad faith or shown "willful and wanton disregard" for anyone's safety. Charlie Kirk was addressing about 3,000 people when he was shot in the neck Kirk's family has previously accused the university of serious security failures and hasfiled a wrongful-death notice, a step that can precede legal action. The family's lawyer, Brett Parkinson, said the independent report released on Friday backed up the concerns raised by Kirk's loved ones. "The buck stopped with UVU leadership and law enforcement," Parkinson said in a statement to the Associated Press. "Justice for Charlie and his family requires true accountability for UVU's fatal shortcomings that day." When asked for comment on the findings, Turning Point USA referred to Parkinson's statement. The review makes numerous recommendations aimed at improving security for major campus events. UVU President Jon Anderson said the university must "learn from the findings of this review, and follow through on its recommendations". It has previously been reported that the campus police failed to conduct security procedures that are common practice at US high-profile events, including flying a drone to monitor rooftops or security screening like bag checks and metal detectors. Kirk had been debating UVU students about US mass shootings, as part of a series of events across different university campuses, when he was shot in the neck shortly after noon. He was rushed to hospital but later pronounced dead. His alleged killer, Tyler Robinson, haspleaded not guiltyto aggravated murder in connection with Kirk's death. Prosecutors are seeking the death penalty. Headline: When and how to see the Harvest Moon in 2026
Body: September's full Moon will be visible in UK skies this weekend, just days after the autumn equinox. Known as the Harvest Moon, it will reach its fullest point at 17:49 BST on Saturday 26 September. At that time it will still be below the horizon for much of the UK, but it will rise shortly afterwards and appear almost completely full throughout Saturday evening. It gets its name from being the full Moon closest to the autumn equinox, which this year took place on Wednesday. September's full Moon is traditionally associated with the harvest, because historically, the additional moonlight after sunset was useful to farmers gathering crops. The Royal Observatory Greenwich also lists the Corn Moon as another common name, reflecting the crops traditionally harvested around this time of year. However, it does not always fall in September and if October's full Moon is closer to the autumn equinox, it takes the title instead. Five night sky events to look out for this autumn Your pictures as equinox marks the start of astronomical autumn The 2025 Harvest Moon, seen here rising over the City of London, was on 7 October If you catch the Moon as it rises it may appear yellow, orange or even reddish. This is not a special feature of the Harvest Moon, but simply that when it lies low in the sky and is close to the horizon, its light has to travel through more of the Earth's atmosphere before reaching our eyes. More of the shorter blue wavelengths of light are scattered, allowing the yellows, oranges and reds to become more prominent. A pilot boat passes the rising Harvest Moon in 2021 off Swanpool Beach, Falmouth Many parts of the UK will have favourable conditions for viewing the Harvest Moon, with the longest clear spells expected in the south and east The current forecast suggests Saturday could bring some drier and brighter weather, particularly across parts of England. However, there is some cloud further west and rain for parts of Scotland and Northern Ireland by the evening. The best chance of clearer skies currently looks to be across some southern and eastern parts of the UK, while conditions are expected to be more changeable elsewhere. The exact times of the moonrise will vary across the UK but will be shortly after it  reaches its fullest point. Headline: Azerbaijan pardons Frenchman after EU lifts sanctions on Russian billionaire
Body: Martin Ryan was convicted of spying earlier this year - charges both he and France denied French national Martin Ryan has been pardoned and his release from prison ordered by Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev after he was jailed on charges of spying. His release came hours after the EU agreed to lift sanctions on two Russian billionaires, prompting anger from Ukraine. Diplomats had indicated that France had pushed for an end to restrictions on one of the businessmen, Alisher Usmanov. Ryan, who denied espionage, is one of 20 people pardoned by Aliyev. However, a second Frenchman, Anass Derraz, remains in jail in Azerbaijan accused of accepting a Russian bribe. It was not clear what had led to pressure for sanctions on Russian-Uzbek billionaire Usmanov to be lifted - the EU also agreed to take Russian-Israeli oligarch Mikhail Fridman off its sanctions list. Slovakia is understood to have pressed for Usmanov's name to removed initially, and France then backed the move, highlighting national security concerns. Both men have been under EU embargo since the Russian full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and until now EU sanctions on more than 3,000 "individuals and entities" have had to be renewed every six months. The latest agreement extends the sanctions on the others for three years. Usmanov was cited bythe EU in its 2022 listing,externalas having "particularly close ties" to Russia's President Vladimir Putin, and of having "supported materially or financially and benefited from Russian decision-makers responsible for the annexation of Crimea and the destabilisation of Ukraine". The metals and mining billionaire denied this characterisation of him. He has also been sanctioned by the UK and US governments. Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha bitterly criticised the EU decision to lift sanctions on the two men, complaining that Moscow was "celebrating, because it got what it wanted: a sense of impunity, the humiliation of the EU, and division among Europeans". Latvia had initially opposed the move, but decided to abstain, announcing instead that it would impose its own measures on the two men. Foreign Minister Baiba Braže said it was "dangerous and sends completely the wrong signal at a time when Russia's behaviour is becoming more aggressive".  Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs said later that France's President Emmanuel Macron had agreed to start talks on Latvia's "accession to the French nuclear deterrence initiative". French relations with Azerbaijan have been poor in recent years, largely because of France's close relations with neighbouring Armenia. However, in May, Macron discussed developing ties with Aliyev, who later spoke of a "new era" in their relations. Under Aliyev's decree on Wednesday, Ryan is one of 20 people including Azerbaijanis and Turks given a pardon. Detained in December 2023, he was handed a 10-year jail term last March for espionage, charges denied by the French government. Prosecutors alleged he had co-operated with employees of France's security services in Baku and gathered information about Azerbaijan's relations with Turkey, Iran and Pakistan, as well as companies linked to Russia and China. "I did not spy. I am not a spy, and during the court case I tried to prove this," Ryan had told the court. Another man he went on trial with, Azad Mamedli, was given 12 years in jail. Headline: Tories would prevent long-term jobless spending benefits on alcohol and cigarettes
Body: The Conservatives have promised to prevent long-term jobless benefit claimants from spending their welfare payments on alcohol, cigarettes and gambling. Under the party's proposals, claimants who have been unemployed for more than six months would see their Universal Credit cut by 30% if they have not previously paid enough into the system, despite being able to work. This reduced rate would be paid onto a "Back to Work" card, which would not allow cash withdrawals or spending on these items. The Tories said the proposals were designed to encourage people back into work and cut the soaring welfare bill but Labour branded the scheme "unworkable". A Labour Party spokesperson said: "The Conservatives had 14 years to fix our welfare system but they completely failed to make meaningful reforms. "Now they are proposing an unworkable new card scheme, which does nothing to tackle the numbers of people their system left signed off and written off." It's too easy to claim benefits in UK, Badenoch says Reform proposes £50bn welfare bill cut with changes to disability payments for millions The Tories estimate the proposed changes would move about 350,000 claimants onto the lower rate of Universal Credit, saving around £538m a year. Under the proposals, anyone fit to work would get six months on full benefits to find a job. Every two years a claimant has previously worked would buy an extra year on the full rate of Universal Credit - but those who have not contributed enough would drop to a new "subsistence allowance", worth 70% of the full rate. The party said this would protect "those with a strong employment record". For example, a 58-year-old who has worked since leaving school but has been made redundant would keep the full allowance up to state pension age. Claimants who are sick, disabled or already in work would also be exempt, with only those judged capable of work affected. The Tories said the reduced subsistence allowance would be loaded onto pre-paid card that would not allow cash withdrawals, and would "prevent spending" on alcohol, cigarettes, or gambling. The party is yet to detail how its proposal would work, but shadow welfare secretary Helen Whately said it would be "a version" of the pre-paid Aspen card issued to asylum seekers living in government-funded accommodation. These cards cannot be used to make contactless, telephone or internet payments, whilst asylum seekers whose applications have failed cannot withdraw cash. The Home Office confirmed last year it had tightened the list of permitted retailers where the cards can be used, after reports that some asylum seekers hadused the cards to gamblein sites such as slot machine arcades. Whately said the party would also look to learn from Australia, where certain claimants are issued with debit cards thatrestrict purchases,externalat shops selling alcohol, tobacco products or pornography. Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said the current system "where someone who can work chooses not to, and earns more benefits than someone in a job" was "unfair". "The best welfare is a well-paid job. So, we will be tough on those who exploit the system because the current system is unfair to workers, taxpayers and those who truly need support," she said. "Welfare must be a safety net for those who genuinely need it, not a lifestyle choice for those who can't be bothered." However, Helen Barnard, director of policy and research at the anti-poverty charity Trussell, said the proposals were "deeply misguided". "Universal Credit already falls well short of what people need to afford the essentials like food and heating, forcing people across the UK to the doors of food banks," she said. "We see people's health being damaged and their ability to find and maintain work undermined by the severe hardship so many are facing." Reform UK's economy spokesman, Robert Jenrick, said the Tories had left record numbers on long-term benefits and the proposals "won't even put a dent" in the welfare bill. The Conservatives have already pledged to scrap Personal Independence Payment, the main disability benefit in England, Wales and Northern Ireland, for "low-level" mental health conditions to help cut the welfare bill. The party also wants to make it harder to claim sickness benefits, which it said would mean more people are required to look for work. Spending on benefits has ballooned in recent years and is forecast to rise to £408.6bn in 2030/31, according to figures from the Department for Work and Pensions. Prime Minister Andy Burnham has insisted he will get the welfare bill down, for example by tackling the number of young people not in education, employment or training, but not through "crude cuts". Headline: Space museum launched by Britain's first astronaut
Body: Britain's first astronaut Helen Sharman officially opened the John Dulcamara Space Flight Museum at Grizedale Observatory A new space flight museum has been opened at a Lake District observatory. Britain's first astronaut Helen Sharman visited Grizedale Observatory and Planetarium on Friday to officially open the John Dulcamara Space Flight Museum. The collection was donated by private collector John Dulcamara and includes a piece of the command module from the 1969 Apollo 11 - the first manned mission to land on the moon. Sharman said the collection was "extraordinary". Grizedale Observatory near Ambleside, Cumbria, opened in May 2024, offering public access to telescopes, a planetarium and meteorite laboratory, as well as staging a dark skies festival and other events. The collection includes a piece of the command module from the 1969 Apollo 11 space flight Sharman, who became the first British person to visit space in 1991, said: "It's an extraordinary collection. We've got bits of Apollo 11, bits from the Russian space programme - it's just an amazing collection of artefacts from space flight history. "It tells its own story of space history, but also of the people that went and the items that were important to them. "For it to be on show now in this beautiful way, as part of Grizedale Observatory, what a coup for Cumbria." The museum contains a variety of pieces ranging from autographed photos and signatures of prominent people in space flight to parts of actual space craft. Dulcamara said he first started collecting the artefacts after he attended a shuttle launch in 1996 and kept the ticket. "That's what started my 30 year collection off," he said. "There's thousands of pieces on display, I hope people will come and have a look." Observatory director Gary Fildes said that the collection presented some "fascinating stories". "John asked whether we would be interested in keeping his collection here at the observatory so other people could have the chance to see it. He brought a few samples along and we knew we had to make it happen. "We thought: 'failure is not an option'!" During her visit, Sharman met with local schoolchildren to talk about her time aboard the Mir Space Station, where she carried out scientific experiments and observations of Earth. "To have Helen opening the museum is incredibly special," Fildes said. "What makes this particularly important to us is the opportunity for local children to meet Helen. "You simply don't know where an experience like that might lead." Follow BBC Cumbria onX,external,Facebook,external,NextdoorandInstagram,externaland listen toRadio Cumbria on BBC Sounds. Headline: Eriksen leaves Wolfsburg by mutual consent
Body: Christian Eriksen was fitted with an Implantable Cardioverter Defibrillator (ICD) in 2022 Christian Eriksen has left Wolfsburg by mutual consent, just over three months after collapsing during Denmark's friendly with Ukraine. The former Manchester United midfielder's contract with the German second-tier side had been scheduled to run until June 2027. Eriksen, 34, had previously suffered a cardiac arrest during Denmark's opening European Championship group match against Finland in Copenhagen in 2021. "At the moment, it is important for me to be close to my family in Denmark. I'm pleased that we were able to find a solution together," Eriksen said. "My time in Wolfsburg was marked by many highs and lows. I know that the club is now in good hands as it aims to make its way back to the Bundesliga, and I am convinced that a successful future lies ahead." Eriksen, who has not played since June, joined Wolfsburg as a free agent a year ago after leaving Manchester United and made 34 appearances for the club. The 151-cap international has previously played for Ajax, Tottenham, Inter Milan and Brentford. In a statement, Wolfsburg's managing director for sport, Dieter Hecking, said: "It was clear that the decision about his future had to be Christian's. "We wanted to give him that freedom in this particular situation and have now agreed to his request to terminate the contract. "Despite his short time here, he has left a lasting impression on his team-mates, our staff and the fans." Headline: Orange Order march row goes to heart of ongoing divisions in Northern Ireland
Body: Hundreds of protesters blocked the parade route after it was given clearance for the first time in almost 30 years History shows that when the politics of Northern Ireland are wrapped up in a street dispute, friction is seldom far away. Bitter rows in the Stormont chamber between unionists and nationalists happen almost every week, but ground-level arguments are rare these days. The Drumcree parade dispute in Portadown is a clash of political cultures. The Orange Order is a Protestant pro-British organisation. The area where it wants to walk is largely Catholic, and predominantly inhabited by pro-Irish nationalists. This dispute over a piece of road is not just a local problem. It has the potential to affect other parts of Northern Ireland and the power-sharing arrangements at Stormont. "What happens at Drumcree never stays at Drumcree," was how one retired politician put it. Follow live updates on this story What is the Garvaghy Road dispute all about? When the parade dispute first erupted into violence in the mid-1990s, the disorder spread to other places - and almost derailed the peace process. But while it was never fully resolved, the dispute faded over the next 30 years. Its sudden re-emergence has caught most people by surprise, including many politicians. What happened was that a legal case was brought to court over the dispute early this summer, re-opening the debate. The two largest parties in Northern Ireland, Sinn Féin and the Democratic Unionist Party (DUP), have been on opposite sides of the argument. Sinn Féin are firmly behind the residents. The DUP fully supports the Orange Order. They may be partners in the devolved government at Stormont, but when it comes to Drumcree they could not be further apart. As always in Northern Ireland, the historical context is important. Orangemen waited in the Drumcree church hall for the go-ahead to proceed down the Garvaghy Road Although there has been an uneasy calm in Portadown over the parading issue in recent years, the Orange Order regards the march as unfinished business. In 1998, it was banned from completing its Drumcree march - which includes the Garvaghy Road - and has been repeatedly refused permission to finish the route ever since. It has applied and been turned down more than 1,000 times in the past three decades. It says it is being denied a traditional walk which dates back to the early 1800s. A Parades Commission was set up in the late 1990s to adjudicate on marching disputes and, until now, it has consistently ruled against the route. The Orange Order's legal challenge to a ruling in June this year succeeded on procedural grounds. The order subsequently re-applied for permission to carry out the parade, albeit a scaled-back version with only 35 participants rather than 400 - and was successful. Nationalist residents on the Garvaghy Road were left shocked and angry. For them, the parade is triumphalist and unwelcome in the area. Rather than being about tradition, they see the parade as an act of supremacy and say it re-opens old community wounds. During a last-minute legal battle over the march, a judge appealed for all sides of the dispute to find common ground and come to an agreement. Nobody was surprised when that did not happen. Feelings are running high on the issue on all sides, including among the political parties. Relations in the power-sharing executive are now dangerously close to breaking point. There is a Stormont election next year which means parties tend to dig in, rather than search for compromises. The Drumcree dispute goes to the heart of the divisions which remain in Northern Ireland. Events of recent days are a reminder that the peace process is not over, it is ongoing - and there is still work to be done on the ground and at Stormont.

Headline: Analysis: Lib Dems leave conference buoyed by Davey's message
Body: This was a more sombre, more serious, Sir Ed Davey. The stunts - from falling off paddleboards to hurtling down rollercoasters – were scaled back at this year's Liberal Democrat party conference. "This is the fight of our lives," he repeatedly told his party. The focus, much like his conference speech last year, was on Reform UK. But the announcement he'd held back for his speech was aimed at Conservative-leaning voters: tax cuts worth billions. And not just for lower income earners, but for those in the higher 40% rate of tax too. Part of the announcement – raising the amount you can earn before you pay income tax altogether – was the same policy Davey's bête noire, Reform UK, announced at their conference a couple of weeks ago. The dividing line he drew was over how it was paid for. Nigel Farage's party would reduce spending on benefits to fund the tax cut. The Lib Dem leader said he would pay for it through the economic growth he believes could be gained by rejoining the EU's Single Market and a customs union. Lib Dems vow to end 'computer says no' economy to boost growth Lib Dems call for one-to-one midwife care during childbirth Davey promises tax cuts for millions if UK rejoins EU single market By putting the European Union at the heart of how he would fund his tax cut, the Lib Dems couldn't be drawing a starker contrast with the Brexit-backing Reform UK and a Conservative Party also committed to cutting welfare. But the plan is speculative. The Lib Dems insist a deal with the EU could be negotiated within a year if the party was in government after the next election. Plenty of economic experts, including the official budget forecaster the OBR, believe the UK's economy could grow if the UK was in the Single Market. But as recent political history teaches us, negotiating a deal with the European Union is often more difficult than party leaders hope. And basing a tax cut on potential future economic growth is a risky business. There is also uncertainty over whether the Lib Dems' sums add up. The independent  think tank, the Institute for Fiscal Studies, said the policy as set out in the press release would cost "much more" than the £17bn the Lib Dems have budgeted for. The party says the tax cut wouldn't come in until the fifth year after the next election. So even if the party got into power and successfully negotiated an EU deal, the tax cut could be eight years away. But the Lib Dem MPs I spoke to afterwards were less focused on these details than the message it sent to voters. Davey came into this conference facing criticism over his leadershipfrom some MPs in privateandothers in his party in publicworrying about the party's ambition and direction. For now those concerns have been dampened. "That was the speech a lot of us have been waiting for him to give," one Davey-sceptic MP told me afterwards. A small number are uncomfortable with the main policy from the party's conference being a tax cut that would most benefit the better off. One told me they would rather the focus had been wooing younger voters by tackling the amount graduates repay in student loans, an old bruise for the Lib Dems. But overall this speech, and this conference, was well received by the Lib Dem faithful. They are a party honing their messaging before the next general election. The strategy is primarily on those 27 seats where the Lib Dems came second in 2024. Most of them are held by the Conservatives and Davey's tax cuts are aimed at appealing to those voters. But already the attack from the Tories has been that the Lib Dems are "Labour's lapdog". That attack is in part because Davey has given his most explicit answer this week on not going into a coalition government with the Conservatives after the next general election. He's done the same for Reform UK. But he hasn't ruled out a pact with Labour. So that attack from the Conservatives will come again and again before the next election. But the Lib Dems leave their Brighton conference buoyed, with sights not just on retaining their record 72 seats won at the last election, but on winning some more. And then? "I've got no ceiling on our ambitions," Davey said this week. He has already served in government once, in coalition with David Cameron's Conservatives. His eyes are on another stint in office. Headline: Glasgow City Council pauses plan to fire and rehire 23,000 staff
Body: Unison members during a previous strike outside Glasgow City Chambers Glasgow City Council has agreed to pause plans to fire and rehire more than 23,000 members of staff. The decision follows online talks between the council and three trade unions, chaired by Deputy First Minister Jenny Gilruth. Negotiations between the council and the GMB, Unison and Unite unions will resume early next week to try to reach a new deal on pay. Letters which had been due to be sent to staff informing them of the fire and rehire plans will not be issued. The SNP-led council had threatened tosack thousands of members of staffand then rehire them on new contracts after negotiations with unions over equal pay proposals broke down. The talks were about the council's plans to replace a pay system found to discriminate against mostly women workers. The changes would see the majority of staff unaffected or better off, but they would cut pay for 11% of staff. Gilruth said the Scottish government did not support fire and rehire schemes and had urged the council and trade unions to get back around the negotiating table. She said: "Given the significance of this situation and the impact on staff, I wanted to bring all parties together to make clear that I expect negotiations between the council and unions to continue so that a collective agreement can be reached and bring an end to discriminatory pay practices. "My expectation is that all parties act in line with the principles of fair work and continue to exhaust all avenues for collective agreement." On behalf of unions Unite, Unison and GMB, the Scottish Trades Unions Congress said: "We are pleased at the lifting of the threat of fire and rehire and that meaningful negotiations will take place next week. "We also welcome the Scottish government's clear statement that the practice of fire and rehire' does not align with the principles and expected practice of fair work." Glasgow City Council to fire and rehire over 23,000 employees Hundreds of council workers face wages cut in end to equal pay row GMB organiser David Hume said the council had initially made the wrong decision - but welcomed its willingness to review and reverse it. "After seven years of hard negotiations, we believe the new structure is ready to be put before our members. They should now be allowed to decide and that should be done as a matter of urgency," he said. One Glasgow City Council worker had earlier described the situation as "heartbreaking". Joanne, a support for learning worker from Glasgow, said the local authority "had a cheek to say they care about their employees" after she read the council's message saying it was dismissing all staff. She was told two weeks ago that she would be one of the workers facing a pay cut under the new system, leaving her "distraught". She will lose about £300 per year. She said: "I came away from my work crying - really, really upset. I couldn't believe that after 25 years' service to Glasgow City Council, I am getting let down yet again." She continued: "I am working with the most vulnerable children in society. I would put it to Glasgow City Council: please come and do my job for one day - one day only. "It is so wrong, and I can't afford to lose money." Glasgow City Council is overhauling its pay and grading structure At a meeting last month, the council agreed to an overhaul of its pay and grading structure after eight years of negotiations. Thecouncil has previously paid over £770mto 19,000 claimants after it emerged that female workers in roles such as catering or cleaning were paid less than those in male-dominated areas such as refuse collection. The new system would see 63% of those affected gain financially, while 11% would have their wages reduced. It was calculated after a job evaluation programme looked at each role within the local authority. This saw staff being given questionnaires to fill out, and in some cases interviewed about their job. Are you a Glasgow City Council employee? How have you been affected by the fire-and-rehire decision? Each evaluation was based around 13 different factors. Categories included physical effort, mental skills, concentration and physical co-ordination. The job evaluation then provided a score for each role within the council, with those scores used to establish which pay grade - out of a possible 12 - each job should sit in. However, this has resulted in some roles being moved onto lower salaries than they were previously on, with the highest drop in wages expected to be around £11,500. The council had said on Thursday that every member of non-teaching staff would be issued with a letter of dismissal, including chief executive Susanne Millar, nursery staff and refuse collectors. They would then be offered new contracts, set to begin on 1 January. Changes to UK-wide employment law will come in effect on the same date. These changes will make dismissing an employee for refusing to accept contract changes automatically an unfair dismissal. Talks between the council and the GMB, Unison and Unite unions fell apart on Wednesday when Unison said it would not ballot its members on a proposed new pay offer. The council accused Unison of "betraying" members by not giving them the chance to vote on it, but the union's education convener Sylvia Haughey accused the council of using "bullying tactics". She toldBBC Radio Scotland Breakfast: "We haven't betrayed anyone, we certainly haven't betrayed our members. We are out fighting for our members. "We are fighting for the members who are... losing big financial amounts, whether its £200 or £12,000. "We have not walked away from anything. We are willing to speak to the council at any time." Glasgow City Council’s communications director, Colin Edgar, said it was a “hellish situation” that “almost no-one” wanted to be in. He acknowledged that staff would feel distressed and anxious, but promised that all those affected would be rehired without a break in their continuity of service. Council staff threaten legal action over contracts Fire and rehire move damaging for council - union Edgar said the council did not want to be in this situation, but it was a consequence of fixing an unlawful pay scheme. “Whenever any council does this exercise, there are people who gain and people who lose - in our case that’s about 11% of people who will earn less,” he said. Both the GMB and Unite unions were in favour of balloting their members over the proposed pay structure, and said they had secured an extra £110m to be added into the salary structure. However, Unison said the extra funding was for "assimilation and arrears", and would not help the staff facing wage cuts. It said the upcoming discussions must be "underpinned by increased funding". The GMB and Unite unions had both criticised the original decision to go ahead with fire and re-hire, with Unite calling it a "scandalous threat". The UK government's Scottish Secretary, Douglas Alexander, said had called for the council's readers to "get back around the table" and find a better way forward. Unite's Scottish secretary, Susan Fitzgerald, said: "Unite was crystal clear that the scandalous fire and rehire threat facing workers had to be lifted in order for meaningful talks to resume. "The immediate threat has now been lifted, and that it is a welcome development, but it should never have escalated to this unacceptable and highly regrettable stage."

Headline: Radio 2 presenter to take on 'greatest ever distance' in Children in Need challenge
Body: BBC Radio 2 host Owain Wyn Evans will ride through the UK's four nations Radio presenter Owain Wyn Evans will cycle through all four UK nations to raise money for BBC Children in Need. The Welsh host of BBC Radio 2's Early Breakfast Show will travel almost 400 miles, setting off from Glasgow and finishing in Cardiff. The five-day challenge will start on Monday, 9 November, and finish on Friday, 13 November - when the fundraiser will be broadcast. The only member of the annual TV fundraiser's hosting team for 2026 to be revealed so far is fellow Welsh presenter, One Show host Alex Jones. The BBC said Evans' challenge would be the "greatest ever distance" covered in a Radio 2 endeavour for the charity. Evans, who is originally from Ammanford, Carmarthenshire, said: "When I said yes to this challenge, I knew it would push me well outside my comfort zone. "It's going to be tough, demanding and probably a little daunting at times, but I'm ready to give it absolutely everything I've got." Alex Jones is among the presenting team for the BBC's flagship fundraiser He said fellow BBC presenters Sara Cox, Paddy McGuinness and Vernon Kay had previously achieved "extraordinary things" for Children in Need, adding: "I've got a lot to live up to." Sports scientist Prof Greg Whyte will be offering support to him throughout the journey. He previously helped Sara Cox when she jogged, walked and ran 135 miles through Northumberland, Durham, North Yorkshire and West Yorkshire. BBC Radio 2 boss Helen Thomas said: "Thank you to Owain for picking up the Pudsey backpack baton from Sara on behalf of the many thousands of children who will benefit." Headline: Mother of woman found hanging in tree shocked as police say body was staged
Body: Tasia Fortune, a 29-year-old mother of four, was found hanging from a tree in August Warning: This story contains distressing details The mother of a woman found hanging in a tree in Mississippi has spoken of her shock after authorities said they believed her daughter was dead before her body was placed at the allegedly "staged" crime scene. Tasia Fortune, a 29-year-old mother of four, was found hanging from a tree at an abandoned home in Jackson in August. The discovery sparked widespread fears in the majority-black city because of the state's deep history of racial violence and lynchings. But on Friday, police said that Fortune had been dead before her body was hanged from the tree. "I have more questions now than what I did before," her mother Christy Spivey told the BBC. The Jackson Police Department said that the medical examiner who conducted Fortune's post-mortem examination had determined that her death was a homicide and that "the scene andthe hanging were staged". Officials have not disclosed the exact cause of death or shared any potential motive behind the allegedly staged hanging. Three people have been arrested in the case, all of whom are black. "I was hoping to be more relieved," Spivey said, adding that the police had not specified how the three suspects were connected to her daughter - or why her death was allegedly staged in this way. "Still no cause of death, no date of death - nothing," she said. "What actually killed her?" Fortune's death left thelocal community on edge and lawmakers demanding federal probes. But the latest developments have created more confusion. Christy Spivey told the BBC she was upset at how the police had handled the investigation Spivey told the BBC that getting the update from the coroner that her daughter did not die by hanging initially gave her peace - at least her daughter did not die in such a gruesome manner, she thought. "When the police called me, I started crying and thanked them and felt a little more at peace than I had before," she said. "I just hope they've got the right person/people." When the latest details surrounding her death emerged this week, she said she was "starting to break down". Police told a court on Friday that Fortune's death was thought to be as a result of a drug-related dispute. A detective said Fortune may have been killed over allegations she stole drugs. Spivey rejected those allegations, but did acknowledge her daughter suffered from addiction. "Tasia has an addiction - had - an addiction problem. She was trying to get better," Spivey said. "If she still was doing drugs, which I'm sure she probably was, she still didn't deserve to be done like that. Nobody does." She said her daughter was homeless at the time of her death, but typically bounced around other people's homes. Her four sons, whose ages range from one to seven, are now living with a mix of family and friends. Two are in the process of being adopted.
