Headline: 'Make women feel seen': Why the Dutch have a new word for labia
Body: Shari Klein spoke at a recent march celebrating the new word Can you imagine seeing the words "shame lips" on your medical notes? The term, which can also be translated as "pubic lips", is the Dutch word for a women's body part. But, for some, it's just one of countless examples that are outdated and loaded with stigma. Last month, leading Dutch dictionary Dikke van Dale said it would include a new term for the labia, "vulvalippen" - in its upcoming online edition - alongside the traditional term "schaamlippen". European campaigners have long been calling for a rewrite of terms used to discuss women's bodies, sexuality and health. What unites them is the desire to move away from terms that are often seen as misogynistic or judgmental. "Language shapes how we see ourselves," says Shari Klein, one of the founders of the Schaamteloos campaign, which targets words that use "schaam" or "shame". "It's crucial people have a more neutral, anatomically correct word - not a word that links to shame, whether consciously or sub-consciously," she says. Calls to use vulvalippen aren't new but campaigners say inclusion in the dictionary may be a sign society is "finally ready for change". Esther Van der Valk, part of prominent Dutch feminist group Dolle Mina, says it's also about sex positivity and reducing body shaming. The campaign's next steps are to convince doctors and officials to use vulvalippen in leaflets and consultations. Signs used during a recent march in the Netherlands, the one on the left translates as "afterall there are no shame balls" Ton den Boon, editor of the dictionary, says adding vulvalippen is justified because it is becoming more established in the language and is being used more in the media, biology text books, medical leaflets and is even seen in veterinary medicine. But whether it will be adopted widely is yet to be seen. Other Dutch words, relevant to both men and women, could carry similar connotations - from "schaamhaar" (pubic or shame hair) or "schaambeen" (pubic or shame bone) to even "schaamluis" for pubic lice. However, critics say changing a word will not necessarily change people's lives. Language around birth should be less judgemental The campaign mirrors attempts in Germany, where in 2018 journalists Gunda Windmüller and Mithu Sanyal started a petition to change Schamlippen to "Vulvalippen". Windmüller says she was compelled to after a gynaecologist told her of the shame some women carry when discussing their bodies and having medical examinations. When writing her article, she realised she couldn't even mention anatomy without including the word shame. "Vulvalippen" has not yet been adopted by a German dictionary, but Windmüller has spotted it in conversations, school textbooks and women's magazines. Her hope is the Dutch move will ignite support closer to home. Similarly, in Sweden a new word for "hymen" was added in the academic dictionary after a 2009 campaign. The association for sexuality education (RFSU) felt traditional term "mödomshinna", which translates as maidenhood skin or virginity membrane, was anatomically inaccurate and did nothing to dispel myths around hymens and virginity. The new term "slidkrans" translates as vaginal corona - reflecting the fact the hymen is often folds of tissue in a ring, rather than a seal that breaks once. "With a new word we can challenge the myths that seek to control women's sexuality and freedom," Sonja Ghaderi of the RFSU says. Ghaderi says slidkrans is used particularly by healthcare professionals and in youth clinics but adds misinformation still exists emphasising the "need to change social constructs". Supporters took to the streets in the Netherlands to celebrate and publicise the new word In the UK, feminist podcast host Nicola Denson-Elliott started a petition to replace the word "hysterectomy" (surgical removal of the womb) with "uterectomy". She argues, as others have, that hysterectomy haslinguistic links with hysteria,external- once seen as a disease of emotional excess in women - and wants a more "anatomically correct term" not one "associated with emotion." The petition describes it as "medical misogyny", adding: "Women deserve terminology that respects them." Linguistics researcher Dr Beth Malory says any changes need to be researched first. "Will people understand uterectomy? Is simply saying removal of the womb better?" New words cannot be ambiguous, she says, it's important to look at the whole system so there is no confusion. Malory also studies language around pregnancy and loss. One phrase highlighted in her research is "incompetent cervix" used to describe the shortening of the cervix that can increase risks of pregnancy loss and early birth. Women told her it made them feel blamed for the medical issue. "Why do we need judgmental words like failure or incompetence?" says obstetricianDr Brooke Vandermolen,external. Even though they appear in medical textbooks, she tells me she's moved away from certain terms, including "failure to progress" - which describes labour not moving forward as expected. "Language is incredibly important and the words we choose can show recognition and make people feel validated and seen." In 2022, the Royal College of Midwives produced guidance offering alternative phrases. But Vandermolen says some traditional terms are still being used and still cause distress. "I hope this change in the Netherlands sparks more conversations here about how we speak about women's bodies. What we say can have a lasting impact." Headline: Rapper Macklemore announces 'Free Palestine' tour after Ed Sheeran fallout
Body: Macklemore performs at the Goldencoast Rap Festival in Corcelles-les-Monts, near Dijon, central-eastern France, on 30 August, 2026 Rapper Macklemore is launching a "Free Palestine" tour, days after being dropped from Ed Sheeran's Loop Tour following pro-Palestinian comments he made  onstage earlier this month. "So, as you all know, my schedule freed up a bit," he said upon announcing the tour on Thursday. The American artist - whose real name is Benjamin Haggerty - said proceeds from the tour, which launches in Dublin next month, will go to organisations supporting Palestinians. Macklemore's onstage comments and subsequent removal from the tour led Sheeran's support acts to drop out, while the British singer stressed that the decision to drop the rapperwas made by his promoter,not by himself. Everything we know about the Ed Sheeran and Macklemore controversy In a statement on Thursday, the rapper said that the last couple of weeks had shown him there had been "a collective awakening around Palestinian liberation, the power of billionaires that try to censor that call, and what we expect from artists right now". "What happened to me is bigger than one artist or one stage," he said. "When the billionaire class can decide which voices are allowed on stage and which ones are too dangerous to hear, everyone should be paying attention." Macklemore said he had spent the last week contacting artists who had used their platforms to stand in solidarity with the Palestinian people, regardless of the consequences. Due to how quickly the tour came together, several details were still being worked out, he added: "But this is a moment of momentum, and there is work to be done." Macklemore's new tour will begin in Dublin on 26 October followed by Paris on 29 October and London on 30 October. US dates will also be added, he said, with additional tickets going on sale next week. This video can not be played "I cannot hide how I feel anymore": Ed Sheeran addresses Macklemore row at show While performing as the opening act for Sheeran at a concert in early September in New Jersey, Macklemore said: "A big part of the reason why I wanted to do this tour in the first place is so that I could stand up in stadiums like this and say two words that are very, very dear to my heart: Free Palestine." The Thrift Shop rapper then performed a song dedicated to pro-Palestinian protesters at Columbia University. After he was taken off the tour on 14 September, Macklemore accused stadium owners of rallying together to push him out. He was also accused by billionaire stadium owner Robert Kraft of hate speech and antisemitic rhetoric surrounding Israel and Gaza. Sheeran early on said that the decision to drop Macklemore from his tour was made by concert promoter Messina Touring Group. His early remarksled to all of his support acts to drop out of the tour in solidarity, and fans to express frustration. Ticket prices for the tour plummeted as well. Sheeranaddressed the controversyhead-on during the start of his set in Philadelphia last week. He said he had made "mistakes" handling the fallout, apologising to fans and taking a stand on the Israel-Gaza conflict, which he said was "a humanitarian issue". He described the 7 October 2023 Hamas-led attacks as "horrific", and also called the situation in Gaza "unjustifiable and disproportionate". Headline: Mohamed Salah given six-month driving ban
Body: Former Liverpool player Mohamed Salah has been banned from driving for six months following the incident Former Liverpool footballer Mohamed Salah has been banned from driving for six months after his Rolls-Royce was clocked speeding. Salah failed to tell police who was at the wheel when the car was caught by a speed camera driving at 36mph (58 km/h) on a 30mph (48km/h) stretch of road in Wilmslow, Cheshire, on 27 March, according to court documents. The 34-year-old did not respond to the notice of the prosecution, brought by Cheshire Police, and did not enter a plea to the charge. He was handed a six-month driving ban and ordered to pay £1,044 in a hearing at Warrington Combined Court. A court spokeswoman said Salah was prosecuted under the Single Justice Procedure, which sees magistrates sit in private hearings, and was convicted of failing to give information relating to the identification of the driver of the Rolls-Royce. The speeding offence came days after the Egypt captain announced he would be leaving Liverpool following nine years with the team. Announcing his departure on 24 March, the club said he had "firmly established himself as one of the greatest players in Liverpool's history". He scored 257 goals in 442 appearances for Liverpool, before transferring to Turkish side Trabzonspor following the 2025-26 season. Headline: Horner a distraction for Ferrari says Vasseur
Body: Horner's remarks about Ferrari have been a distraction, Vasseur (right) says Christian Horner is proving a distraction for Ferrari by "looking for a job", team principal Frederic Vasseur says. Horner, dismissed as Red Bull team principal in July 2025, used an interview with the Times this week to say that Ferrari are the only Formula 1 team he would work for without being given a shareholding,describing it as "the dream",external. Vasseur outlined his frustration with Horner following Saturday's Azerbaijan Grand Prix - at which Charles Leclerc finished fourth and his Ferrari team-mate Lewis Hamilton was sixth. He said: "We are not working in the perfect serenity. "For me, first, but for everybody in the team, for the media, for 50% of the questions [to be] about this, it's a bit of a frustrating situation. "We are fighting for P3 [third place] in the championship, and at the end of the day, we are all speaking a lot about this, and even for the guys in the garage, to discuss about this, it's the best discussion that we can have. "But it is what it is, it's not in my hands. Mr Horner is looking for a job - that everybody knows - everywhere. But what can I do? Just try to do my best to push the team, to rise them to be motivated, focus on what is better today." After the race in Baku, Hamilton was asked by Sky Sports whether he was confident Ferrari were on a good path under Vasseur's leadership. The seven-time champion replied: "Yes." Vasseur was asked whether he was joking about Horner, and replied: "I was very serious." And asked whether he would consider working with Horner, he replied: "This you have to ask my assistant." That remark appears to be a reference to the circumstances surrounding Horner's departure from Red Bull in July 2025. Horner was accused of sexual harassment and coercive, controlling behaviour by a female employee. The allegation became public in February 2024 but the accusations were dismissed by Red Bull following two internal investigations. Horner wasfired from his role as chief executive officer and team principal by Red Bull after the 2025 British Grand Prix. That decision followed a tumultuous 18 months in the wake of the employee's allegations, during which a number of senior team figures left - including chief technical officer Adrian Newey - and there was a slump in form. Red Bull have never given a public explanation for Horner's dismissal. The two parties agreed on a settlement said by sources to be worth 60m euros (£51.5m). Ferrari entered this season hoping to be title contenders following the introduction of new chassis and engine rules in F1. But while their car was acknowledged as the best in the corners as the season began, their engine has lacked performance compared to those of Mercedes and Red Bull. This lack of power was exposed on the long straights of the Baku circuit, as Leclerc slipped back in the race after qualifying second. Vasseur said on Saturday: "With the situation that we are in the engine, we are losing one position per lap, and then we lose the path of the race. "Honestly we were surprised to be in the first row, because Baku is the most demanding in terms of engine, and was not expecting to do so. But we knew even starting from the first row that the opening laps, or in case of restarting safety car and so, it would be difficult. And it was." Asked whether he was still committed to his position at Ferrari, Vasseur said: "Motorsport is my life, it's my business. I'm trying to do my best. I'm there to do my job. I have the best job in the world, heh. But, it is like it is. We have still seven races to go, and I will push until the last corner." Ferrari have not won a world championship since 2008, and have rarely had a fully competitive car since then. Horner said in his interview: "Would I consider Ferrari? I mean, Ferrari is the biggest brand in Formula 1. It's the dream. And arguably it's the sleeping giant of Formula 1." Headline: U2 celebrate 50th anniversary at the school where they formed
Body: This video can not be played Watch: U2 return to school where everything started for their 50th anniversary Exactly 50 years after they formed, U2 returned to Dublin to play a gig at the school where they met. "We've escaped from the lab," declared Bono, as the quartet took to a stage in the playground. "How's the experiment working for you?" The pupils of Mount Temple Comprehensive may not have been born when U2 were the world’s biggest band, but they gave them a hero's welcome, waving signs that said, "I love U2", "It's a beautiful day - no school", and, "Bono, my mum says hi!" The group treated them to a career-spanning set that included hits like I Will Follow, Vertigo and With Or Without You, as well as their latest single, Silencio. As they played, teachers pulled down pupils who’d climbed on their classmates' shoulders, before getting swept up in the moment and dancing along themselves. As he looked out from the same stage where U2 made their debut in 1976, Bono became emotional. "Thanks for, er… Yeah... I didn't… Wow," said the frontman, temporarily lost for words. U2 were all pupils at Mount Temple Comprehensive School in the mid-1970s The band played their first gig at a school talent competition, covering Peter Frampton's Show Me The Way and Bye Bye Baby by the Bay City Rollers The band played seven songs at the end of the school day: I Will Follow, Vertigo, Beautiful Day, Out of Control, Silencio, One and With or Without You Pupils clamoured to meet the band, who have sold more than 175 million records worldwide The U2 story began in those same halls and corridors five decades ago, when 14-year-old Larry Mullen Jr pinned a handwritten note to the school noticeboard. "Drummer seeks musicians to form band." Auditions were held a couple of days later, on 25 September, 1976, in Larry's parents' kitchen. Among the hopeful "misfits", as their school-friend Frank Kearns called them, were Bono, The Edge and Adam Clayton – who arrived wearing a full-length Afghan coat. Initially called Feedback, and then The Hype, they conquered the world as U2, transforming themselves from a scrappy punk outfit into stadium-conquering rock titans, whose big ideas and big anthems attracted millions of admirers, and almost as many detractors. Speaking to BBC News, Mullen confessed the infamous wanted advert had been his father's idea all along. "I'd been playing on my own, in my house, and my dad was pretty frustrated," he says. "I wasn't very good at many things, and playing the drums was included in that. So I think he, out of frustration, said I should try and play with other people." "And unfortunately," adds Bono, "he got the three of us." The group honed their skills over dozens of gigs in the Dublin venue McGonagles Bono, then known as Paul Hewson, had actually been tempted to skip the audition. He was two years older, and concerned about looking out of place. "I wouldn't be hanging out with second years, and particularly really good-looking ones," he says. Eventually, his friend Reggie Manuel persuaded him to attend, even giving him a lift on his rickety old motorbike. "I can tell myself it was a Harley Davidson," the singer jokes, "but really it was a Yamaha DX100." The first band practice didn't exactly show promise. There was more talking than playing. Clayton, a bassist who couldn't play bass, was selected on account of having "the best hair". And Bono, who wanted to be the guitarist, didn't bring a guitar. "I was never any good with gear," he reflects. "Carrying it, unpacking it, that kind of thing." The quartet have remained friends since 1976, partly due to a decision to split all their earnings equally Even so, there were signs the band would attract an adoring legion of fans. Half-way through the rehearsal, a group of screaming girls tried to climb the garden wall. For Clayton, that was the moment that sealed the deal. "Larry already had a fan club, and we thought, 'Well, if he's got a fan club, that looks pretty good to us. Maybe if we hang out with this guy, it might stretch a little further'." Mullen, forever the band's stoic moral compass, was not impressed by the invasion. "As I recall, Larry Mullen took a hose to the fans," laughs Bono. "I don't know what possessed me," the drummer grimaces, while trying to insist the hosing  "was an act of kindness and love because it was a hot day". "They enjoyed it," he protests. "It was playful." Bono jumps in to save his friend's embarrassment…. Well, kind of. "It's been the story of our lives ever since. He doesn't even want to have fans, but we quite like them."  The 1992 Zoo TV Tour pushed the boundaries of what was possible in a stadium show, ushering in an era of video screens and multimedia backdrops From that kitchen in Rosemount Avenue, U2 became the world's biggest rock band. Anthems like With Or Without You, One and Beautiful Day have always sounded majestic yet personal; powered by The Edge's cascading guitar tone and Bono's lyrics which, for all their proselytising, remain grounded in a belief in humanity. They made a stylistic swerve in the 1990s, embracing electronics, dance music and irony on the albums Achtung Baby, Zooropa and Pop. Along the way, they reinvented stadium concerts with the Zoo TV tour, whose stage was crammed full of multimedia screens and satellite feeds, while Bono made nightly prank calls to the White House. The Edge, real name Dave Evans, puts their longevity down to a lack of formal training. "It's been a guiding light, in some ways, the limitations of the band," he explains. "We're in this place where, musically, we never know what's about to happen. It can fall apart or it can become something extraordinary. "And that's the beauty of U2.” Back on stage at Mount Temple, Bono paid tribute to his alma matter for allowing the band to flourish. The support of teachers allowed them to realise that “maybe all we needed was around us, just under our feet,” he said. And he dedicated the performance to school councillor Jack Heaslip, who later became a “travelling pastor” on the band’s tours, before his death from motor neurone disease in 2015. U2 then closed their set with an orchestral arrangement of One, assisted by students from Ireland's Music Generation education programme, which they helped fund and establish 15 years ago. A few hours earlier, the band announced their 16th studio album, Carnaval de Luz, which will be released in November. It's a companion piece to February's angry, impassioned EP, Days of Ash, which tackled headlines about ICE killings in America, the war in Ukraine and the Israel-Palestine conflict. That was followed by themore sedate Easter Lily EPin April; with Carnaval de Luz rounding off the story. The Edge described it as "a messy, provocative, sacred collection of songs", while Bono promised "loud guitars, deep bass [and] ecstatic rhythms." Closing out the album's 12 tracks is Torn, a song co-written by Dolly Parton, which was the country icon's final recorded performance before her death last month. In a press release, the track was described as "a tender country song detailing broken family ties, that holds wider resonances". BBC News will run an interview about that song, and the rest of the album, in the coming weeks. Headline: Top South African police officer charged with raping woman, 18, and grooming 16-year-old girl
Body: Arrest of Shadrack Sibiya comes as country reels from cases of femicide and alleged police corruption and criminality One of South Africa’s most senior police officers has been charged with raping an 18-year-old woman and grooming a 16-year-old girl, as the country’s police face allegations of corruption and failing to tackle violence against women and girls. Shadrack Sibiya, who was already suspended from his role as deputy national police commissioner over allegations he interfered with political killings investigations, was arrested on Monday. He is facing charges of rape, people trafficking, promoting the sexual grooming of a child and two counts of grooming a child. Sibiya appeared briefly in a Johannesburg court on Tuesday. He was then taken to prison in the capital, Pretoria, before a bail hearing on 29 September, as prosecutors had argued he was an escape risk. South Africa is reeling after the discovery ofnine women’s bodiesacross Ekurhuleni, the municipality east of Johannesburg, in September. Meanwhile, the Madlanga Commission judicial inquiry has been examining allegations of corruption and criminality within the police for the last year. Puleng Dimpane, the acting national police commissioner, said: “Police officers are entrusted with protecting women and children. They cannot themselves be implicated in conduct that undermines this responsibility. As the country continues to confront the scourge of gender-based violence and femicide, there can be no room for anyone within the police service who is alleged to abuse their position or violate the rights of women and children.” Sibiya is accused of raping an 18-year-old woman at a hotel in May in the Sandton business district of Johannesburg. The alleged rape took place “whilst she was passed out due to intoxication administered by the accused”, according to a copy of the charge sheet. The alleged grooming of the 16-year-old girl took place over WhatsApp between 20 July and 3 August, according to the charge sheet. This allegedly included Sibiya sending the girl naked photos of herself, which she had not sent to him. Sibiya did not enter a plea at the hearing on Tuesday. His lawyer told the court that they needed more time to consult with and get instructions from him, according toNews24. Firoz Cachalia, the acting police minister, said: “We strongly condemn the alleged conduct. “Where allegations of sexual offences are made against a member of the service, they must be investigated without fear or favour.” When Sibiyaappeared before the Madlanga Commissionin February he denied allegations that he had moved 121 political killings investigations from KwaZulu-Natal province to the national head office without explanation. Sibiya also denied that he hadreceived a gift of 20 impalasfrom Vusimuzi ‘Cat’ Matlala, a businessman who received an allegedly fraudulent 360m rand (£16.7m) police health services contract soon after the alleged gift. Matlala, who has been charged with attempted murder, alongside several other charges including fraud and money laundering,declined to commenton the impalas when he appeared at the Madlanga Commission in August. He said he did not want to incriminate himself as the matter was under investigation.

Headline: RBA expected to hike cash rate to 4.6%, its highest level since 2011
Body: Outcome of meetings of Reserve Bank on Monday and Tuesday will affect Australian mortgage rates, household budgets and house prices Get ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcast Australia’s key interest rate is expected to hit its highest level since 2011, drag down house prices and add more than $100 to typical monthly mortgage repayments. The Reserve Bank board is poised to hike the cash rate from 4.35% to 4.6% on Tuesday, which would be the fourth increase in 2026 and push typical home loan interest rates to 6.5%. For someone with an average-sized new mortgage of $731,000, now paying a rate of 6.2%, an increase would add about $119 to their $4,477 monthly repayments. That would take the total rise in repayments since January to nearly $480. The share of borrowers behind on their home loan repayments is small but rising, S&P data analysed by Westpac shows. Household budgets have also been strained byrising petrol pricesamid the US war on Iran, now 80c higher since the start of the year, adding $44 to the cost of filling up a vehicle with a 55-litre tank. Consumer spending is already slowing, with Commonwealth Bank data showing households cut back on purchases of education, motor vehicles and household goods in August. House prices would fall further after a fourth rate rise. Comparison website Canstar estimated a hike would cut $11,200 from the borrowing capacity of someone earning an average annual full-time wage of $108,650, taking the total lost borrowing power to $47,400. Shrinking borrowing capacities have locked buyers out of markets. Three rate rises and the Albanese government’s investor tax reforms have seen home loan inquiries slump from nearly 15,000 a week at the start of 2026 to just over 12,000 in August and September, Equifax data shows. Home prices around Australia have fallen more than 4% from their peak earlier this year, Cotality data shows. On Friday, the bank predicted prices would fall 7.3% by mid-2027, then begin rising again if the RBA prepared to cut rates. Westpac has predicted falls of 10% in Sydney and 8% in Melbourne, suggesting new buyers in some areas may find housing more affordable even after accounting for higher interest rates. But most capital cities are not expected to see significant price drops, meaning housing affordability would not improve after accounting for higher interest rates and repayments. When the cash rate last rose above 4.35% in 2010, inflation was 3%, housing markets were buoyant and the mining boom was boosting household incomes. Rates stayed above that level until the end of 2011. Nearly 15 years later, the RBA is poised to return interest rates to the same level despite a weak economy and slumping house prices because inflation has persisted above the target range of 3%. Senior RBA staff in recent weeks have highlighted the risk households could be starting to expect high inflation will endure beyond the disruptions to oil prices from the conflict in the Middle East. Shane Oliver, AMP’s chief economist, said on Saturday the central bank was at risk of losing financial markets’ confidence if it did not raise rates again. “After more than five years of inflation being above target, threatening RBA credibility, it does not have the luxury of continuing to wait and assess,” Oliver said. Financial markets expect an additional cash rate rise early next year.

Headline: Baby bank's urgent appeal as demand for help grows
Body: Chantal Nogbou founded Leeds Baby Bank in 2017 and the charity marks its first decade in January The founder of a charity which provides essentials like Moses baskets, prams, nappies and clothes to struggling families across Leeds has said it urgently needs more donations to help keep up with demand. Chantal Nogbou said there had been a "massive increase" in the number of people referred by health and social care professionals to Leeds Baby Bank in recent months. Nogbou said staff had helped an "unprecedented" 550 families in Leeds since the start of June, and were expecting numbers to rise as winter loomed. "We get even more people needing help then because they want to put the heating on, but they still need to buy nappies and feed and clothe their child," she said. Nogbou founded Leeds Baby Bank in 2017 when she was a single parent of four children, including twins, and she realised how many other families were struggling. More families than ever have been referred to Leeds Baby Bank for help since the start of June, according to the charity The charity will be 10 years old in January and Nogbou said that staff had seen a change in the families who needed their support over time. "When we started, pre-Covid, maybe one in five children in Leeds lived in relative poverty," she explained. "Now, you're looking at one in two children in some parts, and that's just a shocking number that really shouldn't be happening." Nogbou said that about 70% of the children they helped had a parent who was working and she said many were "not managing to manage the bills with energy and fuel prices going up". According to government statistics, 27% of children in the Yorkshire and Humber region lived in relative low income families - the joint highest proportion, alongside the West Midlands, in the country. A relative low income family is one living on less than 60% of the median national household income for that year. Chantal Nogbou said people did not realise how far a small financial donation could go Nogbou said the rise in referrals meant more financial challenges for the charity, especiallyafter moving from a city centre office to a larger and more accessible building in Armleywhich could now provide more services. "All that has cost money and obviously bills for us have also gone up when it comes to the utilities, so it's definitely a scary thing as a charity," she said. She added that it was the donations of items and money from the community that had kept the charity going. "It's the people that, instead of buying a coffee every day, set up a direct debit and send £5 to Leeds Baby Bank every month," she said. "That £5 can buy something like a brand new mattress for a Moses basket." Your Voice Listen to highlights fromWest Yorkshire on BBC Sounds, catch up with the latestepisode of Look North. Headline: Ex-GTA developer's studio faces closure after debut game flopped
Body: MindsEye, released in June 2025, was Build A Rocket Boy's debut game A video game studio founded by a former senior Grand Theft Auto developer is facing closure 15 months after the disastrous release of its debut game. Edinburgh-based Build A Rocket Boy (Barb) launched MindsEye in June 2025 to a string of bad reviews and player complaints, with some calling it "the worst game" of the year. Former workers said development of the game was chaotic and accused its boss, Leslie Benzies, of mismanaging the studio. Barb has now gone into administration - a process which could result in it being sold to a new owner or closed down. BBC Newsbeat has contacted Barb for a response. Leslie Benzies, pictured at the 2025 Bafta Game Awards, is regarded as a key figure in the development of Grand Theft Auto Benzies set up Barb in 2016 - the same year he left Grand Theft Auto maker Rockstar Games after a legal row over unpaid royalties. It began work on Everywhere, intended to be a multiplayer role-playing game set in a futuristic city, before pivoting its focus to action-adventure MindsEye. The project attracted a lot of interest and,according to company documents,external, Barb had managed to attract more than £233m of investment by 2024. Former staffpreviously told BBC Newsbeatthe development process had "no coherent direction" and accused senior managers of failing to listen to their concerns. Following the game's turbulent launch, between 250 to 300 members of staff were made redundant. Shortly before this, during an all-staff call, Benzies alleged "internal and external" forces had conspired to hinder MindsEye's release, and vowed to root out "saboteurs" within the company. When Newsbeat asked Barb about this, it released a statement saying: "Leslie and the entire senior management team take full responsibility for the initial launch [of MindsEye]. "The version of the game that was released did not reflect the experience our community deserved." Since its release, the company has failed to attract a bigger audience to the game with a series of fixes and content updates. After further layoffs, reports last week suggested the remaining workers at the studio had also been let go. A company goes into administration when it can no longer pay its bills - referred to as insolvency. Any payments to creditors - people or companies they owe money - are put on hold while proposals to restructure the business are drawn up. An administrator from a qualified accountancy firm is put in charge while this process takes place, and one of their main jobs is to keep the business running, usually until a new owner can be found. They must also make sure creditors are paid back as much money as possible. This is usually done by selling off assets such as equipment, furnishings and anything else that can be sold to raise cash. Administration can take months and, in the worst-case scenario, a company can be put into liquidation and shut down if it has no way of making any more cash. According to Barb's most recent accounts, for the period up to September 2025, it incurred a £36.2m loss and had £10.5m in net assets. Headline: Netanyahu calls Macron's remarks on West Bank in UN speech 'grotesque'
Body: A French diplomatic source said there had been a "misinterpretation" of Emmanuel Macron's words Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has condemned French President Emmanuel Macron after he criticised Israel's actions in the occupied West Bank during his address to the UN General Assembly. "Look at what's happening in the West Bank, where day in, day out, we are seeing violations. And in the name of what? Hamas was never very active in the West Bank," Macron said in French, according to the UN's interpreter. Netanyahu called the remarks a "grotesque absurdity" and said members of the Palestinian armed group there "carry out attacks against Jews almost every day". There was no response from Macron's office, but one French diplomatic source said there had been a "misinterpretation". The source told the Jerusalem Post,externalthat the meaning of the French sentence spoken by the president, "Le Hamas n'a jamais sévi en Cisjordanie," was, "Hamas has never governed the West Bank." Macron also rejected US President Donald Trump's assertion that he had ended the war between Israel and Hamas in the Gaza Strip. Violence there has continued despite last October's ceasefire, including almost daily Israeli strikes, while humanitarian conditions remain dire "Some boast of a supposed peace. But that peace has not reopened humanitarian access for a single second," he said. "Are we simply to stand by and watch this spectacle that should shame us all?" After the address, the Israeli prime minister's office said in a statement: "The grotesque absurdity of Emmanuel Macron's statement is staggering." "On Sunday, the eve of [the Jewish holy day of] Yom Kippur, just two days ago, Netanel Shukrun - a French citizen and father of six - was murdered in his car by a Hamas terrorist in Judea and Samaria," it added, using a biblical term for the West Bank. "Hamas terrorists carry out attacks against Jews almost every day. They have murdered countless Israeli civilians in Judea and Samaria." The US ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, also denounced Macron's remarks as "out of touch with reality". Shukrun, 36, was shot dead when a Palestinian opened fire on a group of Israelis at a spring near the West Bank settlement of Neve Tzuf, according to Israeli police. The suspect was arrested later at a hospital in the city of Ramallah, they said. Hamas praised the attack but did not say it was behind it. The group - which is designated as a terrorist organisation by Israel, France and other countries - is a rival of the Fatah-dominated Palestinian Authority, which governs parts of the West Bank that are not under Israeli control. Israel has built about 160 settlements housing 700,000 Jews since it occupied the West Bank and East Jerusalem - land Palestinians want, along with Gaza, for a hoped-for future state - during the 1967 Middle East war. An estimated 3.3 million Palestinians live alongside them. The settlements are illegal under international law. Headline: Four men down - but Australia still beat South Africa
Body: Australia will open the 2027 World Cup against Hong Kong in Perth International Test match Australia (24) 42 Tries:Ikitau 2, Donaldson, Wilson, JorgensenCons:Lonergan 4Pens:Lonergan 3 South Africa (17) 38 Tries:Grobbelaar, van der Merwe, penalty try, van den Berg, NcheCons:Pollard 2, Mngomezulu 2Pens:Pollard Australia were reduced to 11 men but dug in for an extraordinary win against a much-changed South Africa side as they beat the world champions 42-38 in Perth. The Wallabies excelled with some vibrant attacking rugby, scoring five tries against the back-to-back World Cup winners to lead by 25 points with 16 minutes left. But then a manic spell of four yellow cards in nine minutes left the hosts overrun, with South Africa mounting a comeback that ultimately fell just short. The visitors made 13 changes after beatingNew Zealand in Baltimorebut still fielded a strong starting XV, which boasted 240 caps in the second row alone. But a year out from hosting the World Cup, and a year on from being soundly beaten on home soilby the Lions,it was the home side who impressed before their bizarre late collapse. The teams traded early penalties before Springboks hooker Johan Grobbelaar drove over for the first try of the match after a powerful maul. Australia responded well with a wave of pressure which was rewarded when centre Len Ikitau drove over from a metre out. Ikitau then flew over for his second after the Boks made a mess of a high ball kicked through, but the lead lasted just three minutes. South Africa played the ball quickly and flung it out wide with Edwill van der Merwe on the end of a stunning break to score in the corner. The high level continued as the hosts took the lead again before the break. After 14 patient but quick phases, the Wallabies whipped the ball from right to left to find fly-half Ben Donaldson free to score in the corner. The Springboks had strength in depth to call on, and coach Rassie Erasmus made all eight changes early in the second half with his side down by 10 points. But it was Australia who continued to dominate. Captain Harry Wilson was denied a try as his foot was in touch but just seconds later he did burrow over the line close to the posts. Wing Max Jorgensen then sprinted the length of the pitch to score a stunning solo score after South Africa fumbled the ball to make it 42-17. Wilson was then sin-binned and South Africa finally got their first score of the second half with a penalty try, with Ryan Lonergan yellow carded as well. The Wallabies were down to 13 and a crossfield kick found Van der Merwe in the corner but the wing dropped the ball before he could ground it. Australia wing Joseph-Aukuso Sua'ali'i was then sin-binned as well to leave Australia three men down and replacement scrum-half Morne van den Berg scrambled in to cut the lead to 11 points. Remarkably Australia then appeared to have scored again as Tom Wright intercepted a pass to run in - only for the try to be ruled out and Hunter Paisami shown a fourth yellow card for a dangerous tackle in the build-up. South Africa had so much space and scored again through Ox Nche to cut the lead to four but time ran out. Headline: From weeks to hours - the rapid new test transforming brain tumour diagnosis
Body: The test means patients can be diagnosed within hours rather than weeks, like Steve Palmer whose case the BBC followed A rapid new test for brain tumours that the NHS has started using can slash the time it takes for an accurate diagnosis from up to eight weeks to two hours. The test, which is used by doctors to diagnose which type of tumour a patient has, should mean patients can start treatment including radiotherapy and chemotherapy sooner, and are spared weeks of uncertainty. Steve Palmer, 55, from Nottingham, is among those to benefit from the new technology - and it meant surgeons were able to get his result while they were still operating to remove his tumour. "Getting that quick diagnosis removed weeks of anxiety," he told the BBC. NHS England said that the genomic test, which works by quickly analysing the genetic code of a sample of the tumour, will be piloted in specialist centres around England. There are around 150 different types of brain tumour ranging from slow-growing to aggressive cancers, each of which can respond differently to treatment. Steve was diagnosed with a brain tumour after he collapsed at the gym, and the test revealed it to be a grade 4 glioblastoma. "It wasn't the result I wanted to hear but it means I can get on with the next phase of treatment and recovery, and get on with fighting whatever it is I've got to fight," he told the BBC. Consultant neurosurgeon Stuart Smith, who led Steve's operation at Queens Medical Centre, part of Nottingham University Hospitals NHS Trust, told the BBC the test "seems almost magical." "The diagnosis of brain tumours relies on molecular and genetic analysis but it can take up to six to eight weeks to get the full information back. Here it is done while we are still operating." Diagnosing the type of tumour while the patient is still on the operating table could impact how surgeons operate. Smith explained: "For some tumour types, which are curable, surgery needs to be as radical as possible to remove every last bit of tumour that we can find. "Other types, sadly, are too aggressive, and beyond what surgery can remove, so we would be more cautious in order to lower the risk of causing damage to the brain." Neurosurgeon Stuart Smith, who points to a screen during Steve's surgery, says it means patients will also have quicker access to clinical trials The test works by sending small tissue samples taken from the tumour to the pathology lab. The samples are prepared for loading into a shoebox-sized sequencing machine made by Oxford Nanopore, which uses specialist software developed at the University of Nottingham, in partnership with hospital clinicians. The molecules of DNA pass through a nanopore - a tiny hole - which reveals the tumour's unique genomic fingerprint. In Steve's case, after the nanopore machine was running for 20 minutes, the neuropathology team called the theatre to tell them that the tumour was likely to be a glioblastoma. Dr Simon Paine, consultant neuropathologist at Nottingham University Hospitals NHS Trust, explained that the genomic test was transformative in comparison to what he could determine by looking at tumour cells down a microscope. "I'm crystal ball gazing and can do it reasonably well on a good day, but nowhere near with the clarity of the nanopore, which gives a comprehensive molecular classification," he said. More than 12,000 people in the UK are diagnosed with a primary brain tumour each year. It is the biggest cancer killer of children and adults under 40. Prof Frankie Swords, NHS medical director, said: "For people with suspected brain tumours, getting the right diagnosis quickly can feel like a race against time, while waiting weeks for answers can be agonising for them and their families. "This remarkable rapid test has the potential to completely transform how we diagnose brain tumours, with results reaching patients in a matter of days rather than weeks. "This is a huge leap forward for patients - a faster diagnosis means they can start the right treatment or access clinical trials sooner, while for some patients it could mean surgeons can make potentially life-changing decisions about their surgery while on the operating table." Speaking to BBC Breakfast, she called the pilot scheme a "world first" and said "no other health service" is rolling the technology out across multiple hospitals. The NHS England pilot will involve five specialist centres in Nottingham, Birmingham, London and Newcastle - they are Nottingham University Hospitals NHS Trust, University Hospitals Birmingham NHS Foundation Trust, Great Ormond Street Hospital NHS Foundation Trust, King's College Hospital and Newcastle Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust. It will later be extended to sites in Bristol, Oxford, Leeds and Manchester. The pilot builds on an earlier project already under way in Nottingham and Birmingham. The BBC watched the surgery to remove Steve's tumour, shown here on the scan, at Queens Medical Centre, Nottingham Prof Dame Sue Hill, chief scientific officer for England and senior responsible officer for genomics in the NHS, said: "This is another world-leading development for NHS genomics, taking pioneering science and testing how we can use it safely and consistently in patient care. "Rapid genomic testing could dramatically shorten the wait for answers for brain tumour patients and, in some cases, give surgeons vital information before an operation is even over. "Our ambition is to build the evidence for this testing to become part of routine NHS care, so patients across the country can benefit equally from faster, more precise diagnosis." Smith added:  "For patients it will mean not only mean quicker access to results and treatment, but because we have a full genetic profile of the tumour, more rapid access to clinical trials." Headline: Rick Wakeman performs piano concert to 150 rescued moon bears in Vietnam
Body: Former Yes musician plays at sanctuary to raise awareness of animals that remain stuck in cages at ‘bile farms’ Rick Wakeman has played to all kinds of people around the globe, but he has now performed to an audience he had never encountered before – an enclosure of 150 bears. The former Yes musician, who has gone on to have a prolific solo career, played the piano at a Vietnamese bear sanctuary. “Before you ask, I won’t be playing the teddy bear’s picnic,” he joked ahead of the performance. Wakeman, who is a supporter of animal welfare causes and has rescue dogs and cats of his own, is conducting the concert to raise awareness of moon bears kept in cruel conditions for the extraction of their bile. He said he was a bit worried about how hot it is going to be. “You know the heatwave we had in England? It’s double that,” he said. “They offered to rig up a fan for me, but I figured that will just blow more hot air around.” His concert was performed live on a Yamaha grand piano positioned inAnimalsAsia’s bear sanctuary in the Tam Dao national park, and Wakeman had written some new compositions especially for rescued bears. Asked whether the bears would enjoy the music, he said: “They’ve not got much choice, really. It’s a well-known fact that all animals react to music, especially gentle melodic music. So what I am going to do is piano music that is melodic, and I can only hope that they will come up to the perimeter of the sanctuary and have a listen.” Wakeman has been sponsoring rescue bears since 2016 and recently adopted a new one: “He’s only 20 months old, a big fella, I went to see him today. He came out right to the edge and stood on his back legs and just stared at me, it was brilliant.” Bile is extracted from bears for traditional Chinese medicine by putting a needle into their gall bladder and drawing it out. The bears are kept in poor conditions in countries including China and in Vietnam, where it has just been banned, but where some bears are still in captivity in cramped enclosures. It is the fourth-biggest market in the illegal wildlife trade in east Asia, resulting in a dramatic decline in the Asiatic black bear populations in Vietnam, with nearly a third of their numbers lost around the world in just 30 years. Of the sanctuary, which he has been visiting this week, Wakeman said: “To see the bears be rehabilitated, having a life they never had before, some have never put their feet on grass before. They are so wonderful, that we can do such horrendous things to animals is beyond belief. Before this, they were chained in cages sometimes for 10 or 20 years in conditions where they couldn’t even turn around.” He is playing to raise awareness for the bears still stuck in cages in Vietnam and tourge the governmentto get them released: “We have 150 bears at the sanctuary, but there are 125 bears left in cages in the old bear bile farms, and there are four dying a month. We have to get them out quick and into the sanctuary.” He treats his rescue dogs and cats to music back at home in Suffolk. “I had one cat who used to jump on the grand piano, and if I stopped playing he would put his paw in the strings and rattle them until I played again. I know if my dogs don’t like it, they will get up and walk out, and my cats don’t like metal, grunge or rap. They want a melody.” Wakeman spends hours watching the bears. “If you see these bears it is hard to put into words, they are almost human the way they look at you,” he said. “If you see them, you can’t help but be moved. They aren’t tame but they are very safe, very happy, they play, they romp. I witnessed two today jumping in a bubble bath and playing. They’ve got a life back.” Dr Jill Robinson, the founder and CEO of Animals Asia, said: “We are beyond blessed to have Rick’s support for Animals Asia and the bears. His love for them is immeasurable and can be heard in the beautifully haunting music he has written for them. We’re all so excited to hear his performance in the open air at our sanctuary in the stunning setting of Tam Dao national park. I can’t wait to see how the bears respond.” Wakeman added: “I hope they lay down and have a listen, that would make my day. I would have a big grin on my face.”

Headline: Man cautioned over Reform conference assaults
Body: Nigel Farage's speech to the conference on 4 September was marked by protests A man has been given a caution by police as part of an investigation into assaults on protesters at the Reform UK party conference in Birmingham earlier this month. Footage appeared to show protesters being manhandled by audience members as they were thrown out. One woman had her hair pulled, and was was hit with a walking stick. West Midlands Police said it was investigating assaults on five people and two other men had been voluntarily interviewed, as inquiries continued. It said the man who was given a conditional caution had also volunteered for interview. The force has asked alleged victims and anyone with information to come forward. Activists disrupted the Reform leader, Nigel Farage, four times during his speech at the NEC on 4 September, before they were removed by security. A West Midlands Police spokesperson said: "Our investigation into a number of assaults that took place at the Reform UK national conference at the NEC continues. "One man has been given a conditional caution after being voluntarily interviewed as part of the investigation." Cautions are offered by police if they have enough evidence to convict and the person involved has admitted their part in a crime. Conditional cautions are the more severe of the two types of caution. Agreeing to a caution is an admission of guilt. People who agree to conditional cautions can be subject to certain terms, which can include a fine, reparations to the victim or rehabilitation. Headline: I'm not tempted to call an early election, Burnham says
Body: This video can not be played Burnham: 'No election anytime soon' Andy Burnham has insisted he is not tempted to call an early general election, arguing it would throw "the country into a backward-looking process". During a round of BBC interviews ahead of Labour's annual conference, the prime minister said his focus was on helping people with the cost of living and supporting businesses. Recent polling has suggested Labour's position has improved since Burnham replaced Sir Keir Starmer in Downing Street in July, although Reform UK and the Conservatives are not far behind. An early general election could give Burnham a mandate of his own and free him from commitments made in Labour's 2024 manifesto. The next general election must be held by August 2029. Asked by ITV Calendar if the next election would be in 2029, he replied: "Yes, that's when the next election will be. "All of this speculation on an early election, I can knock that dead." New policies, election speculation: What to expect from Burnham's first Labour conference as PM Burnham heads to his first Labour Party conference as prime minister this weekend, with speculation over the prospect of a snap election likely to be a topic of conversation among some of those attending the event in Liverpool. Labour has been projected to lose its majority but remain the largest party in the House of Commons if there were a snap election, according to recent polling. It comes amid media reports that some of the prime minister's advisers have been weighing up the prospect of an election as early as next year. But Burnham sought to rule out this prospect during interviews with BBC regional political editors ahead of the conference opening on Sunday. Asked by BBC West political editor Paul Barltrop whether he was tempted to call an early poll, Burnham replied: "No, not particularly. No, I'm not. "I see all the speculation and it just races ahead," he said. "No election anytime soon. I'm focused on the job as prime minister, doing what I said I would do." He was later asked by BBC East Midlands political editor Peter Saull if there would be a general election next May, alongside council elections in the area. The PM replied "no" before adding: "Not having a general election." Burnham also said he wanted to use the conference to say more about "the direction I want to take the country in", adding: "The focus is on that, helping people with the cost of living, helping businesses with the cost of running a business. "These have got to be the priorities right now, rather than throwing the country into a backward-looking process where we're arguing again amongst ourselves." Burnham said he wanted to ensure people were "feeling a bit of hope in their lives again", adding: "That's what I'm trying to do, and I hope to take it further in the coming period, rather than putting people back into an election cycle." The prime minister was also asked about the number of migrants crossing the English Channel in small boats. It comes after 781 people were recorded arriving in 10 boats on Wednesday, the highest total for a single day so far this year. Burnham said his goal was that he did not want to see any crossings "at all". He declined to put a timescale on this ambition, but said his government would "not stop" working until crossings went "right down". He argued that Brexit had hampered the UK's ability to stop the arrivals, saying it had led to a "loss of collaboration with neighbours". Elsewhere in the series of interviews, he said: He would not do any "special interviews" with the Sun -he told the BBCin 2015 that he had not forgiven the newspaper for its coverage of the 1989 Hillsborough disaster Tourists would not "begrudge paying a few extra pounds" as a result of his proposal to allow regional mayors in England tocharge new taxon visitors' overnight stays The government would "do what we can within the resources that we've got to support people" in the Budget next month Sign up for our Politics Essential newsletterto keep up with the inner workings of Westminster and beyond.

Headline: 'We're all broke': Would you chase a friend for £5?
Body: This video can not be played Watch: We ask New Yorkers to share the smallest amount they'd ask a friend to pay back You pick up the bill for dinner, pay for the taxi home or grab a friend's coffee with the promise they'll pay you back later, but days go by and the money never arrives. At what point do you ask them for it again and how small is too small to chase? For some, $5 (£3.70) is worth a reminder, while for others, asking a friend to repay anything under $20 (£15) feels more awkward than simply taking the hit. Henry Payne says he's "sent a request for $8.50, but I wouldn't go lower than $8". The 21-year-old New Yorker adds that he will chase someone once but "two requests is insane". "I would rather swallow the $8.50 than send another request." He does admit that he's sometimes the person on the other side of the transaction and can be forgetful himself. "For everyone that I haven't sent back money to, I just forgot, feel free to double request me." Nouria (left) and Kaz are two students in New York who say money conversations with friends can be very awkward Kaz Jahanbini, 19, says needing to ask to be paid back in the first place can be frustrating. "If someone bought me something, I'm immediately paying them back. So then I'm thinking for them, what's the delay?" His rule for navigating friendship and finances is to "keep your wallet close but your friends closer". His friend Nouria agrees and says as a student "every extra dollar counts" but she would usually only ask for money back from a friend if it was more than $10. A recent study,externalfound that 76% of Gen Z who have fronted money for a group expense, like a trip or event, say they were not fully repaid, and 55% say it created tension or negatively affected a relationship. Betsie believes there's a cultural difference between Brits and Americans For British student Betsie Brooke-Taylor, 19, the threshold to ask for money back is a fiver as she says "every little helps". She sees a cultural difference between the UK and US and even though "we are all broke, I think Americans are a bit more generous". Betsie also thinks technology makes settling small debts easier in the US, where payment apps such as Venmo are widely used. Venmo lets users send and request money through an app which includes the function of sending a reminder if someone hasn't paid you. In the US,more than 95 million people have a Venmo account,external. "In the UK you have to ask for the account number and sort code, and not everyone has that on hand," she says. Annika (left) and Hanako feel very differently about confronting a friend who hasn't paid them back For 19-year-old Annika Violet, the amount she would ask back from a friend depends on whether she's consistently paying for them. "I prefer to do something where I get them this time and they get me next time but if I'm consistently paying and you're not, then I will request the $5." Unlike many, Annika doesn't find money conversations uncomfortable. "I am so confrontational, I do not find it awkward. If you're my friend, you would pay me back." Annika's friend Hanako Stepper says she finds it awkward asking for money but wishes she didn't. "I've never chased anyone - I'm just sad if I don't get paid back." Annika's advice to those who do struggle to ask is to "be brave and bold". "If they are going to give you flak about it, maybe it's a sign they are not a good friend." Money expert Laura Pomfret says many people feel embarrassed about asking to be paid back, and Britons in particular can find it awkward. "We're often very British about asking for money back," she says, suggesting people may be worried about being judged as a "cheapskate". Her top tips for asking friends to pay up are: She adds that you shouldn't convince yourself that a debt is too small to justify asking for it as "if you want the money paid back then the amount shouldn't matter". And if the same friend repeatedly fails to pay, Pomfret suggests remembering it the next time you're about to pay for them and think twice. Ella (left) and Katrina have a few friends who rarely pay them back Several people the BBC spoke to said the amount itself mattered less when somebody repeatedly failed to pay. New York student Ella Feuille, 21, says $15 is roughly the point at which she would consider requesting money. If a significant amount was owed, Ella says she would ask around three times before giving up but wouldn't necessarily forget about it. "I have friends who I know now it has to go on their card because they're not going to pay me back." Her friend Katrina Dimingot agrees and says she much prefers a method where "we don't pay each other back, we just take it in turns to get things for each other". Headline: Ministers reject dog ownership licence scheme
Body: Pet owners will not have to pay a fee to own a dog, after the government ruled out introducing a licensing scheme. In a report, published on Thursday,,externala panel of animal experts suggested the government should consider new legal requirements for dog owners. The panel did not reach an agreement on which rules should be adopted but the taskforce said any new laws should aim to promote better dog control, reduce the risk of dog attacks and avoid placing an "undue burden" on owners. A spokesperson for the environment department said: "This is a welcome report and ministers are considering the taskforce's recommendations, however we will not be introducing a new dog licensing scheme." The Dog Control Coalition - which includes the RSPCA, Battersea Dogs & Cats Home and the Royal Kennel Club - said it supported the recommendations in the report and that it was "vital" for the government to take action "as a matter of urgency". A spokesperson for the coalition said: "Dog bite incidents continue to have serious consequences for people and dogs, and the time that has passed since the publication of The Middlesex Report, in 2021, makes it imperative that we now see progress." The report made 20 recommendations including calling for councils to provide a service to tackle low-level dog control issues, improved recording of dog bite wounds and legal requirements for dog walkers. Dog attacks are still rising - even after the XL bully ban What are the rules for having an XL bully dog? Dog licences explored to tackle ownership issues The Responsible Dog Ownership Taskforce was established by the government in 2022, following a series of high-profile dog attacks. The taskforce's report noted that since 2011 the dog population in the UK had grown by 35%, while hospital admissions relating to dog bites in England had risen by 77%. It said pet ownership had spiked during the Covid pandemic at a time when it was harder to access support services. "This led to less experienced owners struggling to access services and finding it harder to get help," the report said. Until 1987, dog owners in England, Wales and Scotland had to pay an annual fee to get an ownership licence. The scheme was scrapped on the grounds that the amount of money it raised was outweighed by the operating costs. Dog owners in Northern Ireland still have to buy a licence of £12.50, or £5 if the owner receives an income-related benefit. In France, owners of the most dangerous dogs have to get special permits which can involve passing a training course and putting the dog through a behavioural assessment. Switzerland previously required potential dog owners to complete a knowledge test, followed by a practical, but this condition has been scrapped. The report said that most members of the taskforce backed introducing legal requirements for dog owners but "further consideration would be needed regarding the form that this should take". "Any legal requirement would need careful consideration of its objective and not appear as a tax on already responsible dog owners. "Reintroducing a universal dog licence may amount to another database of responsible owners or an administrative exercise with little public safety benefit or opportunity to promote responsible dog ownership." It said options could include focusing a scheme on high-risk dogs, introducing background checks on owners and requiring potential owners to pass a knowledge test. The Dogs Trust and the RSPCA have commissioned research into the costs and benefits of different systems and their conclusions are due to be published later this year. In a ministerial foreword to the report, environment minister Baroness Hayman of Ullock said: "In recent years, we have seen a concerning rise in dog attacks, alongside changes in patterns of dog ownership." She said the taskforce's report was an "important and timely contribution", adding: "As ministers, we are carefully considering the recommendations alongside the wider programme of work already under way." Headline: Why Premier League faces uncertainty and chaos after Man City ruling
Body: This video can not be played Kieran Maguire on potential sanctions for Man City If you were getting the impression that the saga overManchester City's 115 charges was almost over, think again. Two years and 10 days since the hearing began, and 1,329 days after City were charged, we now knowa verdict has been reached, with the club guilty of the majority of financial rule breaches. That is not because the Premier League orManchester Cityhave told us - it is thanks tothe Athletic finding out and breaking the story.,external BBC Sport was later told the verdict was sent during the week to club executives, who had to sign a non-disclosure agreement to open the file. A process can appear to be completely watertight, as this one certainly had been, but when the circle of trust is expanded, the chance of information getting out increases. Despite this, public silence from the Premier League continues. City did not address whether they had been found guilty in a statement making it clear - with an appeal expected - that the "process remains ongoing" from their point of view. It all points to the suggestion that the long-awaited decision of the independent panel was not a case of this process nearing an end, but perhaps instead reaching the end of the beginning. It appears the chaos and uncertainty is only going to increase now. City fans, and the rest of football, are left to guess what the punishment might be. And when this all might reach a definitive conclusion. The charges are so serious that some form of points deduction now appears inevitable, subject to the appeal by City, who have always insisted they have done nothing wrong. When and how any punishment is applied will be crucial not just for City, but the Premier League as a whole. And that's before we get to the prospect of clubs suing City for compensation. Enzo Maresca's side go toLiverpoolon 11 October when the Premier League resumes after the international break. They could go six points clear at the top. But is that now rendered meaningless? Let's look at possible scenarios - none of which are particularly appealing. No Premier League appetite to strip Man City of titles - but threat remains Deciding the punishment should be quicker than ascertaining guilt, but nothing is certain in this case. As the charges have been denied, it will have to go to a sanction hearing convened by the independent panel. BBC Sport has been told this hearing could still be months away, and the result may not be published until the appeal is completed. At the hearing, everything will be on the table. Fines, points deductions and even demotion. This differs fromChelsea's case earlier this year, asthe Stamford Bridge club self-reported and admitted guilt. That allowed them to negotiate with the Premier League and reach a sanctioning agreement. It is possible that City could decide to hold their hands up and try to agree a deal - which would be better for the league - though that seems unlikely given the club's consistently strong denials over many years. The panel will have to comb through the hundreds of pages of evidence and determine the punishment. Remember,Evertonwere docked six points, reduced from 10 on appeal, and then two points in separate cases for breaches of profit and sustainability rules (PSR).Nottingham Forestwere deducted four points. These were considered to be minor breaches, while City faced seven separate charges on PSR breaches in the Premier League alone, as well as a further five related to Uefa competitions. This aspect alone suggests a large points penalty. That is before you get into the inflated sponsorship revenue allegedly channelled through the companies' accounts as a means of meeting financial fair play rules, payments to players and managers, and a failure to comply with investigations. Take all this into account, and it places an asterisk against the Premier League between 2009 and 2018. ChelseaandManchester City, two of the competition's most successful clubs, have been part of that. WhileChelseaadmitted effectively cheating, City have been found guilty. They got around the financial rules to put them in a position to be able to sign more expensive players than their finances should have permitted. And if this season passes with no decision on the sanction while it is known City were guilty of the majority of counts, what does that mean for the integrity of the competition? Could a penalty be backdated to this season when finally awarded? Unlikely. So what ifManchester Citywin the league? Coventry are third from bottom right now. What if they finish in that position, are relegated, but would have stayed up had City's punishment come this season? This inertia is terrible news for the Premier League as a competition. There's a strong argument that a sanctioning agreement is the cleanest way out of this. But that may not be palatable to the league as they would have to negotiate with City, who would presumably want a lesser punishment. Clubs seek legal advice over Man City charges compensation Man City fans face up to reality of guilty verdict Man City legal fight could spiral out of control - Purslow The usual process when any points penalty is handed down is that it is applied immediately, subject to appeal. It could be a points deduction so large that it is effectively a relegation. Alternatively, if City's membership of the Premier League was revoked, it is unclear how that might be applied mid-season. It could also be that the punishment is a huge fine, although that would seem unlikely given points deductions to other clubs. The question would be how soon we hear, and how long after the appeal is heard. Usually, the league asks for an expedited process from the independent arbitration company which handles disciplinary cases. But, as ever in this case, the complexities indicate this is not straightforward. There is the chance, though slim, that the punishment is only applied to the league table after the appeal. That would surely lead to protests from impacted teams this season, who will demand it should, as usual, come into effect immediately. Manchester City vs The Premier League For the integrity of the Premier League, so all clubs know what they are playing for, this would need to happen sooner rather than later. Last season, apoints deduction for West Bromwich Albionrelated to breaches of profit and sustainability regulations was not announced until 24 April. While ultimately they stayed in the Championship, it plunged them back into a relegation fight when they thought they were safe. It also gave some hope to the teams in the relegation zone. The Premier League does not want this to drag on until the penultimate month of the season, but nothing is guaranteed in this story. In this scenario, let's not forget City could also win their appeal, like theydid over Uefa's punishment back in July 2020. While this would be celebrated at Etihad Stadium it would likely not be the end of the acrimony over the case. Manchester City won seven domestic trophies during the period of the alleged offences Premier League clubs are seeking legal advice about compensation fromManchester Cityover the case. One source, who held a senior executive position at two Premier League sides, said they expected clubs to submit individual compensation claims againstManchester City. Another leading lawyer told the BBC that process could even be centralised by the league. Premier League rules allow clubs to seek legal action against each other for compensation. In June,Evertonwere told they must pay Burnley £35m after they broke PSR over a three-year period. Burnley argued the breach impacted their chances of staying in the Premier League, and sought compensation for the losses associated with being relegated. Evertonare appealing, with sources previously saying they would "robustly and thoroughly" contest the ruling, but it provides an interesting backdrop to theManchester Citycase. There is uncertainty over a statute of limitations, which would set a cut-off point for claims. Arsenal,Manchester United,LiverpoolandTottenham Hotspurreportedly preserved their rights to claim compensation two years ago. This is not just aboutManchester United(twice) andLiverpool, who finished as runners-up to City in their title-winning seasons. It is about those clubs who just missed out on the Champions League, or failed to make Europe, or even those who were relegated. And it could even result in claims over the prize money for each Premier League place, or the potential commercial earnings lost by rival clubs. Kieran Maguire, professor of football finance at the University ofLiverpool, told BBC Sport it would be considered a "denial of an opportunity" by complainants. Maguire explained that the "statute of limitations is not referenced" in the Premier League's traditional handbook, though that could be subject to a legal challenge from City. But what of the compensation? Just looking at Champions League qualifying could bring huge financial claims. "The Champions League in those days was worth a minimum of £30m," Maguire said. "I think by the time we got to 2018, it was probably worth £60m or £70m, and that's in prize money. "On top of that, you could claim for loss of gate receipts, loss of sponsor bonuses. This is highly unlikely, but it's certainly being discussed. "Players get bonuses for qualifying for the Champions League. Those bonuses, if you talk to people connected to the elite clubs, are normally in the region of 25%. "An average salary in those days would probably, if you go back to 2012, be in the region of £80,000 or £90,000 a week. Twenty-five percent of that is four or five million pounds a year. That's how the issues stack up." Points deductions, fines, and compensation claims. This is an extremely messy situation for the Premier League, and it does not look like being resolved anytime soon. Headline: Survey to show 'vital insight' of children's lives
Body: The chief statistician said the survey provided a "vital insight" into the lives of young people A survey for young people on topics including health, wellbeing, school life and social media is set to open in October. Statistics Jersey said the survey would be offered to students from Year 4 to Year 12 and would run from 5 to 16 October.  It said the 2026 Children and Young People's Survey was voluntary, anonymous and could be completed online. Officials said it would be the first time the survey would ask participants about social media apps and generative AI tools, including how often they use them. Chief statistician Ian Cope said it provided a "vital insight" into the lives of children and young people on the island. Statistics Jersey said it would explore whether young people had caring responsibilities and enough food for each day. It said the results would be used across the Government of Jersey to inform policy and improve services. "We have worked directly with students this year to help shape the content, ensuring it reflects the issues that matter most to them," Cope added. "New questions on social media, generative AI, caring responsibilities and food security will help build a more complete picture of the opportunities and challenges facing young people today." The final report is due to be published in Spring 2027, officials said, alongside a child-friendly version for schools. More news stories for Jersey Listen to the latest news for Jersey Statistics Jersey said the last survey, carried out in 2024, achieved strong participation. Response rates were 87% for Years 4 and 8, 84% for Years 6 and 10, and 78% for Year 12, with 4,360 children taking part, it said. Follow BBC Jersey onX,externalandFacebook,external.
