Headline: Booker Prize judges reveal shortlisted novels after selection 'tussle'
Body: The Booker Prize 2026 judges are Rebecca Liu, Jarvis Cocker, Dame Mary Beard, Raymond Antrobus and Patricia Lockwood Past Booker Prize winners Marlon James and Douglas Stuart have been shortlisted for the prestigious literary award again, after a selection process that the judges described as "a tussle". Jamaican writer James is nominated this year for his latest novel The Disappearers; while Scottish author Stuart is shortlisted for John of John. This year's other contenders are award-winning US novelist Elizabeth Strout, and British authors M John Harrison, Luke Kennard and Rebecca Perry. But seven books that appeared on the longlist in July have been jettisoned, and Dame Mary Beard, who chaired the judging panel, said agreeing on the final six "has been, to put it mildly, hard work". Scroll down to find out more about this year's nominees. James previously won the Booker Prize in 2015 for A Brief History of Seven Killings, while Stuart won in 2020 for Shuggie Bain. Praising this year's entries, Dame Mary added: "English language fiction now is full of talent – talent old and talent new. "It's full of wit, seriousness, pleasure, challenge, discomfort and real brilliance, and I think we should be rewarding our novelists a lot more than we do." The other judges included former Booker Prize-shortlisted US novelist Patricia Lockwood, who said she discovered she was "bossier than I believed myself to be" when making the case for or against particular books in the judges' meetings. "I was sort of standing up a lot and tossing books across the room and being really active. I was like, 'Wow, yeah, I didn't know I had it in me'." Another judge, poet Raymond Antrobus, told reporters: "All of us individually had a different idea for a shortlist and then it was a tussle." Lockwood jokingly added: "A tussle, yeah. We wrestled like pigs in the mud!" Antrobus said the final choices are connected because they are books that "as well as having heart, also took risk". "These books, we truly believe, cannot be replicated by artificial intelligence. These are very human books for the way they talk about and navigate a lived experience." The judging line-up was completed by journalist, editor and critic Rebecca Liu and Pulp frontman Jarvis Cocker, who said being on the selection panel was "a bit like being in a band". He said: "The way a band makes an appealing noise is by everybody combining, in a way, and if you don't like that then you have to go solo. "You get something that you couldn't get [alone] and no-one's in control of it and you make a good noise together. So I hope that's what this shortlist is, a nice noise." Cocker read some of the entries while on tour, and said he joined one judges' meeting online while wearing a dressing gown in a hotel room in Australia at 02:00 local time. "When you're on tour, it's quite dull when you're travelling so it was quite good to have something to read," he said. "I became known for being in those meetings wearing a towelling robe." The End of Everything by M John Harrison An unexplained catastrophe, and the arrival of mysterious alien beings, have turned British society upside down - and a man and his elderly aunt muddle through on the Kent coast. It's the author's first Booker nomination, and he'd be the oldest ever winner at 81. The judges said: "The End of Everything can be read as a thriller, a mystery, a satire, a dystopia, a road novel, a work of realism. The landscape may be bleak, the catastrophe may be immersive, yet there still were moments we found ourselves laughing aloud." The Disappearers by Marlon James This epic, visceral story revolves around a violent attack on eight gay men who had gathered to rehearse a queer play in Kingston, Jamaica, in 1988, and its aftermath. The New York Times called it "a masterpiece, the novel of the decade and possibly of the century thus far". The judges said: "A Jamaican epic from one of the most impactful Caribbean novelists today; readers will love the shifting register of the dialogue and poetic phrasings, often pierced through with sharp, double-edged humour." Black Bag by Luke Kennard An out-of work actor gets a new role - being locked in a black bag during psychology lectures for an entire term as a professor's experiment. The story unfolds into a humorous and poignant satire that makes sharp observations about the state of modern masculinity and creative life. The judges said: "In a wonderfully quirky campus novel, Kennard combines an absurd experiment with a moving story about human frailty, passion, confusion and identity. There's something for everyone here." May We Feed the King by Rebecca Perry A modern-day museum curator is commissioned to recreate a past scene in a historic palace, and becomes immersed in the world of the young, reluctant king whose life she uncovers. It is the debut novel by Perry, who is also a poet and a former competitive trampolinist. The judges said: "An affecting and lush jewel of a novel that moves between our present-day world to a medieval court and unsettles the idea that there's ever one universal historical truth." The Things We Never Say by Elizabeth Strout Strout, a former Pulitzer Prize winner and double Booker nominee, tells the story of a high school history teacher in his 50s who feels adrift in modern America. When a secret emerges, he must face big questions about his relationships and life choices. The judges said: "A novel that engages with the deeply divisive politics of present-day America, without itself becoming divisive. This is the kind of book we need now: a calm antidote to contemporary events." John of John by Douglas Stuart The third novel by Stuart is about a fashion student who is drawn back to his home in a small, religious community in the Outer Hebrides in the mid-1990s. He and his father both nurse secrets. And both are called John. The judges said: "A rich and moving novel about a father and son who live on a remote Scottish island in the 1990s, where small-town secrets and buried shame reverberate to surprising, devastating and even joyous effect." The winner will receive £50,000 and will be announced in London on 9 November. The ceremony will be broadcast live on a special edition of BBC Radio 4's Front Row. Longlisted books that did not make the final cut included Emma Cline's Switzy, which had been seen by some as a frontrunner for the prize. "Believe me, this is a nailed-on Booker winner," critic Giles Coren wrotein the Times,externalthis weekend. "If this one doesn't win, I'll eat Mary Beard." Dame Mary responded on Tuesday: "I know Giles Coren said he wants to eat me if Switzy isn't on the shortlist. "Well, I'm going to get the cooker prepared and ask him how he wants me done." Headline: Invitation for men to 'experience hot flushes'
Body: A common symptom of the menopause is a hot flush Partners of women going through the menopause are being invited to experience one of the symptoms at a forthcoming support event. At the Menopaus'ull Support Network event in Hull next month, health group Over The Bloody Moon will be taking one of its MenoVests, allowing people to experience a hot flush – one of the symptoms of the menopause. Sarah Weichardt, who co-manages the project, said: "We're particularly interested in getting men along to come and experience the MenoVest, just so that they can understand what women go through." The event will be at Princes Quay shopping centre on 17 October, from 10:30 until 14:30 BST. "It's not just a hot flush, it's what the hot flush brings with it," said Weichardt. "So it could be panic, it could be anxiety. It's experiencing it all at the same time." She said she hoped the vest would give people a "better understanding of what women are going through". "The more people we can get to experience it, the better," she added. The menopause describes the end of a woman's reproductive years, and often happens at about the age of 50. The period leading up to this is called the perimenopause, which is when many women notice their periods becoming unpredictable. Other symptoms can include mood shifts, difficulty sleeping, and discomfort during sex. Weichardt said her organisation had a banner with nearly 40 symptoms on it. Many women "don't necessarily know that they're going into the menopause or they're perimenopausal" until they see the banner – and then they sometimes have a "lightbulb moment", she said. Once women have "accepted it and are happy" they are menopausal or peri-menopausal, they can seek the support they need, she added. There is also a Menopaus'ull Support Network event in Beverley on 10 October between 10:30 and 13:30 BST at the Toll Gavel Church. Headline: Ed Sheeran's next US concerts cancelled due to storm warning
Body: Ed Sheeran's concerts in Massachusetts on Friday and Saturday have been cancelled because of severe weather warnings in the area. The singer had been scheduled to perform two shows at the Gillette Stadium in Foxborough, near Boston, as part of his current US tour. The tour has been in the headlines because of a row over a decision to drop Sheeran's support act Macklemore for making pro-Palestinian comments on stage. Stadium owners including the Gillette Stadium's Robert Kraft lobbied for his removal. Astatement from the venue,externalsaid: "Due to the severe weather warnings in place in Boston and across New England throughout the weekend and following consultation with local officials, the promoter and tour have made the difficult decision to cancel the Ed Sheeran concerts at Gillette Stadium." It added: "The decision was made with the safety of fans, staff and everyone involved in the shows as the top priority. "Refunds are available now at the point of purchase. Ticketholders who purchased through Ticketmaster will be automatically refunded." Weather warnings for high winds are in force in the area until the early hours of Sunday, and officials have told drivers to minimise travel. Sheeran was at the eye of a very different storm last week after the decision to drop Macklemore from his tour. The decision came after the rapper made on-stage comments at earlier concerts including calling for "free Palestine" and referring to "genocide" in Gaza, as well as showing images of Gaza. Kraft, who is Jewish, accused the US rapper of hate speech and said Macklemore would not be allowed to appear at the Gillette Stadium, the home of his New England Patriots American football team. Sheeran said the decision to drop Macklemore was made by his promoter, not by him. The promoter said venue owners including Kraft would have refused to let the concerts take place if Macklemore was on the bill. Macklemore's removal from the tour led Sheeran's other support and backing artists to pull out in protest, and sparked a heated debate over free speech and the role of politics in music. Returning to the stage last weekend, Sheeran told fans he "had to take and make difficult decisions - and I am making mistakes - and I'm so, so sorry". Headline: Badenoch registers gift of £8,177 for Murdoch meeting in Greece
Body: Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has registered gifts worth £8,177 covering travel and accommodation for a meeting with media mogul Rupert Murdoch in Greece. Badenoch, along with her husband Hamish and shadow minister Alex Burghart, were flown to Athens on 24 August - with the costs paid for by the Murdoch family's News Corp UK organisation. Badenoch's spokesperson said: "Kemi was pleased to meet Rupert Murdoch and senior News Corp and News UK executives. "The visit has been declared in full in the usual way." The spokesperson added: "Kemi values serious engagement with Britain's major media organisations and the people who run them (including at the BBC) and will continue to make the case for a free and independent press." The figureswere published,externalin the latest register of members' financial interests, in which MPs must report gifts worth more than £300 within 28 days of receipt. In the latest list, Prime Minister Andy Burnham registered three tickets worth £677.34 for seats in the directors' lounge at Everton's first game of the Premier League season. In the record of her meeting with Murdoch, Badenoch lists the following gifts for her and her husband from News Corp UK: An outbound flight from Rome to Athens and a return flight to London, amounting to an estimated value of £4,000 Ground transportation and transfers costing £1,752.50 Accommodation costing £2,425.45. She describes the purpose of the visit as an "off-site meetings with Mr K R Murdoch and other senior executives from News Corp and News UK". Burghart, the Conservative shadow Northern Ireland secretary, also attended the meeting and has registered a gift of £4,088.97, covering flights, accommodation and transportation. The meeting took place shortly after Badenoch met Italian Prime Minister Georgia Meloni in Italy. Badenoch previously met Murdoch, along with other News Corp executives in 2022, when she was an international trade minister. Murdoch stepped down as News Corp chair in 2023 transitioning to the role of chairman emeritus. His son Lachlan became chair of the company, which owns UK media organisations including Virgin Radio, TalkSPORT, and the newspapers the Sun and the Times. UK politicians over the years have sought to develop good relationships with Murdoch and in 2011 Labour's Tony Blair became godfather to his daughter. Murdoch's publications have switched political allegiances throughout the decades, backing the Conservatives in the 1980s and early 90s and switching to Labour in 1997, before returning to the Conservatives in 2010. Headline: 'I was angry at my husband - I didn't know he had dementia'
Body: Helen said she thought her husband was "just being a grumpy middle-aged man" Helen Beaumont spent years arguing with her husband before realising he had a terminal illness. Helen, who lives in Manchester, married Clive when she was 21 and the couple had their two children two decades later. While she expected parenthood to change things - when elements of Clive's personality appeared to shift she spent years frustrated. She wondered why he had stopped listening, had become unreliable, was unable to get a job and had been diagnosed with depression. About five years later, when Clive was 46, he was diagnosed with young onset dementia. He died aged 51. Helen, now 75, said if Clive had received an earlier diagnosis they could have had "at least two years when we weren't fighting all the time". Clive Beaumont spent more than two decades working for the army before developing young onset dementia Since Clive's death in 1999, Helen has been working as a dementia researcher, raising awareness of his condition and continuing his legacy through her charity, The Clive Project. She continues to tell her story because there is still "more to be done" to help dementia patients and their families, she said. Helen described her late-husband as a calm, level-headed and "very active guy" who used to run marathons, even "before it was popular". "Clive was unflappable," she said. "He reckoned he failed if he lost his temper." But as Clive approached his 40s things began to change. "You can't really tell at what stage somebody's behaviour changes," she said. "Younger people in particular are always going to be difficult to diagnose. "And he covered up some things. He never admitted to me that he was having problems with reading and writing." While Helen had never before heard of dementia in younger people, she said she "knew there was something wrong". "I would make plans and he would forget he was looking after the children," she said. "We had very many arguments about it. "He said, 'I'm just growing old' - and he was early forties then." Clive first went to the GP about his symptoms at age 40 and he was diagnosed with depression Clive was made redundant when he was 44 and after taking on odd jobs, he struggled to get another permanent role. "I had to fill in his job application forms," Helen recalled. "He couldn't do it." Helen said Clive's symptoms began to lead to tensions between them. "He went shopping, he bought things like cream and chocolates instead of fish fingers and bread," she said. "And I just couldn't understand it. "I was cross with him - really cross with him for quite a lot of the time. "We could have a conversation and then it was like it had never happened." "I didn't know it was dementia. "With hindsight you think, 'How could I have been so silly?'. "But I talked to a medic friend and I said, 'I think there's something wrong. He might have something like dementia'. "And she said he couldn't possibly - not at his age." Clive's diagnosis came six years after he first went to his GP presenting symptoms Finally, when Clive was 46, he was sent for neurological tests. "Clive was never depressed," Helen said. "The symptoms had been confused. "For a long time they refused to admit that a healthy man in his early 40s could have dementia. "Eventually he got to see a neurologist and six months later I was told over a telephone call that he was very sorry to say my husband had pre-senile dementia, [as it was then referred to]. "There was no treatment and very little support." Dementia is associated with an ongoing decline of brain functioning Symptoms can include memory loss, slower thinking speed, and lower levels of understanding, judgement and mood,according to the NHS,external The condition is often associated with old age, butaccording to Dementia UK,external, 7.5% of people with dementia in the UK have young onset dementia, meaning their symptoms began below the age of 65 Young onset dementia often develops in people between the ages of 45 and 65 but can affect people of any age Helen said caring for Clive was like having a third child For about a year Helen balanced her job with raising her then three and four-year-old children - while also caring for Clive. "I just had three children," she said. "Two of them I could pick up when I wanted them somewhere where they weren't. And Clive, I had to cajole along." Helen said the family were able to do normal activities like going to the park or the cinema for some time - but then Clive became more difficult to care for. "There was a time where we were on the M14 and he tried to get out of the car," she said. "And in he last couple of years he could be quite aggressive." She said when he left the house and went missing she knew he would need full-time care in a residential home. "Fortunately, somebody noticed how uncomfortable he was walking and asked him in for a cup of tea and then got in touch with the police," she said. Clive in 1996 , three years before he died Helen said she felt "fortunate" that the NHS had covered the costs of social care for Clive. Nonetheless, finding care for Clive was not easy. "He was moved three times," Helen said. "And as he got worse, it got more difficult for them to manage him. "Looking after somebody like Clive counts as social care - not medical care." Five years after his initial diagnosis, Clive died in a residential home in 1999, aged 51. After Clive died, Helen said: "I was very depressed. "I kept going. It took me a long time to get back to having some joy in my life" In 2008, at the age of 58, Helen made a big change. "My daughter and son had left home to go to university and I moved from Oxford to Manchester to pursue a new career as a dementia researcher," she said. She did a PhD in 2015 and specialised in using magnetic resonance imaging to investigate brain changes in people with dementia with the aim of improving diagnosis. "What brings me to the university every day is a determination to ensure other families don't have to go through the years of anguish I went through with my husband Clive," she said. According to Dementia UK,external, the average waiting time for a diagnosis of young onset dementia in the UK is just under four years and five months - as opposed to an average of  just under two years and two months for a diagnosis of dementia in over 65s. Helen said she felt "very sad" that she had spent so many years being angry at Clive for something which had been out of his control. "I was trying to get him to do things that he was no longer capable of doing. "It makes me feel very sad. "And that's why I go out and talk to people now so that people can understand." Helen said awareness of young onset dementia had grown since the 90s - but diagnoses still took too long. "It still takes four or five years to get a diagnosis and I'm absolutely certain it's no easier now than it was back then to find suitable care, she said. "There are treatments becoming available. "But you will not treat it if you can't diagnose it. "There is more to be done." Headline: Gaming pays me double what I earned as a teacher
Body: Jarvs Tasker is the director and founder of Jarvs Indie Insights and left her teaching career behind seven years ago In 2019, Jarvs Tasker was forced to give up her teaching career due to chronic illness when she was just 28. Fast forward seven years, and she earns double her former annual salary, running Jarvs Indie Insights, which provides communication and marketing within the gaming industry. She visited the University of Suffolk's e-sport building in Ipswich to celebrate independent game developers and studios on Wednesday. "I can comfortably say it probably would have taken me about 20 years in teaching to earn what I make now," she said. When Tasker left teaching, she initially started volunteering for PlayStation's YouTube channel, but she said there was lots of crossover between the two industries. "Managing a community is very similar to managing a class of kids, so there's a lot of crossover skills there, but actually, video games is one of those industries where a lot of people come into it later on in life." Tasker, who lives in Exeter, believed young people might not know the "many pathways" available in the industry. "The video games community is very strong, and they will champion people that love what they do, but they'll also notice if you're in it just for the money," she continued. "Passion is the most important thing." Asked about the impact of AI, she said she believed the industry was doing a "really great job" at rejecting it, because players hated it. "I think as an industry we should be really proud of the fact that we're still championing human creativity and that the audience is also on board with that," she added. Mark Backler of Game Anglia says the group works to raise awareness about careers in the gaming industry Tasker had been in Suffolk as part of an event hosted by Game Anglia to showcase the growing independent gaming industry in the East of England. Mark Backler from Game Anglia said the industry wasnow one of the biggest in the UK, and while he agreed it was competitive, it was "more possible than ever to develop and release your own independent games". "It's like being a content creator - it's tricky to be one of the standout ones, but it is doable," he said. He added it was difficult to tell how AI would change things, but a lot of players were against its use. Developer Sam Read-Graves says the industry is growing in the East of England Sam Read-Graves is a developer at Read Graves and works specifically in the East. At the event, he said the gaming industry had "grown massively in the past 10 years". "Because of schemes like Game Anglia across Suffolk, Essex, Cambridgeshire, Norfolk, there are really great clusters of a lot of students and a lot of developers, and I like to think that this has started to bring in studios who could make the big games. "When it comes to those games like Call of Duty or FIFA, those at the minute aren't going to come out of the East of England because we don't have big studios. "But when it comes to independent developers, there's no reason those games can't financially be as big." Abbygale Dunn studied game design and programming at university Abbygale Dunn, 22, is the founder and director of Astral Forge, an independent game development company based in Essex. She said there was "so much space for women" in the industry today. "It's obviously daunting. When I studied, there were only about three women in my course," she said. "Everyone is so kind; it's really not as bad as it seems, especially nowadays. "As a programmer myself, which is more rare for women to be in, I've never felt out of place." Game scout Omar Khalil says it can be hard to create the next big game Omar Khalil is game scout lead at Entity and said there was "no shortage of talent in the UK", but it was challenging to create the next big game. "There are so many games out there right now, and it's not like there aren't enough good games; it's how do you get visibility on those games?" he explained. "I think that's the biggest challenge." Headline: Students strike across Germany in protest against military service
Body: School strikes are taking place across Germany to protest against the possible reintroduction of compulsory military service. One of the organisers of the strike, Bela Breitner, from School Strike Against Compulsory Military Service said the federal government was "serious about gradually reintroducing compulsory military service". At one protest in Hamburg, demonstrators waved flags and held up banners emblazoned with the words "We won't take part in your wars". German Chancellor Friedrich Merzhas made boosting Germany's militarya priority following Russia's invasion of Ukraine. A new law introducingvoluntary military service came into force in January, with the aim of recruiting volunteers to increase the number of soldiers. However, if the security situation worsens or if too few volunteers come forward, a form of compulsory military service could be considered by Germany's Parliament, the Bundestag. Under the law, all 18-year-olds in Germany are being sent a questionnaire asking if they are interested and willing to join the armed forces. One protester, 16-year-old Elias Bernhard, from Hamburg, said that the responses to the questionnaires "show that young people do not want to join the Bundeswehr [Germany's armed forces]". "That is why I am out on the streets today. That is why we are serious about striking until compulsory military service is off the table. We will carry on." The questionnaire is mandatory for men and voluntary for women. All 18-year-old men will have to take a medical exam to assess their fitness for possible military service. The organisers of the protests, say the trigger came after some 18-year-olds in the northern German towns of Kiel and Flensburg, were sent official invitations for medical exams, even though they expressed no interest in joining the army on their registration forms. The group says over a hundred demonstrations are planned across Germany, including in Kiel, Hamburg, Berlin and Frankfurt. A spokesperson for the Defence Ministry told the BBC that under the law, the obligation to undergo a medical examination applies "to all men liable for military service who were born after 31 December 2007". This also applies to people who have stated that they have no interest in compulsory military service. The spokesperson said that since July around 1,000 18-year-old men, who showed no interest in the army, have had the medical exam. During the Cold War, Germany, like many other European countries, had a large army. But it reduced its armed forces during the 1990s after the fall of the Iron Curtain. Germany's former Chancellor, Angela Merkel, ended compulsory military service in 2011. But now, in the face of perceived threats from Russia and heavy pressure from Germany's traditional ally, the US, Merz has vowed to transform the Bundeswehr into Europe's strongest conventional army. The Bundeswehr currently has around 186,700 troops. By the early 2030s, Germany wants to raise the number to 260,000, supplemented by around 200,000 reservists, in order to meet new Nato force targets and strengthen Germany's defences. Headline: Nigerian football enduring 'worst time in history' - Odegbami
Body: Nigeria's men failed to qualify for both the 2022 and 2026 Fifa World Cups As Nigeria begin their 2027 Africa Cup of Nations (Afcon) qualifying campaign, former international Segun Odegbami, who won the tournament on home soil in 1980, says the country is experiencing the "worst time" in its football history. Over the past 12 months both the Super Eagles and Super Falcons failed to qualify for their respective Fifa World Cups. But beyond the failure of the senior national teams, Nigeria has also endured disappointing results at age-group level and in African club competitions - although the West Africans recently reached the quarter-finals of the Under-20 Women's World Cup. Odegbami says the diminishing returns represent a "tectonic shift" for one of the continent's traditional powers. "It has never been this bad in our entire history that we didn't qualify for the World Cup," the 74-year-old told BBC Sport Africa. "Our girls (the Super Falcons), who were African champions, failed to win a competition (the 2025 Women's Afcon) that was just there for their taking. All our junior teams are not doing well. "Our local league is not bringing in money. Something is definitely wrong." The crisis has already triggered major changes within the Nigeria Football Federation (NFF). Its president Ibrahim Gusau, general secretary Mohammed Sanusi and multiple members of the federation's executive committeeresigned last month following mounting criticism. Odegbami says Nigerian football had not been represented by its "first XI administrators" and has called for a restructure to create the conditions for long-term development. "The outcry by Nigerians was total. Everybody wanted them out, to the extent that the President of the country himself (Bola Tinubu) made the pronouncement that he wanted reforms," he said. "Everything came together like a jigsaw puzzle and is working now for us to produce a blueprint that will cover every aspect of our football development." Nigeria to miss Women's World Cup after South Africa and Ghana win play-offs 'Motherhood should not be the end of anyone's story' A joint delegation from world governing body Fifa and the Confederation of African Football (Caf) has been involved in discussions with the National Sports Commission (NSC) over the future structure of Nigerian football. The parties are working towards a roadmap for comprehensive reforms but NFF elections, scheduled for 27 September, have been suspended. President Tinubu stated his desire for reform to overcome what he called "repeated failures". Emmanuel Ikpeme has been appointed NFF interim general secretary, with Ademola Olajire the interim deputy general secretary. The changes have prompted renewed debate among stakeholders over whether the country needs a deeper restructuring. Nigerian sports journalist Fisayo Dairo believes any reform must extend beyond a change in leadership. "The reform should be the setting up of a proper framework and structure that our football can thrive on," Dairo told BBC Sport Africa. "[We need to] develop national teams, harness talent from the grassroots and have governance that incorporates all forms of stakeholders. "The corporate world has to be fully represented so that the administration is able to generate funds." Segun Odegbami scored 23 goals in 47 appearances for Nigeria and was named in the team of the tournament as the Super Eagles won Afcon 1980 For Odegbami, the current situation is a stark contrast to the era in which he helped transform the Nigerian game. Nicknamed 'Mathematical' for his precision and skill on the ball, the forward was part of the Super Eagles side that won the country's first continental title in 1980, beating Algeria 3-0 in the final in Lagos. "We had unprecedented support and fortunately the stars aligned with us," he said. "It was an indescribable atmosphere during that period. "That experience you can't even describe and compare. [It remains] indelible in our minds." Nigeria lifted the Afcon trophy again in 1994 and 2013, and finished as runners-up at the 2023 edition. The team also finished third in 2019 and at this year's finals in Morocco. However, Odegbami argues sport has "not been a priority" of successive governments and believes his nation has been failed by football administrators since the mid 1990s. "The pilots are not guiding us well, they haven't guided us well," he said. "And that has affected every aspect of our football development: the grassroots, the discovery of players, the development of the players, the establishment of the institutions that will take care of them, the academies, the clubs that they will go into both locally and internationally. "What is the coaching methodology? What is the philosophy of our football in the country? "What is our culture, what is our style?" Nigeria's Super Eagles currently play their home matches at Godswill Akpabio Stadium in Uyo Yet, alongside the failure to reach the past two men's World Cups, concerns over deteriorating infrastructure and inadequate investment have become recurring themes in discussions about the state of the Nigerian game. Across Africa, meanwhile, other nations have continued to invest in hosting major competitions. Senegal will be the venue for theYouth Olympic Gamesnext month, South Africa, Zimbabwe and Namibia are holding next year's men's Cricket World Cup,Kenya will stage the 2029 World Athletics Championship,and Morocco will co-host the 2030 World Cup with Spain and Portugal. Odegbami has bemoaned the fact that top-class stadiums which Nigeria used to possess have fallen into disrepair after being neglected. He name-checked the National Stadium in Surulere, Lagos, which hosted games during the 1980 and 2000 Afcons, the Liberty Stadium (now Obafemi Awolowo Stadium) in Ibadan, Kaduna's Ahmadu Bello Stadium and the UJ Esuene Stadium in Calabar. "I weep when I think of the amount of damage they have done to Nigerian football - the infrastructure that we had in the country, some of the historic monuments that were facilities for football in this country," he said. "Whether it was wilful, whether it was ignorance, they did irreparable damage to what was Nigeria's heritage. "Uyo is the best we have in Nigeria, but it is not half as good as what we had from the 1960s to the 90s." The Super Eagles will begin their Afcon 2027 qualifying campaign against Madagascar at the Godswill Akpabio Stadium in Uyo on Friday (16:00 GMT) before travelling to Guinea-Bissau on 29 September. Former African Footballer of the Year Victor Osimhen has been ruled out of Eric Chelle's squad through injury.

Headline: Police get more time to quiz suspects in alleged plot against Jewish community
Body: The men can now be detained up until 4 October Detectives have been granted an extra week to question two men arrested as part of an investigation into an alleged plot to target the Jewish community in Manchester. The extension means the men - both in the 30s - can now be detained until 4 October. The men were arrested in the Northern Quarter area of Manchester on 20 September - the eve of Yom Kippur, when thousands of British Jews were in synagogues. A spokesperson for the Metropolitan Police, which is leading the investigation, said their work was "ongoing and officers continue to pursue a number of lines of enquiry". The two men were detained on suspicion of offences under Section 41 of the Terrorism Act 2000, the force said on Tuesday. Sources told the BBC thatthe suspected plot was "fairly imminent"and in the later stages of planning. Police said searches at properties on Epworth Street in Liverpool and Lancaster Road in Salford had also taken place. Yom Kippur is considered to be the holiest day in the Jewish calendar. A spokesperson for the Community Security Trust, which coordinates security for Jewish communities in the UK, said on Tuesday that the suspected plot was "utterly chilling coming so close to the anniversary of the terrorist attack at Heaton Park Synagogue last year". They added: "[This] is another reminder of the serious terrorist threat facing Jewish communities in this current time." Headline: Andy Burnham refuses to back third runway at Heathrow
Body: Prime Minister Andy Burnham has refused to say whether he backs a third runway at Heathrow after it emerged that the expansion of the London airport could be delayed by up to four years. Burnham - who, as Mayor of Greater Manchester, opposed the project - told Sunday With Laura Kuenssberg: "I think principally, it's a matter for London and Londoners." He added: "I think we ought to hear the voice of people there first. It's not right for me to just jump straight in on the back of the consultation." Former Chancellor Rachel Reeves had championed the runway to boost the economy, with a schedule to open by 2035 but Heathrow indicated on Saturday it may not be operational before 2039. As Manchester's mayor, Burnham had been against the project over concerns that it would delay investment in transport for the north. When he took office, he said he was "open-minded" about the scheme. As he prepared for his first annual Labour Party conference as prime minister, Burnham said: "There's a consultion but there are different views and you have to take those views seriously in coming to a decision." In response, Heathrow said: "We agree with the prime minister that local voices must be heard. We know from consistent polling over the last decade that communities support our plans for expansion and support is only growing over time." The project, estimated to cost £33bn, has attracted opposition from environmental campaigners and local resident groups as well as Mayor of London Sadiq Khan. A third runway would mean demolishing hundreds of homes, diverting rivers and rerouting a section of the M25 motorway through a tunnel. But it is estimated it would create 100,000 jobs and provide a major boost to the UK economy. The number of flights from the site, currently capped at 480,000 a year, could go up to 720,000, or nearly 2,000 a day on average. A new runway has been backed by the unions Unite and the GMB. Sharon Graham, Unite's general secretary said: "A third runway at Heathrow is essential and we need to get going with it. "This is more than just infrastructure. It's about investing in the workforce, securing the future of good, unionised jobs and a guaranteed market for UK steel." Earlier this weekend, Heathrow conceded that meeting the original deadline would be increasingly difficult without further steps to simplify the planning process. It said it hoped to secure planning permission by 2029 and then open the runway "within a decade". The Department for Transport said the timeline had "always been ambitious" and it would continue to work with stakeholders "at pace" on the matter. Headline: BBC upholds complaints over Victoria Beckham slur on Have I Got News For You
Body: Complaints about the broadcast of a swear word in connection with Victoria Beckham during an episode of BBC One's Have I Got News For You have been upheld, the corporation's executive complaints unit (ECU) has ruled. The show, from 7 November last year, hosted by comic and presenter Katherine Ryan, featured an email allegedly sent by Sir David Beckham in which the word was used. Ryan told the show's panellists: "I don't know that we are allowed to broadcast the c-word, but you did reference Victoria Beckham earlier and we'll allow that." Two viewers complained that this was gratuitously offensive, andthe BBC saidthere was no justification for a comment which "presented Victoria Beckham as equivalent to a particularly offensive word". The ECU finding has been reported to the management of BBC Content. As a result, a version of the programme edited in light of the finding will replace the version currently on iPlayer. The ECU statement in full said: "The relevant BBC Editorial Guidelines do not require programmes to avoid giving offence, but do require that any offence should be editorially justified. "In the ECU's judgement, while the inclusion of the c-word in the programme derived editorial justification from David Beckham's alleged use of it and the satirical reflections this prompted, there was no such justification for a comment which presented Victoria Beckham as equivalent to a particularly offensive word." In November, the ECU responded to complaints from viewers it said were "unhappy with the inclusion of strong language in the programme". It said "the use of the strong language was editorially justified as the panel were discussing a current news story about Sir David Beckham and directly quoting from leaked emails in which he had used the word in question, leading to further discussion". It added that it was "common practice" to carry a clear verbal warning at the start of post-watershed programmes with very strong language, which was what happened for this particular episode of the show. "It is never our intention to offend our audience," the statement added.

Headline: Some BBC channels and radio stations may well have to close, director general says
Body: This video can not be played 'We can't guarantee any programme or channel forever'  - BBC Director General Matt Brittin The BBC's financial situation and changing audience habits "may well mean" some channels and radio stations have to close so resources can be invested in on-demand services, its director general has said. As the BBC seeks £500m savings, Matt Brittin told BBC One's Sunday With Laura Kuenssberg that "we wouldn't guarantee any programme or any channel will exist forever". He said: "The tight financial situation means that we're having to look at some of those decisions a bit sooner than we might like." Audience behaviour is also rapidly changing, he said. "If most of an audience is getting things on demand, we have to look at the value and the cost of all of those different services." Brittin said his focus when making savings was to "minimise the impact on audience". He explained: "We might have some channels and services where maybe 100,000 people are watching the broadcast service but 500,000 are getting those programmes on iPlayer. "When's the right time to migrate that service fully to being on-demand? And part of my job is to safeguard value for money for the licence fee payer." The BBC should go "in different ways to reach audiences and we're locked into yesterday's model of how people consume content, and actually the audience is always already living in tomorrow's world", he said. In recent months, the BBC has announced a series of closures of jobs and programmes including Blankety Blank, Celebrity Mastermind, Live At The Apollo and Football Focus, and further cuts are expected. Brittin took over as BBC director general in May after a decade as president of Google in Europe, the Middle East and Africa. Asked by Kuenssberg if he would allow a programme to be made and presented by AI, Brittin replied: "I would do, within guardrails." He added: "We want to experiment with this technology and understand what it can and can't do, but I'm here because I believe in human creativity. "I don't think anything we do should be replaced by AI. I think there are lots of places where AI can help us make the licence fee go further, but also help us in our decision-making and creativity. But it's not a substitute for humans." He also warned of the danger of a handful of tech companies having too much control over information in the future. "We're also in this moment where AI is in takeoff. So I think there's a danger that six companies will control access to information in future and the creation of information and misinformation," he said. "Six companies, none of them European, let alone British. In that world, here's the BBC. It's the most trusted organisation by over half a billion people." Asked if he trusted big tech companies he replied: "There's a lot of platforms out there, so I wouldn't trust any platform innately. "And I think what you do is you keep under review how those things work and whether your content can show up in the right place and fulfil its mission. "I think the BBC and our apps and services should be the antidote to the algorithm. Everywhere else you go is driven by some commercial interest." The interview will be available on BBC Sounds and YouTube on Saturday 26 September, then on Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg on BBC One andiPlayerat 09:00 BST on 27 September. Headline: US and Iran hold first talks since June after Trump's 'annihilation' threat
Body: This video can not be played Watch: Trump threatens to 'annihilate' Iran if no deal reached Top Iranian and US officials have held talks at the UN in New York on a day when the US leader said he could "annihilate" the Islamic Republic if the conflict went unresolved. No breakthrough has been reported from the meeting mediated by Qatar and involving Iran's foreign minister and US President Donald Trump's envoy Steve Witkoff - the first since a June ceasefire unravelled. Witkoff said a round of discussions had been completed "that we hope will prove constructive and promising". Iran repeated its demand for the US to end its "acts of aggression". The US and Israel launched air strikes on Iran on 28 February. Iran responded by attacking Israel and US bases in the Gulf and Arab Gulf allies of the US - as well as blocking the Strait of Hormuz. Some 20% of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas used to pass through the strait before the war and its closure has caused wild fluctuations of prices. It has also increased pressure on Trump to find a way of ending the conflict - particularly as the US heads to Congressional elections in November. In his address at the annual meeting of the UN General Assembly in New York on Tuesday, Trump began by touting his accomplishments on the economy, immigration, the border and tackling violent crime - remarks that sounded more pitched to voters the US midterms than the diplomats in the hall. He spent much of his address justifying the war with Iran - a huge contrast with remarks earlier by UN Secretary General António Guterres, who warned global divisions were deepening and underscored the "interdependence" of the world's peoples. The US president argued that the conflict had prevented Tehran from obtaining a nuclear weapon and demonstrated the value of what he described as peace through strength - ultimatums rather than deal-making or compromise. "Will a deal be made with Iran that lets them rebuild and create a far greater country than it ever was before?" he said. "Or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy people and countries again? Do I drive them into hell?" Trump said he believed an Iran deal, which has so far eluded him, would come right after November's elections. The remarks were indicative of his foreign-policy strategy of coercive diplomacy - threatening overwhelming force while keeping negotiations open. Trump later told reporters that American officials had had a "very productive" three-hour meeting with the Iranian delegation on the sidelines of the general assembly. Iran state TV confirmed that Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi had met Witkoff. Iranian foreign ministry spokesman Esmail Baghaei, quoted by state broadcaster IRNA, later said negotiations took part through a Qatari mediator who communicated Tehran's conditions, including an end to the war on all fronts and to US "acts of aggression". The BBC asked Witkoff how the meetings had gone as he was leaving the UN building and he responded with a thumbs up. Witkoff later confirmed on X that the talks had been held "through the mediators, who shuttled between the two sides throughout the day". "They successfully completed a round of discussions that we hope will prove constructive and promising," Witkoff said. "The mediators will continue their work." Since the ceasefire collapsed, both sides have intermittently exchanged fire. Iran has attacked vessels it says have attempted to cross the Strait of Hormuz without authorisation. The US has attacked Iranian sites in the strait - as well as Iranian tankers off the country's coast. The US has also maintained a blockade of Iranian ports, causing a huge disruption to the Iranian economy. In an effort to force Tehran to agree a deal to end the conflict, President Trump has also threatened sanctions against any country that continues trading with Iran. But so far, there has been no indication of a change of course in Iran, which insists the US and Israel end their war, including against the Iran-backed Shia group Hezbollah in Lebanon which Israel has been attacking. Yemen's Houthis - also allied to Iran - have recently intesified attacks aimed at disrupting oil shipping from Saudi Arabia, promting an escalation of the conflict with the kingdom. Headline: Barrecore and Boom Cycle owner suddenly shuts studios
Body: The fitness company behind high-end exercise classes Barrecore, Boom Cycle, and Kobox has suddenly shut all its studios. Common Bond emailed customers announcing its locations, all of which are currently in London, were closed "until further notice". The firm describes itself as a wellness collective and charges £2,400 for 12 months of unlimited classes. It also runs Reformcore and Triyoga brands and said in August last year it had ten sites. Its website is no longer publicly accessible. The BBC has contacted Common Bond for comment. The email sent to customers on Wednesday seen by the BBC said: "We're sorry to let you know that all Common Bond studios are closed until further notice. "We sincerely apologise for the inconvenience and disruption this may cause . We understand this is frustrating, and we appreciate your patience while we work through this." Instructors have told the BBC they were told last week they would not be paid on time and that they only found out about the studios closures from the Wednesday email. One instructor said she and her colleagues were told their pay would be delayed on the day it was due on 14 August. She said: "In good faith, I continued to teach my classes without any news on when or if payment would be made. I have heard absolutely nothing since." The Wandsworth branch of Common Bond's London Barrecore locations It is not clear how many instructors and customers have been hit by the sudden decision to shut the studios down. Companies House filings for Common Bond show the company was incorporated in June last year, so has it has not yet published any accounts. The most recent filings show a director, Ben Allen, left the role last month. Gaspar Lipszyc, listed as a Belgian national living in Spain, is the only currently shown director of the company. Barrecore is a brand specialising in barre, a fitness discipline that combines pilates, ballet, and yoga. Headline: 'This is the final offer,' says NI secretary over £1.5bn Stormont funding package
Body: Northern Ireland Secretary Chris Bryant, pictured in early September The Northern Ireland Secretary of State has said the government's £1.5bn financial package for Stormont is his "final offer" and has given executive parties until next Thursday to respond. Sir Chris Bryant said there was "no more money" available and that the Northern Ireland Executive needed to agree on a budget. He said he would have to consider "every eventuality" if the executive failed to reach an agreement, including the possibility of a budget being passed at Westminster but wanted to "sit down and I'll be as cooperative as I possibly can". However some parties have criticised the deadline with the DUP's Diane Dodds describing it as "reckless". Earlier this month, Bryantmade an offer of a financial package worth about £1.5bn over the next three years- that was a rise from an initial proposal of £1.1bn. But executive parties said it did not go far enoughand have argued that significant gaps remain before they can agree to a deal that would allow them to set a budget. Some six months have passed since the executive should have set a budget for this financial year. Speaking to BBC Newsline, Sir Chris said he had given executive parties until noon next Thursday to come back to him with a plan for agreeing a budget for this year and the following two years. "It's my final offer. It's a good offer," he said. He added: "There is no more money. The financial situation in the UK government at the moment is very, very tight." Asked whether he was prepared to introduce a budget at Westminster if the executive did not accept the offer, Sir Chris said: "I've got to look at every eventuality. Of course I have. I've got to be responsible about this." He said he did not want to legislate for a budget and would prefer to work with executive parties to reach an agreement. "If it's impossible to set a budget through the executive, then somebody else will have to do it for them," he said, adding that he was "not at that stage yet". Sir Chris also said the executive would have to consider raising additional revenue, but that it was not his job to tell ministers how to do so. He said he had not specifically raised the introduction of water charges with executive parties. "We've been underfunded for over a decade, so how do we ever catch up," Kimmins told The View Infrastructure Minister Liz Kimmins said Northern Ireland had been"underfunded for over a decade".,external The NI Fiscal Council has found that Scotland and Wales are currently funded above their levels of assessed need while NI isat or slightly below its assessed funding need. Speaking to BBC's The View programme, the Sinn Féin minister said: "The people here pay their taxes, they're entitled to good public services." "We'll continue to stand up for that and ensure that message is heard loud and clear and I think the executive is united in that," she added. Diane Dodds says the secretary of state's deadline is "reckless and unrealistic" DUP MLADiane Dodds described the Northern Ireland Secretary's final offer,externalas "reckless" and "unrealistic". "He needs to be honest with people in Northern Ireland. Is he....going to stand over the decimation of public services in Northern Ireland and severe cuts to those public services or is he going to be realistic and sit down with parties instead of haranguing people over the media on this issues," she told The View. She said Sir Chris knew Northern Ireland was "underfunded relative to need and relative to other parts of the United Kingdom". Executive parties have been in negotiations with the government in a bid to get increased funding. Finance Minister John O'Dowd previously said the current published financial pressures facing Stormont departments were around £1.6bn, adding: "So we have a bit to go." Northern Ireland Executive parties had rejected an initial £1.1bn package over three years The Ulster Unionist Party (UUP)'s Steve Aiken said that "calling this the final offer does not make it a fair or sufficient offer". "The UK government has moved significantly from its opening position, and that should be acknowledged. However, even with extensive savings, the annual funding on offer would barely meet the pressures in health alone. That puts the scale of the Executive's wider problem into stark perspective." He said it had been made clear during meetings that public services need to "deliver to our citizens the same standard of health, education, policing and other services as is available in any other postcode in our nation". The offer on the table from the government includes £450m extra for day-to-day pressures this year, as well as an additional £400m in 2027/28 and 2028/29. Headline: Pope says 'scourge' of abuse must be rooted out as he visits Lourdes
Body: Hundreds of thousands of people have gathered to hear the Pope speak during a four-day visit to France Pope Leo has called on French bishops to root out the "scourge" of sexual abuse in the Roman Catholic church, telling them to "maintain the greatest vigilance", ahead of a meeting with abuse survivors. The Pope delivered the message to bishops during a private meeting at the Sanctuary of Our Holy Lady of Lourdes, a holy site in southern France, on the third day of his four-day official visit to France. A 2021 inquiry found that clergy or lay members of the Church had abused about 330,000 people as children in France over 70 years. The Pope said Mass in front of thousands of worshippers in Lourdes, before he was scheduled to meet survivors of abuse privately later. Before giving Mass the Pope told the bishops: "You have faced with determination the painful scourge of abuse of minors committed by members of the clergy or within an ecclesial context. "It is important to persevere along the path you have begun, maintaining the greatest vigilance." The gathering of senior church leaders was held behind closed doors and the remarks were later released to reporters. The Lourdes gathering came a day after an estimated 700,000 people flocked to the Place de la Concorde in Paris to hear the pontiff speak. Huge crowds cheered and waved as he rode down the Champs-Élysées Avenue greeting followers from his open-topped popemobile. On Friday, the Pope also met French President Emmanuel Macron. Pope Leo greeted people from his popemobile at the Sanctuary of Our Lady of Lourdes During Saturday's Mass in Paris, the Pope told worshippers that Catholics should not keep their faith to themselves but "let it overflow so that those you meet may be refreshed". The leader of the Catholic Church alsoaddressed young people in his speech, describing them as "today's Church". "How beautiful it is to see your enthusiasm, energy and commitment, and the joy you bring to Christian communities," he said. The number of regular worshippers  in France has fallen from 35% of the population in 1960 to less than 5% today, while the number of priests has shrunk by two-thirds from 25,000 in 1990 to fewer than 9,000. The Pope said Mass at the Meadow of the Shrine of Our Lady of Lourdes But in recent years there have been signs of a growing interest in religious tradition, with the number of adult baptisms more than doubling in five years to hit 10,000 in 2025. Later on Sunday the Pope will meet staff and residents at the health facility at Lourdes, before taking part in a torchlight procession in the evening. It is the Pope's first official visit to France since being chosen to lead the Roman Catholic church in May 2025. Popes have regularly visited France, a country with an avowedly secular modern political history but deep Catholic roots. Why is the Pope in France? Headline: Fresh bedsheets and dusk walks: Expert tips for sleep-deprived freshers
Body: Twenty-year-old Anna-May manages on about five hours' sleep a night It's the start of university - you're already on your fourth themed night out of the week and have signed up for every quirky-sounding society your campus has to offer. But your relationship with your bed could be key to keeping up with a busy social life, as well as that lengthy reading list. "If you can get out before 11am-ish then there's a part of the brain, just behind the eyes, that responds to light," says Jo Baker, a psychotherapist and student sleep and mental health expert. "Getting daylight early on in the day is really going to help to keep your body in check. How you sleep at night starts with how you wake up in the morning." Sleep is essential to learning and absorbing information. But late nights out, noisy flatmates and a strange new bed can mean good sleep habits go out the window. She tries to stay awake during her commute to uni but admits sometimes "dosing off a bit" For Anna-May, 20, it's her four-hour round trip from Kendal, Cumbria to study dance at the University of Salford that leaves her short of sleep. She gets about five hours a night - the alarm goes at 05:00. "I track my sleep and get worried about how little I will get, and then sometimes that keeps me up," she says. "I can tell I'm more tired towards the end of the week and things can feel harder." Forcing yourself to have an early night isn't going to work, according to Baker, especially if you end up lying wide awake in bed. "Your brain learns this is somewhere I lie and get stressed about not being able to sleep - so the most important thing is a consistent waking time," she says. When you feel groggy, it's tempting to chug multiple coffees or fizzy drinks. But caffeine hangs around in the body and blocks the build-up of sleepiness throughout the day. Too many flat whites and you'll not only be short of cash - you could also develop a sleep problem. Alcohol may also be a tempting way to boost your confidence around new people, but it doesn't help you sleep. "When you fall asleep [after large amounts of alcohol], you're anaesthetised really. It's like having an anaesthetic. You're not asleep," Baker says. In fact, alcohol pushes out the deep sleep which restores you physically, and replaces it with lighter sleep, which doesn't. Emma Young, deputy director of student services for health and wellbeing at Manchester Metropolitan University points out the low-key alternatives during freshers' week. "There are lots of alcohol-free events now, like sip and paint. You can also try wellness and wellbeing clubs, like yoga and crafts, if you don't fancy the sport or music societies." Why caffeine makes some people buzz - and others barely notice Anna-May likes a hot shower or bath before bed, which research suggests helps the body's core temperature to cool down and prepare for sleep. Then the only way she can get to sleep is to watch episodes of Friends on her iPad. "I watch something I have seen time and time again - it's enough to quieten the busy part of my mind and I can fall to sleep," she says. Anna-May, who is studying dance, accepts that watching TV before bed goes "against all the advice" But activities without screens like journalling or reading a book might be best for creating a calm, gradual transition to sleep. Listening to music or a podcast can also work. The natural hormone melatonin rises before bedtime, making us feel sleepy. But watching social media reels or films means your eyes stay active, blocking that process and keeping you awake. Baker also suggests: Switching off screens an hour and a half before bed Avoiding a heavy meal just before going to bed Washing your sheets so they are nice and clean to get into Chucking a throw over your laptop, books and desk so you know work is done for the day Going for a walk at dusk - the changing light is a signal to the brain Keeping your bed for sleeping in (rather than eating, working or watching YouTube) Student sleep expert Jo Baker says making your bed in the morning can help signal that sleep is over Feeling unwell can of course impact your sleep patterns. Freshers' flu is tricky to avoid, but good hand hygiene - washing regularly or using antibacterial hand gel - might just reduce your chances of getting a fever, sore throat and blocked nose, and spending a day or two in bed. Meningitis is far more dangerous and requires urgent medical help (call 999). It can look a lot like freshers' flu but if it's not diagnosed, it can progress very quickly and lead to seizures, brain damage and sepsis.That's why a free NHS vaccine called Men B is now on offer to all freshers students. Many universities recommend planning ahead in case you feel ill and need some medical help at some point, especially if you're living away from home. A typical to-do list should include: Registering with a local GP Finding your nearest chemist Registering with an NHS dentist Finding out where the closest A&E is You might also want to check out what your uni has to offer in terms of mental health support. Some pair up students for peer support and run dedicated 24-hour phone lines. Websites likeStudent Minds,externalhave lots of useful advice and information. And if you're not feeling like yourself, Young suggests a regular call home, to family or a best friend. Have you been affected by issues covered in this story?  Share your experiences. Headline: Tenth woman's body found as South Africa police probe killings
Body: File photo of South African Police Service officers in Johannesburg Police in South Africa have discovered another body in Ekurhuleni, to the east of Johannesburg, bringing the number of women found dead there in recent months to 10. The body was found on Saturday morning and was identified by the friend with whom she had been at a bar the previous evening. The local police commissioner said his force could not rule out the possibility that there was a serial killer on the loose, noting similarities acrossthe 10 deaths in Ekurhuleni, as well as another in Soweto. The deaths have sparked a national outcry about the scale of violence against women in the country, which has one of the highest rates of gender-based violence in the world. The latest body was discovered at a cemetery in the Tembisa neighbourhood north-east of central Johannesburg. Police issued a statement a short while later saying crime scene investigators were at the scene gathering evidence. Officials have yet to publicly identify the victim. The woman's friend told national broadcaster SABC that she recognised her friend's clothes from the previous night when shown a picture of the body. "I don't know what I'm going to say to her children," she said while wiping away tears. "It's painful." Gauteng Police Commissioner Tommy Mthombeni said that, at this early stage in the investigation, it was too soon to say whether the woman's death was linked to the others. He told reporters that the other bodies shared a "similar victimology" that indicated a shared "modus operandi" of killing, which would allow police to determine whether this latest death was linked to the others. "For now, it's not something which we can overrule to say there's a serial killer, but we cannot conclusively indicate as such," Lt Gen Mthombeni said. South Africa has one of the highest homicide rates, with 5,427 people murdered between April and June this year alone. But it is the nature of the recent killings around Johannesburg that has left many women there reeling from the growing death toll. The 10 other bodies have been found in similar circumstances to one another since July. Most of them were found in Kempton Park, one neighbourhood over from Tembisa. Many of the bodies were those of young women and almost all had suffered extreme violence prior to their deaths. The deaths have increased pressure on the national government less than a year after ministers declared gender-based violence a national disaster. While South African police statistics do not differentiate victims by gender, the South African Human Rights Commission said last week that 569 women were killed and 1,052 others survived attempted murder between April and June this year. Three men appeared in court earlier this week accused of being involved in one of the nine prior murders, with police working to track down others who may have been involved. Headline: Can you take the 'London' out of London Fashion Week?
Body: As London Fashion Week comes to a close, an initiative has launched to help talent from outside the capital to get into the industry The curtain might have fallen on London Fashion Week (LFW) - but bosses hope the runway of the future will start to look a bit different. Fashion Britain is the British Fashion Council's initiative to open up access to talent outside of London - so how do you shift the focus away from the traditional centre of that world? The council told BBC Newsbeat it has been working with LFW on a series of pop-up events in England, Wales and Scotland to show this year's eventwas "bigger than London". Northern Ireland wasn't included as a location for this year's initiative - but will be included next year, the council said. A recentHouse of Commons report,externalfound that more than half (51%) of the creative industries' economic output was generated in London in 2022. However, it did report that there are "clusters of creative industries" across the country, which included cities like Manchester and Leeds. "A lot of people think in order to make it big, you have come to this big city because it has the schools here," says Charles Jeffrey, founder and creative director of international fashion label Loverboy. "But actually, there is so much amazing education that happens in different places," the Scottish designer tells Newsbeat. "I first started [in] a tiny studio in Dalston [in east London] and we were having to use fabrics from these cheap fabric shops that you would probably only really get in London because of the rag trade," he recalls. "Now a lot of them have gone and what made London a capital city for fashion has been taken away, so you're probably better getting your fabrics from a little fabric shop in Manchester - it's probably ten times cheaper." Charles Jeffrey says there is more than one way into the fashion industry Jeffrey supported Fashion Britain this year, with the aim of opening doors in the industry for creatives outside of London, but how feasible will that be? Birmingham City University graduate Imarnie Bennett knows a bit about the struggle. She travelled to the capital to showcase her project with fellow BCU fashion graduates to an audience at Somerset House. "London is such a big city, it's really well known and there are lots of opportunities," says the 22-year-old. "You hear Birmingham and it's a bit like, 'will they get us the same opportunities as London?', but I feel like Birmingham is becoming more noticed for what we do." Bennett says you can harness the power of being different. "Even colours, some cities are brighter and warmer than others, so it changes people's perspectives on things," she says. Yet fellow designer Sean Pajarillo says he is hopeful about job opportunities because of how the technology and fashion industry is moving. "The merging of industries is what's going to create new opportunities for someone in the future," says the 25-year-old. Birmingham City University (BCU) Fashion Design graduate Sean Pajarillo says he feels positive about opportunities in the industry - despite not living in London Natalie Potter is network director at the British Fashion Council, and says the Fashion Britain initiative is "about recognising that British fashion is bigger than London". Potter says that in the run up to LFW there were events in London, Bristol, Manchester, Liverpool, Newcastle, Edinburgh, Dundee and Cardiff. But what happens after the catwalk leaves town? Potter says the aim of Fashion Britain is that it will connect talent to "the infrastructure and opportunities that they need to grow". "So working with the big global businesses that we do across the country to make sure that they've got routes to retail, to give them active mentorship," she explains. Potter says this will happen "locally and regionally".  Designer Priya Ahluwalia says practical help can go a long way to opening doors for people This is something that British designer Priya Ahluwalia believes is vital. "I do think there is a genuine issue with London being seen as the centre of the universe in terms of fashion," she says. "There is incredible talent from all over the UK, some of the best designers have come from the north, come from Wales, Scotland". Ahluwalia spoke to Newsbeat after showcasing her archive at Westfield Stratford City shopping centre as part of Fashion Week. The designer explained how practical help is important in helping talent access the industry. "Whether we decentralise or not, London is still going to be the centre of UK fashion. "There needs to also be support for people to be able to travel to London, show up in London", Ahluwalia says. For Jeffrey, formal training isn't the only way into the fashion world. "Sometimes having a university degree does kind of put your foot in the door - but honestly, I really think it's just about the work and work ethic." Headline: At Trump meeting, Xi Jinping lays out terms to avoid US-China military conflict
Body: Chinese president’s proposals for lessening tensions come amid period of intense competition between the two countries over AI and trade Xi Jinping has called for extensive cooperation with Washington to avoid the“Thucydides trap”that could put the US and China on a military collision course amid rising tensions over artificial intelligence, trade and Taiwan. At the start of his summit meeting withDonald Trumpin the White House, the Chinese president laid out terms for a mutual understanding that he said could steer the two competing superpowers away from future military conflict and on to a road of mutual gain. Rather than confrontation, conditions for “achieving the great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and making America great again go hand in hand” and should be the goal, Xi said, citing Trump’s political catchphrase. “We should strengthen communication.Chinaand the United States are different in national conditions, but through candid, in-depth and continued dialogue, our two countries can understand each other better, seek common ground while shelving differences, and build up mutual trust,” said Xi, with Trump looking on. “We should coexist in peace. China and the United States, as two major countries, stand to gain from cooperation and will both lose in confrontation. Our two militaries should maintain regular dialog and improve mechanisms for crisis communication and prevention.” With such conditions in place, Xi said, “the Thucydides trap can be overcome”, referring to the phenomenon, defined by the Greek historian, of tensions that arise when an emerging power challenges the dominance of an established power. Xi invoked the phrasein his meeting with Trump in Beijing in May, asking the US president how he planned to avoid it. His proposals for lessening tensions – which also included the invitation of 100,000 young Americans to visit China on student exchanges – come amid a period of intense competition between the two powers over artificial intelligence and trade, with each side imposing tariffs on the other. Trump had earlier welcomed Xi and his wife, Peng Liyuan, to the White House, noting that he was the first Chinese leader to make a second state visit to the US. The previous visit occurred in 2015, when Barack Obama was president. “President Xi and Madame Peng arrive at an important moment for America, the 250th anniversary of our founding,” he said. Trump said he had forged “a truly great friendship” with Xi. “President Xi and I have made tremendous strides on the issues facing our two countries,” he said. “Our teams have been working to encourage a more balanced trading relationship, including the new market access for American farmers and ranchers.” He said the current visit would include discussion over security, technology and AI – which he called “super intelligence”, a term he introduced in his speech to the United Nations general assembly on Tuesday. Xi also extolled his personal relationship with his American counterpart, saying: “President Trump and I have respect for each other. We have built personal rapport and stayed in touch.” Addressing Trump directly, he said: “During your visit to China this year, we agreed to build a constructive China-US relationship of strategic stability. I am ready to work with you to steer the giant ship of the China-US relationship on a steady course towards the future.” The White House welcome ceremony came after Trump had taken the unusual step of going to Andrews air force base in Maryland the evening before to greet the Chinese leader and his wife on the tarmac. Much of the same pageantry was repeated in Thursday’s ceremony, with both countries’ national anthems being played. Trump was flanked by his wife, Melania, while members of his cabinet and senior aides – including Natalie Harp, Trump’s dedicated assistant nicknamed “the human printer” by fellow staffers – looked on. Trump and Xi held bilateral talks after the ceremony and the welcoming speeches. Later on Thursday, Trump hosted Xi at the White House for a state dinner. Notable invited guests from the tech world included Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, Apple chair Tim Cook, SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk, and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman. Trump gestured to the titans of the industry in his remarks to the dinner, recounting when Chinese diplomats first arrived in the US 158 years ago, meeting American intellectuals like Henry David Thoreau and prominent political figures. “Tonight, we revive the spirit of that first encounter here on American soil as we are joined by some of the top leaders in business, culture and government from our own time,” he said. “On one side, China draws on thousands of years of history and tradition from Sun Tzu to Sun Yat-sen. For Americans, we inherit a legacy of faith from Jerusalem to Rome, democracy of ancient Athens, the triumphs of Sparta and the freedom proclaimed in Philadelphia 250 years ago.” Trump also touted his relationship with the Chinese leader. “President Xi and I both understand we represent different systems, but the ties between our people endure, and we’ve never gotten along better,” he said. Xi also addressed the dinner, saying talks with Trump during the visit had yielded “common understanding on many issues”, and suggesting the US and China find a new approach to working together. “China ⁠and the United States must act as responsible major countries,” he said. Despite the harmonious tone adopted by both leaders, analysts have voiced scepticism about the possibility of longstanding stable arrangements being arrived at over a host of issues. Inthe race for AI, the US has placed strict export controls on microchips, semiconductors, software and chip-making equipment in a bid to slow China’s development. Atruce agreed between Trump and Xi in South Korealast year aimed at keeping tariffs lower had been due to expire in November but has now been extended until February, the US treasury secretary, Scott Bessent said. Analysts believe the extension suggests Trump continues to be dissatisfied with Xi’s concession offers on trade and wants to keep the pressure on in the hope of getting a better deal if the two meet again at the G20 summit scheduled to be held in Miami in December. Despite the trade war between the two countries,Chinese imports have continued to surgeinto the US. China is on course to run a $1tn trade surplus for the second year running. Uwa Ede-Osifo contributed reporting This article was amended on 24 and 25 September 2026. Misspellings ofXi Jinpingin the headline and text were corrected. And China is on course to run a $1tn trade surplus, not deficit.
