Headline: £170 a bag? Protein users squeezed as prices soar
Body: The cost of the whey protein Amarpreet Singh buys has almost tripled since 2020 Amarpreet Singh has been drinking protein shakes since he was 16. The 30-year-old, who lives in London and works in banking, started going to the gym at a time when he says protein supplements were mostly associated with bodybuilders. Fourteen years later, shakes are still part of his routine, but they have become considerably more expensive. He says a 4.5kg bag of the whey protein he buys cost around £60 in 2020. By last year, the price had gone up to £120, though he managed to get one from eBay for £90. Now the same bag is £170. "I was a bit gobsmacked," he says. Among his gym friends, the rising prices have even been given a nickname – "proteinflation". Student Evie says the tub she buys is quite expensive for the size of it Over the years, protein powders and shakes have attracted a much broader customer base, while food manufacturers now offer high-protein versions of everything from bagels to water. Evie Lewis is a more recent buyer of protein powder. The 19-year-old University of Manchester student began using it a few months ago because she felt she wasn't getting enough protein in her diet. "You hear a lot more about protein now on social media," she says. But at £32.99 for a 420g tub, she's feeling the high price and tries to make the product stretch. "I've been rationing it and using less than what's suggested," she admits. Max Longman, 32, from Manchester, works in real estate and has been taking protein supplements for 10 years, originally to help him gain weight. He now drinks a protein shake every day and says his monthly spending on whey protein has risen from around £45 a year ago to £60 now. "Loads of foods have protein added to them now. Up until a few years ago, I'd never heard of high-protein yoghurt, and now I eat it three or four times a week," he says. Max Longman has been taking protein supplements for 10 years More recently, weight-loss drugs such as Wegovy and Mounjaro have added another source of demand. People taking these drugs typically eat less, and are often encouraged to make sure they get enough protein while losing weight to help preserve muscle. But that growing appetite for protein is running up against a problem - supply has not kept pace. And the result has been a sharp rise in the wholesale price of some key ingredients, and consumers are feeling the squeeze. High whey protein prices take chunk out of THG profits Food firms scramble to meet the high-protein craze According to global market intelligence platform Expana, the European price of one widely used type of high-protein whey was 130% higher in late August than a year earlier, and more than four times its level three years ago. There is no equivalent UK measure, but Expana says the UK market is closely linked to mainland Europe, where some British businesses source their whey protein. Other dairy proteins have also become more expensive, with another type of whey protein up 60% over the year, while one type of milk protein concentrate was up 80%. Manufacturers say that increasing production takes time and is costly, as producing high-protein whey requires specialist processing and drying equipment. So some are starting to adapt what they make, by changing recipes or looking for cheaper sources of protein. Kieran Fisher's company Warrior is launching a product using cheaper sources of protein Warrior, a UK sports nutrition company, is one of those looking for alternatives. "Our whey protein powder was £12.50 on the shelf last year. We've put that up to £17.99 and we're still subsidising that from other aspects of the business," says its founder Kieran Fisher. The company is now launching a product using other sources of protein, which Fisher says costs around half as much as whey. The effects are also being felt outside the fitness market. Dairy proteins are used in infant formula, and Expana says higher dairy protein costs have contributed to price rises there too. There are, however, early signs that the market is starting to adjust. Wholesale prices for high-protein whey have begun to level off over the past couple of months, although they remain much higher than they were a few years ago. For now though, the higher prices aren't putting off Max. "It feels like protein is so important now, a lot more than it used to be. It's pushed out everywhere," he says. "If you're doing exercise and not taking any, you feel like you wouldn't be recovering properly." But for students like Evie, managing on a much tighter budget, it's a different story. "It was affordable on my gap year [when she was working], but now I'm at university, I don't think I'll continue buying it. It's not a necessity right now," she says. Amarpreet says he will continue buying protein, but admits "it's becoming a luxury". Headline: Netherlands to return to Eurovision after 2026 boycott
Body: The Netherlands last took part in Eurovision in 2025, when they were represented by Claude The Netherlands will return to the Eurovision Song Contest next year despite a boycott by the broadcaster that was previously in charge of the country's participation. Dutch network Avrotros withdrew in 2026 and said it would also not take part in 2027 because the competition could "no longer be considered neutral" given divisions over Israel's involvement and the Gaza war. The NPO, which oversees public broadcasting in the country, has now stepped in, saying coverage of the contest will be provided by broadcasting organisation NOS, while an independent panel will select the Dutch participant. Jurre Bosman, NPO's director of media, said: "It is important that, as a public broadcaster, we remain part of this unifying European event at this moment in particular." Israel's participation in the contest has become highly controversial, and five countries, including the Netherlands, boycotted this year's event. Eurovision organiser the European Broadcasting Union (EBU) has subsequently announced a number of changes, including to exclude any country involved in an armed conflict from hosting the competition. That means that, although Israel can still compete, the EBU would ask another country to host if it won. The EBU has also proposed changes to to the voting, saying politically motivated voting has become "persistent" and is widely seen as "deeply worrying". However, Avrotros said those changes did "not provide sufficient confidence that the independent and neutral character of the Eurovision Song Contest has been restored". In a statement on Wednesday, the NPO said the EBU has "taken significant steps regarding the rules" of the contest, and that the Netherlands will return. Acknowledging that the contest provokes "mixed feelings" in the Netherlands, the NPO said it had "explicitly asked the EBU to once again make the unifying character of the festival an important part of the event". The NPO also said the Dutch entrant would be chosen by "an independent team of experts" who would "carefully guide the process surrounding the act". Eurovision director Martin Green said in a statement: "We are delighted to welcome the Netherlands back to the Eurovision Song Contest in 2027. "We value the constructive conversations we have had with NPO and look forward to working together to reinforce the Contest as a place that truly reflects the spirit of 'United By Music'." Iceland, Spain, Ireland and Slovenia all pulled out of the 2026 contest in addition to the Netherlands. The 2027 contest will take place on 14 May in Burgas, after Bulgarian singer Dara won this year's contest with Bangaranga. Last month, it was announced thatCanada will enter the contest for the first time. Headline: Pope Leo urges healing of ‘deep wounds’ before meeting child sexual abuse survivors in France
Body: Pontiff also uses visit to Catholic shrine at Lourdes to criticise assisted dying as ‘false compassion’ The pope has called on the Catholic church to heal “deep wounds” and “painful errors”, before a meeting with survivors of child sexual abuse as he continues his four-day visit toFrance. Addressing a crowd in a large field near the Catholic shrine of Lourdes on Sunday,Pope Leo XIVcalled on the church to reckon with its past, without directly referencing sexual abuse scandals in France that affected at least 330,000 children over seven decades. “In order to heal the deep wounds, infidelities and ⁠painful errors that have occurred within [the church], we must humbly place ourselves under the Lord’s purifying gaze,” the first US pope told the estimated crowd of 150,000 people. Leo was due to privately meet seven survivors of child sexual abuse by French clergy on Sunday after leading an open-air morning mass at Lourdes, one of the most popular Catholic sites for pilgrims and reputed as a place of healing. During a homily to the faithful, the pope also attacked medically assisted dying as immoral “false compassion”, in a staunch articulation of the Catholic church’s teaching that all human life must be defended from conception until natural death. After years of debate, France formally adopted legislation last monthallowing incurably ill adults the right to “aid in dying”, joining a small number of countries with similar laws, including Belgium, the Netherlands, Switzerland and Canada. The pope said: “It is impossible to regard causing death as something normal. What is legal is not necessarily moral.” The pope was due to take part in six events while in Lourdes, including a meeting with staff and patients at the shrine’s care centre. Lourdes has drawn millions of sick and disabled believers seeking a cure from its spring waters since the Catholic church officially recognised visions of the Virgin Mary reported by a local girl in 1858.Arriving there in a white popemobile on Saturday night, however, Leo would have been reminded of the church’s dark and painful legacy, as he passed boarded-up mosaics by a Jesuit priest who is accused of abusing more than two dozen women over three decades. Marko Rupnik, one of the Catholic church’s best-known mosaic artists, is on trial in a Vatican court,accused by more than two dozen womenof having psychologically, spiritually and sexually abused them from the 1990s, including during the creation of his artworks. The bishop of Lourdes ordered the works covered up, reasoning that survivors of abuse seeking succour at the site should not be forced to see them. Rupnik is not known to have commented publicly on the allegations, Reuters reported. Among the survivors who will meet the pope is a former pupil of the nearby Catholic boarding school Notre-Dame de Bétharram, whose former students have recounted their experiences of violence, rape and sexual assault in what is thought to bethe biggest child sexual abuse scandal at a school in French history. In an interview published last year, the pope spoke of the “crisis” of clerical sexual abuse in the church. He also said “victims must be treated with great respect and with an understanding that those who have suffered very deep wounds because of abuse, sometimes carry those wounds for their entire life”, according to a transcript on Vatican News, the Holy See’s official news site. Thefirst official papal visit to France in 18 yearsfollows an announcement last week by the country’s Independent National Authority for Recognition and Reparation that about 2,000 people who reported sexual abuse by clergy or other church representatives were seeking reparations. Sign up toHeadlines Europe A digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week day after newsletter promotion France’s Catholic bishops conference agreed to provide compensation aftera landmark report in 2021 estimated that 330,000 children were sexually abusedover seven decades by predatory priests or other Catholic figures. The two-and-a-half-year independent inquiry found that vast numbers of children were subjected to sexual violence by priests and clergy and that the crimes were covered up in a “systemic way” by a deliberate “veil of silence” in the church. On the day Leo arrived in Paris, a group of survivors published an open letter voicing fears that his visit would change nothing, criticising that the seven he was due to meet in Lourdes were “carefully selected” by the church, rather than survivors’ groups. “You will merely ask us for forgiveness. This is not enough. One does not ask for forgiveness for a crime; one is responsible for a crime,” they wrote in the letter published in the newspaper Libération. The pope arrived to celebrate mass on Sunday morning to a rapturous reception from the faithful, who waved flags and cheered, as they thronged the streets of Lourdes to catch a glimpse of him. The Holy See’s live stream showed Leo making stately progress in his popemobile, stopping frequently to greet and bless babies that were passed to him. The south-western town near the Spanish border is one of the most important Catholic sites in the world, attracting 3 million pilgrims a year. The Associated Press reported that the pope’s visit had caused accommodation prices to soar, with the price of some one-night hotel stays reaching more than €2,000 (£1,700). In the UK, theNSPCCoffers support to children on 0800 1111, and adults concerned about a child on 0808 800 5000. The National Association for People Abused in Childhood (Napac) offers support for adult survivors on 0808 801 0331. In the US, call or text theChildhelpabuse hotline on 800-422-4453. In Australia, children, young adults, parents and teachers can contact theKids Helplineon 1800 55 1800, orBraveheartson 1800 272 831, and adult survivors can contactBlue Knot Foundationon 1300 657 380. Other sources of help can be found atChild Helplines International

Headline: Xi got Trump's red carpet welcome - but not everything he wanted
Body: This video can not be played Watch: The world’s two most powerful men just met. How did it go? President Xi Jinping's summits with Donald Trump have one clear aim. China believes the United States is trying to contain its rise as a superpower, and it wants Washington to stay out of its way - particularly when it comes to trade, technology and Taiwan. On this visit, however, despite Trump rolling out the red carpet for him, the Chinese leader didn't get everything he wanted. The trade truce that saw both countries pause a tit-for-tat tariff war and prevent a further escalation, was extended by only a few months - from November to January. Beijing had hoped for at least a year as Xi looks to ride out the remainder of Trump's presidency. This means key disputes on tariffs, China's dominance on rare earth supplies and access to advanced US chips are being kicked forward into yet another round of negotiations. This suggests the US wants China to do more to fulfil its side of the bargain before offering longer-term concessions. Trump and Xi attend a dinner at the White House The uncomfortable truth for Xi is that his domestic economy is in trouble. While the country sells a record number of goods around the world, consumers at home are holding back. Youth unemployment remains stubbornly high and property prices have slumped in a country where 80% of people own their own homes. Trade is helping to prop up growth, making access to overseas markets more important than ever. Xi needs to protect those exports from the kind of debilitating tariffs the US imposed last year. On Taiwan, Xi once again made clear that US arms sales to Taiwan are a red line for China. The US is bound by law to provide the self-governing island with the means to defend itself. In May, Xi warned Trump that mishandling the issue could cause the two countries to "collide or even enter into conflict". Trump then delayed the approval of a $14 billion arms package for Taiwan, describing it as a "very good negotiating chip" with Beijing. Xi may have seized on that opening during the talks and likely argued that restraining support for Taiwan reduces the risk of conflict. On Thursday he reiterated his hope that the US would adhere to the "correct position" of opposing Taiwan independence. However,  Trump - who is coming under some bipartisan pressure to continue US support to Taiwan - is yet to make any public response to the Chinese leader's comments. Trade is helping to prop up growth The two leaders did at least discuss artificial intelligence (AI) although it's unclear whether they agreed to any safeguards. All eyes were on whether they would make any concrete decisions on AI - such as an agreement to hold a summit - in the wake of an essay by Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei calling for the slowing down of AI development to make it safer. That followed a warning by a top safety researcher from the company that there was a "greater than 10% chance" that AI could cause the extinction of humans. But besides Xi talking about the importance of ensuring AI "is always under human control" we didn't get much else. Trump has most recently dismissed fears of human extinction from the technology as a "hoax". And, of course,let's not forget the pandas. The gift of Ping Ping and Fu Shuang to Atlanta was first heralded in April, but Xi has now announced they will arrive in just a few days as China's panda diplomacy resumes. There may be more announcements to come as the two prepare to have tea and visit the national archives on Friday. Pandas have played an important role in Chinese diplomatic measures But for now, one of the summit's biggest victories for Beijing may have been the optics. The lavish welcome, a personal greeting at the airport and a state banquet featuring sesame crusted sea bass and braised baby bok choy have been welcomed by those watching from China. It will have helped cement Xi's image at home as Trump's equal. Memes contrasting the two leaders have spread widely on Chinese social media. One popular image shows Trump grimacing as bomber jets fly overhead, while Xi remained impassive. Xi has found a way to manage one of the world's most unpredictable leaders. But while Trump talks of a "truly great friendship", China's leader is focussed on something bigger: securing China's place alongside the United States as a superpower. The pandas, the pageantry and the warm words may help smooth this relationship. But beneath the spectacle, the competition between the world's two most powerful countries remains as fierce as ever. Headline: Switzerland rejects stricter interpretation of its neutrality
Body: Russia openly backed the initiative, which would have required Switzerland to seek UN approval for sanctions Voters in Switzerland have overwhelmingly rejected a stricter interpretation of the country's tradition of diplomatic neutrality. More than 70% of Swiss voters rejected proposals that would have prevented the European nation from imposing sanctions without UN approval, official results showed. The move would have also prevented Switzerland from pursuing closer ties with the Nato military alliance. Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine has reopened the debate around Switzerland's centuries-old non-alignment. Moscow openly backed the initiative, which was supported by the right-wing Swiss People's Party (SVP) and opposed by the federal government and all other major parties. Lukas Golder, co-director of research institute Gfs.bern told Swiss public broadcaster SRF that Swiss voters had not rejected embracing its neutrality but that the vote showed Switzerland was in favour of sanctions against Russia. "People have a clear idea of what Switzerland's neutrality is supposed to achieve," he said. Swiss Foreign Minister Ignazio Cassis said during a recent televised debate that "neutrality has always been applied with a degree of flexibility". While Switzerland had no plans to lift a ban on selling arms to countries in conflict, including Ukraine, he stressed that "neutrality does not mean indifference". He added that Switzerland would "not look away when we see violations of the very international rules that allow us to live in peace". Switzerland was internationally recognised in 1815 when the country was granted "eternal neutrality" at the Congress of Vienna, during a period of war and upheaval in Europe. This neutrality was legally defined by the Hague Convention of 1907, which forbade Switzerland supplying weapons to countries at war. It previously rejected a request from Germany for ammunition for tanks being sent to Kyiv. Switzerland remained neutral through World War Two. It also banked gold looted by the Nazis and, in a move designed to keep Nazi Germany from invading, turned away thousands of Jewish refugees. Switzerland apologised for the policies in the 1990s. Switzerland's system of direct democracy means major political decisions are often deferred to the voters through referenda.

Headline: Child's hidden letter found after 44 years
Body: The letter would have been written before Michelle Harwood was born A letter written by a 10-year-old girl in the 1980s and hidden in the cavity of the stairs at her home has been found 44 years later. The house in Hockley, Essex, was undergoing renovation work when a worker found the scrap of paper and passed it to Michelle Harwood, who now lives there. Filled with curiosity, the 36-year-old charity worker examined it - noting "really neat" handwriting for a child - and posted on her local Facebook community group on Thursday morning to track down the author. Within an hour, multiple people had found and tagged Rachel Miles, now a 54-year- old teacher in Milton Keynes, Buckinghamshire. And she responded. The BBC contacted Miles almost half a century after she wrote the letter. She explained that time capsules were popular in the 1980s because of the influence of Blue Peter, and recalled writing the letter after her dad found a cavity behind the stairs. "I just thought it would be quite nice to basically post a letter for the future and I'm obviously quite delighted to see that someone had found it," she said. Harwood said she had "goosebumps" when she read the words Miles said it was "lovely" reliving her Essex childhood and "really nice" to see how many people remembered her, despite her moving out of the county. "It's nice to hear familiar names that I knew and to be reconnected with the area," she said. She added it amused her that, out of her whole family, she had only named her cat, Kizzy, who was a "legend of those parts". Harwood described the moment she saw the letter. "[Reading] 'to the finder' just immediately gave me goosebumps," she said. "I couldn't believe that note had been there longer than I've been alive." "I couldn't really believe my handwriting", said Miles The letter is dated 12 August 1982, eight years before Harwood was born. While the Harwoods have lived at Betts Farm Estate for 11 years, Miles said her family were there when it was just a building site that she and her friends would play on. The letter is now stuck to the Harwood family fridge Harwood noticed parallels between her own life and that of Miles. Miles was born in Bury St Edmunds, Suffolk, near where Harwood's husband, Jonathan, lived as a child. They also both owned cats while living at the house, which explained why a catflap was already at the back door when the Harwoods arrived. Harwood said in her social media post that it was "a long shot" and she had no expectations of finding the writer at all, let alone in the same morning. "I think social media is great for things like that, because so many people are connected," she said Do you have a story suggestion for Essex? Contact us below. Headline: Republic of Ireland to wear black armbands for Israel game
Body: FAI chief executive David Courell confirmed one player has withdrawn from the Republic of Ireland squad in protest Republic of Ireland players intend to wear black armbands "in recognition of all lives lost in the [Gaza] conflict" for Sunday's Nations League game against Israel in Hungary, after confirming they will go ahead with the fixture. Football Association of Ireland (FAI) chief executive David Courell confirmed one player has withdrawn from the squad before the match. But he added that a vote among the squad produced a "significant majority" in favour of playing. As well as the intention to wear black armbands for Sunday's 'away' game against Israel in Debrecen, Courell said the players will make further gestures for the initial game and the return 'home' fixture against Israel next Sunday in Serbia. The fixtures have been embroiled in controversy since the two teams were drawn to play each other in Group B3. Republic of Ireland players faced calls to withdraw from the games because of theongoing Israel-Gaza warwith a "Stop The Game" campaign - organised by the pressure group Irish Sport for Palestine - gathering pace. "One of their requests is to remove their media obligations for the remainder of this window," Courell said at Saturday's delayed news conference. "They also have the intention to wear black armbands in recognition of all lives lost in the [Gaza] conflict. "There will be elements of the pre-match ceremony not be partaken in by the Republic of Ireland and it is also the intention of the players to make a significant contribution to charitable donation by virtue of both [Israel] match fees and also the fixture against Austria at the Aviva [Stadium in Dublin on Thursday]." This video can not be played FAI CEO David Courell delivers a statement before Israel game There appeared to be real doubt on Saturday morning whether the fixture would take place. A pre-match news conference with manager Heimir Hallgrimsson and a player, scheduled for 09:15 BST, was postponed just 15 minutes before it was scheduled to start, with reporters informed it would instead take place after the team's training session which was also delayed. The players were locked in a meeting back at their hotel after it emerged a player, goalkeeper Gavin Bazunu, withdrew from the game in protest with several other expressing their concerns about fielding. About 13:00, players began to filter out of the meeting room, with it then confirmed the news conference would indeed go ahead, back at Nagyerdei Stadion at 14:30, with training to follow. More than five hours after the initial news conference was scheduled to begin, Courell - flanked by Hallgrimsson and FAI director of football John Martin - confirmed a players' vote passed by a "significant majority" to play the game. "This morning, a player expressed their discomfort at the fixture and indicated their intent to withdraw," Courell said. "This new variable required time for the rest of the squad to consider and what proceeded was another four hours of conversations, predominantly among the players, but also at times with coaching staff and the [FAI] executive. "There were a lot of positions presented and the association is fully respectful of everyone's right to their respective opinion." Later on Saturday, Bazunu posted on social media explaining his decision, one that he said he had "not taken lightly". "I am a man of strong faith and try my best to be a person of character and principle, therefore I feel it would be wrong to participate in the upcoming fixtures against Israel," he said. "My decision is based purely upon my personal belief that the killing of innocent people is wrong. "It is important to note that my stance is not in opposition of the Israel people or the Jewish community but against the atrocities in the region. "There are few times when you get a chance in life to stand up for something bigger and I strongly believe that this is one of them." Neutral venues and no 'away' fans - how Israel v Republic of Ireland became so contentious Republic of Ireland squad will meet to discuss Israel games This video can not be played 'It's a situation you can't win' - Heimir Hallgrimsson Former Republic of Ireland manager Brian Kerr and ex-international James McClean are among those to have backed calls for a boycott of the fixtures. The armed Palestinian group Hamas attacked Israel on 7 October 2023, killing about 1,200 people and taking 251 hostages. In response, Israel launched a massive military offensive in Gaza, during which more than 73,000 people have been killed, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the United Nations. Hallgrimsson relayed that nobody "can understand the pressure that has been going on these players" and said the lengthy meeting on Saturday stemmed from "a change of mind for one of the players to play the game". "All of the rest of the players are training today," he confirmed. "The balance [to play] changed with this [withdrawal] and obviously it was an ongoing discussion but we came to a conclusion and the game is going ahead. "We will train and there will probably be more discussions tonight and probably tomorrow. It's a unique situation and we are just trying to limit the damage." The Republic of Ireland lost their opening Nations League fixture in Kosovo on Thursday, a match overshadowed in the build-up by the Israel games. Asked whether the far from ideal preparation for Sunday's game would affect the players, the Irish boss said "we will see". "Nobody is comfortable but it's about limiting the damage, both personally and for Irish football, that we need to find some solution on it," Hallgrimsson added. "There is no action we do that everyone will agree to, so we need to find a solution to limit the damage for us as a group, for Ireland as a nation and the association for football in Ireland. "We don't know the consequences if we don't play the game but a lot of players share a common feeling, so there are two choices and both are tough. It's a situation you can't win." A spokesperson for the Irish governement insists any decision regarding the fixtures lie firmly at the door of the FAI and Uefa. "The FAI had decided to play the fixtures against Israel in accordance with their obligations as members of Uefa. Following engagement with players today decision stands," they said. "The FAI has strongly represented the views of its membership that Israel should be excluded from international football competitions, including bringing a motion to Uefa to this effect last year. The reality is that this motion was not passed by Uefa and that the FAI was obliged to fulfil the fixture." Israel FA's director of communications Shlomi Barzel confirmed they will appeal Sayed Abu Farhi's red card in the 3-1 defeat by Austria Israel Football Association [IFA] head of communications Shlomi Barzel commended the Republic of Ireland team for confirming they will play, saying "football has won". Barzel began Israel's news conference with a statement before requesting  questions regarding the game-only were directed towards captain Dor Peretz and head coach Ran Ben-Shimon who remained on script. "The separation between football and politics must be maintained, any other approach spell chaos," he said, confirming Israel players intend to shake hands before the game. "The Irish football association [FAI] and the national team players did the right thing by recognising this, even if it took a bit longer than it should. Yet, it is better to be late than never. "The one who certainly lost today are those who want to intimidate to separate and turn the football pitch into a political arena. Uefa, the IFA [Israel Football and the FAI stood strong together to prevent it." Barzel also confirmed the IFA intend to appeal both yellow cards shown to Sayed Abu Farhi inThursday's 3-1 defeat by Austria. Abu Farhi was shown a second yellow for his goal celebration which Barzel insists was not mimicking the firing of a gun, but an "imitation of a snooker player, like the legendary Ken Doherty."

Headline: The moment Antonelli knew he had been transformed as an F1 driver
Body: Kimi Antonelli leads the drivers' championship by 81 points going into the Azerbaijan Grand Prix Kimi Antonelli says he knew from the first moment he drove this year's Mercedes that he would be transformed as a Formula 1 driver in 2026. The 20-year-old Italian, who is running away with the world championship in only his second season in F1, is reflecting on his breakthrough year in the sport in an exclusive interview with BBC Sport. A difficult debut season last year had left external expectations of Antonelli low at the start of 2026. But on a typically damp and cold January day at Silverstone, he already sensed that something special might be on the cards. "It was just a few laps in the wet," Antonelli says, "but I just felt better in the car, much better than I felt last year. Also the car felt well, but I just felt better mentally in the car. Less tense, more relaxed and more mature." Last year, he says, was "not great". "I was driving very tense most of the time, I wasn't able to extract the potential out of me," he says. "This year, it's a lot different. The mindset has been the biggest change." Fast forward eight months and the effects of that new headspace are plain to see. After 14 grands prix, and with either eight or nine remaining depending on the war in the Middle East, Antonelli is a massive 81 points clear of team-mate George Russell. Not only that, but he looks so in control. Always fast, always composed, a factor in every grand prix. Everyone knows the championship is basically over, barring some kind of dramatic misfortune. Even then, Antonelli says he is "still finding my way" in F1. The journey Antonelli has been on in the past two years is remarkable, and he says even he is "surprised" by the extent of his progress this year. He was comprehensively outperformed by Russell in 2025. So when it was obvious that Mercedes would startthe new regulatory erawith an advantage, it was the Briton who started the season as championship favourite. Russell duly won the opening race in Australia, but Antonelli was less than three seconds behind him at the flag. This, he says, was the second moment of realisation of what might be possible. "I had a big, big crash in FP3," Antonelli recalls. "But then thanks to the mechanics - who all throughout the season have done an incredible job, but on that specific occasion, it is a miracle - I was able to go back in the car and push again in the high speed and getting close to the limit. "The crash, definitely it compromised a little bit qualifying and the race because we couldn't set up properly the car. I mean, the car was still very quick. But it was not easy. "Still being able to stay close despite that, I was like, 'OK, you know, it's not going to be a walk in the park. It's going to be very tough', but I knew already that it was a different story compared to last year. "If it would have happened last year, I wouldn't have been able to overcome that." Antonelli climbs out of his Mercedes after crashing in first practice for the 2024 Italian Grand Prix at Monza Antonelli's first season in F1 was haunted by an incident that happened the first time he drove on a grand prix weekend. At the 2024 Italian Grand Prix, the day before they formally announced Antonelli was the replacement for Ferrari-bound Lewis Hamilton, Mercedes gave him an outing in first practice at Monza. He was blindingly fast on his first flying lap - but then crashed heavily on his second. Team principal Toto Wolff played it down at the time, saying he was well aware there would be mistakes from Antonelli as he found his feet in F1. But behind the scenes the incident had had a big impact on the young man. "Monza stayed in my head for a very long time," Antonelli says. "I think all throughout last season, at least. Definitely that was a big thing that was kind of slowing me down. "This memory of being afraid to do a mistake, also because going through the difficult period (in the middle of 2025), this memory was even stronger in my head, if you know what I mean. "Because it was already a difficult period and I was like, 'If I even do a mistake or I crash, it's even worse.' "So yeah, it's been a thing that has been bothering me a lot last year. This year I was able to just put it behind." Doing so has involved a lot of work behind the scenes, analysing what happened in 2025, understanding what had gone well, what had not, and why, and what he could do to improve. "The mindset going into this season, it was mainly trying to be able to extract more out of my potential," Antonelli says. "Trying to, first of all, do a better job than previous year. But as well trying to put things more together. "The preparation that I did in pre-season was very, very intense. But it helped me a lot to arrive ready for this season. "Plus, I did a lot of work with my mental coach. Trying to get my head right, my thoughts right on understanding the goal, and understanding that the most important thing is to be ready and to stay present in the moment. "Not trying to think about final results or what would happen if I wouldn't achieve that. But just trying to be present and trying to do the best with what you can do in the moment." Antonelli crowd-surfs with joyful home fans after winning the Italian Grand Prix earlier this month Still, though, he admits to be "definitely surprised" at how much progress he has made. "I knew that I was going to be better than my first year," he says. "Obviously, because I think last year, towards the end of the season, I started to put things more together, starting to extract more performance. But still, it was still not great. "Whereas this year, it's a lot different. Also as well, withthe first win,the first pole, it took a lot of weight off my shoulder." Antonelli has blossomed. Everything seems to be coming so easily to him. If he drops back in a race, he recovers seamlessly and quickly. Overtaking moves are done quickly and decisively. There's not been a circuit on which he has lacked pace. Russell, by contrast, has admitted to struggling and - while not trying to take anything away from Antonelli, who he is always quick to praise - has expressed his opinion that his his driving style does not suit this year's new cars. All of which raises a key question - how much of what is happening this year is Antonelli stepping it up, and how much Russell falling back? "That's a very difficult question," Antonelli says. "I've definitely stepped up. "This year definitely everything is new. So it requires also a little bit of a different approach. And trying to adapt to a different car, which hasn't been easy." His consistency this year, he says, has come from the fact he has found "a nice rhythm in the season". "I always try to follow my routines," Antonelli says, "the way I approach the weekend. I try to approach it all the time the same. "I'm still finding my way, but I've found a way that helps me to be consistent and also helps me to be consistently ready when I go in the car." There are still moments when he misjudges things, though. He cites the Barcelona-Catalunya Grand Prix, just days after hisoutstanding win in Monaco,one of the most dominant at that storied track for years. "Monaco was a very high moment for me in the season, and then I went to Barcelona and I was probably a bit too excited, especially over a single lap," he says. "So I was overdriving, I was chasing the lap time and the result didn't come in qualifying. I was actually a bit far back and didn't do a good lap. "But that's because I was trying to do a bit too much after a very high moment in my career. And then I understood that that is not the way." The lesson was applied after hisspellbinding win from 19th on the grid at Monza,his home race, a result that Wolff said "closed a cycle" from his 2024 crash. Antonelli says: "After Monza, I reminded myself, 'Don't make the same mistake as you did after Monaco.'" He won the Spanish Grand Prix seven days later, an eighth victory from 14 races so far this season. Success has inevitably led to fame, and with it attention. "Life has changed a lot," Antonelli says. "I'm not going to lie. It's been a big change, but it's nice to see so much support. Definitely, one side is very nice, but on the other side, you have to be careful. You've got to protect yourself a bit more because obviously you're more exposed." All year, Antonelli has talked about focusing on process, about doing the best he can on every single day, not thinking about the big picture. Now, though, for the first time, he acknowledges the title - an achievement that would make him the youngest world champion in F1 history - is on his mind. "Yes, I thought about it," he says. "But again, thinking about it, I came always to the same conclusion that the earlier I finish all this, the better it is. "So I've got to just keep pushing. I keep doing the best I can every race. Because, yeah, that's the way. Just not finish. And until it's done, it's not over." Headline: Germany's saviour? How Klopp is looking to turn fortunes around
Body: Jurgen Klopp has picked a split squad for Germany's opening Nations League games It has been quite the ride since Jurgen Klopp was announced as Germany's head coach in July. In his first news conference, Klopp admonished the media, urging them to treat him fairly and refrain from any attacks against his family. Last Thursday, during another media conference, Klopp called for "positive patriotism" amid political turmoil in the country. When asked whether he considers himself an ambassador for Germany in his new role, Klopp's answer was a serious one. "From my perspective as a sportsman, I can say that I would very much like to reclaim the flag for myself, for all of us," said Klopp. "I want it so that when someone waves it, no-one thinks: 'What is wrong with you?' Instead, I want people to understand: You are happy and realise how lucky you were to be born, grow up, or move to this wonderful country." His statement was made in light of the success of the Alternative for Germany (AfD) in the state election in Saxony-Anhalt. The anti-immigration party has since scored another win in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania. Klopp's remarks were widely and positively discussed in the media - the German national team represents a diverse Germany, as several players come from a migrant background. KIopp also remarked about the recent success of Alexander Zverev at the US Open, the women's basketball team at the European Championship and German athletes at the European Athletics Championships, saying sport can ensure "a sense of community". He added: "This is our mission: we need to create a good atmosphere." Klopp knows, intentionally or not, how to make headlines. However, the German Football Association (DFB) didn't hire the former Liverpool boss on an annual salary of £6m to become a commentator on the state of Germany - but to transform a floundering national team. Klopp wants to 'reclaim' flag amid German elections Klopp starts Germany reign by threatening to quit Between the two news conferences, Klopp looked like the busiest national team boss on the planet, making countless visits to league games and training facilities. One day fans could see Klopp sitting in the stands of Dortmund's Signal Iduna Park, his old stomping ground and, not long after, they may have caught a picture of him in the VIP lounge of Mainz's stadium or somewhere near Eintracht Frankfurt's training pitch talking to players. Klopp has approached this new job with open eyes. Initially, the charismatic 59-year-old drew up a list of 57 players who could have been selected for this first international break. "Players will receive chances who don't even expect it yet," Klopp said in July. His first selection wasn't short of surprises. In the flavour of a trial-and-error principle, Klopp and his staff decided to select two almost completely different squads for the upcoming four games. The first squad, including Joshua Kimmich, Kai Havertz and Jamal Musiala, will face arch-rivals the Netherlands at Johan Cruyff Arena on Thursday (19:45 BST) and host Greece on Sunday. The second squad, with Florian Wirtz and Aleksandar Pavlovic, face Serbia at home and Greece on the road in the second half of this international break. The only player who was selected for both is back-up goalkeeper Finn Dahmen. The selection process means we will not see Germany's best starting XI this time around. Instead, Klopp clearly intends to try out new players, some of whom played in Germany's second tier only a few months ago. Take, for example, Felix Keidel, a 23-year-old full-back-midfielder hybrid from recently promoted SV Elversberg. A year ago, Keidel was as far away from the national team as the Oktoberfest from Rio Carnival. Now Keidel - just like Mika Baur, Bambase Conte, Max Rosenfelder, Philipp Treu, and Vitaly Janelt - has the chance to show he could be a valuable cog in the machine. Klopp has never built his success merely on star names - he has always taken a liking to undervalued and overlooked players. He once signed an little-known Polish winger by the name of Lukasz Piszczek and moulded him into one of the best right-backs in Europe who would go toe-to-toe with Cristiano Ronaldo in his prime. And he helped transform Andy Robertson into a force on Liverpool's left side. Klopp's style helps to elevate all the members of his squad - not just the most talented. Fitness and mental readiness are highly important, and some newcomers might just have that to impress the new manager. But man-marking is prevalent in Germany's top flight, while Klopp prefers his teams to close down the player in possession to create superior numbers around the ball. So some of the Bundesliga players will have to adapt quickly. "It is not important who plays but how someone plays," Klopp said last week. "I expect a lot from the beginning. It could be a bit wild, but I accept that. It just has to be lively." Klopp has chosen younger squads compared to the ones we saw in the past couple of years. Manuel Neuer, Antonio Rudiger and Pascal Gross have retired from international football, and other 30-somethings might just not receive a chance to get into the team again. "I think it is about time to wish the new generation best of luck," Gross said after Brighton's win over Arsenal on Saturday. "I still enjoy playing football here in the club, but there's a change in Germany and rightfully so." This video can not be played Germany head coach pinnacle of my coaching career - Klopp Both squads for this international break have an average age between 24 and 25. Youth and energy seem to be preferred. "I have the desire to work with guys who cannot wait to wear this jersey, who want to play the kind of football everybody enjoys and who perform even better wearing the national team jersey," Klopp said. We can expect from him to simplify Germany's approach to ball possession. Predecessor Julian Nagelsmann bent over backwards to hide some of the flaws he detected in his squad and thus created highly complex tactical systems. On the contrary, Klopp intends to put an emphasis on the wings and break defences there. We saw what he was able to achieve with the likes of Mohamed Salah, Trent Alexander-Arnold and Sadio Mane from wide areas. While underwhelming at the past couple of international tournaments, Germany still possess a deep talent pool. Cologne's rising star Said El Mala and 18-year-old Bayern Munich talent Lennart Karl will get chances to show their skills on the wings. Freiburg's Derry Scherhant and Barcelona's Karim Adeyemi provide plenty of speed, just like Brentford's Kevin Schade who has returned to the squad after being left out for the World Cup. There is potential for an exciting Germany side we have not seen in quite a while. Finally, the emotional component plays a role in Klopp's entire approach. He works towards a fresh start for the national team and a new spirit in the country. Last Thursday, he wore a cap that read "One of 83 million". It was a clear indication he wants to unite all 83 million Germans behind this team and they are all in it together. Klopp has spent plenty of time thus far attempting to shape narratives off the field - but now the spotlight turns to his ability to get the best out of his group of players on the pitch. Headline: Fuel costs putting off meal delivery driver applicants
Body: The service delivers meals to about 100 people, four days a week A delivery service offering meals to people in need has spoken about the challenges of recruiting new volunteers due to rising fuel costs. Maureen Bougeard said Meals on Wheels Jersey had received £38,000 from the Jersey Community Foundation to fund work supplying hot meals to islanders who are unable to prepare meals themselves. She said the service packed and delivered meals to about 100 people, four days a week - but addedfuel costs were having an impact. She said: "Very often volunteers say, you know: 'The petrol's getting expensive.' We're looking for new volunteers and I send the information out which says you drive your car at your own expense and I don't hear from them again." The secretary said the organisation had more than 200 volunteers. "Our complete organisation is run by volunteers," Bougeard said. "We don't have any paid staff at all." Bougeard said some of the voluntary meal delivery drivers drove the length of the island twice in a day, adding most volunteers were retired people. "I'm not saying everyone has a poor pension, not everyone is on the basic pension, but some are and they still manage to come and volunteer, which is absolutely fabulous," she said. More news stories for Jersey Listen to the latest news for Jersey The service said people who receive the meals currently pay a cost price of £5. It said the grant from Jersey Community Foundation covered the charge to the government of Jersey's health and community services, which supply and facilitate the preparation of the meals. The service said the grant had been offered for 2026 and 2027. Meals on Wheels said it hoped to renegotiate the service level agreement with the government to allow it to continue. Headline: Traitors star burgled after sharing holiday photos
Body: Paul Gorton believes he was targeted after sharing his holiday snaps on social media Traitors star Paul Gorton did not think twice about sharing photographs on social media while enjoying a family holiday with his wife and two young children. But when he returned home he discovered that his house in Cheshire had been burgled just days earlier. "The eerie bit is at 21:10 BST I posted that me and Kate were by the side of the pool, we've got full bellies, the kids are in bed, we're actually having our little bit of the holiday," he said. "About 20 minutes later, little did we know, our house has been broken into." Paul's bike as well as several sentimental items including an irreplaceable ring from Kate's grandmother were stolen in the burglary on 28 August. The perpetrators managed to break in through the bi-fold doors at the back of the house by using a technique known as lock snapping before cutting the broadband connection. Paul's home in Cheshire was targeted while he was on holiday Paul, who was a contestant on the second series of the popular BBC series, said he reported the burglary to Cheshire Police, with the force describing it as a "one-off hit". As a result, Paul believes it was a "targeted attack". "They said they normally see people come in from far and wide and they [target] a couple of houses in a night but this isn't the case," said Paul, who is originally from St Helens. "This makes me suspect that it could be someone that follows me. "They've seen that I've posted that I was away and then thought 'let's go in the house and see if we can get ourselves some goodies'." Paul said he hoped other people would learn from his misfortune. "I think the key message is for people to be a little bit smarter, more conscientious when they're posting and post when they're back at home. "Hopefully people can learn from my mistakes. "I guess the aim is the worst thing that's happened to us could be the best thing that will happen to you because you can protect yourself moving forward and that's the whole reason behind the campaign." Following the burglary, Paul has joined forces with Compare the Market, which commissioned a licensed private investigator to examine the publicly available digital footprints of nine volunteers. They were able to identify seven home addresses by using publicly available information. The fastest home address was identified in 15 minutes, with the first lead found in only 50 seconds. "It's not just about social media," said Paul. "I've learned to think about the whole picture with locks, alarms, lights, what you're posting online and whether you're accidentally advertising that nobody's home." Cheshire Police confirmed investigations were ongoing into the burglary but no arrests had been made. Headline: White casts doubt on Fury-Joshua after 24 hours of chaos
Body: Anthony Joshua and Tyson Fury were officially announced to fight in Cardiff on 11 December but fresh uncertainty has emerged over the contest Two days after the announcement British boxing had waited a decade for, Dana White - the UFC president and Zuffa Boxing chief named as one of the figures promoting Tyson Fury against Anthony Joshua - was asked whether the fight would actually happen. "I don't know," he said. White was speaking at London's Copper Box on Saturday, whereBritish heavyweight Johnny Fisher beat Michael Pirottonon his Zuffa Boxing debut. But for much of the media in attendance another heavyweight fight dominated the evening. Asked whether Wednesday's scheduled Fury-Joshua news conference in London would take place, White added: "I have no idea." On Thursday, Fury and Joshuawere officially announced to meetat Cardiff's Principality Stadium on 11 December, live globally on Netflix. By Friday, thatcertainty had unravelled. A dispute over who is entitled to promote the event led to claims of contractual breaches, talk of possible replacement fights and another flurry of cryptic social-media posts. Even by boxing's recent standards, the past 24 hours have been extraordinary - and not a particularly flattering look for the sport. White (right) has become increasingly involved in Turki Alalshikh's boxing plans, with the pair working together through Zuffa Boxing Netflix and Saudi powerbroker Turki Alalshikh's fight announcement was striking for who it included - and who it did not. The event was presented as a collaboration involving Alalshikh's The Ring and White. There was no mention of Matchroom's Eddie Hearn, who has promoted Joshua throughout his professional career, or Queensberry's Frank Warren, Fury's long-time promoter. White's involvement was not entirely unexpected. The Zuffa Boxing promoter has been saying for weeks he would be involved in Fury-Joshua. Hearn has been equally adamant he would not. After Thursday's announcement, Hearn said Joshua's contract specifically prevented White and American sports entertainment company TKO from having a promotional role, claiming Netflix had not been made aware of that provision. Hearn said there had been breaches of the agreement which needed to be resolved and cast doubt on whether Wednesday's news conference would go ahead. Fury says a similar restriction originally appeared in his own contract but was removed because he wanted White involved. Warren has taken a more pragmatic position.Speaking to BBC Sportbefore the latest dispute escalated, he said his understanding was White had helped secure the Netflix deal and compromises had been necessary to get the fight made. On Saturday, White was generally non-committal on the future of the contest but much clearer in his criticism of Hearn. "The guy who is supposed to be helping the fight has been hurting the fight," White said. "He hasn't done the fight any favours." This video can not be played 'None of this is unusual' - Warren on AJ v Fury fight timings The uncertainty intensified on Friday evening. Reports emerged that Fury-Joshua could be in jeopardy and alternative fights for 11 December were being discussed, including Ryan Garcia against therecently retired three-weight undisputed champion Terence Crawford. Crawford appeared as surprised as anyone, publicly questioning the suggestion he could be fighting Garcia. Then Fury intervened. In avideo posted on social media,he claimed Joshua and Hearn were "trying to pull out" and blamed the dispute largely on Hearn's objection to White. There has been no announcement from Joshua saying he intends to withdraw. On Instagram, Alalshikh posted pictures of himself with White and later shared a cryptic message in Arabic about somebody attempting to "stab you where you told them it hurts", although he made no explicit reference to Fury-Joshua. Hearn, meanwhile, posted a picture with a shushing emoji and the message: "Bet against me." For a fight negotiated so publicly for so many years, the familiar mix of claims, counter-claims and cryptic posts had returned almost immediately. Among the media in east London on Saturday, much of the conversation centred around Fury-Joshua. Who had heard what? Was the fight genuinely in danger? Would Wednesday's news conference happen? And, with White in the building, would he provide any clarity afterwards? Instead, his post-fight comments only underlined the uncertainty. White has been openly critical of Hearn, while the precise nature of his own role in Fury-Joshua remains at the heart of the dispute. That distinction could prove significant when lawyers examine exactly what Joshua's contract permits. During Saturday's US broadcast of the Zuffa Boxing card, it was suggested White was helping Alalshikh on a personal level rather than acting as a promoter. White rejected that interpretation. "I don't know where that came from," he said. "That was weird." And White offered another tease when asked whether he would attend Wednesday's news conference if it does go ahead. "I guess I'll leave that as a surprise," he said. This video can not be played 'I think Tyson will knock Joshua out' For now, officially, yes. As of Saturday night, Netflix continued to list Fury against Joshua at the Principality Stadium on 11 December and said the fighters would attend Wednesday's news conference. But the contractual disagreement remains unresolved. The unusual position is that, little more than 48 hours after the fight was officially announced, one of the central figures in its promotion cannot say whether it will happen - or whether its first major launch event will go ahead. There is too much money, time and work invested in Fury-Joshua for anyone involved to walk away lightly. But if the past decade has taught boxing anything, an agreement does not necessarily mean the fight is safe. Fury-Joshua is once again waiting for another hurdle to be cleared. Headline: Priest killed and four injured in knife attack at Polish abbey
Body: Polish police have sealed off the area around the abbey A priest has been killed and four other people injured in a knife attack in south-east Poland, officials have said. A 31-year-old Ukrainian man was arrested after the stabbings on the grounds of a Catholic abbey in the town of Jarosław. Polish President Karol Nawrocki said Thursday's attack "has shaken us all and demands a firm response from the state", while his Ukrainian counterpart Volodymyr Zelensky said "we are shocked by this evil". Reports in Polish media said the attacker first injured a priest in a nearby cafe, and then another four people inside the abbey itself. A police investigation into the attacker's motives is now under way. Polish police said four men and one woman were stabbed in the attack on Thursday morning on the abbey grounds. The name of the murdered priest has not been publicly released. Polish Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński said psychological support was now being provided to all those affected by the incident. Meanwhile, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said the perpetrator "will be punished with the full severity of Polish law". Echoing his words, President Zelensky said "the perpetrator of this evil must bear full responsibility according to the law", adding that Ukraine was counting on "a quick and thorough investigation of all circumstances". The Ukrainian embassy in Poland also condemned the attack. In a statement, it said: "In such difficult moments, it is especially important to support each other, remain steadfast in respect for human life, and not allow pain to escalate into hatred or new violence. Responsibility for a crime must be based solely on the law." Poland has recently seen a number of often violent incidents involving its citizens and Ukrainians, many of whom have fled their home country after Russia's full-scale invasion.

Headline: British rapper Yung Filly to face rape retrial in Australia next June
Body: Yung Filly will face a retrial next June after a jury in Australia failed to reach a verdict on three rape charges British rapper Yung Filly will face a rape retrial in Australia next June after a jury failed to reach a verdict during an earlier trial. In July, a jury acquitted the 31-year-old - whose real name is Andres Felipe Valencia Barrientos - of three counts of rape, one of assault and one of strangulation but found him guilty of two assault charges. No decision was reached for three rape charges, which he has denied. A fan, aged 20 at the time, alleges Barrientos repeatedly raped and assaulted her in his hotel room in Perth, Western Australia, after a 2024 concert. The court previously heard that Barrientos and the woman had consensual sex before she alleged it turned violent and he refused to stop. On Friday, Perth's District Court set 15 June as the start date for the retrial which is expected to last eight days. Barrientos was not required to appear in court and is understood to have returned to the UK after the court granted him permission to leave Australia as part of his bail conditions. Sentencing for the two assault charges that the jury found Barrientos guilty of in July will take place after the retrial. Barrientos, who was born in Colombia and brought up in the UK, is known for his work with the YouTube collective Beta Squad. He has appeared in the celebrity version of Bake Off on Channel 4 and presented BBC Three shows.

Headline: Off sick? You need to phone your boss, back-to-work adviser says
Body: People off sick from work should keep in phone contact with their boss, government-appointed back-to-work expert Sir Charlie Mayfield has said. Getting bosses and workers to have a conversation, rather than simply exchanging emails and sicknotes, could help get people back into work, Sir Charlie, who is leading the Keep Britain Working taskforce, said. His latest report said health-related economic inactivity was costing Britain around £210bn a year in benefit payments and lost output. Talking on the phone was just "one piece of the jigsaw" he said on Wednesday. The report calls for more workplace support,externalfor people with health conditions and disabilities and the establishment of a Workplace Health System alongside the NHS. But improving communication was also a way to "rehumanise" the workplace and help prevent people dropping out of work altogether, Sir Charlie said. Why calling in sick makes you feel guilty The report does not suggest that someone struck down by flu needs to croak through their symptoms over the phone or that bosses need to provide down-the-line sickbed sympathy if an employee is off with food poisoning. "I'm not worried about a day here and a day there. It is more about longer term issues," Sir Charlie told the BBC's Today Programme. But he said Britain was doing a "poor job" of handling sickness in the workplace, leading to more people becoming disengaged and dropping out altogether. "I have met so many people who have said to me, 'You know, I was signed off sick and I was off sick for a month, two months, three months, and I had almost no contact with my employer'," Sir Charlie said. Around 300,000 people leave work every year with a health condition, much of which is preventable, the report said. Sir Charlie said employees sometimes feared talking about long-term health issues with their employer. "But the fear is also felt by employers as well because they're afraid of causing offence or creating a complaint or a grievance," he added. Fear on both sides can create a distance and lack of understanding, he warned, with longer absences making it much more likely a worker will drop out of the labour force altogether. "If you can keep more people in work, there's a massive opportunity for us to add billions to the economy and, frankly, to people's livelihoods," Sir Charlie said. "To get that, though, you need to have people talking to each other, and you've got to more actively manage sickness and ill health in the workplace." Employers need to do more, he said, and employees need to engage with it. Other ways for bosses to support staff include ensuring access to treatments such as physiotherapy and talking therapies, he said. Have you been affected by issues covered in this story? Headline: Italy ministers agree to ban burqa and niqab in school and cap foreigners in class
Body: The Italian government has approved a ban on the burqa and niqab in schools, along with a limit on the share of pupils who speak little Italian in any one class. A 30% cap will be imposed on children without Italian citizenship or poor knowledge of the Italian language in the first year of primary, middle and high school. Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni described the measures as "common-sense tools that do not divide but really help to integrate". Opposition parties accuse the government of pandering to the policies of the hard-right Futuro Nazionale party, ahead of a general election next year. Education Minister Giuseppe Valditara has said the limit is "purely linguistic" rather than one of citizenship, while he has sought to frame the ban on the niqab and burqa as a matter of gender equality. "You must go to school with your face uncovered," Meloni said while announcing the plans on Sunday, adding that no-one could decide that a young woman should hide herself in the name of tradition. There were several drafts of the decree ahead of Thursday's council of ministers meeting, however the core details were clear. The veil ban would apply to the burqa and niqab, but not the hijab, which leaves the face visible. The niqab is a veil for the face that leaves the area around the eyes clear. However, it may be worn with a separate eye veil. It is worn with an accompanying headscarf. The burka is a one-piece veil that covers the face and body. Often there is a mesh screen around the eyes to see through. Non-Italian citizens make up 11.6% of pupils in Italy's schools, according to the research institution Fondazione ISMU. The 30% limit on pupils who speak limited Italian will cover separate stages of education differently. In primary schools, it would cover non-Italian citizens who have either not been born in Italy or who have not attended at least two years of nursery school. In lower- and upper- secondary schools, it would cover pupils without Italian citizenship who have not successfully completed at least three years in the Italian school system. Local school offices would be asked to spread pupils with little Italian language skills more evenly among nearby schools. Where that is not possible, exemptions would apply, with extra Italian teaching. The aim was to avoid "ghetto classes", the education minister explained. The draft also goes further on parents, according to the Ansa news agency. Schools would have to report to social services cases in which persistent language barriers among those with parental responsibility hinder a child's integration. Free Italian courses would be offered. The measure is a decree law, meaning it can take effect immediately, but must be ratified by parliament within 60 days. Italy already has guidance on Italian language at schools. A 2010 ministerial notice under then-Education Minister Mariastella Gelmini set a 30% limit "as a rule" on pupils without Italian citizenship. The new decree puts the limit into law. The political opposition says the plan is as much about politics as schools. Opponents accuse Meloni of pandering to Roberto Vannacci, a retired military general who leads the hard-right Futuro Nazionale party and is seen as a threat to the governing coalition's right flank. The leader of the centre-left Democratic Party (PD), Elly Schlein, called the plan propaganda and impossible to implement. PD deputy and chamber vice-president Anna Ascani also accused the government of propaganda at the expense of schoolchildren. Valditara, speaking by video link from New York at a press conference rejected the charge. "We are not chasing Vannacci; if anything, he is chasing us," he said. Vannacci said he agreed with the measures, but they should have come years ago. The League's Matteo Salvini, who launched a separate package of measures on what he called "political Islam" on Wednesday, accused Vannacci of "continually voting against the government". Salvini said he hoped Futuro Nazionale would back the League's new proposals. Headline: Schools not ready for AI and 'crying out' for government guidance, report warns
Body: Schools are "crying out" for guidance from government on how pupils and teachers can use AI safely and effectively, a new report has warned. Sir Anthony Seldon, former head teacher and author on AI in education, says the technology is being used more and more frequently, but that its introduction has been "chaotic and anarchic". His report calls for the government to roll out a national framework for adopting AI in education in England, including training teachers on how to use it, which schools should use to develop their own "AI strategies" by September next year. The government says its changes to the curriculum in England will give children digital skills and help them spot disinformation. Sir Anthony's report, co-authored with venture capitalist Tim Bunting, says schools have not been prepared for AI's arrival. Sir Anthony co-founded the group AI in Education, which was set up in 2023 to help educational institutions navigate AI safely. His report argues that getting a grip of AI requires the same level of national urgency as wars and epidemics, and requires a taskforce modelled on the one which helped to roll out the Covid vaccine. Sir Anthony Seldon's report says "standing still is not an option" on AI The report recommends a 10-point plan for AI in education in England, including: The prime minister delivering a landmark speech to set out the importance of aligning education with how AI is used in the real world Schools and colleges developing their own AI strategies, and having Ofsted assess their implementation as part of its inspections A mass information campaign to set out the opportunities and risks of AI Using AI to transform the way schools and colleges collect and use data to track pupil progress Reforming assessments into a "two-lane" system of both exams and a "continuous evaluation of a student's understanding" using AI The report says its poll of young people suggests many of those who responded thought AI was making education less important in their lives, with some saying it could eventually replace teachers and make universities "useless". "Put simply, education has not kept pace with how – and how much – young people are already using AI, and that gap is starting to show up as a loss of perceived value in the institution itself," the report says. A spokesperson for the Department for Education says ministers take the "significant opportunities and challenges" of AI "incredibly seriously". As well as refreshing the curriculum in England, they say they are building new AI tutoring tools and introducing new vocational routes to get children into successful careers. Some schools have already embedded AI into the curriculum. Benjamin Barker, principal at King's Leadership Academy Wavertree, says he wants his students to learn how to use tools safely, while also developing their critical thinking skills. Student Emma, 12, says she uses AI for her robotics projects, as well as proof-reading her English homework, and believes more students should be taught how to use it responsibly. "AI is coming into the future. It's getting more advanced," she says. "There's no way we're going to completely pull back from it. So I think that we should use it to be better people."
